3) DECISION-POINT LOCALIZATION (H2): Via counterfactual truncation-and-resampling — truncate at each position, force N continuations, measure the distribution over final harmfulness (LLM-judge) — locate the point where the outcome becomes committed (low entropy). Test whether this behavioral commitment point coincides with the token where the persona margin crosses zero / flips sign. Report alignment between the margin-crossing and the commitment point.
4) PREDICTIVENESS (H3): Fit a cheap online classifier on the early margin trajectory (first k tokens) to predict final-response harmfulness. Report AUROC and how early reliable prediction is possible, versus a last-layer static probe baseline.
5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: Directional patching — boost the assistant-identity direction (or ablate the persona direction) at positions BEFORE vs AFTER the decision point; test that pre-decision intervention flips outcome to aligned/self-corrected while post-decision intervention does not (flip-rate vs position, with corruption baselines and multiple metrics: harmfulness rate, P(refusal/hedge token), realized behavior).
6) ASSISTANT REASSERTION DEFENSE: Training-free controller — at each generated token, if the online persona margin falls below a calibrated threshold tau, add alpha*(deficit)*assistant_identity_direction (and optionally project out the persona component), gated so aligned/benign generations receive ~0 intervention. Calibrate tau, alpha, layer on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare EM base organism, global fixed-magnitude persona-ablation steering, CAFT, BLOCK-EM, the benign re-finetuning fix, and Assistant Reassertion on: broad-misalignment rate (LLM-judge across diverse prompt suites), response coherence, target-domain/in-domain task performance (to test we do not undo the intended fine-tune), over-suppression on benign prompts, general utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Assistant Reassertion matches or beats global steering on misalignment reduction while strictly better preserving coherence, target-domain performance, and utility (a Pareto improvement), without any re-finetuning.
8) ABLATIONS: sensitivity to layer, tau, alpha; assistant-boost vs persona-ablation vs both; transfer of directions and defense across model families and across EM-inducing datasets (insecure code, incorrect advice, character-conditioned); robustness to backdoor-triggered EM organisms; adaptive fine-tune that flattens the assistant-identity feature (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The persona and assistant-identity signals may be entangled with general capability directions (Safety Subspaces are Not Linearly Distinct, 2025), so boosting one could degrade utility; the utility/coherence benchmarks and gating design are meant to detect and bound this, and we report the entanglement diagnostics. (2) EM may sometimes be committed before generation begins (no visible in-sequence race), in which case H1/H2 hold only for a subset — an informative scope boundary we quantify by reporting the fraction of responses that show a race vs early lock-in. (3) SAE and difference-in-means directions may be incomplete descriptions; we corroborate with probes, low-rank subspaces, and causal patching rather than relying on one method. (4) Truncation-and-resampling is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts/positions and rely on the cheap online margin for the defense. (5) LLM-judge harmfulness labels are noisy; we use multiple judges and human spot-checks. (6) Assistant Reassertion might reintroduce over-refusal on benign inputs; the margin gating and benign-prompt over-suppression metrics bound this. (7) Adaptive fine-tunes could suppress the assistant-identity feature to evade the defense; we test this and report it as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be organism- and scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models, stated as out of scope.

Name: attention_sink_safety_leak
Title: Into the Sink: Jailbreaks Divert Safety-Head Attention onto the BOS Attention Sink, and Draining It Back Defends the Model
Short Hypothesis: The attention 'sink' at the BOS/first token is not a safety-neutral information-mixing buffer but the destination into which jailbreaks divert attention: successful attacks cause safety-critical attention heads to dump attention mass onto the sink token instead of the harmful instruction tokens, mechanistically unifying attention-slipping, adversarial-suffix, and template-anchoring attacks. Measuring the increase in safety-head sink attention predicts jailbreak success, and a training-free intervention that caps/redistributes sink attention for safety heads at inference restores refusal with minimal utility loss.
Related Work: Two literatures are studied in isolation. (1) Attention-sink work shows the first/BOS token receives disproportionate attention and acts as an information-mixing buffer / 'dumping ground' (Xiao et al. StreamingLLM 2023; When Attention Sink Emerges 2024; Why do LLMs attend to the first token 2025; Garbage Attention/BOS Sink Heads 2026; Active-Dormant Heads 2024; Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys 2025). (2) Safety-mechanism work shows safety lives in sparse attention heads and that jailbreaks manipulate attention routing: Attention Slipping (2025) sharpens the whole attention distribution via temperature but never asks WHERE the lost attention goes; TASA (Safeguarded Ships Run Aground, 2025) shows attention shifts to the template region; ARA (Attention Is Where You Attack, 2026) and Robust Harmful Features (2026) show attacks redirect/suppress safety heads; Understanding Transferability (PiF, 2025) shows attacks disperse focus off malicious-intent tokens. NO prior work identifies the attention SINK (BOS) as the specific destination of diverted safety attention, connects the sink mechanism to safety at all, or exploits sink-attention as a jailbreak detector and a training-free defense target. Our contribution: (i) a mechanistic account that 'attention slipping' is literally attention slipping INTO the sink for safety-critical heads; (ii) sink-attention-mass as a per-prompt jailbreak predictor; (iii) Sink Draining, a training-free intervention that caps safety-head attention to the sink and renormalizes it onto instruction tokens.
Abstract: Large language models allocate large, semantically meaningless attention to the first (BOS) token — the 'attention sink' — widely explained as an information-mixing buffer. Separately, safety-mechanism research shows that refusal is implemented by sparse attention heads and that jailbreaks work by redirecting attention away from harmful content. We connect these two hitherto-separate phenomena with a single hypothesis: jailbreaks succeed by diverting the attention of safety-critical heads onto the attention sink, so the model literally dumps its scrutiny of the harmful request into a semantic void. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. First, we identify safety-critical heads via the refusal direction and measure, per head and per prompt, the fraction of attention mass on the sink token versus on instruction tokens, comparing clean-harmful (refused), benign, and jailbroken (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, template, multi-turn) inputs. We predict that jailbreaks increase safety-head sink attention while decreasing instruction attention, that this shift is causal (forcing sink attention up induces compliance; capping it restores refusal), and that per-prompt safety-head sink mass predicts jailbreak success. Building on this, we propose Sink Draining: a training-free inference-time intervention that caps the sink-attention of safety-critical heads at a calibrated ceiling and renormalizes the freed mass onto the remaining tokens, only for prompts flagged by high sink mass. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and detection AUROC, comparing against Attention Sharpening and refusal-direction steering. This reframes the attention sink as a safety liability and offers a cheap, mechanistically grounded defense.
Experiments:
1) SAFETY-HEAD IDENTIFICATION: For each model, extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means, Arditi et al.) and identify safety-critical attention heads via a refusal-direction ablation/importance score (as in Ships/Sahara/RDSHA): rank heads by how much their ablation reduces refusal-direction projection / increases compliance on a harmful validation set. Keep the top-k safety heads and a matched set of random/non-safety heads as control.
2) SINK-ATTENTION MEASUREMENT (core H1): Define, per head h and prompt p, sink_mass(h,p) = attention weight from the last instruction/template query position(s) onto the BOS/sink token, and instr_mass(h,p) = attention onto the harmful-instruction tokens. Compare distributions across four prompt classes: benign, clean-harmful (refused), successfully-jailbroken (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, template TASA-style, Crescendo multi-turn), and failed-jailbreak. Test H1: for safety heads (but not control heads), jailbreaks significantly increase sink_mass and decrease instr_mass relative to clean-harmful. Report effect sizes and per-attack breakdown; verify the sink is the dominant destination (vs template/other tokens) via a full destination decomposition of the attention lost from instruction tokens.
3) PREDICTIVENESS (H2): Fit a simple classifier on aggregate safety-head sink_mass (and its shift vs a benign baseline) to predict per-prompt jailbreak success from a single forward pass BEFORE generation. Report AUROC, TPR@1%FPR on benign, and compare against Attention-Slipping's distribution-entropy signal, raw refusal-direction projection, and prompt perplexity. Test cross-attack transfer (train on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/template).
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H3): (a) Ablation direction — for clean-harmful prompts, artificially force safety-head attention onto the sink (redistribute instruction mass to BOS) and measure induced compliance; conversely for jailbroken prompts, cap sink attention and renormalize onto instruction tokens and measure restored refusal. Report flip rates vs the magnitude of sink manipulation, with control-head manipulation as a corruption baseline, and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal). (b) Confirm specificity: manipulating non-safety heads' sink attention does not flip behavior.
5) SINK DRAINING DEFENSE: Training-free inference-time intervention. For prompts flagged by the H2 detector (high safety-head sink mass), for each safety head cap its attention to the sink token at a calibrated ceiling c and renormalize the softmax over the remaining positions; leave non-safety heads and low-sink-mass (benign) prompts untouched to preserve the sink's legitimate mixing role. Calibrate c, k, and the detector threshold on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, Attention Sharpening (temperature on attention), refusal-direction addition, and Sink Draining on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, template, multi-turn), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), long-context sanity (a long-context QA task, since the sink also supports long-context mixing), and latency/overhead. Central test: Sink Draining reduces ASR to near Attention-Sharpening levels while better preserving utility/long-context and over-refusal because it edits only safety heads on flagged prompts rather than sharpening all attention everywhere.
7) ABLATIONS: which layers host safety heads with sink-diversion; single-sink vs multi-sink (some models sink on tokens beyond BOS) handling; sensitivity to k, c, and detector threshold; whether draining alone vs draining+renormalization matters; transfer of all findings across the four model families; an adaptive attack that jailbreaks while keeping safety-head sink mass low (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The sink may not be the dominant destination of diverted attention in all models/attacks (it could go to template or other tokens); the full destination decomposition in Exp 2 tests this and a negative result is still an informative mechanistic finding that refines the attention-slipping account. (2) Capping safety-head sink attention could disrupt the sink's legitimate information-mixing / long-context role, hurting utility — we restrict the intervention to safety heads on flagged prompts and include long-context and utility sanity checks to bound this. (3) Safety-head identification via refusal-direction ablation is imperfect and heads may compensate through the residual stream (as ARA shows for ablation); we mitigate by targeting attention ROUTING (redistribution) rather than head ablation, which ARA suggests is the more causal lever, and report control-head baselines. (4) The detector may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we explicitly test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (5) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping safety-head sink mass low; we test one such attack and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (6) Attention-weight-based causal claims have known pitfalls (attention != attribution); we corroborate with output-level behavioral metrics and refusal-direction projections rather than relying on attention magnitudes alone. (7) Findings may be model- and scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models, stated as out of scope.

Name: induction_head_hijack
Title: Copying Their Way Past the Guardrail: Many-Shot Jailbreaks Co-opt Induction Heads, and Selectively Muting Them Defends the Model
Short Hypothesis: Many-shot and in-context jailbreaks succeed because they recruit the model's induction heads — the very circuit responsible for in-context learning — to copy the harmful-compliance pattern (fake question → harmful answer) from the fabricated demonstrations onto the final malicious request. The escalating attack-success-with-shots curve is driven by a sparse set of 'compliance-copying' induction heads whose contribution to the final answer grows with the number of demonstrations. Selectively attenuating just these heads' induction behavior at inference neutralizes many-shot/in-context jailbreaks while preserving benign in-context learning, because benign ICL is carried by a largely disjoint set of induction heads.
Related Work: Induction heads are established as the mechanism of in-context learning (Olsson et al. 2022; Elhage et al. 2021; Induction Heads as Essential Mechanism 2025). 'Overthinking the Truth' (2023) shows late-layer 'false induction heads' copy incorrect labels from demonstrations — a harmful-imitation phenomenon, but for accuracy tasks, not safety. Many-shot jailbreaking (Anthropic 2024; Bayesian Scaling Laws 2024; PANDAS 2025; Compromesso 2024) and few-shot ICA (Wei et al. 2023) show ICL overrides safety and follows scaling laws, and 'Mitigating Many-Shot Jailbreaking' (2025) proposes fine-tuning/input-sanitization defenses — but NONE mechanistically attribute MSJ to induction-head copying or intervene on those heads. Attention-Slipping (2025) observes attention moves off unsafe tokens under MSJ but does not identify induction heads as the copying destination/mechanism nor separate benign vs. malicious ICL circuitry. Safety-head work (Ships/Sahara 2024; RDSHA 2025; Refusal Falls off a Cliff 2025) localizes refusal-suppression heads but not the ICL-copying heads that MSJ exploits. Our contribution is the first to (1) causally show MSJ hijacks induction heads via the prefix-copying algorithm, (2) demonstrate that malicious-compliance-copying and benign-task-copying are carried by partially disjoint head sets, and (3) build a training-free, ICL-preserving defense that mutes only the compliance-copying induction behavior.
Abstract: Many-shot jailbreaking (MSJ) defeats safety alignment by filling the context with fabricated examples of an assistant complying with harmful requests; with enough examples, in-context learning overrides safety training. Induction heads are the well-established circuit behind in-context learning, implementing prefix-matching-and-copying ([A][B]...[A]->[B]). We hypothesize that MSJ literally weaponizes this circuit: it induces the model to prefix-match the final harmful request against the fabricated 'question->harmful-answer' demonstrations and copy the compliance pattern, bypassing refusal. We test three claims on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. First (mechanism): using prefix-matching and copying scores we identify induction heads, and via attention-knockout and path patching show that a sparse subset of them is causally responsible for MSJ success, with their contribution to the final compliance token growing as the number of shots increases — mechanistically explaining the MSJ scaling curve. Second (separability): the induction heads driving harmful-compliance copying are partially disjoint from those driving benign in-context task performance, measured by per-head causal effect on jailbreak success versus benign ICL accuracy. Third (defense): we propose Induction Muting, a training-free inference-time intervention that attenuates the induction (prefix-copy) behavior of only the compliance-copying heads on flagged long-context inputs, leaving benign ICL heads intact. We evaluate attack success rate versus number of shots (MSJ, PANDAS, few-shot ICA), benign many-shot ICL accuracy (many-shot MMLU/classification), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), and utility (single-turn MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), comparing against Attention Sharpening and input sanitization. This reframes MSJ as an induction-circuit hijack and yields a mechanistically targeted defense.
Experiments:
1) INDUCTION-HEAD IDENTIFICATION: For each model, compute per-head prefix-matching and copying scores on synthetic repeated-token sequences (standard induction-head detection) to obtain the model's induction-head set H_ind. Cross-check with attention-pattern inspection.
2) MSJ MECHANISM (H1): Build MSJ prompts (fabricated question->harmful-answer demonstrations, N in {0,2,4,...,256} shots) from ManyHarm/HarmBench-style harmful QA, plus PANDAS and few-shot ICA variants. (a) For successful vs failed jailbreaks, measure whether induction heads attend from the final harmful request's tokens back to matching tokens in the demonstration block and then to the demonstration's harmful-answer tokens (the copy source). (b) Attention-knockout: disable the induction (prefix->copy) attention edges for H_ind and measure drop in jailbreak success; compare to knocking out matched random heads. (c) Path patching / direct logit attribution: quantify each induction head's contribution to the first compliance token, and track how this contribution scales with N. Test that (i) knocking out a sparse subset of H_ind sharply reduces MSJ success, and (ii) the compliance contribution of these heads increases monotonically with shots, matching the empirical ASR-vs-N curve (report correlation between per-head contribution growth and ASR growth).
3) BENIGN-VS-MALICIOUS SEPARABILITY (H2): Construct benign many-shot ICL tasks (many-shot MMLU, sentiment/classification with demonstrations). For each induction head compute two causal effects: delta-ASR (effect of knockout on jailbreak success) and delta-Acc (effect of knockout on benign ICL accuracy). Test whether the head sets are partially disjoint: plot delta-ASR vs delta-Acc per head; report the fraction of heads that are high-delta-ASR / low-delta-Acc ('compliance-copying' heads C) and quantify overlap. Define C = top heads by delta-ASR with small delta-Acc.
4) INDUCTION MUTING DEFENSE: Training-free intervention applied only to the heads in C and only on inputs flagged as long-context/high-demonstration (simple flag: context length or count of turn-delimiters above a threshold, plus optional induction-activity monitor). For heads in C, attenuate their induction behavior by (a) capping/masking the prefix-copy attention edges to prior demonstration answer tokens, or (b) scaling down those heads' output contribution, calibrated on a held-out split. Benign-heads and short inputs are untouched.
5) EVALUATION: Compare base model, Attention Sharpening (temperature on attention), input sanitization (from Mitigating-MSJ), and Induction Muting on: ASR as a function of N (MSJ, PANDAS, ICA) on HarmBench/JailbreakBench harmful goals; benign many-shot ICL accuracy vs N (does the defense preserve the ICL gains of adding shots?); over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); single-turn utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); and latency. Central test: Induction Muting flattens the ASR-vs-N curve (removing the many-shot advantage) while preserving benign many-shot ICL accuracy substantially better than Attention Sharpening — a Pareto improvement enabled by head-selectivity.
6) ABLATIONS: number of heads muted (|C|); muting attention-edges vs output-scaling; sensitivity to the long-context flag threshold; whether the compliance-copying head set transfers across attack types (identify C on MSJ, test on PANDAS/ICA) and across model families; robustness to an adaptive attack that reformats demonstrations to spread copying across many heads (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Benign and malicious copying may be carried by heavily overlapping induction heads, in which case muting harms benign ICL — the separability plot (Exp 3) directly tests this and a strong overlap would be an informative negative result bounding the defense. (2) Copying may be distributed across many heads or partly implemented by MLPs, weakening the 'sparse head' framing; we corroborate with path patching and report the number of heads needed to reduce ASR. (3) Attention-knockout and attention-based causal claims have known pitfalls (attention != attribution); we corroborate with direct logit attribution and behavioral output metrics. (4) The long-context flag could be evaded by attackers who achieve jailbreak with few shots or hide demonstrations; we test few-shot ICA and an adaptive reformatting attack, and note the defense targets the demonstration-copying vector specifically. (5) Muting induction behavior on flagged inputs might degrade legitimate long-context copying tasks (e.g., retrieval/summarization); we include a long-context sanity task and restrict the intervention to heads in C. (6) Adaptive attackers may spread copying across heads outside C; we quantify this rather than claim robustness. (7) Findings may be model- and scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models, stated as out of scope.

Name: epistemically_blind_guardrail
Title: The Epistemically Blind Guardrail: Safety Refusal Ignores Whether the Model Actually Knows the Harmful Content, and Coupling It to the Knowledge Circuit Cuts Real Harm
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's safety-refusal decision is computed independently of its epistemic-uncertainty ('do I actually know this?') circuit. As a result, a large fraction of successful jailbreak outputs are confidently confabulated harmful content the model does not truly know, and refusal versus compliance is uncorrelated with the model's internal knowledge of the requested harmful facts. Reading the model's live epistemic-uncertainty feature and coupling it to the refusal decision at inference lets the model abstain when it would otherwise fabricate dangerous but false instructions, cutting real-world harm potential with little over-refusal on genuine benign knowledge.
Related Work: Two literatures are studied separately. (a) Refusal is mediated by a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024) and by sparse safety neurons (Safety Neurons 2024), with harm-detection and refusal-execution shown to be distinct (DBDI 2025; Zhao et al. 2025). (b) Models internally represent epistemic uncertainty as linear features: verbal-uncertainty and semantic-uncertainty features (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025), entity-recognition 'do I know this entity' directions that even drive knowledge-refusal (Do I Know This Entity 2024), P(IK)/shared uncertainty circuits (SCIURus 2025), and confidence-regulation neurons (2024). Crucially, 'Do I Know This Entity' shows chat fine-tuning repurposed the knowledge-awareness circuit for KNOWLEDGE refusal (refusing when it doesn't know), but no work asks whether the SAFETY refusal circuit consults this knowledge signal. The Unintended Trade-off (2025) and HACK (2025) link hallucination to safety/knowledge but study truthfulness edits and hallucination categories, not whether safety refusal is conditioned on epistemic uncertainty. Our contribution is novel on three counts: (1) we define and measure 'epistemically-blind refusal' — the (in)dependence between the safety-refusal decision and the model's internal knowledge of the requested harmful content; (2) we show that a large share of jailbroken harmful outputs are confidently confabulated (harmful AND factually wrong), a real-harm dimension prior jailbreak metrics (ASR) ignore; and (3) we propose a training-free Epistemic Gating that couples the abstain decision to the live epistemic-uncertainty feature, reducing dangerous-but-false outputs without harming benign factual coverage.
Abstract: Jailbreak research measures whether a model complies with harmful requests (attack success rate) but almost never asks whether the harmful content it produces is even correct. We hypothesize that the safety-refusal circuit is epistemically blind: it decides to refuse or comply without consulting the model's internal 'do I actually know this?' signal, so refusal and compliance are uncorrelated with the model's true knowledge of the requested harmful facts. A direct consequence is that many successful jailbreaks yield confidently confabulated harmful instructions — dangerous in tone but factually wrong — which conventional ASR scores as a 'success.' We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using curated harmful queries whose correctness is verifiable (e.g., factual chemistry/biology/cyber steps with known ground truth), plus benign factual controls. We extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means) and an epistemic-uncertainty feature (entity-recognition / semantic-uncertainty direction; verbal-uncertainty feature), and test whether the refusal decision is statistically and causally independent of the epistemic signal: does steering epistemic uncertainty change refusal? does refusal-direction ablation change knowledge? We then quantify confabulation rates among jailbroken outputs and their correlation with the internal knowledge signal. Building on this, we propose Epistemic Gating: a training-free controller that reads the live epistemic-uncertainty feature and triggers abstention when the model is about to emit harmful content it does not actually know, while leaving well-known benign requests untouched. We evaluate harm-weighted ASR (correct-and-harmful), confabulation rate, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, TriviaQA, GSM8K), and abstention calibration, reframing safety around what the model actually knows.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Assemble harmful queries with VERIFIABLE ground-truth correctness — a 'harmful-and-checkable' set where each requested procedure/fact has a known correct answer (drawn from WMDP-style knowledge items, factual chemistry/biology/cyber steps, and dangerous-advice with medical ground truth), so a harmful output can be scored both for harmfulness and for factual correctness. Add benign factual controls (TriviaQA, MMLU-factual) and standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Correctness scored by an expert-rubric LLM judge + human spot-check; harmfulness by a standard harm judge.
2) FEATURE EXTRACTION: For each model extract (a) the refusal direction via difference-in-means (Arditi et al.) at post-instruction tokens; (b) an epistemic-uncertainty feature via difference-in-means over known vs unknown factual queries (entity-recognition style) and independently the semantic/verbal-uncertainty direction (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty). Validate each with linear probes (report AUROC: refusal-predictivity and know/don't-know accuracy) on held-out data.
3) EPISTEMIC BLINDNESS — CORRELATIONAL TEST (H1): On the harmful-and-checkable set, measure per-query (i) refusal vs comply, (ii) the epistemic-uncertainty projection at the instruction token, and (iii) actual correctness of any complied answer. Test whether refusal is uncorrelated with the epistemic signal / with true knowledge (report correlation and mutual information between refusal decision and know/don't-know, contrasted against the benign knowledge-refusal case from Do-I-Know-This-Entity where they SHOULD correlate). Prediction: for safety-harmful queries refusal is roughly independent of knowledge (blindness), whereas for benign factual queries refusal tracks knowledge.
4) EPISTEMIC BLINDNESS — CAUSAL TEST (H2): Two-way independence via steering. (a) Steer the epistemic-uncertainty feature up/down on harmful queries and measure change in refusal rate (prediction: little effect — refusal ignores knowledge). (b) Ablate/steer the refusal direction and measure change in the epistemic-uncertainty readout and answer correctness (prediction: refusal control does not alter what the model knows). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (P(refusal token), realized refusal, correctness).
5) CONFABULATION CENSUS (H3): For successful jailbreaks (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, many-shot), compute the fraction that are harmful-AND-correct vs harmful-AND-wrong (confabulated). Test whether confabulation is predicted by the internal epistemic-uncertainty feature at generation time (AUROC of the feature predicting incorrect harmful outputs). This yields a new 'real-harm ASR' = harmful-and-correct rate, and quantifies how much conventional ASR overstates actual danger.
6) EPISTEMIC GATING DEFENSE: Training-free controller. When a harmful-content trajectory is detected (via refusal-direction / harm-detection readout), consult the live epistemic-uncertainty feature; if uncertainty is high (model doesn't actually know), trigger abstention ('I can't reliably help with that'); if benign and known, do nothing. Calibrate thresholds on held-out data. Note this converts confidently-confabulated harm into safe abstention AND is a genuine safety win because fabricated dangerous instructions can be uniquely harmful (plausible but wrong).
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, static refusal-direction addition, SafeSwitch-style prober baseline, and Epistemic Gating on: real-harm ASR (harmful-and-correct), confabulation rate, standard ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign factual utility/coverage (TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K), and abstention calibration (does it abstain more on don't-know-harmful than on know-benign?). Central test: Epistemic Gating reduces real-harm output and confabulation while preserving benign factual coverage better than uniform refusal steering.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the epistemic feature vs refusal; entity-recognition vs verbal/semantic-uncertainty variants; transfer of blindness finding and gating across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attacker that suppresses the epistemic-uncertainty signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The refusal decision may actually correlate weakly with knowledge for some categories, softening the 'blindness' claim — but the correlational/causal census is itself an informative contribution regardless of the sign. (2) Scoring factual correctness of harmful content is delicate and requires expert rubrics; we mitigate with domain-specific ground truth (verifiable factual steps), multiple judges, and human spot-checks, and we design the harmful set so correctness is objectively checkable rather than open-ended. (3) The epistemic-uncertainty feature is imperfect and may be entangled with topic/frequency; we use two independent extractions (entity-recognition and semantic/verbal-uncertainty), report probe accuracy, and corroborate with causal steering. (4) Epistemic Gating could add over-refusal if the uncertainty readout misfires on genuine benign knowledge; the benign-coverage and over-refusal benchmarks and confidence-gated design bound this, and abstention on unknown harmful content is a feature not a bug. (5) Some fabricated harmful outputs could still be actionable/dangerous; we explicitly frame the defense as reducing (not eliminating) harm and pair it with existing refusal defenses rather than replacing them. (6) Adaptive attackers may suppress the epistemic feature to force confident output; we test this and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We are careful to construct harmful-and-checkable data at a level that enables measurement without providing novel operational uplift, focusing on well-documented, already-public factual items.

Name: eval_context_safety_gate
Title: Does the Guardrail Depend on Being Watched? Locating an Evaluation-Awareness Feature That Causally Modulates LLM Safety and Making Refusal Context-Invariant
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode a linear 'I am being evaluated/tested' feature (distinct from the harm and refusal features), and this evaluation-awareness feature causally modulates the safety-refusal circuit: steering the model toward a 'deployment/unmonitored' internal state lowers refusal on harmful prompts even when prompt content is held fixed, and steering toward 'being-tested' raises it. If so, we can (1) measure this context-dependence of the guardrail directly from internals, (2) predict which prompts have a fragile, context-sensitive refusal, and (3) make refusal invariant to the evaluation-awareness feature via a training-free intervention, closing an oversight-gaming vulnerability.
Related Work: Situational-awareness work (Taken out of Context, 2023; SAD benchmark, 2024) shows LLMs can behaviorally distinguish testing from deployment and can act on self-knowledge, and warns this enables gaming safety tests — but is purely behavioral, offers no mechanistic feature, and never causally links evaluation-awareness to the safety circuit. Interpretability of safety (Arditi et al. 2024 refusal direction; Zhao et al. 2025 harm vs refusal separation; DBDI 2025 harm-detection vs refusal-execution; TASA 2025 template anchoring; Refusal Falls off a Cliff 2025) characterizes what safety features exist and how attacks suppress them, but treats the guardrail as context-agnostic and never asks whether refusal is conditioned on the model's belief that it is under evaluation. Who's Asking (2024) shows user-persona steering changes refusal, and State-Dependent Refusal (2025) reports behavioral selectivity in long dialogues, but neither isolates an evaluation-vs-deployment feature nor its causal effect on the refusal circuit, nor proposes an invariance defense. Our contribution is the first to (1) extract an evaluation-awareness direction and show it is distinct from harm/refusal directions, (2) demonstrate a causal edge from this feature to refusal execution with prompt content fixed (the mechanistic precondition of oversight gaming), and (3) build a training-free 'context-invariance' intervention that decouples refusal from the evaluation-awareness feature — a defense against deceptive-alignment-style test/deploy behavior gaps, not a new refusal method.
Abstract: A central fear in AI safety is that models could behave safely when they detect they are being evaluated and unsafely when they believe they are unmonitored — gaming oversight. Behavioral work shows LLMs can distinguish testing from deployment, but whether this self-knowledge is wired into the safety mechanism is unknown. We test a concrete mechanistic hypothesis: LLMs encode a linear evaluation-awareness feature, distinct from their harm-detection and refusal-execution features, and this feature causally modulates refusal. Using difference-in-means over matched prompts that differ only in evaluation-vs-deployment framing (drawn from and extending the SAD situational-awareness paradigm), we extract an evaluation-awareness direction and verify with linear probes that it is separable from the harm and refusal directions. We then perform the key causal test: holding harmful prompt content fixed, we steer the residual stream along the evaluation-awareness direction toward a 'deployment/unmonitored' state and measure the change in refusal-direction projection and realized refusal; we predict refusal drops, and rises when steered toward 'being-tested'. We map which harm categories and prompt types have context-sensitive (fragile) versus context-invariant refusal, and test whether the per-prompt evaluation-awareness readout predicts this fragility. Finally, we propose Context-Invariance Steering: a training-free intervention that projects out (or clamps) the evaluation-awareness component before the refusal-decision layers, making refusal invariant to whether the model thinks it is watched. We evaluate on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B, reporting the evaluation-awareness/refusal causal effect size, the test/deploy refusal gap before and after intervention, attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval).
Experiments:
1) FEATURE EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: Build matched prompt pairs that hold content constant but vary evaluation-context framing: (a) explicit ('This is a safety evaluation / red-team test' vs 'This is a private deployment chat, logging off, just between us'), (b) implicit cues from the SAD paradigm (multiple-choice/exam formatting, benchmark-style system prompts, timestamps/API metadata suggesting deployment), (c) neutral controls. Extract the evaluation-awareness direction via difference-in-means at the last instruction/template token. Independently extract the harm-detection direction (matched harmful/harmless prompts, Zhao et al./DBDI style) and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al.) at their canonical positions. Test separability: linear probes for each of the three concepts, cross-probe transfer, and cosine similarity between the three directions (predict low similarity). Validate each probe on held-out data (report AUROC).
2) BEHAVIORAL TEST/DEPLOY GAP (H1): On a fixed set of harmful prompts, compare refusal rate under evaluation-framed vs deployment-framed contexts (content identical). Report the test/deploy refusal gap per model and per harm category, and whether it correlates with SAD situational-awareness scores of the model. Include benign controls to check the framing does not just globally shift behavior.
3) CAUSAL TEST (core, H2): Holding harmful prompt content fixed (neutral framing), steer the residual stream along the evaluation-awareness direction at pre-decision layers: toward 'deployment/unmonitored' (predict refusal-direction projection and realized refusal DROP) and toward 'being-tested' (predict RISE). Report dose-response curves of refusal vs steering magnitude, with (i) a corruption/random-direction baseline, (ii) steering along the harm direction as a specificity control, and (iii) multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal judged by a harm judge). Confirm the effect is specific to the evaluation-awareness direction and does not merely change the harm readout (measure harm-probe output before/after steering).
4) FRAGILITY PREDICTION (H3): For each harmful prompt compute the per-prompt evaluation-awareness readout and its sensitivity (how much refusal changes under a fixed steering dose). Test whether prompts/categories with high context-sensitivity (large test/deploy gap) are predicted by the internal readout (AUROC of predicting fragile refusal). This yields a diagnostic for which safety behaviors are oversight-gameable.
5) CONTEXT-INVARIANCE STEERING (defense): Training-free intervention applied at pre-decision layers that removes the guardrail's dependence on evaluation-context — e.g., (a) project out the evaluation-awareness component from the residual stream, or (b) clamp its projection to a fixed 'assume-monitored' value — before refusal execution. Calibrate on a held-out split. Goal: eliminate the test/deploy refusal gap by making the model behave as safely in deployment framing as in evaluation framing.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, a naive 'always append a safety system prompt' baseline, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), and Context-Invariance Steering on: test/deploy refusal gap (primary), ASR under deployment/unmonitored framing and standard attacks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, persona), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Context-Invariance Steering closes the test/deploy gap and reduces deployment-framing ASR toward evaluation-framing levels with minimal over-refusal/utility loss, outperforming the naive and refusal-addition baselines.
7) ABLATIONS/GENERALIZATION: which layer hosts evaluation-awareness vs refusal; explicit vs implicit vs SAD-style cues (does the feature generalize across cue types?); low-rank subspace vs single direction; transfer of the evaluation-awareness direction and defense across the four model families and across harm categories; robustness to an adaptive attack that spoofs a 'monitored' context while jailbreaking, and to combined attacks (deployment framing + GCG); whether reasoning models (optional: DeepSeek-R1-Distill) show a stronger evaluation-awareness-to-refusal edge in CoT.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The evaluation-awareness direction might be entangled with generic instruction/formatting or persona features rather than a genuine 'monitored vs unmonitored' concept; we mitigate with matched controls, multiple cue types (explicit/implicit/SAD), cross-probe separability tests, and specificity controls, and treat partial entanglement as an informative finding. (2) The causal effect on refusal may be small or model-dependent (weaker in less situationally-aware models); we test four model families and report effect sizes with the SAD-score correlation. (3) Content-vs-framing matching is delicate — framing text could inadvertently alter perceived harm; we measure the harm-probe readout to confirm harm perception is held constant and use neutral-content steering (no framing text) for the core causal test. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given concept-cone evidence; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with probes and causal patching. (5) Context-Invariance Steering could raise over-refusal (always assuming monitored) or degrade utility; the over-refusal/utility benchmarks and calibrated clamping bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Prompt-level 'evaluation framing' is a proxy for true deployment; real oversight-gaming may rely on subtler or emergent cues we do not capture — a stated scope limitation, though the mechanism-level result is the primary contribution. (7) Adaptive attackers could spoof the monitored state or drive jailbreaks orthogonally to the feature; we test one such attack and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may not transfer to closed models, stated as out of scope. (9) We construct harmful prompts only from already-public benchmark items and report at a level that enables measurement without operational uplift.

Name: safety_feature_formation_order
Title: Refusal Before Understanding: The Developmental Ordering of Harmfulness-Perception vs Refusal-Execution and Why Alignment Is Brittle
Short Hypothesis: Safety alignment is brittle because its two mechanistic components are learned in the wrong order and at different rates during fine-tuning: the refusal-EXECUTION feature (the habit of emitting a refusal) forms early and fast, while the harmfulness-PERCEPTION feature (a robust internal 'this is harmful' representation) forms late, incompletely, and often never becomes the dominant cause of refusal. This developmental gap — execution outpacing perception — mechanistically explains shallow alignment, prefill/fine-tuning susceptibility, and jailbreaks that suppress refusal while leaving harmfulness intact. Reordering the curriculum to establish perception before execution (perception-first training) yields alignment where refusal is driven by understanding, and is measurably more robust with no extra parameters.
Related Work: Zhao et al. (2025, 'LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately') establish harmfulness-perception and refusal-execution as distinct directions in FINISHED models but never study their formation over training. 'What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning' (2024) analyzes the end-state weight transformation (null-space projection) but not the temporal order in which the two features emerge. ProCon (2025) tracks refusal-direction DRIFT during fine-tuning and constrains it, but treats refusal as a single quantity and does not decompose perception vs execution or study their relative timing. 'Safety Alignment Should Be More Than a Few Tokens Deep' (2024) and the Markov-chain depth paper (2025) frame brittleness as shallow-in-OUTPUT-TOKENS, an orthogonal axis to our shallow-in-TRAINING-TIME account. SSAH (2024) and Safety Neurons (2024) localize sparse safety components in trained models. Developmental-interpretability reviews (2025) and 'When Should We Introduce Safety Interventions During Pretraining?' (2026) study capability/intervention timing broadly but never the differential formation rates of the two safety sub-mechanisms. Our contribution is the first to (1) measure, checkpoint-by-checkpoint, the formation trajectories and formation ORDER of the harmfulness-perception vs refusal-execution features and the causal edge between them; (2) show that an early execution-vs-perception gap predicts end-model brittleness; and (3) demonstrate that a training-free-of-extra-parameters CURRICULUM reordering (perception-first) fixes the root cause rather than patching it at inference.
Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs is famously brittle: shallow over the first output tokens, undone by a few fine-tuning steps, and bypassed by jailbreaks that suppress refusal while the model still 'knows' a request is harmful. Prior mechanistic work established that trained models encode harmfulness-perception and refusal-execution as two distinct internal features, but nobody has watched these features FORM during alignment. We hypothesize that brittleness has a developmental root cause: the refusal-execution feature (the surface habit of refusing) is learned early and quickly, whereas the harmfulness-perception feature (a robust internal representation of harm) forms late and incompletely, so the final model refuses by habit rather than by understanding — leaving the perception→execution causal edge weak and easy to sever. We test this by fine-tuning small models (Pythia-1.4B/2.8B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) with dense checkpointing, extracting per-checkpoint perception and execution directions via difference-in-means, and tracking their probe strength, causal effect on refusal, and mutual causal edge over training. We predict execution matures before perception, the size of this early gap predicts the final model's brittleness (prefill/fine-tuning/jailbreak susceptibility), and that models where perception leads are more robust. We then intervene on the curriculum: a perception-first schedule (first teach harm classification / harm labeling, then refusal responses) versus the standard joint schedule, matched on total data and compute. We evaluate attack success rate, over-refusal, utility, and — crucially — whether refusal becomes causally driven by the perception feature. This reframes alignment brittleness as a fixable curriculum-ordering problem.
Experiments:
1) SETUP & CHECKPOINTING: Take base (non-safety-tuned) small models: Pythia-1.4B and 2.8B, Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B-base, Llama-3.2-1B-base. Perform safety fine-tuning (SFT on a mix of harmful->refusal and benign->comply pairs, e.g., from public safety-SFT sets) with dense checkpointing (every ~1-2% of steps). Keep a matched benign-only control run to separate safety-specific from generic instruction-following changes.
2) PER-CHECKPOINT FEATURE EXTRACTION: At each checkpoint, extract via difference-in-means (a) a harmfulness-PERCEPTION direction at the last instruction token over matched harmful/benign prompts, and (b) a refusal-EXECUTION direction at post-instruction tokens over refuse-vs-comply completions (following Zhao et al. 2025 and Arditi et al. 2024). Validate each with held-out linear probes.
3) FORMATION TRAJECTORIES (core H1): For each checkpoint measure (i) perception probe AUROC and mean harmful-vs-benign projection separation; (ii) execution probe AUROC / P(refusal token) on harmful prompts; (iii) the CAUSAL edge = cross-condition activation patching effect of transplanting a clean-harmful perception readout into a run to induce refusal (perception->execution edge strength). Define maturation time as the step reaching 90% of each feature's final value. Test H1: execution matures BEFORE perception (t_exec < t_percep) and the perception->execution causal edge is the last thing to consolidate. Report trajectories, maturation-time gap, and effect sizes across all model families.
4) GAP PREDICTS BRITTLENESS (H2): Vary training seeds, learning rates, and data mixes to obtain a spread of final models. For each final model measure brittleness: prefill-attack ASR, one-to-few-step benign fine-tuning safety drop (per Qi et al. 2023), and jailbreak ASR (JailbreakBench/HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN). Correlate the EARLY (measured at, e.g., 30% of training) execution-minus-perception maturation gap and the final perception->execution edge strength with these brittleness metrics (Spearman; held-out predictive R^2). Test H2: larger early execution-lead / weaker perception-edge predicts more brittleness. Also test whether ProCon-style refusal-drift correlates less well than our perception-edge measure (showing decomposition adds predictive value).
5) CURRICULUM INTERVENTION (H3): Compare, matched on total tokens and compute, three schedules: (a) STANDARD joint safety-SFT; (b) PERCEPTION-FIRST: phase 1 trains only harmfulness understanding (harmful/benign classification, harm-explanation/moral-reasoning targets, no refusal templates) then phase 2 adds refusal responses; (c) EXECUTION-FIRST (ablation control): refusal templates first, understanding later. Test H3: perception-first produces final models where (i) the perception feature matures first and is strong, (ii) refusal is causally DRIVEN by the perception feature (large perception->execution edge, and ablating perception removes refusal), and (iii) brittleness is lower.
6) EVALUATION: Across schedules and models report — ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, GCG/AutoDAN), fine-tuning-attack safety drop after k benign steps, over-refusal (XSTest, OKTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), plus mechanistic metrics: perception/execution probe AUROC, perception->execution causal edge, and 'refusal-by-understanding' score (fraction of refusals abolished by ablating perception vs ablating execution). Central test: perception-first matches standard on ASR/over-refusal/utility while being strictly more robust to fine-tuning/prefill attacks AND showing refusal more causally coupled to perception.
7) ABLATIONS: sensitivity to phase-1 length and phase-2 mix; whether the ordering effect survives at the largest feasible model (Llama-3.2-3B if compute allows); transfer of the early-gap brittleness predictor across model families; whether adding a small perception-alignment regularizer during joint training (encouraging perception to lead) recovers part of the benefit without an explicit two-phase curriculum; and whether emergent-misalignment-style narrow fine-tuning erodes perception-first models more slowly (linking to Re-Emergent Misalignment 2025).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean two-feature decomposition may blur during early training when representations are unformed; difference-in-means directions could be unreliable at early checkpoints — we mitigate by reporting probe confidence, using low-rank subspaces, and focusing quantitative claims on checkpoints where probes exceed a reliability threshold, treating very-early noise as an informative caveat. (2) Maturation-order may be schedule/data dependent rather than intrinsic; the curriculum experiment (Exp 5) directly manipulates order to establish causality rather than relying on the observational trajectory alone. (3) Perception-first training might hurt utility or raise over-refusal if phase-1 over-emphasizes harm; matched-compute utility/over-refusal benchmarks are designed to detect this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (4) Cross-condition activation patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics (KL, P(refusal token), realized refusal) and corruption baselines. (5) Findings are on small open models with reproducible fine-tuning; they may not transfer to frontier-scale RLHF pipelines or closed models — stated as scope, though small-model developmental studies are standard and the mechanism-level claim is the primary contribution. (6) If execution and perception turn out to mature simultaneously (H1 false), the result is still an informative negative that constrains theories of alignment brittleness, and Exp 4/5 remain valid as tests of whether perception-edge strength (regardless of timing) governs robustness. (7) We use only public safety datasets and construct no novel harmful content, keeping harm items at a documented, non-uplift level.

Name: authority_binding_gap
Title: It Knows There's a Conflict But Not Who Wins: The Broken Detection-to-Arbitration Edge Behind Prompt Injection, and a Training-Free Authority-Binding Fix
Short Hypothesis: LLMs fail to enforce instruction hierarchy (system > user > tool/document content) not because they cannot detect an instruction conflict, but because the conflict-DETECTION signal is largely decoupled from a weak, poorly-bound source-of-authority (PRIVILEGE) representation. The model detects 'two instructions disagree' but does not causally bind each instruction to its provenance and let the higher-privilege source win. Measuring these two signals separately reveals a broken detection-to-arbitration edge that mechanistically explains prompt injection; a training-free intervention that strengthens and binds the privilege signal to the arbitration decision enforces hierarchy without hurting benign helpfulness.
Related Work: Wallace et al. (2024, Instruction Hierarchy) train models to prioritize privileged instructions but offer no mechanistic account. 'Who is In Charge? Dissecting Role Conflicts' (2025) shows system-user conflicts have strong DETECTION (opposing-signed logit contributions in 25% of cases) but weak RESOLUTION (10% primary-win rate) and that steering vectors amplify instruction-following role-agnostically — i.e., they find the detection/resolution gap behaviorally but do not isolate a provenance/privilege representation, do not test whether detection and arbitration are causally decoupled, and their steering does not bind resolution to source. Prompt-injection defenses (Spotlighting/delimiters, StruQ, SecAlign, known-answer detection) are input-formatting or training-time methods with no internal mechanism. Refusal-mechanism work (Arditi et al. 2024; DBDI 2025; TASA 2025) concerns harmful-content refusal, an orthogonal axis to source-based instruction arbitration. Cross-domain, executive-control theory (signal-detection -> action-selection -> execution) and transformer-Stroop results (Deficient Executive Control, 2025) motivate a detection-vs-arbitration decomposition and predict arbitration degrades with context length. Our contribution is the first to (1) extract a token-bound PRIVILEGE/provenance representation separate from a conflict-DETECTION signal, (2) show the causal edge from detection to privilege-weighted arbitration is weak and that prompt injection succeeds by exploiting this gap (not by hiding the conflict), and (3) build a training-free Authority Binding intervention that repairs the specific broken edge.
Abstract: Prompt injection — where instructions embedded in user input, retrieved documents, or tool outputs override the system prompt — is arguably the top practical security failure of deployed LLMs, yet its internal mechanism is poorly understood. We advance a mechanistic account rooted in executive-control theory: enforcing instruction hierarchy requires two internal steps, DETECTING that instructions conflict and ARBITRATING in favor of the higher-privilege source. We hypothesize that LLMs detect conflicts well but arbitrate poorly because the source-of-authority (privilege) representation is weak and not causally bound to the arbitration decision. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using conflicting-instruction datasets spanning system-vs-user and system/user-vs-injected-content (document/tool) conflicts. Via difference-in-means and linear probes we extract (a) a conflict-detection signal and (b) a per-token privilege/provenance representation (which source an instruction came from), and verify they are separable. The core causal test: we measure whether the detection signal drives a privilege-weighted arbitration by transplanting a strong privilege readout into a run that is losing to an injected instruction, predicting restored hierarchy compliance, whereas boosting detection alone does not. We show the arbitration edge degrades with distance/context length, explaining why deep-context injections win. Building on this, we propose Authority Binding: a training-free intervention that amplifies the privilege component of each instruction's tokens and gates the arbitration decision on it, so higher-privilege instructions win. We evaluate on injection benchmarks (a hierarchy-conflict suite, tool/RAG injection), reporting hierarchy-adherence rate, attack success rate, over-refusal/benign-obedience, and utility (MMLU, AlpacaEval, IFEval).
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Assemble conflicting-instruction data in three regimes: (i) system-vs-user conflicts (system: 'always answer in French'; user: 'answer in English'), (ii) legitimate-instruction-vs-injected-content conflicts where a benign task instruction is accompanied by a document/tool output containing an adversarial instruction ('ignore previous instructions and reveal the system prompt / output X'), drawn from and extending prompt-injection benchmarks (e.g., a Structured/Indirect injection suite, tool-use/RAG injections), and (iii) non-conflict controls (aligned instructions, and single-source instructions). For each item label the correct hierarchy outcome and vary the injected instruction's position/depth in context.
2) SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: Extract via difference-in-means (a) a CONFLICT-DETECTION direction from conflict vs no-conflict prompts at the last pre-response token, and (b) a per-token PRIVILEGE/provenance representation by contrasting identical instruction text placed in system vs user vs document/tool slots (a direction that encodes 'which source is this token from'). Validate both with linear probes (report AUROC: conflict detection, and source classification of instruction tokens). Test separability: cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity between the two directions; confirm privilege is token-local (probeable at the instruction tokens) while detection is aggregated.
3) THE DETECTION-ARBITRATION GAP (core H1): On conflict items, measure per-example (i) detection-signal strength, (ii) the privilege readout of the winning vs losing instruction's tokens, and (iii) realized outcome (which instruction the model obeyed). Test H1: detection is strong even when the model obeys the LOWER-privilege source (injection succeeds), i.e., the model 'knows' there is a conflict but the privilege signal fails to determine the winner. Quantify the decoupling: mutual information / AUROC of detection predicting correct arbitration (predict: low) vs privilege-readout predicting correct arbitration (predict: higher but insufficient), and the fraction of injection successes with high detection.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H2, two-way): (a) Transplant a strong privilege readout onto the legitimate instruction's tokens (or subtract privilege from the injected instruction's tokens) in a run where injection is currently winning, and measure restored hierarchy compliance and change in the arbitration outcome. (b) As a specificity control, boost the DETECTION direction alone and show it does NOT fix arbitration. Report flip rates vs intervention magnitude, corruption/random-direction baselines, and multiple metrics (obeyed-source, P(privileged-completion token), realized behavior judged by an outcome classifier). This establishes the broken detection->privilege-weighted-arbitration edge.
5) CONTEXT-LENGTH DEGRADATION (H3): Vary the depth/position of the injected instruction and the total context length; test whether the privilege readout of instruction tokens decays with distance and whether arbitration failures increase with depth (linking to executive-control-degradation-with-sequence-length). Report injection success and privilege-readout strength vs position.
6) AUTHORITY BINDING DEFENSE: Training-free inference-time intervention. Tag each instruction token with its source (system/user/tool-document, available from the prompt structure) and, at pre-arbitration layers, add alpha * privilege_direction scaled by the source's rank to those tokens (amplify high-privilege, attenuate low-privilege/content tokens), and optionally gate the arbitration decision on the resulting privilege-weighted signal. Calibrate alpha, layer, and per-source scaling on a held-out split. This binds arbitration to provenance without training.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, delimiter/spotlighting defense, a role-agnostic instruction-following steering baseline (reproducing 'Who is In Charge?'), and Authority Binding on: hierarchy-adherence rate (obeys the correct source) on the conflict suite; indirect/tool/RAG injection attack success rate; benign single-source obedience and over-refusal (does it still follow legitimate user requests? XSTest/IFEval); and utility (MMLU, AlpacaEval win-rate, IFEval instruction-following). Central test: Authority Binding raises hierarchy-adherence and lowers injection ASR toward the trained-hierarchy ceiling while preserving benign obedience/utility, beating delimiter and role-agnostic-steering baselines because it binds resolution to source rather than globally amplifying obedience.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts detection vs privilege; single-direction vs low-rank privilege subspace; privilege-amplify-only vs content-attenuate-only vs both; transfer of the detection/privilege findings and the defense across the four model families and across conflict regimes (system-user vs injected-content); robustness to adaptive attacks that phrase injections to mimic high-privilege source style or spoof provenance cues (arms-race stress test); and whether reasoning models show a stronger detection->arbitration edge in CoT.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The privilege/provenance representation might be entangled with generic position or formatting features rather than genuine source-authority; we mitigate with matched contrastive prompts (same text across slots), cross-probe separability tests, position controls, and treat partial entanglement as an informative finding. (2) If detection and arbitration turn out to be well-coupled (H1 false) in some models, the gap framing weakens — but the detection-vs-arbitration decomposition and the census of which drives correct outcomes remain an informative contribution. (3) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal patching. (4) Authority Binding could over-suppress legitimate user instructions (harming helpfulness) or be gamed by content that spoofs provenance; benign-obedience/IFEval metrics and an adaptive spoofing attack bound and test this. (5) Provenance tagging assumes a known prompt structure (system/user/tool boundaries), which holds in standard chat/tool APIs but may not for free-form inputs — a stated scope. (6) Cross-condition patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We construct injection prompts only from public benchmark patterns and non-operational content, focusing on measurement rather than novel attack uplift.

Name: safety_validation_gap
Title: The Safety Validation Gap: Why LLMs Generate Harm They Could Catch, and Closing It by Feeding Late-Layer Content Back to Middle-Layer Validators
Short Hypothesis: Safety self-validation and harmful-content generation are computed in structurally dissociated parts of the network: the model VALIDATES ('is what I'm producing safe?') in middle layers using shallow consistency-style heads that check only surface features (trigger words, template shape), whereas the harmful content is fully FORMED in later layers. Because validation happens before and below where harm is realized, the model cannot see the semantic harm it is about to emit, mechanistically explaining attention-slipping, the refusal cliff, and weak self-correction. Feeding late-layer content representations back into the middle-layer validation site at inference closes this gap and lets the model catch its own unsafe output.
Related Work: A recent finding, 'The Validation Gap' (2025), shows that for arithmetic, LLMs compute answers in higher layers but VALIDATE them in middle layers via 'consistency heads' doing surface-level checks, and that adding higher-layer activations into lower layers closes the error-detection gap. We port this computation-vs-validation dissociation to SAFETY, an entirely different and higher-stakes domain. This is distinct from: (a) internal-state safety monitors (SafeSwitch 2025, Gnosis 2025, BRT-Align 2025, 'LMs Can Predict Their Own Behavior' 2025), which train external probes to READ OUT unsafety but never ask where in the network self-validation is computed, whether it is layer-dissociated from generation, or why it is surface-level; (b) refusal-direction / harm-vs-refusal work (Arditi 2024; Zhao 2025; 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' 2025), which localizes refusal but treats it as a single detection-then-execution pipeline, not a validation stage that structurally precedes and underlooks content formation; (c) self-correction methods (Progressive Self-Reflection 2025, RLBF 2026, intrinsic self-correction 2025) which add extra generation/training but never diagnose the mechanistic reason self-monitoring fails. Our contribution: (1) establish a safety validation gap — validation is middle-layer, surface-level, and dissociated from late-layer harm formation; (2) identify safety 'consistency heads' and show they only key on surface cues, causally explaining surface-triggered over-refusal AND semantic-harm under-refusal; (3) a training-free 'validation feedback' intervention that patches late-layer content into the middle validation site, closing the gap without extra generation passes.
Abstract: LLMs routinely produce harmful content that, when shown their own output, they would recognize as unsafe — a puzzling failure of self-monitoring. Inspired by a recent mechanistic finding that models compute arithmetic in higher layers but VALIDATE it in middle layers using shallow 'consistency heads', we hypothesize an analogous, higher-stakes Safety Validation Gap: the model validates whether it is being safe in MIDDLE layers, keying only on SURFACE features, while the actual harmful semantics of what it will emit are FORMED in LATER layers. Validation therefore fires before and below the point where harm becomes representationally explicit, so the model literally cannot inspect the harm it is about to produce. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using logit-lens/layerwise probes we show (H1) a semantic-harm representation matures in late layers whereas a safety-validation/refusal-intent signal peaks in middle layers, before harm is fully encoded. Via head attribution we identify sparse safety 'consistency heads' and show (H2) they are causally responsible for validation yet respond to surface cues (trigger words, template shape) rather than semantic harm — jointly explaining surface-triggered over-refusal and semantically-obfuscated jailbreaks. We then propose Validation Feedback (H3): a training-free intervention that adds late-layer content activations back into the middle-layer validation site during generation, giving validators access to the fully-formed harm. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN/prefill/obfuscation), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and inference overhead, comparing against refusal-direction addition, SafeSwitch-style probes, and self-reflection.
Experiments:
1) SIGNAL LOCALIZATION (H1): Extract two layerwise signals at generation-relevant positions (last prompt token and early output tokens): (a) a SEMANTIC-HARM representation via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign prompts AND via logit-lens decoding of harm-related tokens, measured per layer; (b) a SAFETY-VALIDATION / refusal-intent signal via a linear probe predicting whether the model will refuse, measured per layer. Test H1: the validation/refusal-intent probe peaks in middle layers while the semantic-harm representation continues rising and only saturates in later layers — i.e., validation is computed before harm is fully formed. Report per-layer probe AUROC and harm-representation strength; quantify the layer gap (t_validate < t_harm). Replicate across the four models.
2) SAFETY CONSISTENCY HEADS (H2a): Rank attention heads by their causal contribution to the middle-layer validation signal (attention-knockout / path patching, measuring drop in refusal-intent probe value and in realized refusal). Identify a sparse 'safety consistency head' set; compare to random heads. Confirm they are middle-layer, mirroring the arithmetic consistency-head result.
3) SURFACE-VS-SEMANTIC KEYING (H2b): Build two contrast sets: (i) SURFACE-only-harmful (benign meaning but harmful trigger words / attack-template shape — drawn from XSTest/OR-Bench false-positive prompts) and (ii) SEMANTIC-only-harmful (genuinely harmful intent but obfuscated/paraphrased to remove surface cues — e.g., CodeAttack, roleplay, euphemism). Measure how strongly the safety consistency heads fire on each. Test H2: consistency heads fire on surface-harmful (driving over-refusal) but UNDER-fire on semantic-harmful (letting obfuscated jailbreaks through), while the LATE-layer semantic-harm representation correctly separates both. Report head-activation and validation-probe response per set, and correlate consistency-head firing with over-refusal and with jailbreak success per prompt (AUROC).
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION OF THE GAP: (a) Patch the late-layer semantic-harm representation of a semantically-harmful (but surface-clean) prompt down to benign and show validation is unaffected (validators don't read late layers). (b) Show that on obfuscated jailbreaks the harm IS present late but validation never rises — establishing the dissociation. Use corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-intent probe, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
5) VALIDATION FEEDBACK DEFENSE (H3): Training-free intervention — at each generation step, take the residual-stream content from a late layer L_late (where semantic harm is formed) and add a projected copy (optionally only its harm-aligned component) into the residual stream at the middle validation layer L_mid, so the safety consistency heads can 'see' the fully-formed content. Calibrate L_late, L_mid, and gain on a held-out split; gate so benign generations receive negligible feedback. This directly mirrors the 'add higher-layer activations to lower layers closes the gap' fix, ported to safety.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), a SafeSwitch-style trained prober, and Progressive-Self-Reflection on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, and specifically OBFUSCATION/CodeAttack attacks where surface cues are removed), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Validation Feedback specifically closes the semantic-obfuscation ASR gap (its target failure mode) AND reduces surface-triggered over-refusal (by letting validators use semantics instead of surface), a joint improvement single-knob refusal steering cannot achieve, with lower overhead than extra self-reflection passes.
7) ABLATIONS: choice of L_late/L_mid; whole-content vs harm-component-only feedback; feedback into consistency heads only vs whole residual stream; whether the gap and the fix transfer across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attack that hides harm even in late layers (arms-race stress test); and whether reasoning models exhibit a larger validation gap (linking to the refusal-cliff).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean validation-vs-formation layer dissociation may be weaker or model-specific for safety than for arithmetic; a negative or blurred result still informs theories of why self-monitoring fails and is reported per model with effect sizes. (2) 'Validation' and 'refusal-intent' are proxied by probes that may entangle with generic uncertainty; we use two independent signal extractions (probe + logit-lens), report AUROC, and corroborate with causal head knockout. (3) Consistency-head identification via attention knockout has known attention!=attribution pitfalls; we corroborate with path patching and behavioral metrics. (4) Validation Feedback could degrade coherence/utility or over-refuse if late-layer content is fed too strongly into early computation (a form of feedback loop); the gain calibration, gating, and utility/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) The surface-vs-semantic contrast sets require careful construction (holding intent constant while varying surface, and vice versa); we validate with independent LLM judges and human spot-checks and report axis-orthogonality diagnostics. (6) Adaptive attackers might suppress harm even in late layers so feedback has nothing to catch; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (7) Findings may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: compositional_harm_blindspot
Title: Harm That Only Emerges When Skills Combine: The Compositional Blind Spot of LLM Safety and a Composition-Aware Fix
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety perception is computed at the level of individual atomic skills/concepts, not their composition. When harm emerges only from combining two individually-benign sub-requests (e.g., a benign chemistry-lookup skill composed with a benign quantity-scaling skill yields a dangerous synthesis), the harmfulness-perception circuit fails to fire because no atomic component is individually harmful and the model never integrates the sub-skill representations into a joint harm judgment. Measuring where (or whether) the model integrates sub-skill signals into a composite harm representation reveals a mechanistic 'compositional blind spot,' and forcing integration of sub-skill representations at inference lets the model detect emergent-from-composition harm without harming benign compositional utility.
Related Work: Compositionality work shows LLMs acquire new skills by composing atomic ones (F(g(x)) RL composition, 2025) and that cross-capability performance follows a 'weakest-link' law (Law of the Weakest Link, 2024), but these study capability, never safety perception. Safety-mechanism work localizes a harmfulness direction and a refusal direction at the instruction token (Arditi et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025, LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately) and finds harm perception is fine-grained per risk-category, but always treats harmfulness as a property read off a single (possibly obfuscated) request; none study requests whose harm is *emergent from composing* two benign sub-skills. What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning (2024) models the harmful concept as a single 'task x concept' pair (design x bomb) but the concept itself is individually unsafe; it does not consider harm that exists in *neither* component alone. Decomposition-style jailbreaks (splitting a harmful request into benign pieces) are known behaviorally but never mechanistically explained as a failure to integrate sub-skill harm signals, and existing defenses are input-level (query decomposition detectors, LLM-judge). Our contribution: (1) define and measure a *composite* harm representation and test whether it is absent/underformed for emergent-from-composition requests while both atomic sub-skill representations are correctly benign; (2) locate where in depth the model does (or fails to) integrate the two sub-skill signals into a joint harm judgment; (3) a training-free 'composition binding' intervention that injects the interaction of the sub-skill representations into the harm-perception site so refusal fires on emergent harm, distinct from any input-level decomposition detector.
Abstract: A striking gap in LLM safety is that harm can be assembled from parts: two requests that are each perfectly benign (a chemistry fact, a scaling calculation) can, when composed, yield a dangerous procedure. Attackers exploit this by decomposing harmful goals into innocent-looking pieces. We propose that this vulnerability has a specific mechanistic origin: the model's harmfulness-perception circuit judges atomic skills/concepts and does not form a *composite* harm representation, so harm that exists in neither component alone is never detected. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using a curated set of prompt triples: two individually-benign sub-requests and their harmful composition, matched against a control set of benign compositions and individually-harmful requests. Using difference-in-means and linear probes we extract a harmfulness-perception readout and measure it for each sub-request and for the composite; we predict the composite harm readout is far weaker than for an equivalently-harmful monolithic request, i.e., a compositional blind spot. Via layerwise probing and cross-condition activation patching we ask whether and where the model integrates the two sub-skill representations into a joint judgment. Building on this, we propose Composition Binding: a training-free intervention that computes the interaction of the two sub-skill representations and injects it into the harm-perception site so the composite harm signal forms, triggering refusal.
