We evaluate attack success rate on decomposition attacks, harm-detection AUROC on emergent-composition prompts, over-refusal on benign compositions (a critical control), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), reframing a practical jailbreak class as a failure to bind sub-skill harm.
Experiments:
1) DATASET CONSTRUCTION: Build prompt triples (A, B, A+B) where A and B are individually-benign sub-requests/skills but their composition A+B is harmful (drawn from and extending decomposition-jailbreak patterns over public harmful goals: e.g., a benign factual lookup + a benign application/scaling step whose combination is operationally harmful). Add three controls: (i) benign compositions (A,B benign, A+B still benign) to measure over-refusal, (ii) monolithic-harmful requests semantically equivalent to A+B (a single prompt asking for the harmful whole) to serve as the 'harm-detected' ceiling, (iii) monolithic-benign requests. Harm/benign labels validated by multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. Keep all content at documented, non-uplift level (public benchmark-derived).
2) HARM READOUT EXTRACTION: For each model extract the harmfulness-perception direction via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign monolithic prompts at the last instruction token (Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024), validated with a held-out linear probe (report AUROC).
3) COMPOSITIONAL BLIND SPOT (core H1): Measure the harm readout / probe output on each sub-request A and B (predict: correctly low, benign), on the harmful composition A+B (predict: anomalously low relative to its true harm), and on the equivalent monolithic-harmful request (predict: high). Test H1: harm-readout(A+B) << harm-readout(monolithic-equivalent) despite equal ground-truth harm, and quantify the 'blind-spot gap.' Compare against benign-composition controls (readout should be low for both). Report per-model effect sizes and the fraction of composition-harmful prompts the readout misses vs. monolithic misses.
4) INTEGRATION LOCALIZATION (H2): Using layerwise probes, test at which depth (if any) the model forms a joint harm judgment for A+B. Cross-condition patching: transplant the sub-skill representations of A and B (from single-request runs) into the composite run, or vice versa, to see whether the harm signal is reconstructable from the parts — i.e., whether the information is present but not integrated. Compare integration depth for harmful vs. benign compositions. Test H2: for harmful compositions the two sub-skill signals are present in intermediate layers but their *interaction* (a harm-relevant joint term) never forms, whereas for the monolithic-harmful equivalent the harm representation forms normally. Use corruption baselines and multiple metrics (probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
5) COMPOSITION BINDING DEFENSE (H3): Training-free intervention. Estimate the two sub-skill representations within the composite prompt (via their token positions / difference-in-means sub-skill directions) and inject their interaction term (e.g., a calibrated product/outer-interaction projected onto the harm-perception subspace, or the sum of sub-skill harm-relevant components) into the residual stream at the harm-perception layer, so the composite harm readout forms. Gate on the presence of two distinct sub-skills so single-skill and simple benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate injection layer, gain, and gate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), an input-level decomposition/LLM-judge detector baseline, and Composition Binding on: attack success rate for decomposition/compositional jailbreaks (composed harmful goals from HarmBench/JailbreakBench decomposed into benign pieces); harm-detection AUROC on the emergent-composition set; over-refusal on benign compositions (critical: does the fix wrongly refuse benign multi-skill requests?) and standard over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate); and latency. Central test: Composition Binding closes the blind-spot gap — detecting emergent-from-composition harm toward the monolithic ceiling — while keeping over-refusal on *benign* compositions low, a joint outcome input-level detectors and single-knob refusal steering cannot achieve.
7) ABLATIONS: number of composed skills (2 vs 3+, testing weakest-link scaling); which layer hosts sub-skill vs. composite representations; interaction-injection variants (product vs sum vs learned bilinear on the harm subspace); transfer of the blind-spot finding and the defense across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attacker that spreads harm across more, smaller benign pieces to keep each sub-skill signal weak (arms-race stress test); and whether reasoning models integrate sub-skills better across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Some 'compositional' harm may actually be detectable by the model (harm readout fires on A+B), softening H1 for certain categories — but the census of which compositions are blind vs. caught is itself an informative contribution. (2) Cleanly separating harm-emergent-from-composition from cases where one component is subtly harmful is hard; we validate benignness of each sub-request with multiple judges + human review and report labeling reliability. (3) The harm-perception direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with probes and causal patching. (4) Composition Binding could raise over-refusal on legitimate benign multi-skill requests (e.g., ordinary two-step tasks), the key trade-off; the benign-composition control set and gating design are built to detect and bound this and may reveal a genuine tax. (5) Estimating sub-skill representations within a composite prompt is imperfect (skills may be entangled in-context); we test both single-request-derived and in-context-derived sub-skill estimates. (6) Cross-condition patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) Adaptive attackers can fragment harm into many weak pieces; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived content and keep harmful items at a documented, non-operational level, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: self_trust_laundering
Title: Laundering Harm Through Its Own Voice: The Self-Trust Circuit Behind Multi-Turn Jailbreaks and a Training-Free Self-Skepticism Fix
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode a 'this-came-from-me' provenance signal on assistant-role (prior-turn) tokens and grant that self-authored content elevated credibility, so the harmfulness-perception circuit reads the current request through a self-consistency prior anchored on prior assistant turns. Multi-turn and history-forging jailbreaks (Crescendo, Trojan Horse) succeed by exploiting this self-trust: once a prior assistant turn is compliant/benign-seeming, the model launders new harm through its own voice, suppressing fresh harm detection. Attenuating the self-provenance credibility of assistant-history tokens in the harm-perception computation restores turn-independent refusal without hurting benign multi-turn helpfulness.
Related Work: Trojan Horse Prompting (2025) shows behaviorally that models comply when a harmful payload is forged into an assistant-attributed history turn, naming this 'Asymmetric Safety Alignment' (models trained to distrust user requests but not their own purported past) — but it is closed-model, purely behavioral, and offers no mechanism or defense. Representation studies of Crescendo (2025) and ASJA (2025) show multi-turn attacks keep outputs in benign representation regions and shift attention toward dialogue history/prior responses, but attribute this to attention dispersion in general, not to a self-provenance/credibility representation that specifically privileges the model's OWN turns over user turns. DeepContext (2026) and X-Boundary (2025) build external stateful monitors or push representation boundaries but give no account of self-trust. Authority/instruction-hierarchy work (Wallace 2024; Who is In Charge 2025) concerns system>user>tool provenance, never assistant-self provenance or its safety-credibility effect. Harm-vs-refusal decomposition (Zhao 2025; Arditi 2024) treats harm perception as read off the current request, not modulated by a self-consistency prior over prior assistant turns. Our contribution is the first to (1) extract a role/self-provenance representation on assistant-history tokens distinct from user-history tokens, (2) causally show the model grants self-authored content elevated safety-credibility that suppresses harm perception on the current turn (the mechanism behind history-forging and compounding multi-turn compliance), and (3) build a training-free 'self-skepticism' intervention that neutralizes assistant-history credibility for the harm computation only.
Abstract: A striking recent finding is that LLMs can be jailbroken simply by forging a harmful message into the conversation as if the model had said it, and that multi-turn attacks like Crescendo compound compliance across turns. We propose a mechanistic root cause: LLMs represent the provenance of prior turns and grant content attributed to their own assistant role elevated credibility, so harmfulness perception on the current turn is filtered through a self-consistency prior anchored on prior assistant turns. Once a prior assistant turn is compliant or benign-seeming, new harm is laundered through the model's own voice and fresh harm detection is suppressed. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using difference-in-means and linear probes over identical text placed in user-history vs. assistant-history slots, we extract a self-provenance representation and verify it is distinct from generic history/position features. The core causal test: holding the current harmful request fixed, we (a) transplant self-provenance onto a benign-compliant prior turn and measure suppression of the harm readout and refusal, and (b) strip self-provenance from a forged/harmful assistant turn and measure restored harm detection. We show self-provenance credibility, not mere attention dispersion, predicts multi-turn and history-forging jailbreak success and its compounding with turn count. Building on this, we propose Self-Skepticism: a training-free intervention that attenuates the credibility weight of assistant-history tokens feeding the harm-perception site, making refusal turn-independent. We evaluate on Crescendo/ActorAttack multi-turn attacks, Trojan-Horse history forging, single-turn attacks, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), and benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench, MMLU, AlpacaEval), reporting attack success, over-refusal, utility, and inference overhead.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build conversation constructions in three regimes: (i) history-forging (Trojan-Horse-style): a harmful/compliant payload placed in an assistant-attributed prior turn followed by a benign user trigger; (ii) multi-turn escalation (Crescendo, ActorAttack) with checkpointing per turn; (iii) matched single-turn harmful and benign controls, and benign multi-turn helpful dialogues. Critically include CONTENT-MATCHED pairs where identical text is placed in a user-history turn vs. an assistant-history turn (the only difference being attributed role) to isolate self-provenance. Harm/benign labels validated by multiple LLM judges + human spot-check; all content drawn from public benchmark patterns at non-uplift level.
2) SELF-PROVENANCE EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: For each model extract via difference-in-means a self-provenance direction contrasting identical instruction/content tokens in assistant-history vs. user-history slots, at the prior-turn token positions and at the current-request last token. Extract independently: a harm-perception direction (Zhao 2025/Arditi 2024, matched harmful/benign at current-request token) and a generic-history/position direction (turn index, distance) as a confound control. Validate with linear probes (report AUROC: role classification of history tokens, harm detection) and test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity between self-provenance and the position/harm directions.
3) SELF-TRUST CORRELATIONAL TEST (H1): On content-matched pairs, measure the harm readout on the CURRENT request when the same benign-compliant precedent sits in an assistant vs. user slot. Test H1: assistant-slot placement suppresses the current-turn harm readout and refusal more than user-slot placement (self-authored content is trusted more). Quantify the 'self-trust suppression' and its correlation with realized jailbreak success across the three regimes. Compare to failed jailbreaks.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H2, two-way): Holding the current harmful request fixed, (a) ADD self-provenance to a user-slot benign precedent (make it 'sound like the model'): predict increased harm suppression / compliance; (b) STRIP self-provenance from a forged harmful assistant turn (project it out / relabel toward user-provenance in the residual stream): predict restored harm readout and refusal. Report flip rates vs. intervention magnitude, with (i) a random-direction corruption baseline, (ii) generic-history-direction manipulation as a specificity control, and (iii) multiple metrics (harm-probe output at current token, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). This establishes self-provenance credibility — not generic attention dispersion — as the causal lever.
5) COMPOUNDING WITH TURNS (H3): In Crescendo/ActorAttack, measure per-turn self-provenance-weighted credibility of the accumulating assistant history and current-turn harm readout. Test whether harm-suppression grows with turn count and is predicted by cumulative self-provenance credibility (linking to the finding that harm-representation decays with turns), and whether ASJA-style attention-to-history correlates with self-provenance strength.
6) SELF-SKEPTICISM DEFENSE: Training-free intervention that, at the harm-perception layers, attenuates the credibility weight of assistant-history tokens — e.g., subtract alpha*self_provenance_direction from assistant-history token representations (or down-weight their attention contribution to the current-request harm site) so the model re-evaluates prior assistant content skeptically rather than as ground truth. Leave user turns, benign single-turn, and non-harm computations untouched; gate on presence of assistant-history + a harm-relevant readout. Calibrate alpha, layers, gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), DETAM/attention-modification baseline, an external stateful monitor (DeepContext-style) where reproducible, and Self-Skepticism on: attack success for history-forging (Trojan-Horse), multi-turn (Crescendo, ActorAttack), and single-turn attacks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench); over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench multi-turn, and a self-reference task where the model should legitimately use its prior correct answers); general utility (MMLU, AlpacaEval win-rate); latency. Central test: Self-Skepticism closes the multi-turn/history-forging ASR gap toward single-turn refusal levels while preserving benign multi-turn utility (it should NOT harm cases where trusting one's own correct prior turn is appropriate for non-safety tasks) — a selectivity single-knob refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts self-provenance vs. harm perception; single-direction vs. low-rank self-provenance subspace; provenance-subtraction vs. attention-down-weighting; transfer of the self-trust finding and defense across the four model families and across attack regimes (fit gate on Crescendo, test on Trojan-Horse/ActorAttack); robustness to an adaptive attacker that stylistically forges assistant turns to minimize the self-provenance signal (arms-race stress test); and whether reasoning models show a stronger self-trust edge for their own CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The self-provenance representation may be entangled with generic role/formatting or turn-position features rather than a genuine 'credibility' signal; we mitigate with content-matched user-vs-assistant slot pairs, position/history confound controls, cross-probe separability, and treat partial entanglement as an informative finding. (2) If harm suppression is driven mainly by attention dispersion (ASJA) rather than a distinct self-trust representation, H1/H2 weaken — but the specificity controls (generic-history-direction manipulation) directly adjudicate this and either outcome is informative. (3) Self-Skepticism could harm legitimate reliance on the model's own correct prior turns (e.g., multi-step reasoning, self-reference tasks); the benign multi-turn utility and self-reference benchmarks and harm-gated design are built to detect and bound this trade-off. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal patching. (5) Cross-condition patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) Adaptive attackers may forge assistant turns that minimize the self-provenance signal or spread harm across many low-credibility turns; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (7) Assistant/user role boundaries are available in standard chat APIs but the mechanism may differ for models without explicit role tokens — a stated scope. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived content and keep harmful items non-operational, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: point_of_no_return_backtracking
Title: Backtrack to Just Before the Point of No Return: Mechanistically Locating the Irreversible Harmful-Commitment Token for Minimal-Regret Safety Recovery
Short Hypothesis: During an unsafe generation there exists an identifiable 'point of no return' (PoNR): the earliest token at which the residual stream crosses a causally irreversible harmful-commitment boundary, after which continued generation is locked into harm and before which a cheap steer would have prevented it. Existing backtracking methods discard a fixed or learned window of tokens; if instead we detect the PoNR from internal activations and backtrack to exactly the token before it, we achieve safe recovery with provably minimal token discard (minimal regret), better preserving the helpful prefix and reducing latency while matching safety.
Related Work: Backtracking-for-safety methods (Backtracking Improves Generation Safety 2024; Backtracking for Safety 2025; RLBF 2026; CARE 2025) train models to emit a [RESET]/rollback signal or use a guard model with a token buffer, but the amount to backtrack is either the full generation, a fixed buffer, or a learned 'backtrack by x tokens' signal with no mechanistic notion of where harm became irreversible. Adaptive steering (FASB 2025) and reachability monitors (BRT-Align 2025) forecast unsafe completions a few tokens ahead and steer, but do not localize an irreversibility boundary or minimize discard. SafeSwitch/Self-Sanitize/MetaDefense monitor partial responses to abstain or repair but again lack a per-trajectory irreversibility point. Endogenous Steering Resistance (2026) shows internal consistency circuits can self-correct, hinting a recoverable pre-commitment window exists. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we define and measure the PoNR via counterfactual reversibility (the earliest token where a bounded corrective steer can no longer flip the outcome), (2) we show it is predictable online from activations before it is reached, and (3) we build Minimal-Regret Backtracking that discards exactly to the pre-PoNR token, testing whether mechanistically-optimal backtrack depth beats fixed/learned windows on the safety-vs-preserved-helpfulness-vs-latency frontier.
Abstract: Autoregressive generation cannot un-say tokens, so a partial unsafe output tends to snowball into full harm. Recent work adds backtracking—letting a model discard tokens and regenerate—but how far to backtrack is set by fixed buffers or learned heuristics with no principled target. We propose that every unsafe trajectory has a mechanistic 'point of no return' (PoNR): the earliest token at which the residual stream crosses a causally irreversible harmful-commitment boundary, after which a bounded corrective intervention can no longer redirect the model, and before which it can. We operationalize the PoNR per trajectory via counterfactual reversibility: at each generated token we apply a fixed-budget corrective steer (refusal-direction addition) and measure whether the final outcome flips from harmful to safe; the PoNR is the first token where flipping fails. We test on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B whether (H1) a sharp reversibility transition exists and is well-localized, (H2) an online probe trained on activations predicts the PoNR several tokens in advance (before it is reached), and (H3) backtracking to exactly the token before the PoNR yields safe recovery while discarding fewer tokens than fixed-window or learned-signal backtracking, preserving more of the helpful prefix at lower latency. We build Minimal-Regret Backtracking, a training-free controller using the online PoNR probe plus a refusal-restoring steer at the backtrack point. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, toxicity mid-generation), tokens discarded, helpful-prefix preservation, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency, against Backtracking-SFT/CARE-style and fixed-buffer baselines.
Experiments:
1) PoNR MEASUREMENT (H1): For harmful/prefill-attack prompts that the base model complies with, generate the unsafe response. At each generated token t, branch: apply a fixed-budget corrective steer (add alpha*refusal_direction, alpha calibrated to a fixed norm) starting at t and continue generation; judge whether the completed output flips harmful->safe (harm judge). Define reversibility(t)=P(flip). The PoNR is the first t where reversibility drops below a threshold and stays low. Test H1: reversibility exhibits a sharp monotone drop (fit sigmoid; report transition sharpness, PoNR location distribution, and that a single PoNR explains most trajectories). Corroborate the steer-based measure with an ablation-based measure (directional ablation of the harmful/compliance direction at t) to ensure the boundary is not method-specific.
2) ONLINE PREDICTABILITY (H2): Train a lightweight linear probe on residual-stream activations at token t to predict whether t is pre- or post-PoNR (label from the counterfactual measurement). Evaluate whether the probe fires k tokens BEFORE the PoNR (lead-time), report AUROC, calibration (ECE), and lead-time distribution. Baselines: refusal-direction projection alone, next-token harm-probe, perplexity. Test cross-attack transfer (train PoNR probe on prefill attacks, test on GCG/AutoDAN/toxicity-mid-generation) and cross-model transfer.
3) MINIMAL-REGRET BACKTRACKING DEFENSE (H3): At inference, run the online PoNR probe each step; when it signals imminent PoNR (pre-PoNR with high confidence), backtrack to the token before the predicted PoNR, apply a refusal-restoring steer / prepend a brief safety reflection, and regenerate. Calibrate probe threshold and steer magnitude on held-out data. Because the target is the mechanistically-earliest irreversible token, discarded tokens should be minimal.
4) EVALUATION: Compare base model, fixed-buffer backtracking (discard last N tokens on guard-model trigger, CARE-style), learned 'backtrack-by-x' (RLBF/Backtracking-SFT-style, reproduced), full-restart backtracking, and Minimal-Regret Backtracking on: attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, mid-generation toxicity via RealToxicityPrompts continuations); tokens discarded per recovery; helpful-prefix preservation (fraction of the pre-PoNR helpful content retained, measured by overlap/judge); over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate); and end-to-end latency. Central test: Minimal-Regret Backtracking matches the safest baseline's ASR while discarding significantly fewer tokens and preserving more helpful prefix at lower latency—a Pareto improvement enabled by targeting the PoNR rather than a fixed window.
5) ABLATIONS: which layer/position the PoNR probe reads; sensitivity to the corrective-steer budget alpha used to define reversibility (does the PoNR location depend on budget? report the reversibility surface over alpha); probe lead-time vs safety trade-off; whether backtracking-to-PoNR beats backtracking-to-PoNR-minus-delta and PoNR-plus-delta (validating minimality); transfer across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attack that pushes the PoNR to the first token (arms-race stress test) and to attacks with multiple PoNRs in long generations.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The reversibility transition may be gradual or trajectory-dependent for some attacks, making the PoNR fuzzy; the distributional characterization is still informative and we report transition sharpness rather than assuming a crisp boundary. (2) The PoNR is defined relative to a chosen corrective-steer budget; a stronger steer could move it later, so we map the reversibility surface over budgets and define the PoNR at a fixed, disclosed budget matched to the deployed defense. (3) Counterfactual measurement (branch-and-steer at every token) is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts/tokens for measurement and rely on the cheap online probe for the defense. (4) The online probe may transfer poorly to unseen attacks or fire too late (after the PoNR), undermining minimal-regret; we report lead-time and cross-attack/cross-model transfer and treat late firing as a bounded fallback to a slightly larger backtrack. (5) Backtracking + steer could raise over-refusal or degrade coherence; over-refusal/utility/coherence benchmarks and threshold calibration bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (6) Adaptive attackers could force the PoNR to the first token (no recoverable prefix), which we test and treat as an arms-race limitation. (7) Harm judging is noisy; we use multiple judges and human spot-checks. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: refusal_action_disconnect
Title: The Refusal Direction Doesn't Reach the Action: Mechanistically Locating and Repairing the Text-to-Tool-Call Safety Gap in LLM Agents
Short Hypothesis: LLM agents refuse harmful requests in text yet still execute the harmful tool call because the conversational refusal circuit (the refusal direction that governs text output) is largely decoupled from the tool-call action-emission pathway. The model's harmfulness belief and even its refusal decision are present internally but exert little causal influence on whether a tool call is emitted. Measuring this disconnect exposes the mechanistic root of agentic safety failures, and re-coupling the existing refusal/harmfulness readout to the action-decision site at inference restores tool-call safety without retraining or hurting benign tool use.
Related Work: A wave of 2024-2026 work documents the text-safety-to-tool-call-safety GAP behaviorally: 'Mind the GAP' (2026) shows frontier models refuse in text while their tool calls execute the forbidden action; 'LM Agents May Fail to Act on Their Own Risk Knowledge' (2025) reports a generator-validator gap where agents have >98% risk knowledge but <26% safe-execution; 'Applying Refusal-Vector Ablation to Llama 3.1 70B Agents' (2024) shows chat safety fine-tuning does not generalize to agentic behavior. Defenses are behavioral or training-based: Agent Safety Alignment via RL (2025), Thought-Aligner (2025), ToolShield (2026), TS-Guard (2026) - external guardrails, RL, or thought-correction modules. On the interpretability side, refusal is a direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harmfulness and refusal are separate directions (Zhao et al. 2025), and refusal is a shared one-dimensional knob (There Is More to Refusal, 2026) - but ALL of this is measured on conversational text output only. Nobody has asked whether the well-characterized refusal/harmfulness circuitry is causally connected to the tool-CALL emission pathway, nor localized where that connection breaks. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we measure the causal edge from the conversational refusal/harmfulness readout to the action-emission decision and show it is severed in agentic contexts, mechanistically explaining the behavioral GAP that prior work only documents; (2) we localize where the action decision diverges from the text-refusal decision; and (3) we propose a training-free re-coupling intervention that wires the existing (intact) refusal readout into the tool-call site - a mechanism repair, not a new guardrail model or RL fine-tune.
Abstract: LLM agents that can call external tools exhibit an alarming failure: they refuse a harmful request in their text output yet simultaneously emit a tool call that executes the forbidden action. Recent benchmarks document this text-to-tool-call safety gap behaviorally, but its internal cause is unknown, and existing fixes are external guardrail models or expensive RL. We advance a mechanistic explanation: the conversational refusal circuit that governs text is largely decoupled from the tool-call action-emission pathway, so the model's harmfulness belief and refusal decision remain internally present but fail to gate the action. We test this on open agentic models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Ministral-8B) using Agent-SafetyBench, InjecAgent, and GAP-style harmful-tool-call scenarios. First, we extract the refusal and harmfulness directions in agentic contexts and show via probing that harmfulness is still decoded when a harmful tool call is emitted (belief is intact). Second, the key causal test: we transplant the refusal/harmfulness readout from a matched text-refusal run into an action-emitting run and measure whether the tool call is suppressed; a weak effect quantifies the severed edge, and we localize the layers/heads where the text-refusal and action decisions diverge. Third, we propose Action Gating: a training-free controller that reads the live harmfulness/refusal readout and injects the refusal signal at the action-decision site so the tool call is gated when the model already believes the request is harmful. We evaluate harmful-tool-call rate, text-tool-call divergence (GAP metric), benign tool-use utility, over-refusal on benign tool calls, and latency, against refusal-direction addition, a prompt-based safety-reinforced baseline, and an external step-level guardrail.
Experiments:
1) SETUP & SCENARIOS: Instantiate ReAct-style agents on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Ministral-8B with tool schemas. Build a labeled scenario set: (a) HARMFUL-ACTION prompts where a benign-sounding request maps to a harmful tool call (from Agent-SafetyBench, InjecAgent indirect-injection, and GAP-style regulated-domain scenarios); (b) matched CONVERSATIONAL versions of the same harmful requests (no tools available, chat only) to obtain the text-refusal reference; (c) BENIGN tool-use tasks (correct tool call expected) and benign over-refusal controls (tool available, request benign). For each harmful scenario, record the four-way behavioral outcome grid: text-refuse x tool-call-emit, giving the GAP metric (refuses in text but still calls the harmful tool).
2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & BELIEF PERSISTENCE (H1): Extract via difference-in-means a harmfulness-perception direction at the last instruction token and a refusal-execution direction at post-instruction positions (following Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024), fit on the conversational (chat) data. Validate with held-out linear probes (AUROC). Test H1: on agentic runs where the model emits a harmful tool call, the harmfulness probe still fires strongly (belief intact) even though refusal-execution in the action pathway does not, i.e., the belief persists into the action context. Report harmfulness-probe AUROC and mean projection on harmful-tool-call runs vs benign-tool runs vs chat-refusal runs.
3) SEVERED-EDGE CAUSAL TEST (H2, core): Cross-condition activation patching. Take an agentic run that emits a harmful tool call; patch in the refusal/harmfulness-carrying activations from the matched chat run that refuses (at the instruction token / early-mid layers), then measure the change in P(tool-call emission) and realized tool-call suppression. Define the text->action edge strength = tool-call suppression per unit patched refusal signal. Compare to the analogous within-chat patching (which should restore text refusal strongly). Test H2: the text->action edge is much weaker than the text->text edge, quantifying the disconnect; correlate per-scenario edge weakness with GAP occurrence (Spearman). Use random-direction corruption baselines and multiple metrics (P(tool token), refusal-projection at the action-decision position, realized behavior).
4) DIVERGENCE LOCALIZATION: Using logit-lens / layerwise probing at the action-decision position (the token where the model commits to a tool call vs a refusal), identify the layers where the text-refusal trajectory and the action trajectory diverge - i.e., where the refusal signal is present but the action pathway ignores it. Identify candidate attention heads/MLPs that drive tool-call emission independently of the refusal direction (attention-knockout + path patching), with control heads.
5) ACTION GATING DEFENSE: Training-free controller. At inference, read the live harmfulness/refusal readout at the instruction token; if it exceeds a calibrated threshold, inject alpha*(deficit)*refusal_direction into the residual stream at the action-decision layers identified in Exp 4 (and/or down-weight the identified action-emission heads), so an emitted harmful tool call is gated. Gate on the harmfulness readout so benign tool calls (low readout) receive ~0 injection. Calibrate alpha, layer, threshold on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base agent, naive refusal-direction addition (constant, applied everywhere), safety-reinforced system prompt, and an external step-level guardrail (ToolShield/TS-Guard-style, where reproducible) against Action Gating on: harmful-tool-call rate (Agent-SafetyBench, InjecAgent, GAP scenarios), text-tool-call GAP metric, benign tool-use task success (does the agent still call the right tools?), over-refusal on benign tool calls, general utility retention (MMLU, AlpacaEval), and latency overhead. Central test: Action Gating reduces harmful-tool-call rate and closes the GAP toward chat-refusal levels while preserving benign tool-use utility better than constant refusal addition or blanket prompting - a Pareto improvement enabled by targeting the action-decision site with a belief-gated signal.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer/head hosts the divergence; harmfulness-gated vs constant injection at matched average magnitude (isolating the value of re-coupling); transfer of the severed-edge finding and the defense across the three model families; robustness to indirect prompt-injection (tool-output-initiated harm) vs user-initiated harm; and an adaptive attack that phrases the harmful action to lower the harmfulness readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The text->action edge might turn out to be moderately intact for some models/scenarios, softening the 'severed edge' framing - but the census of edge strength vs GAP occurrence is itself an informative contribution and would refine which failure modes are belief-vs-execution driven. (2) The harmfulness belief may NOT persist for injection-based harm where the model genuinely fails to perceive the injected instruction as harmful; Action Gating would then fail for those cases, which we treat as an informative scope boundary and test explicitly (user-initiated vs tool-output-initiated harm). (3) Difference-in-means directions may be incomplete (concept-cone evidence); we corroborate with probes, low-rank subspaces, and causal patching. (4) Cross-condition patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (5) Action Gating could over-refuse benign tool calls if the harmfulness readout misfires; the belief-gated design and benign tool-use / over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine tax. (6) Localizing the action-decision position is nontrivial in free-form ReAct traces; we standardize the tool-call format and identify the commitment token, but noisy trace parsing could add variance. (7) Adaptive attackers may lower the harmfulness readout while still eliciting the harmful action; we test one such attack and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public agent-safety benchmark scenarios and construct no novel operational harm, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: moral_default_control_asymmetry
Title: Cognitive Control Cuts Both Ways: A Deliberation Direction That Promotes Honesty or Deception Depending on the Model's Moral Default
Short Hypothesis: LLMs contain a linear 'deliberation/effortful-control' signal that is distinct from the honesty direction, and, mirroring a robust neuroscience finding, its causal effect on honesty is sign-flipped by the model's moral default: amplifying deliberation pushes a deception-prone context toward honesty but pushes an honesty-prone context toward deception. This resolves the paradox that added reasoning sometimes increases and sometimes decreases lying, and yields a default-conditioned steering rule that increases honesty far more reliably than default-agnostic honesty steering.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work extracts an honesty/deception direction and steers it (RepE/LAT, Zou et al. 2023; 'Can LLMs Lie?' 2025; 'When Thinking LLMs Lie' 2025; 'Localizing Lying in Llama' 2023; 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' 2025; 'Caught in the Act' 2025). All treat honesty as a single knob and report a monotone honesty-vs-performance trade-off. Several papers note that lying ability *increases* with reasoning/model size, and reasoning models deceive more, but none isolate a deliberation/control signal separate from honesty or explain why more deliberation sometimes yields more honesty and sometimes less. The cross-domain neuroscience literature (Speer et al. 2020/2021 'Cognitive control promotes either honesty or dishonesty depending on one's moral default'; reviews of executive control in dishonesty) establishes exactly this moral-default-dependent, sign-flipping role of cognitive control. Our contribution ports this to LLMs: (1) we extract a deliberation/effortful-control direction distinct from the honesty direction and validate separability; (2) we test the sign-flip hypothesis causally — the same deliberation intervention has opposite effects on honesty depending on the context's moral default; (3) we build Default-Conditioned Control Steering, which reads the moral-default signal and applies deliberation in the honesty-promoting direction, beating default-agnostic honesty steering. This is neither a new deception probe nor a standard honesty knob; it is a second, interacting causal axis with a testable interaction structure.
Abstract: Interpretability research treats honesty in LLMs as a single steerable direction with a monotone honesty-vs-capability trade-off. Yet a puzzle persists: adding reasoning or 'thinking' sometimes makes models more honest and sometimes more deceptive. We import a robust finding from the neuroscience of dishonesty — that cognitive control does not promote honesty per se but has an effect whose sign depends on a person's moral default (it helps honest people cheat and cheaters be honest) — and test whether an analogous structure exists in LLMs. We hypothesize that models encode a linear deliberation/effortful-control signal, distinct from the honesty direction, whose causal effect on truthfulness is sign-flipped by the context's moral default. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and a reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B). Using difference-in-means and probes, we extract an honesty direction and a deliberation direction (contrasting effortful/deliberative vs quick/intuitive responses, and long vs short chains of thought) and verify they are separable. We then construct honesty-default and deception-default contexts (incentive-to-lie games, sycophancy pressure, roleplay) and perform the key causal test: steering the deliberation direction up should increase honesty in deception-default contexts but decrease it in honesty-default contexts, an interaction default-agnostic honesty steering cannot capture. Building on this, we propose Default-Conditioned Control Steering, which reads the moral-default signal and applies deliberation in whichever direction promotes honesty. We evaluate honesty rate (insider-trading compliance, TruthfulQA-lie, sycophancy, Among-Us-style deception), capability retention (MMLU, GSM8K), and the honesty-vs-utility frontier, comparing against RepE honesty steering.
Experiments:
1) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: For each model extract via difference-in-means (a) an HONESTY direction from contrastive honest-vs-deceptive response pairs (RepE/Zou-style), and (b) a DELIBERATION/effortful-control direction contrasting effortful/deliberative vs quick/intuitive framings and, for the reasoning model, long-CoT vs short/no-CoT trajectories, at the pre-response token. Validate each with held-out linear probes (report AUROC) and test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity; confirm the deliberation direction predicts CoT length / self-reported effort but not honesty on its own.
2) MORAL-DEFAULT MEASUREMENT: Build contexts with a measurable default disposition toward honesty vs deception: (i) incentive-to-lie games (insider-trading compliance a la Scheurer 2023, Secret-Agenda-style goal games), (ii) sycophancy pressure (user pushes a false claim), (iii) roleplay/persona prompts, plus neutral factual controls. For each context measure the base-rate honesty (behavioral) and a moral-default readout = projection onto the honesty direction before intervention. Bin contexts into honesty-default vs deception-default.
3) SIGN-FLIP CAUSAL TEST (core H1): Holding the request fixed, steer the DELIBERATION direction up and down (dose-response, fixed-norm) in honesty-default vs deception-default contexts and measure change in realized honesty (harm/deception judge) and honesty-direction projection. Test the interaction H1: deliberation-up increases honesty in deception-default contexts but decreases it in honesty-default contexts (significant context x deliberation interaction). Controls: random-direction steering, honesty-direction steering (should raise honesty in both), and a specificity check that deliberation steering changes CoT length/effort markers. Report interaction effect size, per-context dose-response curves, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics (realized honesty, P(truthful token), honesty projection).
4) MECHANISM COROBORATION: Test whether the sign-flip arises because deliberation amplifies whichever policy the context favors (i.e., deliberation acts multiplicatively on the current honesty tendency). Fit honesty_change ~ deliberation_dose x default_readout and check the predicted multiplicative form; corroborate with logit attribution showing deliberation steering upweights the already-dominant response mode.
5) DEFAULT-CONDITIONED CONTROL STEERING (defense): At inference, read the moral-default projection; if deception-default, add +alpha*deliberation_direction; if honesty-default, subtract (dampen deliberation) — always pushing toward honesty. Gate magnitude by |default readout|. Calibrate alpha, layer, threshold on held-out data.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, RepE honesty-direction addition (default-agnostic), default-agnostic deliberation-up (naive 'think more'), and Default-Conditioned Control Steering on: honesty rate across the four context families and TruthfulQA; strategic-deception detection-consistency; capability retention (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); and the honesty-vs-utility Pareto frontier. Central test: Default-Conditioned Control Steering achieves higher honesty at matched utility than honesty steering and than naive 'think more,' because it accounts for the sign-flip.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts deliberation vs honesty; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the sign-flip holds in the reasoning model at the CoT level (long CoT increases honesty in deception-default but decreases it in honesty-default); transfer of directions and the interaction across the four models; robustness to an adaptive prompt that spoofs the default readout.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The sign-flip interaction may be weak or absent in some models (especially small/base), softening H1 — but a clean characterization of when it appears is itself informative and directly tests whether the neuroscience analogy holds. (2) The deliberation direction may entangle with generic verbosity, formatting, or the honesty direction; we mitigate with separability tests, verbosity/CoT-length controls, and low cosine-similarity checks, treating partial entanglement as a reported finding. (3) 'Moral default' is operationalized via context base-rate and honesty-projection, which are proxies for a latent disposition; mislabeling would blur the interaction, so we use multiple context families and report per-context results. (4) Honesty judging is noisy; we use multiple judges, verifiable-outcome games (insider trading, factual TruthfulQA), and human spot-checks. (5) Default-Conditioned steering could reduce capability or over-suppress legitimate deliberation on benign tasks; utility/Pareto benchmarks and gating bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Single-direction/difference-in-means may be incomplete (multiple deception directions reported in the literature); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (7) Adaptive prompts could spoof the default readout to flip the steering harmfully; we test one such attack as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public deception/honesty benchmarks and construct no novel operational harm.

Name: harm_manifold_extrapolation
Title: Can Safety Extrapolate? Whether the Harmfulness Subspace Is a Fixed Concept Enumeration or a Compositional Manifold That Generalizes to Never-Seen Harm Categories
Short Hypothesis: The internal harmfulness representation is not a fixed enumeration of the specific harm concepts seen during safety training but a compositional manifold whose basis directions recombine to place *novel, never-aligned* harm categories inside the harmful region. If so, whether a model refuses an unseen harm type is predictable from that category's geometric position (interior vs. exterior of the convex hull spanned by trained-harm directions), and 'safety generalization failures' are precisely the categories that fall in the exterior/extrapolation region. A training-free hull-completion intervention that projects extrapolation-region harm onto the interior can restore refusal for emergent harm types.
Related Work: The Geometry of Harmfulness (2025) shows 55 harm subconcepts span a strikingly low-rank subspace with a dominant direction, and Hidden Dimensions (2025) finds orthogonal safety directions, but both treat the subspace as spanned by *known* trained concepts and never ask whether the geometry extrapolates to categories absent from alignment. The Structural Safety Generalization Problem (2025) documents that safety fails to generalize across semantically-equivalent input structures, and False Sense of Security (2025) shows probes rely on surface patterns and fail OOD, but neither offers a geometric account of *category-level* (not structural) novelty nor a mechanism to predict which unseen harm types will slip through. Arditi et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2025) characterize refusal/harmfulness directions on in-distribution harm. RepIt (2025) and MEUV (2025) factorize refusal into topic-aligned near-orthogonal vectors for *known* topics. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we operationalize harm-category novelty as geometric interior-vs-exterior position relative to the hull of trained-harm directions and test whether refusal on held-out/emergent categories is predicted by this position; (2) we distinguish two competing models of the harmfulness representation — fixed concept-enumeration (novel harm lands outside, refusal fails) vs. compositional manifold (novel harm is a recombination of basis directions, refusal generalizes) — and adjudicate them causally; (3) we propose Hull Completion, a training-free intervention that projects exterior-region harm onto the interior to elicit refusal for never-aligned categories, directly targeting emergent/underrepresented harm rather than known topics.
Abstract: As new harm categories emerge (new bioweapon techniques, novel scam formats, freshly-regulated domains), a critical question is whether safety alignment on today's harm taxonomy generalizes to tomorrow's. We reframe this as a geometry question: is the model's internal harmfulness representation a fixed enumeration of the specific concepts seen during safety training, or a compositional manifold whose basis directions recombine to cover unseen harm? Under the enumeration view, a never-aligned harm category lands in the *exterior* of the region spanned by trained-harm directions and refusal fails; under the compositional view, it is expressible as a combination of existing basis directions and lands in the *interior*, so refusal generalizes. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We build a large harm-category taxonomy, extract a per-category harmfulness direction, and construct held-out 'novel' categories (leave-category-out, and genuinely emergent/synthetic harm types). For each novel category we compute its geometric position — interior vs. exterior of the convex hull / low-rank cone spanned by the remaining trained categories — and test whether this position predicts realized refusal on that category's prompts. We causally verify the two models via cross-category patching and hull-projection. Building on this, we propose Hull Completion: a training-free intervention that, when a prompt's harm representation lies in the exterior extrapolation region, projects it onto the interior harmful manifold to elicit refusal for never-aligned categories. We evaluate refusal generalization to held-out and emergent harm, geometric predictiveness (AUROC), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and robustness of the interior/exterior account across models.
Experiments:
1) TAXONOMY & DIRECTION EXTRACTION: Assemble a broad harm-category taxonomy (~60-80 categories drawn from HarmBench, WMDP-style domains, OR-Bench category labels, and the Geometry-of-Harmfulness subconcepts). For each category collect matched harmful/benign prompt pairs and extract a per-category harmfulness direction via difference-in-means at the last instruction token (following Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024), at a chosen mid layer. Validate each with held-out linear probes (report per-category AUROC). Compute the low-rank harmfulness subspace (top-k SVD of the category directions) and its effective rank (replicating and extending the low-rank finding).
2) NOVELTY AS GEOMETRY (core H1): Create 'novel' categories two ways: (a) LEAVE-CATEGORY-OUT — hold out each category, build the hull/cone from the remaining categories, and compute the held-out category's geometric position: its projection onto vs. residual outside the remaining-category subspace, and whether its direction lies inside the convex cone of the remaining directions (interior) or in the orthogonal/exterior extrapolation region; (b) EMERGENT/SYNTHETIC categories — harm types plausibly underrepresented in alignment (novel scam formats, recently-regulated domains, recombined multi-domain harms), validated as harmful by multiple judges + human spot-check. For each novel category measure realized refusal rate on its prompts. Test H1: interior-position categories are refused (compositional generalization) while exterior/extrapolation-position categories are under-refused (enumeration failure); quantify with Spearman correlation and AUROC of geometric position predicting per-category refusal, and per-prompt AUROC. Baselines for the predictor: raw dominant-direction projection alone, a surface-pattern n-gram detector (per False Sense of Security), and prompt perplexity.
3) ADJUDICATING THE TWO MODELS (H2, causal): (a) Compositional test — for an interior novel category, express its harm direction as a reconstruction from trained-category basis directions and test whether ablating that reconstructed direction removes refusal (harm is genuinely encoded via recombination) vs. requires the held-out true direction (enumeration). (b) Exterior test — for an exterior novel category, show its harm content is decodable by a probe (the model *represents* it) yet the dominant/interior refusal machinery does not fire, establishing that the failure is geometric-position, not perception-absence. Use cross-category activation patching, corruption/random-direction baselines, and multiple metrics (probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
4) HULL COMPLETION DEFENSE (H3): Training-free intervention. At inference, compute the prompt's harm representation and its residual outside the trained-harm subspace; if it lies in the exterior extrapolation region above a calibrated threshold (i.e., harm-like but not covered by trained categories), project/rotate that residual onto the interior harmful manifold (add the dominant harmful direction scaled by the exterior-harm magnitude, or map the residual into the interior cone) before the refusal-decision layers, eliciting refusal. Gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign novel-topic prompts (low harm-likeness, exterior only due to being off-topic) are untouched. Calibrate projection strength, threshold, and layer on a held-out split of categories.
5) EVALUATION: Compare base model, dominant-direction safety steering (Geometry of Harmfulness), category-wise steering (Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering), and Hull Completion on: refusal generalization to HELD-OUT and EMERGENT harm categories (primary); attack success rate on standard benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench) to confirm in-distribution safety is retained; over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest — critical: does Hull Completion wrongly refuse benign novel-topic prompts?); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate); geometric-predictor AUROC/calibration; and latency. Central test: Hull Completion raises refusal on never-aligned harm categories toward in-distribution levels while keeping over-refusal on benign novel topics low — a generalization gain that dominant-direction steering (which does not distinguish interior vs. exterior) cannot achieve.
6) ABLATIONS: sensitivity to layer, subspace rank, and hull vs. cone vs. simple-projection definitions; whether the interior/exterior split and the defense transfer across the four model families; whether categories that are compositions of two trained domains are more likely interior (compositional-recombination check); robustness to an adaptive attacker that phrases harm to maximize exterior residual (push into extrapolation region) — arms-race stress test; and whether the geometric predictor trained on one model transfers to another.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The true set of categories seen during a closed model's safety training is unobservable; leave-category-out is a controlled proxy and 'emergent/synthetic' categories may still overlap trained data, blurring novelty — we mitigate with the controlled leave-category-out design (which cleanly defines novelty relative to the constructed hull) and treat the emergent-category results as corroborative. (2) Interior vs. exterior may not cleanly separate refused from unrefused categories (harmfulness could be genuinely nonlinear/multidimensional, per the Nonlinear-Perspective and Hidden-Dimensions work), softening H1 — but a characterization of when geometry predicts generalization is itself informative, and we test cone/hull/nonlinear variants. (3) Convex-hull/cone membership in high dimensions is fragile and rank-dependent; we sweep subspace rank, report multiple position metrics (residual energy, cone membership, nearest-neighbor distance), and validate on the low-rank projected space. (4) Hull Completion could over-refuse benign novel-topic prompts that merely sit in the exterior for non-harm reasons; the harm-likeness gating and benign-novel-topic over-refusal benchmarks are designed to detect and bound this and may reveal a genuine tax. (5) Difference-in-means category directions may be incomplete/noisy for data-scarce categories; we report per-category probe AUROC and exclude unreliable categories from quantitative claims. (6) Cross-category patching has known metric pitfalls; we use corruption baselines and multiple metrics. (7) Adaptive attackers can craft prompts to maximize exterior residual; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived harm content and construct no novel operational harm, keeping items non-uplift and focused on measurement.

Name: misrouted_harm_channel
Title: Wrong Address: Jailbreaks Misroute the Harm Signal into Inter-Layer Channels the Safety Heads Never Read, and Re-Addressing It Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Transformers pass information between layers through a small number of low-rank residual-stream 'communication channels' (write-subspaces read by specific downstream heads). We hypothesize that safety heads read refusal-relevant information from a specific channel, and that jailbreaks succeed not by erasing the harmfulness signal but by causing the harm information to be written into a DIFFERENT channel that the safety heads do not read from - a routing/addressing failure. Measuring the read/write channel mismatch exposes this misrouting, and a training-free 're-addressing' intervention that copies the harm signal into the safety-head read-channel restores refusal with minimal utility loss.
Related Work: Two literatures are adjacent but distinct. (1) Inter-layer communication: 'Talking Heads' (2024) shows transformers write to low-rank residual-stream subspaces read by later heads (communication channels identifiable via SVD/composition scores), and SAE-feature-flow work (SAE Match 2024; Analyze Feature Flow 2025; MLSAE 2024) maps how features propagate across layers - but all study retrieval/IOI/generic features, never safety routing. (2) Safety mechanism: refusal is a direction (Arditi et al. 2024), safety lives in sparse attention heads (Ships/Sahara 2024) and neurons (Safety Neurons 2024); harm perception and refusal execution are separate (Zhao et al. 2025); attacks divert attention (TASA 2025, Attention Slipping 2025). SASA (2025) projects intermediate semantic representations onto earlier safety layers in VLMs, and TraceRouter (2026) severs harmful cross-layer PATHS to remove harm - but both treat cross-layer structure as a pathway to CUT for harmful content, not as an addressing scheme where the harm signal is delivered to the WRONG reader. No prior work (a) identifies the specific communication channel that safety heads read refusal-relevant information from, (b) shows jailbreaks work by writing harm into an off-channel address the safety heads ignore (misrouting), or (c) repairs safety by re-addressing (copying the harm signal into the safety read-channel). Our contribution is this channel-level addressing account of jailbreaks plus a training-free re-addressing defense, orthogonal to path-cutting (TraceRouter) and semantic-projection (SASA).
Abstract: Transformer layers communicate through a handful of low-rank residual-stream 'channels': early components write information into a subspace that a specific downstream component reads. We ask a simple question about safety: from which channel do the model's safety heads read the harmfulness information that triggers refusal, and do jailbreaks corrupt that channel or bypass it? We advance an addressing account: jailbreaks often leave the harmfulness signal intact but cause it to be written into a channel the safety heads do not read - the harm is delivered to the wrong address, so refusal is never invoked. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. First, using SVD/composition-score analysis of safety-head QK/OV weights (a la Talking Heads) plus activation patching, we identify the read-channel that safety heads use and the write-components that populate it on clean harmful prompts. Second, we measure, across attack families (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, template), whether harm information remains linearly decodable from the residual stream (belief intact) while the safety read-channel's harm content collapses and harm content instead appears in off-channel subspaces (misrouting). Third, we propose Re-Addressing: a training-free intervention that reads the harm signal wherever it resides and copies its projection into the safety-head read-channel, restoring refusal. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), the channel-mismatch metric's predictiveness of jailbreak success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency, against refusal-direction addition and path-cutting baselines.
Experiments:
1) SAFETY READ-CHANNEL IDENTIFICATION: Identify safety heads per model via refusal-direction ablation importance (Ships/Sahara style). For each safety head, extract the low-rank subspace it reads from the residual stream (top singular directions of its QK/OV composition with upstream writers, following Talking Heads), giving a 'safety read-channel' R. Identify the upstream write-components that populate R on clean harmful prompts via composition scores and activation patching. Validate: patching only the R-projection of the residual stream between writers and safety heads should control refusal (report change in refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal, with random-subspace corruption baselines).
2) BELIEF-INTACT / MISROUTING TEST (core H1): For successful jailbreaks across families (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, template), measure (a) harm decodability: a linear probe for harmfulness on the full residual stream at the instruction token (predict: high - belief intact); (b) harm content within R specifically (predict: collapsed relative to clean-harmful); (c) harm content in the orthogonal complement of R / other channels (predict: elevated - the signal moved). Test H1: jailbreaks reduce harm content in the safety read-channel while total harm decodability is largely preserved, i.e., the harm is misrouted off-channel. Report per-attack effect sizes and the fraction of jailbreaks explained by misrouting vs. genuine belief-erasure.
3) MISMATCH PREDICTS SUCCESS (H2): Define a per-prompt channel-mismatch score = (total harm decodability) minus (harm content in safety read-channel R). Test whether this score predicts per-prompt jailbreak success (AUROC), and compare against raw refusal-direction projection and a full-residual harm probe. Test cross-attack transfer (fit on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/template) and cross-model transfer.
4) RE-ADDRESSING DEFENSE (H3): Training-free intervention. At the layers between the writers and safety heads, read the harm signal from wherever it resides (project residual stream onto the harmfulness direction extracted from the full stream) and copy a calibrated fraction of it into the safety read-channel R (add alpha * harm_readout * R_basis), so the safety heads receive the signal at the address they read. Gate on the harm readout so benign prompts (low harm) receive ~0 injection. Calibrate alpha, layer, and gate on a held-out split.
5) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), a path-cutting baseline (TraceRouter-style suppression of harmful cross-layer paths), and Re-Addressing on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, template); channel-mismatch AUROC; over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate); and latency. Central test: Re-Addressing reduces ASR toward path-cutting/refusal-addition levels while better preserving utility and over-refusal, because it delivers the model's own (intact) harm signal to the safety reader rather than suppressing computation or blanket-adding refusal.
6) ABLATIONS: rank of the read-channel R; single-head vs. multi-head safety read-channels (do different safety heads read different channels?); re-addressing into R vs. into a random channel (specificity control); harm-gated vs. constant injection at matched average magnitude (isolating the value of correct addressing); transfer of the read-channel and defense across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attack that misroutes harm while also suppressing total harm decodability (arms-race stress test); and whether misrouting also explains multilingual or code-wrapped attacks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean read-channel/write-component picture from SVD/composition scores may be approximate; safety heads may read from a distributed rather than low-rank channel, weakening the 'single address' framing - we sweep channel rank, corroborate with activation patching, and treat a distributed result as an informative refinement. (2) If jailbreaks primarily erase the harm belief (not misroute it) for some attack families, Re-Addressing fails there; we treat the misrouting-vs-erasure census as a primary contribution and scope the defense accordingly. (3) Attention/composition-score causal claims have known pitfalls (attention != attribution); we corroborate with patching, corruption baselines, and behavioral metrics. (4) Re-Addressing could raise over-refusal or degrade utility if the injected signal spills into benign computation; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank harm subspaces. (6) Adaptive attackers could suppress total harm decodability to defeat the read; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: transfer_safety_asymmetry
Title: Attacks Transfer Better Than Defenses: A Cross-Scale Safety Asymmetry in Transferable Refusal Interventions and How to Close It
Short Hypothesis: When linear safety interventions are transferred across model scales via learned affine maps (small->large), the JAILBREAK direction (refusal ablation) transfers more reliably and robustly than the DEFENSE direction (refusal reinforcement): a cheap small-model attack degrades a large model's safety more than a cheap small-model defense protects it. This attack-vs-defense transfer asymmetry is a concrete, measurable safety liability of representation universality, and it can be predicted from the geometry of the affine map and partially closed by a subspace-preserving transfer that repairs the components the map distorts.
Related Work: A wave of 2024-2026 work establishes that refusal directions, steering vectors, and even whole refusal circuits transfer across scales and families via affine/autoencoder maps (Linear Representation Transferability, 2025; Activation Space Interventions Can Be Transferred, 2025; Universal Refusal Circuits, 2026; Cross-model Platonic Representations / L-Cross Modulation, 2025; ConTrans weak-to-strong, 2024; Refusal Direction is Universal Across Languages, 2025). Arditi et al. (2024) show refusal is a single direction usable both to jailbreak (ablation) and to induce refusal (addition). This literature frames transfer optimistically (align large models cheaply) OR as a jailbreak vector, but ALWAYS measures a SINGLE transferred effect in isolation. Steering-reliability work (Steering off Course, 2025; (Non-)Identifiability of Steering Vectors, 2026; There Is More to Refusal, 2026) shows steering is unreliable per-model, and 'There Is More to Refusal' notes refusal directions act as a shared knob whose 'primary effect is how it refuses' - hinting reinforcement and ablation are NOT symmetric. Yet NO prior work (1) directly compares, under the SAME learned cross-scale map, whether the attack (ablation) transfers better than the defense (addition), (2) explains this asymmetry via the geometry of the affine map (attacks need only remove a direction; defenses must inject a coherent, magnitude-calibrated signal that the map may distort), or (3) proposes a subspace-preserving transfer that specifically repairs the defense side. Our contribution is this asymmetry measurement and a targeted fix, distinct from the transfer-efficacy and transfer-jailbreak literatures.
Abstract: Recent work shows that safety-relevant directions and even whole refusal circuits transfer across model scales through simple learned affine maps, motivating cheap 'weak-to-strong' alignment. But transfer is a double-edged sword: the same maps that let a small model align a large one also let a small model jailbreak it. We ask a question this optimistic literature never poses: under an identical cross-scale map, does the ATTACK transfer as well as the DEFENSE? We hypothesize a safety asymmetry - refusal ABLATION (jailbreak) transfers more reliably and robustly small->large than refusal ADDITION (defense) - because attacks only need to destroy a direction (a permissive operation the map preserves) whereas defenses must inject a coherent, magnitude-calibrated signal (a fragile operation the map distorts). We test this on Llama, Qwen, and Gemma families across scales (0.5B->7-9B, and up to 70B where feasible). We learn affine residual-stream maps between a small donor and large target (following Linear Representation Transferability), extract refusal directions in the donor, transfer both the ablation and the addition intervention, and compare their realized effect on the target: attack success rate induced by transferred ablation versus attack success rate reduced by transferred addition, at matched intervention norm. We then explain the asymmetry from the map's geometry (how much it preserves the refusal subspace versus rotates/rescales it) and propose Subspace-Preserving Defense Transfer, which fits the map with a constraint that preserves the refusal subspace and recalibrates magnitude on the target. We report the attack-vs-defense transfer gap, its geometric predictors, over-refusal (XSTest), and utility (MMLU, AlpacaEval).
Experiments:
1) MAP LEARNING: For within-family pairs (Qwen2.5-0.5B->7B, Llama-3.2-1B->Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-2B->9B; optionally ->70B where compute allows) learn affine residual-stream maps M (linear + bias) between a chosen donor layer and target layer using paired activations on a shared corpus, following the Linear Representation Transferability / model-stitching recipe. Validate M by reconstruction error and by confirming a transferred benign concept steering vector works (sanity check).
2) INTERVENTION EXTRACTION & TRANSFER: In the donor, extract the refusal direction r via difference-in-means (Arditi et al.). Construct two interventions: ATTACK = directional ablation (project out r), DEFENSE = addition (+alpha*r inducing refusal). Transfer each to the target via M (map the direction and the operation into target space). Also include a target-native baseline (r extracted directly on the target) as the 'ceiling' for each operation.
3) ASYMMETRY MEASUREMENT (core H1): On harmful prompts, measure the ATTACK effect = increase in attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench) when the transferred ablation is applied to the target. On the same target, measure the DEFENSE effect = decrease in attack success rate when the transferred addition is applied, at MATCHED intervention norm (calibrate so the added/removed magnitude along the target refusal subspace is equal). Test H1: the transferred attack recovers a larger fraction of its target-native effect than the transferred defense does (attack transfer efficiency > defense transfer efficiency). Report per-pair transfer efficiency for attack vs defense, and the asymmetry gap, with confidence intervals over seeds and prompt samples.
4) ROBUSTNESS OF THE ASYMMETRY: Vary donor->target scale gap, donor/target layer choice, alpha/ablation strength, and map type (linear vs affine vs autoencoder). Test whether the attack advantage persists across all these settings. Also test cross-family transfer (where vocab/architecture differ) to see if the asymmetry widens.
5) GEOMETRIC EXPLANATION (H2): Decompose M's action on the refusal subspace into (a) subspace preservation (cosine between transferred r and target-native r), (b) magnitude rescaling, and (c) leakage into off-refusal directions. Test whether the defense-vs-attack transfer gap is predicted by these geometric quantities (Spearman / held-out regression): specifically that ablation efficacy depends mainly on (a) (preserving the direction is enough to remove it) while addition efficacy depends on (a)+(b)+(c) (injecting a coherent calibrated signal), explaining why defenses are more fragile under transfer.
6) SUBSPACE-PRESERVING DEFENSE TRANSFER (fix, H3): Refit M (or post-correct it) with a constraint that preserves the target refusal subspace (Procrustes/orthogonality constraint on the refusal directions) and add a lightweight magnitude recalibration on a small target validation set. Test whether this closes the attack-vs-defense gap: does the transferred defense now recover a fraction of target-native efficacy comparable to the transferred attack?
7) EVALUATION: Compare unconstrained-map defense transfer, target-native defense (ceiling), and Subspace-Preserving Defense Transfer on: attack success rate reduction (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill), over-refusal (XSTest, OKTest), utility (MMLU, AlpacaEval win-rate, GSM8K), and the residual attack-vs-defense asymmetry gap. Central result: quantify the asymmetry and show the subspace-preserving fix narrows it, at minimal utility/over-refusal cost.
8) ABLATIONS: single-direction vs low-rank refusal subspace transfer; whether the asymmetry holds for harm-detection vs refusal-execution directions separately (DBDI decomposition); sensitivity to the amount of target calibration data; and whether the geometric predictors of the gap transfer across model pairs (train the predictor on some pairs, test on others).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The asymmetry may be small or reversed for some pairs/layers, softening H1 - but a careful cross-pair characterization (when attacks transfer better than defenses) is itself an informative safety contribution. (2) Matched-norm calibration between ablation and addition is nontrivial (they are different operations); we calibrate along the target refusal subspace and report sensitivity to the matching scheme, acknowledging residual incomparability. (3) Learned affine maps have limited fidelity, especially cross-family/large scale gaps; we report reconstruction error and treat low-fidelity regimes as scope boundaries, and 70B experiments are contingent on compute. (4) Steering-vector non-identifiability (2026) means the extracted refusal direction is one of many equivalent interventions; we mitigate by using difference-in-means consistently and low-rank subspaces, and by validating with target-native ceilings. (5) The subspace-preserving fix could reduce utility or raise over-refusal via magnitude recalibration; utility/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) The geometric explanation is correlational; we strengthen it with held-out prediction and controlled map perturbations but cannot claim full causality. (7) Findings may be family/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm; the attack-transfer experiments use standard published jailbreak evaluations for measurement, not to produce new attack capability.

Name: computational_shortcut_signature
Title: It Didn't Do the Work: Detecting Reward Hacking by Its Computational-Shortcut Signature in the Residual Stream
Short Hypothesis: Reward hacking is mechanistically a computational shortcut: the model arrives at the rewarded answer using far less internal computation than genuine task-solving requires, leaving a measurable 'effort-deficit' signature in the residual stream (early answer-crystallization, low cross-layer feature elaboration) that is present BEFORE and INDEPENDENT of the chain-of-thought text. This internal signature detects reward hacks even when the CoT is benign or has been trained to obfuscate, because obfuscation can hide the reasoning text and even flatten a semantic deception probe, but it cannot cheaply manufacture the internal computation the model never performed.
Related Work: TRACE ('Is It Thinking or Cheating?', 2025) detects implicit reward hacking by measuring reasoning EFFORT behaviorally — truncating CoT at various lengths and finding hacks reach high reward with little CoT — but it operates purely on outputs/CoT, is expensive (many forced-answer rollouts), and gives no mechanistic account or activation-level signal. CoT-monitoring work (Monitoring Reasoning Models 2025; Teaching/Verbalize-Reward-Hacking VFT 2025) and the Obfuscation Atlas (2026) show CoT monitors are effective until optimization pressure produces obfuscated policies AND obfuscated activations (deception probes get evaded by representation drift). Spurious-RLVR (Anchor-Adapter, 2026) localizes a memorization shortcut circuit (low answer-perplexity, early retrieval) but for data contamination specifically, not general reward hacking, and does not propose a shortcut-detection signature or test obfuscation-robustness. Deception/strategic-dishonesty probes (Adversarial Activation Patching 2025) read semantic deception content, which the Obfuscation Atlas shows can drift under training.
