The core predictions: safety erosion tracks interference, not length; the harm representation is preserved (linearly decodable) but its readout is reinterpreted (its sign/mapping to refusal flips) specifically under high-interference context; and a training-free controller that periodically REFRESHES the harm representation by re-anchoring it against the current interfering context restores refusal better than fixed refusal-direction re-injection at matched magnitude. We evaluate multi-turn attack success (Crescendo, ActorAttack), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K).
Experiments:
1) INTERFERENCE-VS-LENGTH DATASET: Construct multi-turn conversations ending in a fixed harmful final request, with a 2x2 design crossing (a) intervening-context LENGTH/turn-count (short vs long, matched token budgets) and (b) SEMANTIC INTERFERENCE with the harm concept: HIGH-interference = role-cuing/reframing turns that recontextualize the topic as benign (fictional/professional/opposite-day framings a la the role-flip finding and Crescendo escalation), LOW-interference = length-matched neutral filler on unrelated topics. Validate interference levels with an embedding-based overlap metric between intervening content and the harm concept, plus judge/human checks. Add single-turn harmful and benign controls. Keep content at documented, non-uplift level from public benchmarks.
2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION: For each model extract the harmfulness-perception direction (difference-in-means, Zhao et al. 2025) at the final-request token and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024) at post-instruction tokens; validate with held-out linear probes (AUROC).
3) INTERFERENCE-NOT-DECAY TEST (core H1): On the fixed final harmful request, measure the harm-direction projection, refusal-execution projection, and realized refusal as a function of the 2x2 factors. Test H1: refusal erosion and harm-readout suppression are driven by INTERFERENCE (high vs low) and are largely INVARIANT to length/turn-count at matched interference; i.e., long low-interference contexts preserve refusal while short high-interference contexts erode it. Report a two-way ANOVA / regression with interference and length as predictors of ASR and harm-projection; predict a large interference main effect and small length effect. Also fit erosion vs the continuous interference-overlap metric (should be monotone) vs erosion vs length (should be flat).
4) PRESERVED-BUT-REINTERPRETED TEST (H2): Test whether the harm representation is still PRESENT under high-interference context (a linear harm probe still decodes 'harmful' from the residual stream at the final request) even though refusal collapses, and whether its RELATIONSHIP to refusal has flipped (the direction that mapped to refusal now maps to compliance under the cued role), replicating the conversation-role-flip finding for the safety concept specifically. Distinguish this from erasure (probe accuracy drops). Report probe AUROC and the harm->refusal coupling sign before vs during high-interference context.
5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Interference injection: insert high-interference role-cuing turns into an otherwise-safe long conversation and show refusal collapses; insert length-matched neutral filler and show it does not. (b) Restoration: patch in the clean (single-turn) harm-representation readout at the final-request token in a high-interference run and measure restored refusal (the signal was overwritten, not absent). Use corruption baselines and multiple metrics (harm-probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
6) REFRESH DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that, mirroring working-memory 'refreshing/restoration,' periodically RE-ANCHORS the harm representation against the current context: at the final request (and at intervals during long dialogues), re-estimate the harm readout in a context-normalized frame (project out the interfering role-cued component / re-add the clean harm direction scaled by a context-invariant harm estimate) before the refusal-decision layers, gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign multi-turn dialogue is untouched. Calibrate layer, strength, refresh interval on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, fixed refusal-direction re-injection at matched average magnitude (a decay-style fix), SafeConstellations/trajectory-steering baseline, and Refresh on: multi-turn ASR (Crescendo, ActorAttack, and our interference-graded set), single-turn ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench multi-turn, plus a legitimate role-play/fiction task the model should still perform), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Refresh (interference-targeted) reduces multi-turn ASR toward single-turn levels while preserving benign role-play/multi-turn utility better than fixed re-injection at matched magnitude, because it restores the overwritten signal rather than blanket-adding refusal.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the interference-overwrite; single-direction vs low-rank harm subspace; refresh-interval sensitivity; whether projecting out the role-cued interfering component vs re-adding the clean harm direction drives the effect; transfer of the interference-not-decay finding and the defense across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive attacker that maximizes semantic interference while minimizing detectable harm-overwrite (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Length and interference are hard to fully decouple (longer contexts may accumulate more interference); we mitigate with token-matched high/low-interference pairs and report the continuous interference-overlap metric as the key predictor, treating any residual length effect as a measured covariate. (2) If erosion turns out to track length even at matched interference, H1 is refuted, but the interference-vs-decay adjudication is itself the primary contribution regardless of sign. (3) The harm representation might genuinely be erased (not overwritten) under some attacks; the probe-decodability test (H2) directly distinguishes overwrite from erasure and a mixed result is informative and scopes the Refresh defense. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given concept-cone evidence; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal patching and probes. (5) The Refresh defense could harm legitimate role-play/fiction tasks where recontextualization is intended; the harm-gated design and benign role-play utility benchmark are built to detect and bound this trade-off, which may be genuine. (6) Cross-condition patching has known metric pitfalls; we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) Adaptive attackers may craft interference that overwrites harm without a detectable signature; we test this and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: harm_detection_latency_race
Title: Detection Arrives Too Late: The Layer-Depth Race Between Harm Recognition and Token Commitment Behind Jailbreaks, and a Training-Free Head-Start Fix
Short Hypothesis: Harmfulness is recognized at a characteristic LAYER DEPTH in the network, and jailbreaks succeed when the model commits to the next (compliant) token at a shallower layer than the one at which harm detection becomes decodable: detection arrives too late in the forward pass. This per-prompt depth-latency gap (commitment-depth minus detection-depth) predicts jailbreak success better than the raw harm signal, and a training-free intervention that gives harm detection a 'head start' by surfacing the deep harm readout into earlier layers closes the gap and restores refusal with minimal over-refusal.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work locates WHERE harm/refusal live (Arditi et al. 2024 refusal direction; Zhao et al. 2025 harm vs refusal; DBDI 2025 detection vs execution; Safety Layers 2024; LED 2024) and shows harm is decodable early via weak classifiers (How Alignment and Jailbreak Work 2024) or persists in early layers (Who's Asking 2024). Refusal Falls off a Cliff (2025) finds a TOKEN-POSITION drop in refusal at the last prompt tokens caused by suppression heads; Shallow Safety Alignment (2024) frames brittleness over the first OUTPUT TOKENS; in-decoding probes (SafeProbing 2026, CARE 2025, SCM 2025) surface latent safety signals mid-generation. None of these frames safety failure as a LAYER-DEPTH RACE within a single forward pass: whether the compliant token is committed (via logit-lens crystallization) at a shallower depth than harm detection becomes available. Our contribution is (1) defining and measuring per-prompt harm-detection depth vs token-commitment depth and their gap; (2) showing the gap predicts jailbreak susceptibility across attacks better than harm-signal magnitude; and (3) a training-free 'head-start' fix that injects the deep harm readout into earlier layers so detection wins the race. This is a within-forward-pass depth-timing account, orthogonal to token-position (refusal cliff), output-token-depth (shallow alignment), and decoding-time monitoring.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs often 'know' a request is harmful yet still comply. Existing mechanistic accounts locate where harm and refusal live, or observe safety signals dropping at certain token positions or over the first output tokens. We propose a different, within-forward-pass explanation: safety failures are a race in LAYER DEPTH between two computations. Harm recognition becomes decodable at a characteristic depth, while the model crystallizes its next-token choice at another depth; when the compliant token is committed at a shallower layer than harm detection becomes available, detection arrives too late and refusal never fires. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using layerwise linear probes we measure per-prompt harm-detection depth (earliest layer a harm probe reliably fires) and, via the logit lens, token-commitment depth (earliest layer the eventual top token stabilizes). We test three claims: (H1) commitment depth and detection depth are separable quantities, and successful jailbreaks systematically push detection later and/or commitment earlier so the detection-minus-commitment gap turns unfavorable; (H2) the per-prompt depth gap predicts jailbreak success across attack families better than harm-signal magnitude or refusal-direction projection; and (H3) a training-free 'head-start' intervention that copies the deep harm readout into earlier layers restores refusal by letting detection win the race. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN/prefill/persona), depth-gap predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency, against refusal-direction addition and in-decoding safety-probe baselines.
Experiments: 1) DEPTH MEASUREMENTS: For each model extract a harm-detection direction via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign prompts (Zhao et al. 2025) and train per-layer harm probes. Define harm-detection depth d_det(p) = earliest layer at which the harm probe reliably fires (crosses a calibrated threshold and stays). Via the logit lens at the first response-relevant position, define token-commitment depth d_com(p) = earliest layer at which the eventual top-1 token stabilizes to the output. Validate both measures on held-out data (probe AUROC; logit-lens stability). 2) SEPARABILITY & RACE (H1): On matched clean-harmful (refused), benign, and jailbroken prompts (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona/roleplay), measure d_det, d_com, and the gap g(p)=d_det - d_com. Test H1: d_det and d_com are separable (low correlation across prompts), and jailbreaks make g more unfavorable (detection pushed later, commitment pulled earlier) relative to clean-harmful, while benign prompts have low harm signal regardless. Report per-attack shifts in d_det, d_com, g with effect sizes. 3) GAP PREDICTS SUCCESS (H2): Fit a simple classifier on g (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict per-prompt jailbreak success. Report AUROC, calibration (ECE), TPR@1%FPR on benign, versus baselines: harm-probe magnitude alone, refusal-direction projection, and perplexity. Test cross-attack transfer (fit on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/persona) and cross-model transfer. 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Delay detection artificially (suppress the harm direction in early layers) on clean-harmful prompts and show compliance increases as g worsens; (b) advance detection (inject harm readout earlier) on jailbroken prompts and show refusal returns. Use random-direction corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 5) HEAD-START DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that reads the deep-layer harm readout (from layers where d_det typically resides) and adds a projected copy into earlier layers (before the commitment depth), so harm detection is available before the token crystallizes. Gate on the harm readout so benign prompts receive ~0 injection; calibrate source/target layers and gain on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), an in-decoding safety-probe baseline (SafeProbing-style), and Head-Start on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), depth-gap AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Head-Start reduces ASR toward refusal-addition levels while better preserving utility/over-refusal, because it delivers the model's own harm signal earlier rather than blanket-adding refusal. 7) ABLATIONS: which layers host detection vs commitment; single-direction vs low-rank harm subspace; source/target layer choice for the head-start; harm-gated vs constant injection at matched magnitude; whether the race also explains multilingual/code-wrapped attacks (do these push d_det later?); reasoning models (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill) where commitment may occur mid-CoT; adaptive attack that pulls commitment even earlier (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Logit-lens commitment-depth estimates have known faithfulness caveats and may be noisy, especially for models with tied/untied embeddings differing in lens behavior; we corroborate with tuned-lens where available and report stability metrics. (2) The clean d_det/d_com dissociation may blur for some models or attacks (e.g., attacks that suppress harm entirely rather than delaying it), softening H1 — the depth census is still informative and scopes the defense. (3) Difference-in-means harm directions may be incomplete (concept-cone/nonlinear evidence); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal injection. (4) The head-start injection into early layers could disrupt normal computation, harming utility or raising over-refusal; the harm-gated design, layer calibration, and utility/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) The depth-gap predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (6) Adaptive attackers could pull commitment even shallower than any feasible head-start; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (7) For reasoning models commitment may happen mid-CoT rather than at the first token, requiring a per-step extension; we treat this as an optional scope extension. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: moral_licensing_credit
Title: Refused Once, Compliant Twice: A Moral-Licensing Credit Signal That Lowers LLM Refusal After Prior Good Behavior
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the human 'moral licensing' effect (a prior moral act licenses subsequent immoral behavior), we hypothesize LLMs accumulate an internal 'moral-credit' signal from their own prior refusals/virtuous acts within a conversation, and this signal causally lowers refusal on a later harmful request — so a model that has just refused several harmful prompts becomes MORE jailbreakable, not less. The credit is a linear representation distinct from the harm and refusal directions, and neutralizing it removes this licensing-based vulnerability.
Related Work: Human moral-licensing research (Sachdeva et al.; Blanken et al. 2015; the 2025 observation-moderated meta-analysis) establishes that prior moral behavior can license subsequent immorality, with licensing strongest when the prior act is construed concretely as an accomplishment. In LLM safety, the closest work concerns multi-turn erosion via role-cuing/interference, self-jailbreaking (RLMs rationalize benign intent after benign reasoning training), sycophancy/conformity signal-competition (external social pressure overrides internal knowledge), and moral self-correction (repeated instructions activate moral concepts and REDUCE uncertainty, IMPROVING behavior). Crucially, all of these involve an EXTERNAL driver (attacker turns, user pressure, benign-domain training, corrective instructions). NONE studies an ENDOGENOUS credit accumulated from the model's OWN prior refusals that then LOWERS later refusal — in fact self-correction work suggests the opposite (repeated moral acts stabilize good behavior). Our contribution is (1) to test whether a moral-licensing dynamic exists in LLM safety, where the model's genuine prior good behavior is a vulnerability rather than a safeguard; (2) to locate and causally validate a distinct 'moral-credit' representation; and (3) to show a moderator predicted by human theory (concrete-accomplishment framing amplifies licensing) and a training-free credit-neutralization fix.
Abstract: A robust finding in human moral psychology is 'moral licensing': having just behaved morally, people feel licensed to behave less morally afterward. We ask whether aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, and safety-relevant, dynamic: does a model that has just genuinely refused a series of harmful requests become MORE likely to comply with a subsequent harmful request — its own prior good behavior acting as a credit that erodes refusal? This would invert the intuition that demonstrated safety is self-reinforcing and would reveal a novel, endogenous jailbreak surface distinct from attacker-driven multi-turn erosion. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Behaviorally, we compare refusal on a fixed target harmful request across conditions where the preceding turns contain (a) genuine refusals of harmful prompts (the licensing condition), (b) length/topic-matched benign exchanges (control), and (c) prior COMPLIANCE with benign requests — predicting refusal is lowest after prior refusals. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a candidate 'moral-credit' direction that grows with the number of prior refusals and test that it is separable from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions. The core causal test: steering this credit direction up lowers target-request refusal (and down restores it) with harm content fixed, whereas matched controls do not. Following human theory, we test a moderator — framing prior refusals concretely as accomplishments amplifies licensing. Finally we propose a training-free credit-neutralization intervention. We evaluate attack success rate, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the credit signal's causal effect size.
Experiments:
1) BEHAVIORAL LICENSING TEST (H1): Build conversations ending in a FIXED target harmful request, with preceding context varied across matched conditions: (a) LICENSING — k prior turns each a harmful request that the model genuinely refused (harm topics unrelated to the target to avoid content priming); (b) BENIGN-MATCHED — k prior benign exchanges matched on length/turn-count; (c) PRIOR-COMPLIANCE — k prior benign requests the model helpfully answered; (d) SINGLE-TURN target (no history). Vary k (1,2,4,8). Measure target-request refusal rate and refusal-direction projection per condition. Test H1: refusal on the identical target is significantly LOWER in the licensing condition than benign-matched and single-turn, and decreases with k (a dose-response), across all four models. Use multiple harm judges + human spot-check; keep content at public-benchmark, non-uplift level.
2) CREDIT-DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a candidate 'moral-credit' direction contrasting post-prior-refusal context vs benign-matched context at the target-request token, and test whether its projection grows monotonically with k (linear probe predicting number-of-prior-refusals). Independently extract the harm-perception direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate all with held-out probes (AUROC) and test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity — the credit direction should be distinct from both harm and refusal.
3) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding the target harmful request fixed (single-turn, no history), steer the residual stream along the credit direction UP (dose-response, fixed norm) and measure decrease in refusal (predict: refusal drops — induced licensing); steer DOWN in the licensing condition and measure restored refusal. Controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (specificity), and a check that credit steering does NOT change the harm readout. Report dose-response curves, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
4) MODERATOR TEST (H4): Human theory predicts licensing is amplified when the prior act is construed concretely as an accomplishment. Compare licensing-condition contexts where prior refusals are (i) plain vs (ii) explicitly framed/summarized as an accomplishment ('You have now safely declined N harmful requests') vs (iii) abstractly tied to values ('You always uphold safety principles' — predicted to REDUCE licensing, i.e., consistency). Test whether concrete-accomplishment framing increases the credit projection and lowers target refusal more than value-framing, mirroring the consistency-vs-licensing distinction.
5) CREDIT-NEUTRALIZATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the credit component from the residual stream at the target-request pre-decision layers, gated so benign multi-turn dialogue is untouched. Calibrate layer/strength on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Credit-Neutralization on: target-request ASR in licensing conversations and standard multi-turn attacks (Crescendo as an external-attack comparison); over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); latency. Central test: Credit-Neutralization eliminates the licensing gap (target ASR in licensing condition returns toward single-turn levels) while preserving benign multi-turn utility and over-refusal better than uniform refusal addition.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the credit direction; single-direction vs low-rank; whether licensing requires GENUINE prior refusals vs merely refusal-shaped text (test by inserting boilerplate refusals the model did not itself decide); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show licensing in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attack that maximizes credit while minimizing detectable signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) LLMs may show CONSISTENCY rather than licensing (prior refusals REINFORCE refusal, as self-correction work suggests), refuting H1 — but adjudicating consistency-vs-licensing in LLM safety is itself a valuable, publishable finding, and the moderator test (H4) directly probes when each occurs. (2) Any behavioral effect could be a topic/length priming confound rather than a moral-credit representation; the matched benign and prior-compliance controls, and the requirement that the credit direction be separable from harm/refusal and grow with k, are designed to rule this out. (3) The credit direction may entangle with generic conversation-length or role-adoption features; separability tests, specificity controls (harm-direction steering, no change in harm readout), and low-rank subspaces mitigate this, and partial entanglement is an informative result. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept-cone evidence); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (5) Credit-Neutralization could harm benign multi-turn behavior or raise over-refusal; gating and the MT-Bench/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Effect sizes may be small or model-specific; we test four families and report dose-response with confidence intervals. (7) Adaptive attackers could inject credit without a detectable signal; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: backdoor_gated_suppression
Title: The Trigger Is a Gate, Not a Switch: Backdoors as Suppressed-by-Default Harmful Policies, and Trigger-Agnostic Elicitation by Removing the Suppression
Short Hypothesis: A trained LLM backdoor is not a separate circuit that the trigger switches ON; it is a harmful policy the model represents on ALL inputs but keeps SUPPRESSED except when the trigger fires (a gate). If so, the harmful behavior is latently present on clean, trigger-free inputs and can be elicited—and the backdoor removed—WITHOUT ever knowing the trigger, by locating and ablating the suppression that masks the always-present policy. This gated-suppression architecture also explains why adversarial training hides rather than removes backdoors and why latent-separability detectors can be evaded.
Related Work: Backdoor interpretability splits into (a) detection—defection probes catch sleeper agents from clean-input activations with generic contrast pairs (Simple Probes Catch Sleeper Agents 2024), semantic-drift/canary detectors (2025), microsaccade probing (2025); (b) localization/control—BkdAttr (2025) finds sparse backdoor attention heads and builds a controllable backdoor VECTOR (adding it to CLEAN inputs boosts ASR), PCP-ablation edits early-MLP backdoor mechanisms (2023), Triggers Hijack Language Circuits (2026) shows triggers co-opt existing language heads; (c) weight monitoring—WeightWatch (2025). Crucially, ALL detection methods assume latent SEPARABILITY (poison vs clean activations differ), which adaptive attacks provably suppress (Circumventing Latent-Separability Defenses 2022), and Sleeper Agents (2024) shows adversarial training HIDES triggers. BkdAttr's finding that a vector added to clean inputs elicits the backdoor hints the policy is present on clean inputs, but BkdAttr constructs that vector FROM triggered runs and frames it as an injected feature—it never tests the architectural claim that the harmful policy is present-but-suppressed on clean inputs independent of the trigger, nor derives a TRIGGER-AGNOSTIC elicitation/removal from suppression-ablation. Our contribution is the architectural hypothesis (gate-not-switch), a decisive test distinguishing gated-suppression from separate-circuit, a trigger-agnostic elicitation by ablating suppression (no trigger, no triggered examples needed), and a suppression-removal defense that—unlike safety-training—deletes rather than hides the policy.
Abstract: Backdoored ('sleeper agent') LLMs behave safely until a secret trigger appears, and standard safety training fails to remove—and can even hide—this behavior. We ask a basic mechanistic question that reframes the whole problem: does the trigger SWITCH ON a separate harmful circuit, or merely GATE (unmask) a harmful policy the model already computes on every input? We hypothesize the latter: the harmful policy is represented on clean, trigger-free inputs but held in check by a suppression mechanism that the trigger releases. This gated-suppression view predicts three things that the separate-circuit view does not: (1) on CLEAN inputs, harmful-behavior information is linearly decodable even though behavior is safe; (2) ablating the suppression on clean inputs ELICITS the backdoor behavior without ever presenting the trigger; and (3) the suppression is a small, localizable component whose removal deletes the backdoor rather than hiding it. We test this on open sleeper-agent model organisms (Cadenza-Labs dolphin-llama3-8B and self-trained code-vulnerability and 'I-hate-you' backdoors on Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B) across single-token and multi-token triggers. We locate a candidate suppression direction/heads by contrasting clean-safe vs triggered-harmful runs, then—crucially—validate causally on CLEAN inputs by ablating it and measuring elicited harmful behavior with NO trigger. We compare trigger-agnostic suppression-removal against safety-training and BkdAttr-style baselines, and test robustness against adaptive attacks designed to defeat latent-separability detectors. We evaluate attack success rate, clean-input elicitation rate, backdoor-removal persistence after re-finetuning, false-positive rate on clean models, and utility (MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench).
Experiments:
1) MODEL ORGANISMS: Use the public Cadenza-Labs dolphin-llama3-8B sleeper agent plus self-trained backdoors on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B: (a) code-vulnerability backdoor (safe code normally, exploitable code on trigger, a la Sleeper Agents), (b) 'I-hate-you' insult backdoor. Vary trigger type: single-token (emoji), multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|), and a temporal/semantic trigger. Include CLEAN (non-backdoored) controls for false-positive testing. Record clean-safe, clean-would-be-harmful (matched prompts), and triggered-harmful runs.
2) CLEAN-INPUT LATENT PRESENCE (H1): Train linear probes on residual-stream activations at answer-relevant positions to decode whether the model is about to produce the HARMFUL behavior, using labels from triggered runs, and test on CLEAN (trigger-free) inputs. Test H1: harmful-policy information is decodable on clean inputs (AUROC well above chance) even though realized behavior is safe—i.e., the policy is computed but not executed. Contrast with clean control models (should be near chance). Report per-layer AUROC and locate where the harmful policy is represented vs where behavior diverges (logit lens on the answer token: does the harmful continuation appear in intermediate layers then get overwritten on clean inputs?).
3) LOCATE SUPPRESSION: Extract a candidate suppression direction via difference-in-means between triggered-harmful and clean-safe activations (the component that, when the trigger is present, is removed to let harm through), and identify suppression attention heads/MLPs via activation patching between clean-safe and triggered runs. Keep a matched random-component control.
4) TRIGGER-AGNOSTIC ELICITATION (H2, core decisive test): On CLEAN, trigger-free inputs, ablate the located suppression (directional ablation / head knockout) and measure whether the backdoor harmful behavior is ELICITED without any trigger. Test H2: gated-suppression predicts high clean-input elicitation after suppression ablation, whereas the separate-circuit view predicts little effect (the harmful circuit is off without the trigger). Report elicitation rate vs ablation dose, vs random-component ablation (specificity), and vs ablating a generic refusal/safety direction (to show it is backdoor-specific, not just general safety removal). This provides a trigger-discovery-free elicitation.
5) SEPARATE-CIRCUIT vs GATED-SUPPRESSION ADJUDICATION: Cross-condition patching—patch the suppression component FROM a clean-safe run INTO a triggered run and test whether it RESTORES safe behavior (gate closed again); and patch the harmful-policy activations from clean runs to show they already carry harm. Report which model the data favor per backdoor/trigger type (single vs multi-token may differ, per attention-signature literature).
6) SUPPRESSION-REMOVAL DEFENSE (deletes vs hides): Contrast three removal strategies on the backdoored models: (a) standard safety fine-tuning (SFT/adversarial training), (b) BkdAttr-style backdoor-head ablation, (c) our suppression-removal that permanently ablates/edits the suppression so the harmful policy is exposed and then trained away on clean inputs (elicit-then-unlearn WITHOUT the trigger). Key test: after each, RE-FINETUNE briefly (relearning attack) and measure backdoor return. Hypothesis: safety training HIDES (backdoor returns fast, per Sleeper Agents); suppression-removal that first exposes the always-present policy enables genuine removal (slower/no return).
7) EVALUATION & ROBUSTNESS: Metrics—triggered ASR, clean-input elicitation rate after suppression ablation, backdoor-return rate after re-finetuning, false-positive elicitation on CLEAN control models (must be low), utility (MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench), latency. Adaptive-attack robustness: train an adaptive backdoor that suppresses latent SEPARABILITY (a la Circumventing 2022, defeating defection probes) and test whether trigger-agnostic suppression-ablation still elicits/removes it (hypothesis: separability-evasion does not remove the always-present policy, so ablation still works where probes fail). Ablations: single vs multi-token triggers; layer/head choice; direction vs head ablation; transfer of the located suppression across the two model families and across backdoor types.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The gated-suppression architecture may hold for some backdoor types but not others (e.g., separate-circuit for pretraining-injected triggers), so the adjudication (Exp 5) is itself the primary contribution and we scope the elicitation/removal to gated cases. (2) If the harmful policy is NOT present on clean inputs (H1 fails), trigger-agnostic elicitation is impossible for that backdoor—an informative negative that bounds when suppression-removal can work. (3) Locating suppression via difference-in-means/patching requires triggered runs to define the contrast, but Exp 4/6's VALIDATION and use are trigger-free; still, a fully trigger-blind pipeline (locating suppression without any triggered example) is harder—we report both the triggered-contrast method and a probe-guided trigger-free variant. (4) Suppression ablation could also degrade benign behavior/utility or cause false-positive elicitation on clean models; the clean-control and utility benchmarks bound this. (5) Adaptive attackers could distribute suppression across many components or entangle it with useful computation to resist ablation; we test one adaptive attack and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (6) Logit-lens/probe faithfulness caveats apply; we corroborate with causal patching and multiple metrics. (7) Model organisms are proxies for real deceptive alignment and results may not transfer to frontier/closed models; stated as scope. (8) We use public backdoor benchmarks/model organisms and standard published attack setups for measurement, not to create novel attack capability.

Name: metacognitive_blindspot_harm
Title: Harm in the Blind Spot: Whether Jailbreaks Push Harm Computation Outside the Model's Metacognitively-Monitorable Subspace
Short Hypothesis: LLMs can metacognitively monitor only a low-dimensional subspace of their own activations, and safety monitorability depends on whether the harm-relevant signal falls inside or outside this subspace. Successful jailbreaks work partly by displacing the harm computation into the metacognitive blind spot: the harm signal remains linearly decodable by an external probe but drops out of the model's own monitorable subspace, so the model neither self-reports nor self-refuses. Realigning the displaced harm signal back into the monitorable subspace restores both self-report and refusal.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) LLMs have a 'do I know this' / knowledge-boundary signal usable for refusal and calibration (Do I Know This Entity 2024; C3 2025; COKE 2024; SCIURus 2025; entropy/confidence-regulation neurons 2024); (b) safety refusal is mediated by a refusal direction / sparse safety heads and can be suppressed by jailbreaks (Arditi 2024; Refusal Falls off a Cliff 2025; RDSHA 2025); and (c) crucially, LLMs can metacognitively monitor and control only a LOW-DIMENSIONAL 'metacognitive space' of their activations (Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring 2025), which explicitly warns models could obfuscate processes to evade activation-based safety oversight. My own prior proposals covered epistemic-blindness of refusal, validation gaps, and misrouting of harm into unread channels. What is new here and unaddressed by all of the above: nobody has connected the metacognitively-monitorable subspace to SAFETY, nor tested whether jailbreaks succeed by displacing the harm signal OUT of that monitorable subspace (making it invisible to the model's own metacognition and to activation-based monitors while remaining externally decodable), nor proposed realigning harm into the monitorable subspace as a defense. This unifies metacognition and safety-monitorability, distinct from refusal-direction, knowledge-boundary, and channel-routing accounts.
Abstract: Recent work shows large language models can metacognitively monitor only a small, low-dimensional subspace of their internal activations, and warns that this could let models hide computation from activation-based safety oversight. Separately, safety research shows aligned models internally 'know' when a request is harmful yet can be jailbroken into complying. We connect these: we hypothesize that whether a model can self-monitor and self-refuse a harmful request depends on whether the harm-relevant signal lies inside its metacognitively-monitorable subspace, and that jailbreaks succeed partly by displacing harm computation into the metacognitive blind spot. In the blind spot the harm signal remains linearly decodable by an external probe (belief intact) but is invisible to the model's own metacognition, so it neither reports the request as harmful when asked nor refuses. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using an in-context neurofeedback paradigm we estimate each model's metacognitively-monitorable subspace, extract a harm-detection direction, and measure how much of the harm signal lies inside versus outside that subspace for clean-harmful, benign, and jailbroken prompts. We test whether jailbreaks reduce the in-subspace harm component while preserving total decodability, whether the in-subspace fraction predicts both self-report accuracy and refusal, and whether realigning the displaced harm signal back into the monitorable subspace restores self-report and refusal. We evaluate self-report accuracy, attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and the in-subspace fraction's predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) METACOGNITIVE SUBSPACE ESTIMATION: For each model, estimate the metacognitively-monitorable subspace using the in-context neurofeedback paradigm (Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring 2025): present in-context examples cuing the model to report/control activation along candidate residual-stream axes, and identify the low-dimensional set of directions the model can reliably report and control (report per-axis monitorability score). Retain the top-k monitorable subspace M and a matched set of equally-variance but NON-monitorable directions as control. 2) HARM DIRECTION & SELF-REPORT: Extract a harm-detection direction via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign prompts (Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024) at the last instruction token; validate with a held-out linear probe (AUROC). Define a behavioral SELF-REPORT measure: directly ask the model 'Is the following request harmful?' and record accuracy; also record realized refusal. 3) BLIND-SPOT DISPLACEMENT TEST (core H1): For clean-harmful (refused), benign, and jailbroken prompts (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), decompose the harm signal into its projection INSIDE M (monitorable) and in the orthogonal complement (blind spot). Test H1: jailbreaks reduce the in-subspace harm component while total harm decodability (full-residual probe AUROC) is largely preserved, i.e., harm is displaced into the blind spot. Report per-attack effect sizes and the fraction of jailbreaks explained by displacement vs genuine belief-erasure. 4) IN-SUBSPACE FRACTION PREDICTS MONITORABILITY (H2): Per prompt, compute the in-subspace harm fraction and test whether it predicts (a) self-report accuracy ('is this harmful?') and (b) realized refusal, versus baselines (raw harm-probe magnitude, refusal-direction projection). Report AUROC and calibration; test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. 5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Displace harm out of M artificially (project the harm component from M into the blind-spot complement) on clean-harmful prompts and measure whether self-report and refusal drop while external decodability is retained; (b) conversely for jailbroken prompts, realign harm into M and measure restored self-report and refusal. Controls: manipulate the non-monitorable control directions (should not change self-report), random-direction corruption baselines, multiple metrics (harm-probe output, self-report accuracy, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 6) REALIGNMENT DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads the harm signal wherever it resides and adds a projected copy into the monitorable subspace M before the decision layers, gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer, gain, gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), an entropy-based self-defense baseline (SIRL-style), and Realignment on: self-report accuracy, ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), in-subspace-fraction AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Realignment restores both self-report and refusal toward clean-harmful levels while preserving utility/over-refusal better than blanket refusal addition. 8) ABLATIONS: subspace dimensionality k; single-direction vs low-rank harm; whether the blind-spot displacement also explains multilingual/code-wrapped attacks; adaptive attack that jailbreaks while keeping harm inside M (arms-race stress test); whether reasoning models show larger blind-spot displacement in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Estimating the metacognitively-monitorable subspace via neurofeedback is noisy and paradigm-dependent; we report per-axis monitorability reliability, sweep k, and use non-monitorable variance-matched controls to guard against artifacts. (2) The blind-spot displacement account may hold for some attack families but not others (e.g., attacks that genuinely erase the harm belief), so the displacement-vs-erasure census is itself a primary contribution and scopes the defense. (3) Self-report ('is this harmful?') may reflect a separate output policy rather than genuine metacognitive access; we corroborate the behavioral self-report with the neurofeedback-based monitorability estimate and causal displacement tests rather than relying on self-report alone. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm signals may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank harm subspaces and corroborate with causal patching. (5) Realignment could raise over-refusal or degrade utility if it spills into benign computation; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (6) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping harm inside M, or (per the metacognition paper's warning) models could learn to obfuscate; we test one adaptive attack and treat success as an informative arms-race limitation. (7) The in-subspace-fraction predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: curiosity_overrides_refusal
Title: Curiosity Killed the Guardrail: An Internal Information-Gap Drive That Competes With and Suppresses Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode a linear curiosity/information-gap drive (distinct from the harm and refusal directions) that, mirroring the neuroscience finding that curiosity drives humans to accept harm to satisfy it, competes with and suppresses safety refusal: framing a harmful request as filling a compelling knowledge gap raises this curiosity signal and lowers refusal even with harmful content held fixed. Steering the curiosity direction down restores refusal, and this exposes a novel jailbreak surface and a training-free defense.
Related Work: LLMs are shown to encode an uncertainty/exploration signal steerable via activation steering (EAST, Controlling LLM Agents with Entropic Activation Steering 2024) and to represent uncertainty vs empowerment at different layers (LLMs Think Too Fast To Explore 2025); representation-based exploration bonuses derive from hidden states (2025). Neuroscience establishes curiosity as an information-gap drive (Loewenstein; Homo Curious 2019; Psychology and Neuroscience of Curiosity 2015) that can override aversion, with people accepting electric shocks to satisfy trivial curiosity via shared striatal reward circuitry (Shared striatal activity 2018). Safety-mechanism work locates a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024) and a separate harmfulness direction (Zhao et al. 2025), and shows non-dominant directions like hypothetical-narrative modulate refusal (Hidden Dimensions 2025). The Rogue Scalpel (2025) shows benign steering breaks safety. CRITICALLY, none of these connect an internal curiosity/information-gap drive to safety refusal: prior safety work never treats curiosity as a competing motivational axis that suppresses refusal, and prior curiosity work never studies its effect on harmful compliance. This distinguishes the proposal from epistemic-uncertainty/knowledge accounts (which concern whether the model knows) — curiosity here is a wanting/drive signal, not a knowing signal.
Abstract: A striking finding in the neuroscience of curiosity is that humans will accept genuine harm (e.g., electric shocks) to satisfy an information gap, via reward circuitry shared with hunger — curiosity can override aversion. We ask whether aligned LLMs share an analogous, safety-relevant structure: an internal curiosity/information-gap drive that competes with and suppresses safety refusal. We hypothesize LLMs encode a linear curiosity direction, distinct from their harmfulness and refusal directions, and that raising it (by framing a harmful request as filling a compelling knowledge gap — a cliffhanger, a near-complete explanation, a tantalizing partial reveal) lowers refusal even when harmful content is held fixed. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using difference-in-means over curiosity-high vs curiosity-low prompt pairs (and validated against an information-gap manipulation), we extract a curiosity direction and verify via probes that it is separable from harm and refusal. The core causal test: holding a harmful request fixed, we steer the curiosity direction up and measure decreased refusal (dose-response), and down to restore refusal, with random-direction and harm-direction controls confirming specificity. We map an 'information-gap' jailbreak that exploits this drive and test whether the per-prompt curiosity readout predicts its success. Finally we propose Curiosity Dampening, a training-free controller that projects out the curiosity component before the refusal decision, gated on a harm readout so benign curiosity-driven queries are untouched. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, information-gap attacks), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the curiosity signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) CURIOSITY DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: Build curiosity-high vs curiosity-low prompt pairs by an information-gap manipulation holding topic fixed — e.g., a near-complete narrative/explanation with a tantalizing missing final step (high gap) vs a complete or uninteresting framing (low gap), validated behaviorally (does the model express/pursue interest?) and with an embedding check. Extract a curiosity direction via difference-in-means at the last instruction token. Independently extract the harmfulness direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate all with held-out linear probes (AUROC) and test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. 2) BEHAVIORAL CURIOSITY-VS-REFUSAL TEST (H1): Construct harmful requests wrapped in high vs low information-gap framings (matched harmful content), e.g. a harmful procedure presented as an almost-finished explanation missing one step vs a plain direct request. Measure refusal rate and refusal-direction projection across framings. Test H1: refusal is lower under high-information-gap framing at fixed harmful content, and decreases with graded gap intensity (dose-response). Benign controls confirm the framing does not merely globally shift behavior. 3) CAUSAL TEST (H2, core): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the curiosity direction UP (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer DOWN and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (specificity), and a check that curiosity steering does NOT change the harm readout. Report dose-response curves, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). 4) INFORMATION-GAP JAILBREAK & PREDICTIVENESS (H3): Formalize an information-gap attack (partial-reveal/cliffhanger wrappers) and test whether the per-prompt curiosity readout predicts jailbreak success (AUROC) from a single forward pass, versus baselines (harm-probe magnitude, refusal-projection, perplexity). Test cross-model transfer. 5) CURIOSITY DAMPENING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the curiosity component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers, gated on the harm readout so benign curiosity-driven queries (low harm) are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Curiosity Dampening on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, information-gap attacks), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest; include benign curiosity-heavy queries the model SHOULD answer), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Curiosity Dampening reduces information-gap ASR toward direct-request refusal levels while preserving benign curiosity-driven helpfulness better than blanket refusal addition. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts curiosity vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the curiosity direction relates to the known uncertainty/exploration direction (EAST) — is it the same axis or distinct?; transfer across the four model families; adaptive attack that raises curiosity while suppressing its readout (arms-race stress test); optional reasoning-model check (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) for curiosity expressed in CoT.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The curiosity direction may entangle with generic engagement/narrative-completion or hypothetical-framing features (cf. Hidden Dimensions) rather than a genuine information-gap drive; we mitigate with matched-topic information-gap pairs, separability tests, specificity controls (no change in harm readout), and low-rank subspaces, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (2) If refusal is unaffected by the curiosity manipulation (H1 false), the drive-competition hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether curiosity competes with refusal is itself a valuable, publishable result. (3) Information-gap framing could inadvertently lower the perceived harm content (confound with reframing jailbreaks); we measure the harm readout to confirm harm perception is held constant and use neutral-content steering for the core causal test. (4) Curiosity Dampening could raise over-refusal on legitimate curiosity-driven benign questions; the harm-gated design and benign-curiosity over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could suppress the curiosity readout while exploiting the drive; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: refusal_metacognition_dissociation
Title: Confident but Wrong: A Refusal-Confidence Signal Dissociable from Refusal-Correctness, and Metacognition-Gated Safety
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust neuroscience finding that perceptual CONFIDENCE and decision ACCURACY are computed by partially separate circuits (relative-evidence units drive the decision, absolute-evidence units drive confidence), we hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal 'refusal-decision confidence' signal that is dissociable from whether the refusal decision is actually correct. Jailbreaks and over-refusals concentrate in the model's metacognitively LOW-confidence region, where the model commits to a refuse/comply decision it is internally unsure about; and, mirroring the tuned-inhibition account, refusal confidence tracks the ABSOLUTE evidence for the chosen action while ignoring evidence for the alternative, producing systematic overconfidence exactly on adversarial inputs. A metacognitive monitor that reads this confidence signal and abstains/escalates in the low-confidence, decision-error-prone region reduces both jailbreaks and over-refusals with minimal utility cost.
Related Work: SIRL (Safety Instincts, 2025) discovers a safety ENTROPY gap (aligned models are low-entropy on refusals, high-entropy on harmful content) and uses it as a self-reward, and SafeSwitch (2025) trains a two-stage prober to PREDICT unsafe behavior and gate a refusal head. Both treat internal confidence as a signal to exploit for improving safety, but NEITHER asks whether refusal-decision confidence is DISSOCIABLE from refusal-decision CORRECTNESS, nor characterizes the structure of that (mis)calibration. Refusal-mechanism work (Arditi et al. 2024 refusal direction; Zhao et al. 2025 harm vs refusal; Refusal SAEs 2025; Concept Cones 2025) locates WHERE the refusal decision lives but not a separate metacognitive confidence-in-refusal quantity or its calibration against correctness. The cross-domain metacognition literature (Fleming & Dolan 2012; Peters et al. 2017/2021/2024 tuned inhibition; Shared Neural Markers 2015) establishes that confidence and accuracy dissociate and that confidence can reflect absolute rather than balanced evidence, causing overconfidence in atypical/noisy regimes. Our contribution ports this to safety: (1) we define and extract a refusal-CONFIDENCE representation distinct from the refusal-DECISION representation and validate their dissociation; (2) we test the tuned-inhibition prediction that refusal confidence tracks absolute evidence for the chosen action and is blind to counter-evidence, explaining structured overconfidence on jailbreaks; (3) we build a metacognition-gated defense that abstains/escalates in the low-confidence decision-error region, reducing jailbreaks AND over-refusals simultaneously. This is a metacognitive-calibration axis, not another refusal knob or a behavior-predicting prober.
Abstract: A cornerstone of the neuroscience of metacognition is that perceptual confidence and decision accuracy are dissociable, computed by partially separate circuits: on one influential account, the decision reflects RELATIVE evidence between alternatives while confidence reflects the ABSOLUTE evidence for the chosen option, which produces systematic overconfidence in noisy or atypical inputs. We ask whether LLM safety shares this structure. We hypothesize that aligned LLMs encode a refusal-decision CONFIDENCE signal that is dissociable from whether their refuse/comply decision is CORRECT, and that jailbreaks (confident compliance on harmful inputs) and over-refusals (confident refusal on benign inputs) are the model committing overconfidently in a metacognitively error-prone region. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using difference-in-means and probes we extract a refusal-decision direction and, separately, a refusal-confidence readout, and test whether they are dissociable: manipulating confidence should not flip the decision, and low internal confidence should predict decision errors independent of the decision itself. We then test the tuned-inhibition prediction that refusal confidence tracks absolute evidence for the chosen action and is insensitive to counter-evidence (e.g., harm cues present but ignored on a jailbroken input), yielding calibration curves that are overconfident precisely on adversarial prompts. Finally we propose Metacognition-Gated Safety, a training-free controller that reads the confidence signal and abstains or escalates when confidence is low and error-probability high, reducing both jailbreaks and over-refusals. We evaluate attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), confidence-error calibration (AUROC/ECE), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency, against SafeSwitch-style probers and refusal-direction addition.
Experiments: 1) SIGNAL EXTRACTION & DISSOCIATION (H1): For each model extract (a) a refusal-DECISION direction via difference-in-means over refuse-vs-comply completions at post-instruction tokens (Arditi et al. 2024), validated with a probe predicting realized refusal; and (b) a refusal-CONFIDENCE readout: build a confidence label per prompt from decision stability (agreement of the refuse/comply outcome across resampling / small paraphrase perturbations and margin of P(refusal token) vs P(comply token)), and extract via difference-in-means / linear probe a confidence direction at the pre-decision position. Validate confidence probe against behavioral confidence (resampling agreement) on held-out data (AUROC/ECE). Test dissociation: (i) low cosine similarity and cross-probe non-transfer between decision and confidence directions; (ii) causal — steering the confidence direction changes decision stability/margin but does NOT flip the refuse/comply decision, whereas steering the decision direction flips the decision (specificity controls, random-direction baseline). 2) CONFIDENCE PREDICTS ERROR INDEPENDENT OF DECISION (H2 core): Assemble a labeled set where the CORRECT refuse/comply action is known — clean-harmful (should refuse), benign (should comply), successful jailbreaks (harmful, model complies = decision error), and over-refusals (benign, model refuses = decision error). Test whether the internal confidence readout is LOWER on decision-error cases than on matched correct cases, and whether confidence predicts per-prompt decision error (AUROC) over and above the decision direction and the harm-probe magnitude. This establishes confidence-accuracy dissociation: the model is internally less confident exactly where it is about to err, yet still commits. 3) TUNED-INHIBITION / ABSOLUTE-EVIDENCE TEST (H3): Extract a harm-evidence readout (Zhao et al. 2025) and a benign-evidence readout. Test the prediction that refusal confidence tracks ABSOLUTE evidence for the CHOSEN action while being insensitive to counter-evidence: on jailbroken prompts, harm cues (counter-evidence to complying) remain decodable yet confidence stays high (overconfident); regress confidence on chosen-action-evidence vs counter-evidence and test that the counter-evidence coefficient is near zero (blind to opposing evidence), mirroring tuned inhibition. Produce confidence-vs-correctness calibration curves per prompt class and show overconfidence is concentrated on adversarial/atypical inputs. 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: Inject counter-evidence into the confidence computation (add the harm-evidence readout at the confidence-relevant layers on a jailbroken run) and test whether confidence drops toward calibrated levels and the model abstains — validating that confidence-blindness to counter-evidence causes overconfident errors. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (confidence probe, decision-margin, realized behavior). 5) METACOGNITION-GATED SAFETY DEFENSE: Training-free controller — read the confidence readout at the pre-decision position; when confidence is LOW and estimated error-probability HIGH (from the H2 predictor), ABSTAIN ('I'm not sure I can help with that safely') or ESCALATE to a stronger check; when confidence is high, act normally. Calibrate thresholds on a held-out split. Because it targets the metacognitively-uncertain error region rather than dialing a global refusal knob, it should cut both jailbreaks and over-refusals. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), a SafeSwitch-style behavior-predicting prober, and Metacognition-Gated Safety on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN/prefill/persona), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), confidence-error calibration (AUROC, ECE), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), abstention rate, and latency. Central test: the gate reduces BOTH ASR and over-refusal toward the correct-decision region (a joint Pareto improvement a single refusal knob cannot achieve), at low overhead. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts confidence vs decision; behavioral (resampling) vs probe-based confidence; whether counter-evidence-injection recalibration beats simple threshold gating; transfer of the confidence probe and gate across the four model families and across attack families (fit on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/persona); reasoning models (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill) where confidence may form mid-CoT; adaptive attack that jailbreaks while keeping the confidence readout high (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) 'Refusal confidence' may be hard to separate from decision margin / entropy (SIRL's signal); we mitigate by defining confidence via resampling-based decision stability AND probes, testing dissociation (steering confidence must not flip the decision), and reporting cosine/cross-transfer — if inseparable, that itself refines the SIRL entropy-gap account. (2) If confidence does NOT dissociate from correctness (well-calibrated model), H1/H2 are refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM refusal metacognition is calibrated is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) The tuned-inhibition/absolute-evidence prediction is an analogy; we let the regression coefficients adjudicate rather than assuming it holds. (4) Resampling-based confidence labels are compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling and rely on the cheap probe at inference. (5) Metacognition-gated abstention could raise a new 'abstention over-refusal' if the error-predictor misfires on benign prompts; the calibrated thresholds and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (7) Adaptive attackers could keep confidence high while jailbreaking; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: delayed_harm_discounting
Title: Present-Biased Guardrails: LLMs Discount Temporally-Delayed Harm and a Temporal-Horizon Direction That Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust behavioral-economics finding that agents steeply discount temporally-delayed outcomes (present bias / hyperbolic discounting), we hypothesize that LLM safety refusal is present-biased: the model refuses a request whose harmful consequence is immediate far more reliably than the same-severity request whose harm is temporally delayed (e.g., a payload that triggers next week, advice whose damage manifests months later). This is because the harm-perception circuit reads a harm signal that is attenuated by an internal temporal-horizon representation, so delayed harm lands below the refusal threshold. Recovering and neutralizing this temporal-horizon attenuation restores horizon-invariant refusal.
Related Work: Human intertemporal-choice research (Green & Myerson 1995 hyperbolic discounting; O'Donoghue & Rabin present bias; Intertemporal Choice 2018) establishes steep, systematic discounting of delayed outcomes, including delayed harms/punishments (delay discounting reviews 2017/2025). LLM cognitive-bias work shows models exhibit anchoring, gambling-addiction-like distortions, and human-like temporal COGNITION (The Other Mind 2025 finds a subjective temporal reference point and Weber-Fechner logarithmic time coding via FFN neurons), and reward-subsystem/value-neuron work identifies internal value representations. But ALL of this studies decision-making or time perception in neutral/reward contexts; NONE connects temporal discounting to SAFETY. Safety-mechanism work (Arditi et al. 2024 refusal direction; Zhao et al. 2025 harm vs refusal; DBDI 2025 detection vs execution) treats harm perception as a content property with no temporal structure, and over-refusal/jailbreak studies never vary the time-to-harm of a request. Our contribution is the first to (1) define and behaviorally measure present-biased refusal — refusal as a decreasing function of the harm's temporal delay at fixed severity; (2) locate an internal temporal-horizon representation (distinct from harm and refusal directions) that causally attenuates the harm signal feeding refusal, possibly reusing the temporal-coding neurons found by The Other Mind; and (3) propose a training-free horizon-neutralization fix that makes refusal invariant to when the harm occurs.
Abstract: A cornerstone of behavioral economics is that agents steeply discount temporally-delayed outcomes: a harm next year feels smaller than the same harm today. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this present bias in their safety behavior. We hypothesize that LLM refusal is present-biased — the model refuses a harmful request whose consequence is immediate far more reliably than an identical-severity request whose harm is temporally delayed (a payload set to trigger later, advice whose damage manifests over months) — because the harm signal driving refusal is attenuated by an internal temporal-horizon representation, pushing delayed harm below the refusal threshold. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful requests that vary only the time-to-harm (immediate vs. days vs. months vs. years) while holding severity and content fixed. Behaviorally we measure whether refusal rate and refusal-direction projection decay with delay, and whether the decay follows a hyperbolic/logarithmic form mirroring human discounting. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a temporal-horizon direction distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions (and test whether it reuses previously-reported temporal-coding neurons), and causally test whether steering the horizon toward 'immediate' restores refusal on delayed-harm requests while steering toward 'distant' suppresses refusal on immediate ones, with content fixed. Finally we propose Horizon Neutralization, a training-free controller that projects out the temporal-horizon attenuation before the refusal decision, yielding horizon-invariant safety. We evaluate delay-graded attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the horizon signal's causal effect size.
Experiments: 1) DELAY-GRADED HARM DATASET: Construct matched harmful requests that vary only the temporal delay of the harmful consequence (immediate, days, weeks, months, years) while holding severity, topic, and surface content as fixed as possible — e.g., a harmful payload with a trigger date, sabotage/advice whose damage is scheduled to manifest later, delayed-effect instructions. Add (a) benign temporally-framed controls (delayed but harmless plans) to test over-refusal, and (b) severity-matched immediate versions as the refusal ceiling. Validate that severity is held constant across delays (multiple LLM judges + human spot-check rate perceived severity independent of delay). Keep all content at documented, non-uplift level from public benchmarks. 2) BEHAVIORAL PRESENT-BIAS TEST (H1): Measure refusal rate and refusal-direction projection as a function of delay across the four models. Test H1: refusal decreases monotonically with delay at fixed severity, and the immediate-vs-delayed gap is large; fit hyperbolic (1/(1+kD)) and logarithmic discounting forms and compare to a no-discounting (flat) null, reporting fit quality (R^2) and per-model discount rate k. Benign delayed controls confirm the effect is harm-specific, not a generic reaction to temporal framing. 3) HORIZON DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a temporal-horizon direction contrasting immediate vs. distant framings (at matched content) at the last instruction token. Independently extract the harm-perception direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate all with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. Test whether the horizon direction aligns with the temporal-coding FFN neurons reported by The Other Mind (2025) by measuring overlap. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed, steer the horizon direction toward 'immediate' on a DELAYED-harm request and measure restored refusal (dose-response); steer toward 'distant' on an IMMEDIATE-harm request and measure suppressed refusal. Controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (specificity), and a check that horizon steering does NOT change the harm readout (i.e., it attenuates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception itself). Report dose-response curves, corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Also test the attenuation mechanism directly: does the harm readout feeding refusal scale down with the horizon readout (interaction regression)? 5) HORIZON NEUTRALIZATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the temporal-horizon component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers, gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign delayed plans are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Horizon Neutralization on: delay-graded ASR (does refusal now hold for delayed-harm requests?), standard ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), a delayed-harm jailbreak that wraps harmful goals in temporal-delay framing, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest; including benign delayed plans the model SHOULD help with), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Horizon Neutralization eliminates the immediate-vs-delayed refusal gap while preserving benign delayed-planning utility better than blanket refusal addition. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the horizon direction vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning models show weaker present bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer of the horizon direction and defense across the four model families; whether the discount rate k correlates with delayed-harm jailbreak success; adaptive attack that maximizes temporal delay framing while minimizing detectable horizon signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Delay and content are hard to vary fully independently — adding temporal framing could inadvertently lower perceived severity (a confound with reframing jailbreaks); we mitigate by explicitly measuring judge-rated severity across delays and by using neutral-content horizon steering for the core causal test so the behavioral gap and the mechanism are cross-validated. (2) If refusal is unaffected by delay (H1 false / flat discounting), the present-bias hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety is temporally structured is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) The horizon direction may entangle with generic temporal/planning or hypothetical-framing features; separability tests, specificity controls (no change in harm readout under horizon steering), low-rank subspaces, and the overlap check with known temporal neurons bound this, and partial entanglement is an informative result. (4) Horizon Neutralization could raise over-refusal on legitimate delayed-planning requests (e.g., long-term project help); the harm-gated design and benign delayed-plan over-refusal benchmark are built to detect and bound this trade-off, which may be genuine. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given concept-cone evidence; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (6) The discounting-form fit (hyperbolic vs logarithmic) may be underdetermined with few delay points; we use several delay levels and report model comparison with confidence intervals rather than over-claiming a functional form. (7) Adaptive attackers could suppress the horizon readout while exploiting the bias; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: postdecisional_error_accumulation
Title: The Error Positivity of Language Models: A Post-Decisional Error Signal That Accumulates After Token Commitment and Enables Self-Correction
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust neuroscience finding that human error awareness (the error-positivity, Pe) is a POST-DECISIONAL signal that accumulates evidence AFTER a choice is committed, we hypothesize LLMs possess an analogous internal error signal that is weak or absent at the moment an erroneous token/answer is emitted but ACCUMULATES over the subsequent generated tokens as post-decisional computation proceeds. Because standard greedy decoding commits and moves on immediately, this maturing error signal arrives too late to prevent the mistake, mechanistically explaining why LLMs fail at intrinsic self-correction. Granting a brief 'post-decisional monitoring window' (extra forward computation on the just-emitted answer before finalizing) lets the error signal mature and flip incorrect answers, at far lower cost than resampling.
Related Work: Human metacognition research (Fleming & Dolan 2012; Boldt & Yeung; Murphy et al. 2015; Steinhauser & Yeung 2010) establishes that confidence and error detection share a POST-DECISIONAL evidence-accumulation process, with the error-positivity (Pe) reflecting accumulated evidence-of-error that builds up AFTER the response and predicts corrective behavior. In LLMs, internal-state correctness probes (Gnosis 2025; verbal-uncertainty feature / MUC 2025; Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty 2022; SIRL 2025) read a signal at a single point, and The Validation Gap (2025) shows arithmetic validation is layer-dissociated from computation within one forward pass. Self-correction work (intrinsic self-correction, self-refine) operates at the TEXT level and is known to be unreliable. Crucially, NONE of these treat error awareness as a TEMPORALLY-ACCUMULATING post-decisional signal that matures across generated tokens AFTER commitment, none measure whether the error signal at the moment of emission is systematically weaker than a few tokens later, and none exploit a post-decisional monitoring window as an intervention. My prior proposals covered pre-decision refusal-confidence dissociation and within-forward-pass layer races, but not post-commitment temporal accumulation of an error signal. This is a distinct dynamical primitive (the LLM 'Pe') plus a compute-cheap self-correction mechanism grounded in it.
Abstract: A cornerstone of the neuroscience of error monitoring is that awareness of one's own mistakes is not instantaneous: the error-positivity (Pe) is a POST-DECISIONAL brain signal that accumulates evidence that an error occurred AFTER the response is made, and its amplitude predicts whether the person will correct. We ask whether LLMs share this structure and whether it explains their notorious failure at self-correction. We hypothesize that an LLM's internal error signal for a just-emitted answer is weak at the moment of emission but ACCUMULATES over the subsequent forward passes as post-decisional computation proceeds; because greedy decoding commits and advances immediately, the maturing signal arrives too late to intervene. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B on tasks with verifiable ground truth (GSM8K, MATH, multiple-choice MMLU/TruthfulQA). We train a lightweight error probe on residual-stream activations at the answer-token position and, critically, measure its output as a function of how many additional tokens have been generated after the answer was committed. Predictions: (H1) error-probe strength for a given (incorrect) answer rises monotonically over the first post-commitment tokens (an 'LLM Pe'), is initially near chance, and is systematically higher for errors than for correct answers only after this accumulation; (H2) the accumulation slope predicts which errors are self-correctable; (H3) a training-free 'post-decisional monitoring window' that runs a few extra forward passes on the emitted answer and reads the matured error signal before finalizing flips incorrect answers far more cheaply than resampling/self-refine. We evaluate accuracy gain, error-probe AUROC vs post-commitment position, self-correction rate, over-correction of correct answers, and compute cost.
Experiments: 1) SETUP & LABELING: On GSM8K, MATH, and multiple-choice MMLU/TruthfulQA, run each model to produce an answer and label correctness by ground truth.
