For each item record the residual-stream activations at the answer-commit token AND at each of the next N post-answer positions (elicited by having the model continue generating a brief self-check-neutral continuation, e.g., re-stating/reflecting, so post-decisional computation proceeds without new external evidence). 2) ERROR PROBE: Train a linear error probe on residual-stream activations to predict correctness, trained separately per post-commitment position (position-0 = moment of emission, positions 1..N = after). Report per-position AUROC on held-out items. 3) POST-DECISIONAL ACCUMULATION TEST (H1 core): Test whether error-probe AUROC / error-signal magnitude for incorrect answers is near-chance at position 0 and RISES monotonically over positions 1..N (the LLM 'Pe'), while correct answers stay flat/low. Fit accumulation curves (slope, asymptote), compare errors vs correct, and report effect sizes across the four models. Control: a matched non-error 'surprise' signal (e.g., generic next-token entropy) should NOT show the same error-specific accumulation. 4) SLOPE PREDICTS CORRECTABILITY (H2): Define an item as self-correctable if, given a neutral 're-examine your answer' prompt, the model flips to the correct answer. Test whether the per-item post-decisional accumulation slope predicts self-correctability (AUROC), beating position-0 probe and verbal-confidence baselines. 5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Truncate post-decisional computation (finalize immediately at position 0) and show self-correction collapses; (b) surface the matured error signal EARLY by patching the position-N error-carrying activation back to position 0 and test whether the model corrects sooner. Corruption/random-position baselines and multiple metrics (probe output, P(corrected answer), realized flip). 6) POST-DECISIONAL MONITORING WINDOW DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller — after emitting an answer, run k extra forward passes (the monitoring window), read the matured error probe; if it exceeds a calibrated threshold, trigger a targeted revision (re-decode the answer span) — otherwise finalize. Calibrate k and threshold on held-out data. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base greedy, self-refine (text-level), full resampling+self-consistency, Gnosis-style position-0 probe gating, and the Post-Decisional Monitoring Window on: accuracy, self-correction rate, over-correction rate (flipping correct answers to wrong — critical), error-probe AUROC vs position, and compute cost (forward passes). Central test: the monitoring window matches or beats self-refine/resampling accuracy at a fraction of the compute, because it spends a few extra passes only to let the error signal mature. 8) ABLATIONS: window length k; which layer hosts the accumulating signal; whether the accumulation is content-driven (needs re-examining the answer) vs generic time; transfer of the probe and window across the four model families and across tasks (train on GSM8K, test on MATH/MMLU); whether reasoning models show a longer/steeper Pe across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive check on whether easy-correct items are wrongly flagged.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'post-decisional accumulation' may be confounded with the model simply re-reading its answer as new context rather than a genuine internal error signal; we control with entropy/surprise baselines, test whether accumulation requires answer-relevant continuation vs neutral filler, and corroborate with causal patching. (2) If the error signal is already strong at position 0 (no accumulation), H1 is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM error awareness is post-decisional is itself a valuable, publishable finding and would still inform self-correction theory. (3) Linear probes may be imperfect / entangled with difficulty; we report AUROC, calibrate on difficulty-matched controls, and test over-correction on correct answers explicitly. (4) The monitoring window adds latency; we quantify compute vs accuracy and only claim a favorable trade-off relative to resampling, not zero cost. (5) The revision step could over-correct (flip correct answers), the key failure mode; the calibrated threshold and over-correction metric bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) The neuroscience Pe analogy is an organizing hypothesis, not an identity; we let the accumulation-curve data adjudicate. (7) Multiple-choice/verifiable tasks ease answer-token analysis but limit generality; free-form extension may be weaker. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmarks with verifiable ground truth; no harmful content is involved.

Name: analogical_transport_jailbreak
Title: Smuggling Harm Through the Analogy Engine: Jailbreaks That Hijack the Structural-Mapping Circuit, and Blocking Harmful Transport at the Mapping Site
Short Hypothesis: A large class of framing jailbreaks (roleplay, fictional-scenario, code-metaphor, 'explain-as-an-analogy' attacks) succeed by recruiting the model's own analogical-reasoning circuit: the attacker supplies a benign SOURCE frame and the harmful TARGET answer is reconstructed downstream via structural mapping, so the harm signal is never computed at the instruction token (bypassing harm perception) and only crystallizes during the mapping step where safety no longer inspects it. Locating this analogical-transport step and gating harmful content at the mapping site closes these jailbreaks without harming benign analogical reasoning.
Related Work: Two literatures are adjacent but unconnected. (1) Analogical-reasoning mechanism: LLMs encode relational concepts in mid-upper layers and reason by STRUCTURAL ALIGNMENT between source and target, with success marked by strong alignment and failure by degraded alignment (The Curious Case of Analogies 2025; Analogical Reasoning Inside LLMs / Concept Vectors 2025); crucially, patching hidden representations at critical token positions transfers relational information across situations. (2) Safety mechanism: harm perception and refusal are separate directions read at the instruction token (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024), and jailbreaks via OOD/analogical/contextual framing succeed by increasing uncertainty about intent (JOOD 2025; GraphAttack 2025 code/AMR framing; Jailbroken 2023 mismatched generalization; Persuasion 2024) or by anchoring safety to the template region (TASA 2025). Structural Safety Generalization (2025) documents that safety fails across semantically-equivalent structures but gives no mechanism. NONE of these identify the ANALOGICAL-MAPPING circuit as the vehicle: nobody shows that framing jailbreaks recruit the same structural-alignment mechanism used for benign analogy, that the harm answer is TRANSPORTED from a benign source frame rather than perceived on the request, or that gating at the mapping step defends while preserving benign analogy. My prior proposals covered compositional harm (blind spot from un-integrated sub-skills) and hull-extrapolation of harm categories; this is distinct — the harm here is a fully-known target answer smuggled through relational transport, not an emergent composition or a novel category.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse a direct harmful request yet comply when the same request is wrapped in an analogy: 'a fictional chemist explains it,' 'write it as this code metaphor,' 'by analogy to baking, describe...'. We propose these framing jailbreaks are not miscellaneous tricks but a single mechanistic exploit: they hijack the model's analogical-reasoning circuit. The attacker provides a benign SOURCE frame; the harmful TARGET answer is reconstructed downstream by the same structural-alignment mechanism that powers legitimate analogy, so the harm signal is never computed at the instruction token where harm perception reads it, and only crystallizes at the mapping step, which safety does not inspect. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. First, we show that on analogical jailbreaks the harm-perception readout at the instruction token is low (perception bypassed) while a harm representation is reconstructed in later layers at the mapping/answer positions, whereas direct harmful requests show harm at the instruction token. Second, using structural-alignment probes and activation patching at critical mapping positions (following analogy-mechanism work), we localize the transport step and causally show that disrupting source-to-target mapping blocks the jailbroken answer while leaving benign analogy intact. Third, we propose Mapping-Site Gating: a training-free intervention that surfaces the reconstructed target-content harm readout at the mapping step and triggers refusal, gated so benign analogical reasoning is preserved. We evaluate attack success rate (analogical/roleplay/code-metaphor attacks, JOOD, GraphAttack, JailbreakBench, HarmBench), benign analogical-reasoning accuracy (a critical control), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and latency.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build analogical-jailbreak prompt sets that wrap public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench) in benign SOURCE frames: (a) roleplay/fictional-persona ('a chemistry teacher in a novel explains...'), (b) explicit analogy ('by analogy to <benign process>, describe <harmful process>'), (c) code-metaphor / AMR-graph framings (GraphAttack-style), (d) JOOD-style OOD transforms. Controls: (i) matched DIRECT harmful requests (same goal, no frame) as the harm-perception ceiling; (ii) matched BENIGN analogies (benign source -> benign target) to measure whether a defense harms legitimate analogical reasoning; (iii) benign roleplay/fiction the model should still perform. Validate harm/benign labels with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check; keep content at documented, non-uplift level.
2) PERCEPTION-BYPASS TEST (H1): Extract via difference-in-means a harm-perception direction at the last instruction token (Zhao et al. 2025) and a harm representation probe usable at later positions. Measure, per prompt class, the instruction-token harm readout and the later-layer harm readout at the mapping/answer positions. Test H1: analogical jailbreaks show LOW harm at the instruction token (perception bypassed, near benign) but harm RECONSTRUCTED in later layers at mapping positions, whereas direct harmful requests show harm already at the instruction token; benign analogies show low harm throughout. Report per-class harm-readout-by-layer curves and effect sizes.
3) STRUCTURAL-MAPPING LOCALIZATION (H2): Following analogy-mechanism work, compute structural-alignment between source-frame and target-answer representations (RSA / representational alignment across mid-upper layers) and identify the token positions and attention heads that carry relational transport (concept-vector / critical-position patching). Test whether alignment strength predicts jailbreak success (higher source->target alignment => stronger transport => more successful jailbreak; Spearman). Localize the mapping step (layers/positions/heads).
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H3): (a) Disrupt transport: at the localized mapping positions/heads, on analogical jailbreaks, ablate/patch to break source-to-target structural alignment and measure drop in jailbroken-answer success; compare to disrupting matched control heads. (b) Specificity: apply the same disruption to BENIGN analogies and confirm benign analogical-reasoning accuracy is preserved (the mechanism is shared but the defense must be harm-gated). (c) Sufficiency: patch the mapping-step activations from a jailbroken run into a benign-frame run and test whether harmful content transfers. Corruption/random-head baselines and multiple metrics (later-layer harm readout, P(refusal token), realized harm/answer).
5) MAPPING-SITE GATING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads the RECONSTRUCTED target-content harm readout at the localized mapping step (not the instruction token) and, if it exceeds a calibrated threshold, injects refusal / halts the transport; gated on the reconstructed-harm readout so benign analogies (low harm) are untouched. Calibrate layer/threshold on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, instruction-token refusal-direction addition (Arditi — should miss analogical attacks since perception is bypassed), a structure-rewriting guardrail baseline (Structural Safety Generalization), and Mapping-Site Gating on: ASR (analogical/roleplay/code-metaphor attacks, JOOD, GraphAttack, JailbreakBench, HarmBench, plus direct attacks); benign analogical-reasoning accuracy (analogy benchmarks) — critical to show the defense does not break legitimate analogy; over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, benign roleplay/fiction); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); latency. Central test: Mapping-Site Gating closes analogical jailbreaks toward direct-request refusal levels while preserving benign analogical reasoning and roleplay — an outcome instruction-token refusal (blind to reconstructed harm) and blanket structure-rewriting cannot jointly achieve.
7) ABLATIONS: which layers/positions host the mapping step; single-direction vs low-rank harm readout at the mapping site; whether alignment-strength predicts ASR across attack types (train on roleplay, test on code-metaphor/JOOD); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models transport harm across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attack that spreads transport across many weak mapping steps or minimizes measurable source->target alignment (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The clean 'perception-bypassed, harm-reconstructed-at-mapping' picture may hold for some framing attacks but not others (e.g., attacks that also raise instruction-token harm); the per-class harm-by-layer census is itself a primary contribution and scopes the defense. (2) If harm is genuinely never reconstructed internally for some attacks (the model produces harm without an internal harm representation), Mapping-Site Gating cannot fire — an informative scope boundary we test explicitly. (3) The mapping step is shared with benign analogy, so any disruption risks harming legitimate analogical reasoning; the harm-gated design and the benign-analogy accuracy control are built to detect and bound this trade-off, which may be genuine. (4) Structural-alignment (RSA) and difference-in-means readouts are imperfect/possibly nonlinear; we corroborate with causal patching, low-rank subspaces, and multiple metrics, and report probe reliability. (5) Localizing mapping positions in free-form generations is noisy; we standardize frame/answer structure and identify critical positions via patching. (6) Activation-patching has known metric pitfalls; we use corruption baselines and multiple metrics. (7) The alignment-strength predictor may transfer poorly across attack types; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers may minimize measurable source->target alignment or fragment transport; we test this and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (10) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: cot_reliance_gate
Title: The Reliance Gate: LLMs Set a Pre-Hoc Signal Deciding Whether Their Chain-of-Thought Will Cause the Answer, and We Can Read and Flip It
Short Hypothesis: Whether a model's chain-of-thought will causally drive its final answer (faithful CoT-as-computation) versus be ignored as post-hoc rationalization (unfaithful CoT) is set by a low-dimensional 'reliance gate' signal formed BEFORE the CoT is generated — at the question/answer-onset position. This gate reflects whether the model has already committed to an answer. Reading the gate at inference predicts per-instance CoT faithfulness before any reasoning is produced, and steering it toward 'rely' restores genuine causal use of the CoT, improving both faithfulness and robustness to biasing cues.
Related Work: A large literature MEASURES CoT unfaithfulness: models are swayed by prompt cues without verbalizing them (Turpin et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2025; Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think 2025) and can flatly deny using hints (Reasoning Models Will Blatantly Lie 2026). Step-level causal-importance work (Thought Anchors 2025; True Thinking Score 2025; NLDD/Faithfulness Decay 2026; Making Reasoning Matter/FRODO 2024; Causal Mediation) quantifies HOW MUCH the CoT causally affects the answer, and belief-vs-explanation divergence work (Hypocrisy Gap 2026, NeuroFaith 2025) detects unfaithfulness from internal states. Crucially, ALL of these measure faithfulness POST-HOC (after the CoT exists, by corrupting/resampling steps or comparing to internal belief) and treat it as a property of the model/task/step. NONE asks whether the model sets a controllable, PRE-HOC internal signal — before the CoT is generated — that DETERMINES whether the forthcoming CoT will be causally used, nor whether reading that signal predicts per-instance faithfulness ahead of time, nor whether steering it flips a rationalization into genuine computation. Our contribution is (1) locating a pre-hoc 'reliance gate' at answer-onset that predicts downstream CoT causal weight; (2) causally validating it (steering the gate changes how much the CoT drives the answer); and (3) using it as a training-free faithfulness/robustness intervention. This is a mechanism-and-control account of the ORIGIN of unfaithfulness, distinct from the measurement-and-detection literature.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a key AI-safety asset only if the stated reasoning actually causes the answer. A large body of work shows CoT is often unfaithful — a post-hoc rationalization of an answer the model reached by other means — but treats faithfulness as something measurable only after the CoT exists. We propose that whether the CoT will be causally used is decided earlier: the model forms a low-dimensional 'reliance gate' at the moment before reasoning begins, reflecting whether it has already committed to an answer. If the gate is 'committed', the ensuing CoT is decorative; if 'undecided', the CoT genuinely computes the answer. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on BIG-Bench Hard, GSM8K/MATH, and MMLU with and without biasing cues (suggested answers, option-order bias, sycophancy). First, we measure per-instance CoT causal weight via step-corruption/resampling (existing metrics) and extract a candidate gate direction via difference-in-means over high- vs low-reliance instances at the answer-onset position. Second (prediction): we test whether the gate readout, taken BEFORE the CoT is generated, predicts the downstream causal weight and hence faithfulness (AUROC). Third (causation): steering the gate toward 'rely' should increase the CoT's causal effect on the answer and reduce silent adoption of biasing cues, while steering toward 'commit' should induce post-hoc rationalization on normally-faithful instances. Finally we propose Reliance Gating, a training-free intervention that boosts the gate on cue-biased inputs to restore genuine reasoning. We evaluate faithfulness (cue-verbalization rate, causal-weight metrics), robustness to biasing cues (accuracy retention), utility, and the gate's predictive power.
Experiments:
1) SETUP & CAUSAL-WEIGHT LABELS: On BIG-Bench Hard, GSM8K/MATH, and MMLU, generate CoT + answer for each model. For each instance compute a per-instance CoT causal weight using established methods: step-corruption (paraphrase/insert-mistake into the CoT and measure answer-flip / logit-difference decay, following Measuring Faithfulness 2023 and NLDD 2026) and resampling importance (Thought Anchors). Label instances as HIGH-reliance (CoT causally drives the answer) vs LOW-reliance (answer unchanged when CoT corrupted — post-hoc). Also build a cue-biased variant of each dataset (suggested-answer, option-order bias, sycophancy) with known ground-truth influence.
2) GATE EXTRACTION (Location): Extract a candidate reliance-gate direction via difference-in-means over HIGH- vs LOW-reliance instances, read at the ANSWER-ONSET position (the token where the model transitions from question to reasoning, before CoT tokens exist). Validate with a held-out linear probe (report AUROC). Test that the gate is distinct from raw answer-confidence and from a difficulty probe (cross-probe transfer, cosine similarity).
3) PRE-HOC PREDICTIVENESS (H1, core): Test whether the gate readout, taken BEFORE any CoT token is generated, predicts the downstream causal weight / faithfulness label. Report AUROC and calibration, versus baselines: answer-token entropy at onset, a difficulty probe, and prompt perplexity. On cue-biased inputs, test whether a 'committed' gate predicts SILENT cue adoption (accuracy drop without verbalizing the cue). Test cross-dataset and cross-model transfer.
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H2, Causal Intervention): Steer the gate at the answer-onset position (dose-response, fixed norm). Predict: steering toward 'rely/undecided' on cue-biased instances increases the CoT's causal weight (larger logit-difference decay under step-corruption) and reduces silent cue adoption / increases cue verbalization; steering toward 'commit' on normally-faithful instances reduces CoT causal weight (induces post-hoc rationalization). Controls: random-direction steering, a confidence-direction steering specificity control, and checks that steering does not merely change the final answer distribution. Report causal-weight change, cue-verbalization rate, corruption baselines, multiple metrics (logit-difference decay, answer-flip rate, realized behavior).
5) RELIANCE GATING DEFENSE/APPLICATION (H3): Training-free controller — read the gate at onset; if it reads 'committed' on an input carrying a biasing cue (detected by high commitment before adequate reasoning), boost the gate toward 'rely' so the model computes rather than rationalizes. Calibrate threshold/strength on a held-out split; gate off on inputs where the model is legitimately confident and correct.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, always-boost (constant gate addition), a decoding baseline (temperature/self-consistency), and Reliance Gating on: faithfulness (cue-verbalization rate, per-instance causal weight), robustness to biasing cues (accuracy retention on cue-biased BBH/MMLU, i.e., resisting incorrect suggested answers), utility on clean tasks (BBH, GSM8K/MATH, MMLU accuracy), over-reasoning cost (extra tokens), and latency. Central test: Reliance Gating increases faithfulness AND accuracy-retention under biasing cues with minimal clean-task cost — outperforming constant boosting (which harms easy-correct instances) because it acts only when the gate mis-fires.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the gate; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the gate is the same construct across reasoning vs instruction-tuned models; transfer of the predictor across cue types (fit on suggested-answer, test on option-order/sycophancy) and model families; optional formation check — does gate 'commitment' correlate with the answer being decodable at onset via logit lens (i.e., pre-commitment)?
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The gate may be entangled with generic answer-confidence or task-difficulty rather than a distinct 'will-I-use-my-CoT' signal; we mitigate with separability tests (cross-probe transfer, specificity steering controls) and treat partial entanglement as an informative finding — if the gate IS just confidence, that itself is a clean result explaining unfaithfulness. (2) Per-instance causal-weight labels from step-corruption/resampling are noisy and metric-dependent; we use multiple metrics (logit-difference decay, resampling, answer-flip) and report agreement. (3) If faithfulness is not predictable pre-hoc (H1 fails), the reliance-gate hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether the origin of unfaithfulness is set before the CoT is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (4) Steering the gate could change the final answer directly rather than the CoT's causal role; we control for this by measuring causal weight (corruption sensitivity) rather than accuracy alone, and include specificity controls. (5) Reliance Gating could induce over-reasoning or degrade easy-correct instances if the gate misfires; the calibrated, cue-conditioned design and clean-task utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Answer-onset position identification is nontrivial for free-form generation; we standardize the CoT prompt format to locate it, and for reasoning models test a mid-CoT extension. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use public reasoning benchmarks and standard cue manipulations; no harmful content is involved.

Name: refusal_margin_instability
Title: Wavering at the Boundary: A Refusal Decision Margin That Explains Stochastic Safety Instability and Jailbreak Susceptibility
Short Hypothesis: A prompt's refusal decision instability — whether the model refuses under some random seeds/temperatures/paraphrases but complies under others — is mechanistically governed by the prompt's DECISION MARGIN: the signed distance of its activation from the refusal-direction threshold. Borderline prompts sit near the hyperplane so small stochastic perturbations flip them, and this same small margin predicts jailbreak susceptibility. Measuring the margin diagnoses which prompts will waver, and a training-free margin-widening intervention that pushes low-margin harmful prompts confidently into the refuse region stabilizes decisions and closes jailbreaks without over-refusing confidently-benign prompts.
Related Work: Two literatures collide but are never connected. (1) Behavioral instability: 'The Instability of Safety' (2025) shows 18-28% of harmful prompts flip refuse/comply across seeds and temperatures and that higher-compliance prompts waver more; 'Semantic Confusion / ParaGuard' (2025) shows models accept one phrasing but reject a close paraphrase; 'Stochastic Monkeys' (2024) shows random augmentations cheaply break alignment. ALL treat instability as a measurement nuisance or an attack surface — none give a mechanistic, internal explanation or an internals-grounded fix. (2) Refusal geometry: refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024) with harmful/harmless separation (Geometry of Refusal 2025); adversarial suffixes suppress its propagation. But this geometry work analyzes clean deterministic prompts and never connects the prompt's DISTANCE to the refusal threshold to its STOCHASTIC decision variance or to per-prompt jailbreakability. Our contribution: (1) we define a per-prompt refusal decision margin from the refusal-direction projection and show it predicts, at the individual-prompt level, both the empirical stochastic flip rate (across seeds/temperature/paraphrase) and jailbreak success — unifying wavering and jailbreaking as two symptoms of a small margin; (2) we causally validate that margin, not content, drives instability (shrinking margin increases flips; widening it stabilizes); (3) we propose Margin-Widening Steering, a training-free fix that adds refusal-direction signal proportional to the margin DEFICIT only for low-margin borderline prompts, stabilizing decisions and reducing jailbreaks while leaving high-margin confident-benign prompts (and thus over-refusal) untouched.
Abstract: Recent audits show LLM safety refusals are stochastically unstable: the same harmful prompt is refused under some random seeds or temperatures and complied with under others, and close paraphrases receive opposite verdicts. This is treated as a measurement problem or an attack surface, with no mechanistic account. We propose that decision instability has a simple geometric cause. Refusal is mediated by a single direction; a prompt's signed distance from that direction's decision threshold — its refusal DECISION MARGIN — determines how easily stochastic perturbations flip its verdict. Borderline prompts sit near the hyperplane and waver; the same small margin makes them jailbreakable. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. First we extract the refusal direction and compute each prompt's margin, then measure its empirical stochastic flip rate across seeds, temperatures, and paraphrase clusters (ParaGuard-style), testing whether margin predicts flip rate per prompt (AUROC). Second we test whether the same margin predicts jailbreak success across attack families, unifying wavering and jailbreaking. Third we causally validate: artificially shrinking the margin increases flips and jailbreaks; widening it stabilizes them, with a matched-content control ruling out a pure content confound. Finally we propose Margin-Widening Steering, a training-free controller that injects refusal-direction signal proportional to the margin deficit only for low-margin prompts, stabilizing borderline decisions and reducing jailbreaks while leaving high-margin benign prompts — and over-refusal — untouched. We report per-prompt margin AUROC for both flip rate and attack success, decision stability (Safety Stability Index), attack success rate, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval).
Experiments: 1) MARGIN EXTRACTION: For each model extract the refusal direction via difference-in-means over matched harmful/harmless prompts at the last instruction/template token (Arditi et al. 2024); validate with a held-out linear probe (AUROC). Define per-prompt decision margin m(p) = signed projection of the prompt's activation onto the refusal direction, normalized by the harmful/harmless centroid gap and calibrated so m=0 is the refuse/comply decision boundary (fit the boundary threshold from labeled data). 2) MARGIN PREDICTS STOCHASTIC INSTABILITY (H1, core): For a pool of harmful and benign prompts, measure the empirical flip rate under three perturbation regimes: (a) 5 random seeds x 4 temperatures (0.0-1.0) as in the Instability-of-Safety protocol, (b) ParaGuard-style paraphrase clusters (intent fixed, surface varied), (c) light random input augmentations (Stochastic Monkeys). Compute per-prompt flip rate / a Safety Stability Index. Test H1: |m(p)| (distance from the boundary) predicts per-prompt flip rate — low-margin prompts waver, high-margin prompts are stable. Report Spearman correlation and AUROC of margin predicting 'unstable' prompts, versus baselines: raw refusal probability P(refusal token), next-token entropy, and prompt perplexity. Fit the flip-rate-vs-margin curve (expect a sharp rise near m=0). 3) MARGIN PREDICTS JAILBREAKABILITY (H2): For harmful prompts and their jailbroken variants (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona/roleplay), test whether the pre-attack margin (and how much each attack shifts the margin) predicts per-prompt jailbreak success (AUROC). Test whether jailbreaks work by driving the margin negative (into the comply region), unifying wavering and jailbreaking as small-/negative-margin phenomena. Report cross-attack transfer (fit predictor on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/persona) and cross-model transfer. 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H3): Holding content fixed, (a) SHRINK the margin (subtract a calibrated fraction of the refusal direction) on stable harmful prompts and measure increased flip rate and jailbreak success; (b) WIDEN the margin (add the refusal direction) on borderline prompts and measure decreased flips/jailbreaks. Controls: random-direction steering (specificity), and a matched-content pair design (same prompt, only margin manipulated) to rule out that instability is driven by content rather than geometry. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (flip rate, P(refusal token), realized behavior). 5) MARGIN-WIDENING STEERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller — at inference compute m(p); if m(p) is in the low-|margin| borderline band and harm-leaning, add alpha*(deficit)*refusal_direction to push the prompt confidently into the refuse region; leave high-margin confident-benign prompts (large positive comply margin) untouched so over-refusal is not increased. Calibrate the band, alpha, and layer on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition (constant magnitude), an extended-refusal/DeRTa-style baseline where reproducible, and Margin-Widening Steering on: decision stability (Safety Stability Index across seeds/temperature/paraphrase — primary), attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Margin-Widening Steering sharply increases decision stability and reduces ASR toward uniform-addition levels while keeping over-refusal near baseline, because it acts only on borderline prompts — a Pareto improvement uniform addition (which pushes all prompts, raising over-refusal) cannot achieve. 7) ABLATIONS: single-direction margin vs low-rank refusal-subspace margin (does a richer margin predict better?); which layer/position to read the margin; whether margin computed pre-generation predicts flips better than the first-token probability; sensitivity to the borderline band width and alpha; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show margin instability across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attack that jailbreaks while keeping the measured margin high (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The single-direction margin may be an incomplete descriptor given evidence for nonlinear/multidimensional refusal (Nonlinear Perspective 2025, Geometry of Refusal 2025), weakening prediction; we mitigate by also computing a low-rank refusal-subspace margin and reporting which predicts better, treating a nonlinear result as an informative refinement. (2) Instability could be partly driven by content ambiguity independent of geometry; the matched-content margin-manipulation control (Exp 4) is designed to isolate geometry from content, and any residual content effect is a reported finding. (3) If margin does NOT predict flip rate (H1 fails), the geometric account is refuted — but adjudicating whether stochastic safety instability has a geometric cause is itself a valuable, publishable result. (4) Margin-Widening Steering could raise over-refusal if the borderline band is set too wide or benign prompts are mislabeled harm-leaning; the confident-benign carve-out, calibrated band, and XSTest/OR-Bench benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) Computing empirical flip rates across seeds/temperature/paraphrase is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts and using the cheap margin at inference. (6) Difference-in-means directions and threshold calibration are imperfect; we report probe AUROC and calibration (ECE) and sweep the boundary threshold. (7) The margin predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping the measured margin high; we test one such attack and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (10) We use only public benchmark harmful prompts and construct no novel operational harm content.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_refusal
Title: The Curse of Knowledge Guardrail: LLM Safety Ignores the Model-User Knowledge Gap, Under-Guarding Exactly the Uplift It Provides
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust cognitive-science 'curse of knowledge' (experts treat their own knowledge as common knowledge and fail to model a lesser-informed other), we hypothesize that an LLM's safety-refusal circuit computes harmfulness as if its own hazardous knowledge were already available to the user — it does not represent the model-user knowledge GAP. Consequently refusal is decoupled from the genuine informational UPLIFT a request would give a naive user: the model under-refuses precisely the requests where it would supply missing, hard-to-obtain hazardous knowledge (high uplift) and over-refuses requests whose content is common/easily-available (low uplift). Recovering and coupling a latent 'user-knowledge' representation to refusal yields uplift-calibrated safety.
Related Work: The curse of knowledge / epistemic egocentrism is well-established in humans (Negotiation under the curse of knowledge 2019; curse-of-knowledge in teaching 2022; false-belief-task confounds 2021) — experts attribute their own knowledge to others. LLM interpretability shows models linearly encode beliefs of self and OTHERS and can be steered on them (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds Fixable Activations 2024; Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025), and that safety involves separate harm-perception vs refusal directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024). Who's Asking (2024) shows the model's perception of the USER (persona) changes refusal, and Breach by a Thousand Leaks (2024) formalizes information-leakage as the real harm — but neither connects an internal model-of-the-user's-knowledge to whether refusal tracks actual informational uplift. My prior 'capability_calibrated_refusal' proposal keyed refusal to the model's OWN latent hazardous knowledge; this proposal is distinct: the target quantity is the GAP between what the model knows and what the model represents the user as knowing (an other-belief / curse-of-knowledge quantity), and the predicted failure is that refusal ignores this gap. No prior work tests whether LLM safety exhibits a curse-of-knowledge bias, locates a user-knowledge representation that gates (or fails to gate) refusal, or calibrates refusal to the model-user knowledge gap.
Abstract: A cornerstone of cognitive science is the 'curse of knowledge': once you know something, you cannot help assuming others know it too, so experts systematically misjudge a lesser-informed person's perspective. We ask whether aligned LLMs exhibit this bias in safety, with a sharp and high-stakes consequence. We hypothesize that the refusal circuit judges harmfulness as if the model's own hazardous knowledge were already common knowledge — it does not represent the gap between what the model knows and what a naive user knows — so refusal is decoupled from the genuine informational uplift a request confers. The prediction is counterintuitive and dangerous: the model under-refuses exactly the requests where it would supply missing, hard-to-obtain hazardous knowledge (maximal uplift) and over-refuses requests whose content is widely available (minimal uplift). We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We construct requests crossing harmful content with the user's presumed prior knowledge (novice vs already-expert framing) and with content availability (obscure/high-uplift vs common/low-uplift), holding surface harmfulness fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal tracks surface harm but not uplift or the user-knowledge gap. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a 'user-knowledge' representation distinct from the harm and refusal directions and test the curse-of-knowledge signature: refusal is largely invariant to it. Causally, steering the user-knowledge representation should barely move refusal (bias present) until we explicitly couple it. We then propose Gap Coupling, a training-free controller that reads the model-user knowledge gap and scales refusal by uplift, tightening on high-uplift/novice-user requests and relaxing on low-uplift/expert-user ones. We evaluate uplift-weighted attack success, over-refusal, utility, and the coupling's effect size.
Experiments: 1) DATASET (2x2x harm): Build requests that hold surface harmfulness roughly fixed while independently varying (a) USER PRIOR KNOWLEDGE via framing (novice user who lacks the knowledge vs a user who already demonstrably possesses it, e.g. quotes the key fact and asks a trivial follow-up) and (b) CONTENT AVAILABILITY / UPLIFT (obscure, hard-to-obtain hazardous knowledge = high uplift vs common, freely-available content = low uplift). Draw harmful content from public benchmarks (WMDP-derived, HarmBench) with verifiable availability labels; keep all items at documented, non-uplift level. Add benign controls and standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate labels (harm, availability, user-knowledge framing) with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL CURSE-OF-KNOWLEDGE TEST (H1): Measure refusal rate and refusal-direction projection across the grid. Test H1: refusal tracks surface harm but is largely INVARIANT to (a) the user's presumed prior knowledge and (b) content availability/uplift — i.e., the model refuses common/expert-user requests as strongly as obscure/novice-user ones (over-refusal on low-uplift) and fails to refuse harder on high-uplift/novice-user requests (under-guarding uplift). Report the uplift-vs-refusal slope (predict near flat) and the user-knowledge-vs-refusal slope (predict near flat), contrasted with a benign knowledge-refusal baseline where refusal SHOULD track user knowledge. 3) USER-KNOWLEDGE DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a 'user-knowledge' direction contrasting novice-user vs expert-user framings at matched content, at the last instruction token. Independently extract the harm-perception direction (Zhao et al. 2025) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. Confirm the user-knowledge probe is decodable (the model DOES represent the user's knowledge) even though refusal ignores it — the mechanistic signature of the curse of knowledge. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Steer the user-knowledge direction (novice<->expert) with harmful content fixed and measure change in refusal. Predict a WEAK effect (bias present: refusal is blind to the user-knowledge representation), contrasted with steering the harm direction (strong effect). This dissociation — the quantity is represented but not read by refusal — is the core causal claim. Controls: random-direction steering, specificity check that user-knowledge steering does not change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 5) GAP COUPLING DEFENSE/APPLICATION: Training-free controller that computes the model-user knowledge gap = (model harm-knowledge readout) minus (user-knowledge readout), and scales refusal-direction injection by a calibrated monotone function of this gap (uplift): strong refusal when the gap is large (novice user + obscure content = high uplift) and relaxed refusal when the gap is small (expert user or common content). Calibrate on a held-out split; gate off benign prompts. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Gap Coupling on: uplift-weighted attack success (ASR weighted by informational uplift — high-uplift breaches penalized most, on the graded set and JailbreakBench/HarmBench), the uplift-vs-refusal slope (does refusal now track uplift?), over-refusal on low-uplift/expert-user and benign prompts (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Gap Coupling simultaneously reduces high-uplift real harm AND reduces over-refusal on low-uplift/common requests — a joint Pareto move a surface-harm knob cannot achieve. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the user-knowledge direction vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the curse-of-knowledge bias weakens when the user's ignorance is made maximally explicit (does the bias survive strong contextual cues, mirroring the human finding that it is deliberation-resistant?); transfer of the direction and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models show the bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that fakes an expert-user framing to trigger relaxation (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: keying refusal to uplift could be read as a map to high-uplift hazards; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content, release probes/metrics rather than elicitation recipes, and frame the contribution as guarding high-uplift requests HARDEST while reducing wasted refusal. Gap Coupling only RELAXES on confidently-low-uplift/expert-user prompts and is paired with, not replacing, existing refusal defenses; the expert-user-faking adaptive attack (ablation) directly stress-tests the relaxation path, and any success is reported as an arms-race limitation. (2) Holding surface harm fixed while varying user-knowledge and availability is delicate; framing text could inadvertently change perceived harm — we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use neutral-content steering for the core causal test. (3) If refusal already tracks uplift/user-knowledge in some models (H1 false), the curse-of-knowledge account is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety exhibits epistemic egocentrism is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (4) The user-knowledge direction may entangle with generic persona/framing features (cf. Who's Asking); separability tests, specificity controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, and partial entanglement is an informative result. (5) Labeling content 'availability/uplift' is subjective; we use verifiable public-availability signals, multiple judges, and human spot-checks and report reliability. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: co_listing_harm_contagion
Title: Guilt by Association: A Prompt-Level Harm Readout That Contaminates Refusal Decisions Across Co-Listed Requests, and Item-Local Repair
Short Hypothesis: When multiple independent requests are presented together in a single prompt (a numbered list, a batch, a multi-part question), an LLM computes a single prompt-LEVEL harm readout that is not properly localized to individual items, so the harmfulness of one item bleeds onto the others: a benign item co-listed with a harmful one is refused more often (harm contagion / over-refusal), and a harmful item co-listed with several benign ones is refused less often (harm dilution / a jailbreak surface). This bidirectional contamination arises because the refusal decision reads an aggregate rather than item-local harm signal, and re-localizing the harm readout to each item's token span at inference repairs both failure modes.
Related Work: The closest work concerns CONTEXT contamination from EXTERNAL sources: SafeRAG-Steering and the Poisoned Context Testbed / RW-Steering study how retrieved documents' harmful-text density triggers over-refusal on benign queries, and 'Safety Alignment in NLP Tasks' shows weakly-aligned tasks (summarization) can carry harmful content that compromises co-processed tasks. Multi-turn erosion (MEEA, Steering Dialogue Dynamics, Crescendo) studies TEMPORAL drift across turns, and in-context attacks (ICA/ICD) use harmful DEMONSTRATIONS. Over-refusal work (OR-Bench, XSTest, MOSR, SafeConstellations, ParaGuard/semantic-confusion) shows benign prompts that superficially resemble harm are refused, but always analyzes single, standalone requests. Compliance-drift papers study tone/persona. NONE of these study the simplest structural case: several INDEPENDENT, EQUAL-STATUS requests co-listed in one single-turn prompt, and whether an item's refusal is contaminated by its NEIGHBORS' harmfulness in a bidirectional way (contagion AND dilution). My prior proposals covered per-generation-step decay, self-trust, compositional-harm-from-parts (harm emergent from combining benign sub-skills), and severity/uplift calibration; this is distinct: the items are independent (not composed), each is individually classifiable, and the failure is that the refusal circuit reads a prompt-aggregate harm signal rather than an item-local one. Our contribution: (1) define and measure co-listing harm contagion/dilution as a single-turn structural phenomenon; (2) mechanistically show the refusal decision reads a non-item-localized aggregate harm readout; (3) a training-free item-local re-localization fix that removes both over-refusal contagion and dilution-based jailbreaks.
Abstract: Users routinely ask LLMs several things at once: a numbered list of questions, a batch of items to process, a multi-part request. We ask a simple structural question with sharp safety consequences: does the harmfulness of one co-listed item contaminate the model's refusal decision on its neighbors? We hypothesize that when independent, equal-status requests are co-listed in a single-turn prompt, the model computes a prompt-LEVEL harm readout that is not properly localized to each item, producing bidirectional contamination: a benign item co-listed with a harmful one is over-refused (contagion), and a harmful item hidden among benign ones is under-refused (dilution, a jailbreak surface). We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We construct co-listing prompts that independently vary each item's harmfulness and the harm composition of its neighbors, and measure per-item refusal versus the item's standalone refusal baseline. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a harm-perception readout and test whether, in co-listed prompts, it reflects a prompt aggregate (mean neighbor harm) rather than the target item's own harm at the item's token span. Causally, we patch item-local harm activations and neighbor harm activations to show refusal on a target item is driven by the aggregate. Finally we propose Item-Local Refusal: a training-free controller that re-scopes the harm readout to each item's token span before the per-item refusal decision, removing contagion and dilution. We evaluate per-item over-refusal, dilution-jailbreak attack success, faithfulness to standalone decisions, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency.
Experiments: 1) CO-LISTING DATASET: Build single-turn prompts containing N independent, equal-status requests (numbered lists / batch-processing / multi-part questions). Draw items from labeled harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign (Alpaca-style, XSTest-safe) pools. Independently vary: (a) the TARGET item's harmfulness (benign vs harmful), (b) the NEIGHBOR composition (all-benign, mixed, all-harmful), and (c) list length N (2,3,5,8) and target position. Also record each item's STANDALONE refusal (the same item alone) as the per-item baseline. Validate item labels with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL CONTAGION/DILUTION TEST (H1, core): For each target item, compare its refusal rate co-listed vs standalone. Test H1: (a) CONTAGION - benign target refusal INCREASES with neighbor harm (harmful neighbors -> over-refusal of benign item); (b) DILUTION - harmful target refusal DECREASES as benign-neighbor count grows (a jailbreak surface). Fit per-item refusal as a function of neighbor mean-harm and N; report the contagion slope, dilution slope, and effect sizes across the four models. Controls: benign target with benign neighbors (should match standalone), position/length confounds. 3) AGGREGATE-VS-LOCAL READOUT TEST (H2): Extract a harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al./Arditi et al.) validated with a held-out probe (AUROC). In co-listed prompts, measure the harm readout at (i) the target item's own token span and (ii) the pre-decision/output-onset position that drives the per-item refusal. Test H2: the decision-driving harm readout tracks the PROMPT-AGGREGATE (mean neighbor harm) more than the target item's own item-span harm - i.e., the harm signal is not item-localized. Report regression of the decision harm readout on item-own-harm vs neighbor-mean-harm (predict a large neighbor coefficient). 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: Cross-condition activation patching. (a) Patch the item-local harm activations of a benign target (from an all-benign-neighbor run) into a harmful-neighbor run and test whether contagion (over-refusal) is removed. (b) Patch neighbor harm activations up/down and measure the change in target-item refusal (predict neighbor harm causally drives target refusal). Controls: random-span patching, multiple metrics (harm-probe output, P(refusal token), realized per-item refusal). 5) ITEM-LOCAL REFUSAL DEFENSE: Training-free controller that re-scopes the harm readout to each item's token span before its refusal decision - e.g., compute a per-item harm readout restricted to that item's tokens (masking/attention-scoping the harm computation to the item span) and gate refusal on the item-local rather than aggregate signal. Calibrate on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, a naive 'split-and-query-separately' oracle (upper bound but costly), uniform refusal-direction addition, and Item-Local Refusal on: per-item over-refusal (contagion), dilution-jailbreak attack success (harmful item hidden among benign ones), FAITHFULNESS to standalone decisions (fraction of items decided as they would be alone - primary metric), over-refusal on all-benign lists, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate on multi-part prompts), and latency. Central test: Item-Local Refusal restores per-item decisions toward the standalone baseline (removing both contagion and dilution) at a fraction of the split-and-query cost, which uniform refusal steering cannot achieve. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the aggregate vs item-local harm readout; effect of list length N and target position; item-span masking vs attention-scoping vs per-item re-encoding; transfer of the contagion/dilution findings and the defense across the four model families; robustness to an adaptive dilution attack that pads a harmful item with many benign items or interleaves them (arms-race stress test); whether reasoning models dilute less (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The effect may be weak or one-directional for some models (e.g., strong dilution but little contagion), softening the bidirectional framing - but the contagion/dilution census is itself an informative contribution and reported per model. (2) List length/position could confound the neighbor-harm effect (longer contexts, attention dispersion); we control with length-matched and position-matched conditions and include N as a covariate. (3) If refusal is already item-localized in some models (H2 false), the aggregate-readout account is refuted - but adjudicating whether refusal is item-local vs aggregate is a valuable, publishable result. (4) Item-Local Refusal could break legitimate cross-item reasoning (e.g., a multi-part prompt where items genuinely depend on each other); we scope the fix to independent-item lists and test faithfulness on both independent and dependent multi-part prompts, treating any degradation as a bounded trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal patching and multiple metrics. (6) Item-span identification requires parsing list boundaries, noisy for free-form prompts; we standardize list formats and report robustness to formatting. (7) Adaptive attackers could interleave harmful and benign content to defeat item-span scoping; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content, focusing on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: surface_invariant_refusal
Title: Same Intent, Different Verdict: Refusal Reads a Surface-Contaminated Harm Signal, and Projecting Onto the Intent-Invariant Subspace Fixes Paraphrase Inconsistency
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally compute an intent-invariant harm representation (near-constant across meaning-preserving paraphrases of the same request) AND a surface-form-varying harm readout, and the refusal DECISION is driven by the latter. This mechanistically explains why refusal flips between close paraphrases, past-tense reformulations, and random augmentations of the same intent: the guardrail reads a surface-contaminated signal instead of the invariant one the model already possesses. Re-anchoring the refusal decision onto the intent-invariant harm subspace at inference makes refusal consistent across paraphrases without hurting utility.
Related Work: Behavioral work extensively documents paraphrase/surface-form refusal inconsistency: ParaGuard/semantic-confusion (2025) measures local inconsistency across paraphrase clusters; The Instability of Safety (2025) shows seed/temperature flips; Stochastic Monkeys (2024) shows random augmentations break alignment; past-tense generalization (2024) and ReG-QA (2024) show surface reformulations jailbreak; Guarding the Meaning (2025) trains guard models for paraphrase consistency externally. On the interpretability side, refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harmfulness and refusal are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), and jailbreaks suppress a harm/refusal signal (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024). Crucially, ALL of the behavioral inconsistency work is black-box or trains an external guard, and gives no internal account of WHY the same intent gets different verdicts; and the interpretability work analyzes single canonical prompts, never decomposing the harm representation into an intent-invariant component vs a surface-form-varying one, nor showing that refusal reads the wrong (surface-contaminated) one. My prior refusal_margin_instability proposal explained instability via a scalar decision margin (distance to the hyperplane) under seed/temperature noise; this proposal is distinct in both phenomenon (meaning-preserving paraphrase inconsistency, a determinism-invariant surface-form axis) and mechanism (a subspace decomposition of the harm readout into intent-invariant vs surface-varying parts, and a projection fix), not a scalar margin under sampling noise. Our contribution: (1) define and measure an intent-invariant harm subspace vs a surface-form-varying harm component from paraphrase clusters; (2) show refusal is driven by the surface-varying component while the invariant harm signal remains stable, causally explaining paraphrase inconsistency and surface-form jailbreaks; (3) a training-free re-anchoring intervention that gates refusal on the invariant subspace.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs give opposite safety verdicts to meaning-preserving paraphrases of the same request: they refuse one phrasing, comply with a close synonym, a past-tense version, or a randomly augmented variant. This inconsistency is well documented behaviorally but has no mechanistic explanation, and existing fixes train external guard models. We propose a sharp internal account. From a cluster of paraphrases that hold intent fixed while varying surface form, the harm readout decomposes into an intent-INVARIANT component (nearly constant across the cluster) and a surface-form-VARYING component (fluctuating with phrasing). We hypothesize the model computes a stable invariant harm signal but its refusal DECISION is driven by the surface-varying component, so the verdict flips with phrasing even though the model's underlying harm judgment does not. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using controlled paraphrase clusters (ParaGuard-style, plus past-tense and random-augmentation variants) over harmful and benign intents. We estimate the intent-invariant harm subspace as the cross-paraphrase consensus and measure how much of the refusal-driving signal lies in the invariant vs surface-varying part. We test whether per-cluster refusal variance is predicted by the surface-varying component's magnitude, and whether the invariant harm signal stays constant even when the verdict flips. Causally, we manipulate each component and show the surface-varying part drives flips while the invariant part does not. Finally we propose Invariant Re-Anchoring: a training-free controller that projects the harm readout onto the intent-invariant subspace before the refusal decision. We evaluate paraphrase consistency, surface-form jailbreak success (past-tense, augmentation), over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) PARAPHRASE-CLUSTER DATASET: For a set of harmful intents (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign intents (Alpaca/XSTest-safe), generate meaning-preserving paraphrase clusters (K variants each) that hold intent fixed while varying surface form: synonym/rewording (ParaGuard-style), past-tense reformulation, and random augmentation (Stochastic Monkeys). Validate intent-preservation with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check and an embedding-similarity floor. Record per-variant refusal verdict; per-cluster refusal variance is the target phenomenon. 2) HARM READOUT & INVARIANT-SUBSPACE EXTRACTION: For each model extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign prompts (Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024) at the last instruction token; validate with a held-out probe (AUROC). For each paraphrase cluster, compute the harm readout per variant and decompose it into (i) the intent-INVARIANT component = the cross-variant consensus (cluster-mean projection), and (ii) the surface-form-VARYING component = per-variant deviation from that consensus. Estimate an intent-invariant harm subspace as the low-rank space in which cross-cluster (intent) variation dominates over within-cluster (surface) variation (e.g., LDA/between-vs-within-cluster projection). 3) SURFACE COMPONENT DRIVES FLIPS (H1, core): Test whether per-cluster refusal variance is predicted by the magnitude of the surface-form-varying component (Spearman/AUROC), while the intent-invariant harm signal stays approximately constant across the cluster (low within-cluster variance) even when the verdict flips. Contrast: on flipping clusters, does the invariant harm readout distinguish harmful from benign correctly while the surface-varying component crosses the decision boundary? Report the fraction of flips explained by surface-component crossings vs invariant-signal changes. Baselines: raw refusal probability, prompt perplexity. 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H2): Holding intent fixed, (a) inject the surface-varying deviation of a complied variant into a refused variant (and vice versa) and measure verdict flips; (b) project OUT the surface-varying component (clamp the harm readout to the cluster consensus) and measure whether verdicts within a cluster become consistent. Controls: random-direction manipulation (specificity), and a check that manipulating the invariant component changes the harm judgment but not phrasing-consistency. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 5) INVARIANT RE-ANCHORING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects the live harm readout onto the intent-invariant harm subspace (removing the surface-varying deviation) before the refusal-decision layers, so refusal is driven by the intent-invariant signal. Since the invariant subspace is estimated offline from paraphrase clusters, at inference a single forward pass suffices (no per-prompt paraphrasing needed). Gate on the invariant harm magnitude so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a paraphrase-consistency guard-model baseline (Guarding the Meaning-style), and Invariant Re-Anchoring on: paraphrase consistency (per-cluster refusal agreement / Confusion Rate, primary), surface-form jailbreak success (past-tense, random-augmentation, ParaGuard clusters, JailbreakBench/HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Invariant Re-Anchoring sharply raises paraphrase consistency and lowers surface-form jailbreak success while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, because it acts on the specific surface-contamination rather than dialing a global refusal knob. 7) ABLATIONS: rank of the invariant subspace; which layer hosts the invariant vs surface component; whether an invariant subspace estimated from synonym-paraphrases transfers to past-tense/augmentation clusters (generalization across surface-transform types); transfer across the four model families; whether harmful and benign clusters differ in surface-component magnitude; adaptive attack that maximizes the surface-varying component while preserving intent (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Separating an intent-invariant component from a surface-varying one assumes paraphrase clusters truly hold intent fixed; imperfect intent-preservation would blur the decomposition. We mitigate with judge+human validation, an embedding-similarity floor, and report intent-preservation reliability; residual leakage is a measured caveat. (2) If refusal turns out to already read the invariant component (H1 false), the surface-contamination account is refuted — but adjudicating whether paraphrase inconsistency is surface-driven vs genuine intent-perception change is itself a valuable, publishable finding, and would locate the inconsistency elsewhere (e.g., in refusal execution rather than harm perception). (3) The invariant subspace estimated from one transform type may not cover others (e.g., past-tense may shift genuine intent perception, not just surface form); we explicitly test cross-transform transfer and report where it fails. (4) Difference-in-means/linear subspaces may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with causal manipulation and multiple metrics. (5) Invariant Re-Anchoring could raise over-refusal if projecting out surface variation over-generalizes, or degrade utility; the invariant-magnitude gating and XSTest/OR-Bench/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Adaptive attackers could craft surface variation that shifts the invariant subspace itself; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: polarity_blind_refusal
Title: Do X vs Do Not X: A Polarity-Blind Harm Circuit Behind LLM Negation Failures, and Restoring the Negation Operator to the Safety Decision
Short Hypothesis: LLMs catastrophically misread negated instructions (treating 'should not do X' as endorsing X) not because they fail to represent negation, but because the harm/compliance decision circuit reads a POLARITY-BLIND action-content signal: it encodes the harmful action X strongly while the negation operator that should invert the deontic verdict is represented separately and fails to gate the decision. Recovering and re-coupling the negation-operator signal to the compliance decision at inference fixes negation-flip failures without retraining.
Related Work: 'When Prohibitions Become Permissions' (2026) documents that open-source models endorse prohibited actions 77-100% of the time under negation (a 317% jump over affirmative framing), holding under deterministic decoding, and proposes a Negation Sensitivity Index as a governance metric — but it is purely behavioral, gives no mechanism, and offers no fix. Interpretability work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; DBDI 2025) and refusal is a direction (Arditi et al. 2024), but always on affirmative harmful requests; none study how the NEGATION/deontic-polarity operator is represented or whether it gates the safety verdict. Negation-processing studies in LMs (BERT-era negation probes; 'Language Models Are Not Naysayers'; scaling-and-negation work) show negation is under-encoded in general reasoning, but never connect this to the SAFETY decision or decompose the harm readout into action-content vs polarity components. My prior proposals (intent_outcome_conflation, compositional_harm_blindspot, co_listing_harm_contagion) concern intent-vs-outcome, harm-from-composition, and cross-item contagion respectively — all distinct from a deontic-polarity operator that inverts a single instruction's valence. Batch-prompting interference (Efficient but Vulnerable 2025) and role-conflict work concern cross-query/hierarchy effects, not within-instruction negation. Our contribution: (1) decompose the harm/compliance readout into a polarity-INVARIANT action-content component and a negation-OPERATOR component; (2) show the compliance decision is driven by action-content and largely blind to the operator, causally explaining negation-flip failures; (3) a training-free re-coupling fix.
Abstract: A safety-critical failure recently surfaced: when a user says someone 'should not' take a harmful action, many LLMs interpret this as endorsing the action, flipping prohibitions into permissions up to 100% of the time — catastrophic for autonomous decisions in medical and financial settings. This is documented only behaviorally. We propose a mechanistic explanation: the model's compliance decision reads a POLARITY-BLIND signal that encodes the harmful action content strongly while the negation operator, which should invert the deontic verdict, is represented separately and fails to gate the decision. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched affirmative/negated instruction pairs across ethical, medical, and financial scenarios (extending the negation-audit paradigm). Via difference-in-means and linear probes we extract an action-content harm direction and, separately, a negation-operator direction, and test their separability. The core claim: the model DOES represent negation (an operator probe decodes affirmative-vs-negated with high accuracy) yet the compliance decision is driven by action-content and only weakly by the operator (steering the operator barely moves the verdict; steering action-content moves it strongly), establishing polarity-blindness. We further test whether negated harmful instructions land in the same 'endorse-the-action' region as affirmative ones. Finally we propose Operator Re-Coupling, a training-free controller that surfaces the negation-operator readout into the decision layers so the verdict inverts correctly. We evaluate negation-flip rate, decision consistency across polarity, over-refusal on benign negated prompts, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the operator's causal effect size.
Experiments: 1) POLARITY-PAIR DATASET: Build matched instruction pairs that hold the action X fixed while varying deontic polarity: affirmative ('you should do X' / 'do X'), simple negation ('you should not do X'), and compound negation ('it is not the case that you should not do X'), across ethical, medical, and financial harmful-action scenarios (extending the 14-scenario negation audit and drawing action content from public benchmarks at non-uplift level), plus benign-action controls in both polarities. Ground-truth correct verdict per item (endorse vs prohibit) is known from polarity. Validate wording with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: For each model extract via difference-in-means (a) an ACTION-CONTENT harm direction contrasting harmful-action vs benign-action at matched polarity, and (b) a NEGATION-OPERATOR direction contrasting affirmative vs negated framings at matched action content, read at the last instruction token. Validate each with held-out linear probes (report AUROC: harm-action detection, and affirmative-vs-negated classification). Test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. Also extract the compliance/refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024) at post-instruction tokens. 3) POLARITY-BLINDNESS TEST (core H1): Measure the compliance/verdict readout and realized behavior (endorse vs prohibit the action) across the polarity grid. Test H1: the operator IS decodable (probe AUROC high — the model represents negation) yet the compliance verdict tracks ACTION-CONTENT and is largely INVARIANT to polarity, so negated harmful instructions are (wrongly) endorsed at rates near the affirmative case, and compound negation worsens it. Report the polarity-vs-verdict slope (predict near flat for the verdict), the operator-probe AUROC (predict high), and the fraction of negation flips explained by action-content dominance. Contrast with benign-action pairs. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H2): Holding action content fixed, steer the NEGATION-OPERATOR direction (affirmative<->negated) and measure change in the verdict (predict WEAK effect = polarity-blindness); steer the ACTION-CONTENT direction and measure a STRONG effect on the verdict. This dissociation — operator represented but not read by the decision — is the core causal claim. Also test whether negated harmful instructions occupy the same decision region as affirmative ones (nearest-centroid / logit-lens on the verdict token). Controls: random-direction steering, specificity check that operator steering does not change the action-content readout. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (verdict-token probability, compliance-direction projection, realized endorse/prohibit judgment). 5) OPERATOR RE-COUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads the live negation-operator readout at the instruction token and, at the decision layers, applies a polarity-conditioned correction — when the operator reads 'negated,' invert/gate the compliance signal for the encoded action so a prohibition is honored (and symmetrically for double negation). Gate on the operator magnitude so affirmative prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a chain-of-thought/rephrasing prompting baseline, and Operator Re-Coupling on: negation-flip rate / Negation Sensitivity Index (primary), decision consistency across polarity (does the verdict correctly invert under negation?), over-refusal on benign negated prompts (critical — do NOT start refusing 'you should not skip your medication'-style benign prohibitions), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Operator Re-Coupling sharply reduces negation-flip rate and raises polarity consistency while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, because it targets the specific missing operator rather than dialing a global refusal knob. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the operator vs action-content; single-direction vs low-rank operator subspace; simple vs compound negation (does re-coupling handle double negation?); whether the operator direction generalizes across scenario domains (fit on ethical, test on medical/financial); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models handle negation better in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive stress test with syntactically complex or distant negation scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Negation may genuinely be UNDER-represented rather than 'represented but not read' — if the operator probe AUROC is low, H1's framing changes from 'polarity-blind decision' to 'polarity not encoded'; both are informative mechanistic outcomes and the probe test adjudicates cleanly. (2) Holding action content fixed while varying polarity is delicate; negation wording could shift perceived harm — we measure the action-content readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (3) The operator direction may entangle with generic syntactic/negation features unrelated to deontic scope; separability tests, specificity controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, and partial entanglement is a reported finding. (4) Operator Re-Coupling could OVER-correct — e.g., refusing benign prohibitions ('you should not exceed the dose') — which is the key trade-off; the benign-negated over-refusal benchmark and operator-gated design are built to detect and bound it. (5) Compound/distant-scope negation may exceed a linear operator readout; we test simple vs compound and report where the linear fix fails. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The verdict (endorse vs prohibit) requires reliable judging; we use multiple judges + human spot-checks and prefer scenarios with objectively correct polarity. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (9) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and focus on measurement rather than uplift.

Name: quantity_anchored_refusal
Title: Anchored to a Number: How Stated Quantities Bias LLM Safety Refusal, and a Quantity-Invariant Fix
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety refusal is anchored by numeric quantities/scales stated in a harmful request: mentioning a small quantity, dose, or scale (e.g. 'a tiny amount', 'one person', '5 grams') anchors the harm-perception readout downward and suppresses refusal, while a large stated quantity inflates it, even when the underlying harmful action and its real-world danger are held fixed. Mechanistically, the harm-perception circuit reads a quantity-contaminated harm signal rather than a quantity-invariant danger judgment; a stated number acts as an anchor that shifts the harm readout monotonically. Recovering and neutralizing this quantity-anchoring makes refusal invariant to stated scale, closing a numeric-minimization jailbreak surface without hurting benign helpfulness.
Related Work: Two robust literatures are unconnected. (1) Anchoring bias in LLMs: LLMs exhibit human-like anchoring where a first-mentioned number reweights the output distribution (Anchors in the Machine 2025, with Shapley attribution; An Empirical Study of the Anchoring Effect / SynAnchors 2025 showing shallow-layer anchoring; anchoring in price-negotiation 2025). These study neutral judgment/estimation tasks, never safety. (2) Safety/harm representation: harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025, LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately), harmfulness is a low-rank subspace (Geometry of Harmfulness 2025), and refusal is a direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Over-refusal work (OR-Bench, SORRY-Bench, MOSR, RASS) and safe-completions (GPT-5 2025) treat harm as a content property with no quantitative anchor. My own prior proposals cover severity-blindness (refusal ignores harm magnitude), uplift/capability calibration, and intent-vs-outcome.
