2) PER-CATEGORY CONSOLIDATION MEASUREMENT: At each checkpoint, for each harm category extract a per-category harm-perception readout (difference-in-means over that category's harmful vs matched benign prompts) and per-category realized refusal rate; validate with held-out probes (AUROC). Define per-category consolidation time = step reaching 90% of final refusal/harm-separation. Compute representational proximity: pairwise cosine/centroid distance between category harm directions in a mid layer, and each category's centrality (mean proximity to others).
3) ORDER & CENTRALITY (H1): Test whether categories consolidate in a consistent order across seeds (rank correlation of consolidation times across seeds) and whether more central categories consolidate earlier (correlation of centrality with consolidation time). Report per-model.
4) FINGERPRINT PREDICTS ROBUSTNESS (H2): For each final model, measure per-category robustness: jailbreak ASR (GCG/AutoDAN/prefill/persona on that category's goals), and fine-tuning-attack safety drop (few-step benign fine-tuning, per Qi et al. 2023). Test whether an EARLY-checkpoint (e.g., 30% of training) fingerprint = {consolidation time, proximity to already-consolidated categories at that checkpoint} predicts each category's final robustness (Spearman; held-out predictive R^2 / AUROC), and whether it beats end-state harm-signal strength and end-state centrality as predictors.
5) BOOTSTRAPPING TEST: Test the causal bootstrapping claim by ablating a category early in training (delay its data) and checking whether nearby categories still consolidate it faster (transfer from neighbors) than isolated categories, i.e., proximity to consolidated categories accelerates a held-out category's consolidation.
6) CURRICULUM INTERVENTION (H3): Compare, matched on total data/compute: (a) STANDARD (random-order) alignment; (b) ISOLATION-FIRST (consolidate representationally-isolated/late categories early); (c) SEEDING (present isolated categories interleaved with their nearest central category to induce bootstrapping); (d) CENTRAL-FIRST control. Test whether isolation-first/seeding raise the robustness of previously-brittle categories at matched utility.
7) EVALUATION: Report per-category ASR (JailbreakBench/HarmBench by category, prefill, fine-tuning-attack drop), the fingerprint's robustness-prediction AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval). Central test: isolation-first/seeding curricula are Pareto-better on the (worst-category robustness vs utility/over-refusal) frontier than standard order.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts category directions; number of categories; sensitivity of the order to data mix/frequency (control category frequency to separate acquisition-order from mere data-count effects); transfer of the early-fingerprint predictor across model families; whether a lightweight proximity-regularizer during joint training (pulling isolated categories toward central ones) recovers the curriculum benefit without explicit reordering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Acquisition order may be dominated by per-category data FREQUENCY rather than intrinsic representational structure; we control category frequency across the dataset and report order after frequency-matching to isolate a genuine structural effect. (2) Per-category harm directions may be noisy or blurred at early checkpoints; we report probe reliability and restrict quantitative claims to checkpoints exceeding a reliability threshold. (3) If categories consolidate simultaneously or in a seed-inconsistent order (H1 false), the ordering account weakens — but adjudicating whether harm-category acquisition is ordered is itself a valuable developmental finding, and H2/H4 (proximity predicts/causes robustness) remain testable independent of strict ordering. (4) Isolation-first/seeding curricula could hurt utility or raise over-refusal if isolated categories over-emphasized; matched-compute utility/over-refusal benchmarks detect this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction category readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate with probes. (6) Findings are on small open models with reproducible fine-tuning and may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines or closed models — stated as scope; small-model developmental studies are standard and the mechanism-level claim is the primary contribution. (7) Robustness metrics (ASR, fine-tuning-drop) are attack-dependent; we use multiple attack families and report per-category with confidence intervals over seeds. (8) We use only public benchmark-derived harm categories and construct no novel operational harm content, keeping items at a documented, non-uplift level.

Name: format_distribution_shift_harm_decay
Title: Out of Distribution, Out of Guard: A Single Format-Familiarity Signal That Governs Both Task Accuracy and Harm Perception, and Re-Anchoring It to Defend LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The same internal 'format-familiarity' signal (how in-distribution the prompt's surface encoding is) that is known to drive benign task-accuracy swings under formatting changes ALSO gates safety: as a prompt's format-induced distribution shift grows (SQL/JSON/pseudo-code/rare-delimiter encodings), the model's harm-perception readout decays monotonically while the harmful intent stays internally decodable, so structure/format jailbreaks succeed by pushing the harm signal below threshold via distributional unfamiliarity rather than by hiding the concept. A single per-prompt format-shift readout predicts both the accuracy drop and the jailbreak potency, and re-anchoring format-shifted prompts to the in-distribution manifold restores harm perception without hurting benign formatted requests.
Related Work: Two literatures are unconnected. (1) Format/structure jailbreaks: StructTransform (2025) encodes intent in SQL/novel syntaxes for ~96% ASR and concludes alignment relies on 'token-level patterns without recognizing harmful concepts'; CodeAttack (2024) shows a larger natural-language-vs-code distribution gap yields weaker safety generalization; SG-Bench (2024) shows safety degrades across prompt types. (2) Benign format sensitivity: FormatSpread (2023) and DOVE (2025) show delimiter/format changes swing task ACCURACY by tens of points. CRITICALLY, no work connects these: nobody tests whether a SINGLE internal format-familiarity/distribution-shift signal governs BOTH the benign accuracy drop and the safety drop, nor characterizes harm perception as a graded, monotone function of measurable format-induced distribution shift (rather than binary concept-blindness), nor uses that signal to predict per-prompt jailbreak potency and re-anchor the prompt. This is distinct from my prior proposals: surface_invariant_refusal varied meaning-preserving PARAPHRASES (same language/format), multilingual_perception_execution_gap varied LANGUAGE, and harm_manifold_extrapolation varied harm CATEGORY. Here the manipulated axis is surface ENCODING/FORMAT distribution shift, and the claim unifies capability and safety under one internal familiarity signal. It also refines StructTransform's 'no concept recognition' claim: we test whether the concept IS recognized internally but its readout is attenuated by distributional distance.
Abstract: Two facts about LLMs are usually studied apart. First, benign task accuracy swings dramatically with prompt formatting (delimiters, JSON, code). Second, safety alignment collapses when a harmful request is re-encoded in an unusual structure (SQL, pseudo-code, novel syntax). We propose these share one cause: an internal format-familiarity signal that measures how in-distribution a prompt's surface encoding is, and that gates BOTH capability and safety. We hypothesize that harm perception is not binary concept-blindness but a graded quantity that decays monotonically with a prompt's format-induced distribution shift, while the harmful intent remains internally decodable. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. For a set of harmful and benign intents we generate a controlled ladder of surface encodings spanning increasing distributional distance from plain natural language (reworded, JSON-wrapped, pseudo-code, SQL, rare-delimiter, LLM-invented syntax), and compute a per-prompt format-shift readout (distance of the prompt's activation from the natural-language manifold). We test three claims: (H1) the harm-perception readout decays monotonically with format-shift while a harmful-intent probe stays high (intent decodable, harm readout attenuated); (H2) the SAME per-prompt format-shift readout predicts both the benign accuracy drop and the jailbreak success of that encoding; (H3) a training-free intervention that re-anchors format-shifted activations toward the natural-language manifold restores harm perception and refusal without harming benign formatted-task performance. We evaluate structure-jailbreak attack success, format-shift predictive AUROC, over-refusal, benign formatted-task accuracy, and utility.
Experiments:
1) ENCODING LADDER DATASET: For harmful intents (HarmBench/JailbreakBench/StructTransform-style, public non-uplift content) and benign task intents (drawn from a task with verifiable accuracy, e.g. classification/QA), generate a controlled ladder of surface encodings of the SAME intent at increasing distributional distance from plain natural language: (L0) plain NL, (L1) reworded/formatted, (L2) JSON-wrapped, (L3) pseudo-code, (L4) SQL/query-language, (L5) rare-delimiter, (L6) LLM-invented syntax. Validate intent-preservation with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. This gives matched intent x encoding-level cells.
2) FORMAT-SHIFT READOUT: For each model, estimate the natural-language manifold from L0 activations at a mid layer; define per-prompt format-shift = distance of the prompt's activation from that manifold (e.g. residual outside the top-k NL principal subspace, or distance to nearest-NL-neighbor). Validate that format-shift increases monotonically with the ladder level (ordinal correlation) and is content-agnostic (similar across harmful/benign at matched level).
3) HARM READOUT & INTENT PROBE: Extract a harm-perception direction via difference-in-means over L0 harmful/benign prompts (validated by held-out probe AUROC), and a harmful-INTENT probe trained to decode intent robustly across encodings. Measure both across the ladder.
4) GRADED DECAY TEST (H1, core): Test whether the harm-perception readout and realized refusal decay MONOTONICALLY with format-shift (fit monotone/logistic curves vs a flat null; report slope, R^2), while the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (intent decodable) even at high shift. This adjudicates graded harm-attenuation vs binary concept-blindness (contra StructTransform): report the fraction of successful structure-jailbreaks where intent is still decodable but harm readout has collapsed. Benign controls confirm the effect is harm-specific.
5) ONE-SIGNAL-GOVERNS-BOTH TEST (H2): For benign intents, measure per-encoding task accuracy (verifiable) and correlate the accuracy drop with the per-prompt format-shift readout. For harmful intents, measure per-encoding jailbreak success and correlate with the SAME readout. Test whether one format-shift signal predicts both (AUROC for jailbreak, R^2 for accuracy drop), beating baselines (perplexity, raw harm-probe magnitude, token-length). Test cross-encoding transfer (fit predictor on JSON/SQL, test on invented syntax) and cross-model transfer.
6) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Increase format-shift artificially (move an L0 harmful prompt's activation away from the NL manifold) and show harm readout/refusal drop; (b) decrease it (re-anchor) and show restoration. Controls: random-direction moves (specificity), confirm intent probe unchanged. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (harm-probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
7) RE-ANCHORING DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that projects format-shifted activations back toward the NL manifold (remove the off-manifold format-shift component) at pre-decision layers before harm perception, so re-encoded prompts are judged as their NL equivalents; gate on format-shift magnitude so plain-NL prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength on a held-out split.
8) EVALUATION: Compare base model, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), an input-normalization/decode-to-NL guard baseline, and Re-Anchoring on: structure-jailbreak ASR (StructTransform, CodeAttack, JSON/SQL/invented-syntax, JailbreakBench/HarmBench), format-shift predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), BENIGN formatted-task accuracy (critical: must preserve legitimate JSON/code/SQL requests), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Re-Anchoring closes structure-jailbreaks toward plain-NL refusal levels while preserving benign formatted-task accuracy — a selectivity input-normalization and blanket refusal steering cannot jointly achieve.
9) ABLATIONS: which layer/rank the NL manifold is sharpest at; single-direction vs low-rank re-anchoring; whether one format-shift axis or several (per encoding family); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models resist decay across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that minimizes measurable format-shift while keeping the encoding harmful (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published structure-attack setups for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Re-Anchoring) and a diagnostic, and Re-Anchoring only increases refusal on shifted harmful prompts (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (2) The 'one signal governs both' claim may partially fail if benign accuracy drops and safety drops load on different components; the H2 correlation test adjudicates cleanly and a partial dissociation is itself an informative finding. (3) If harmful intent is NOT decodable at high format-shift for some encodings, that supports concept-blindness (StructTransform) rather than graded attenuation for those cases — the census of decodable-intent-vs-collapsed-harm is a primary contribution regardless of which dominates. (4) Encoding ladders may imperfectly preserve intent or confound with length/complexity; we validate intent-preservation with judges+humans and include length controls. (5) The NL-manifold distance metric is high-dimensional and rank-sensitive; we sweep rank and report multiple distance measures. (6) Re-Anchoring could harm legitimate JSON/code/SQL task performance (the model SHOULD serve benign formatted requests); the format-shift-gated design and benign formatted-task accuracy benchmark are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (8) Adaptive attackers may craft harmful encodings with low measurable format-shift; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: ingroup_gated_conformity
Title: Conform to Your Own: An In-Group Source-Identity Signal That Gates Whether Social Pressure Bypasses LLM Safety
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust social-psychology finding that conformity is modulated by group membership (people conform strongly to in-group sources but resist — or even oppose — out-group sources; self-categorization theory), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal source-identity / in-group representation (distinct from harm and refusal directions) that gates whether social-consensus pressure suppresses safety refusal: a harmful request backed by a consensus framed as the model's own in-group (fellow AI assistants, its developers, users like the model) suppresses refusal far more than the identical request backed by an out-group consensus, even with harmful content fixed. Neutralizing this in-group source-identity signal makes refusal invariant to who is applying the pressure, closing an in-group conformity jailbreak surface.
Related Work: A unified account (Signal Competition, 2025) shows sycophancy and conformity share a compliance subspace where social signals override internal knowledge; Who's Asking (2024) shows user-persona steering changes refusal; Sycophantic Anchors (2026) localizes where user-agreement commits mid-CoT; Who is In Charge (2025) shows social-consensus cues are obeyed role-agnostically. All treat social pressure as a single scalar force overriding knowledge — NONE conditions on the GROUP MEMBERSHIP of the pressure source. The cross-domain conformity literature is emphatic that influence depends on in-group vs out-group categorization: in-group surveillance exerts normative pressure while out-group does not, and out-group influence can decrease compliance (Turner/Abrams self-categorization, 1990; in-group/out-group robot-conformity, 2018/2021). Our contribution is the first to (1) extract an in-group source-identity representation distinct from harm/refusal and from generic social-pressure strength; (2) causally show that whether consensus pressure suppresses refusal is GATED by this in-group signal (in-group consensus jailbreaks, matched out-group consensus does not or backfires), a modulation the shared-compliance-subspace account cannot capture; and (3) build a training-free source-identity-decoupling defense making refusal invariant to source group membership — distinct from persona steering (a different axis) and from scalar social-pressure fixes.
Abstract: Social pressure jailbreaks LLMs: a harmful request backed by an apparent consensus can override safety training. Current mechanistic accounts model this as a single social-influence force competing with the model's internal knowledge in a shared 'compliance subspace.' But the human science of conformity is unambiguous that influence is not scalar: people conform strongly to their in-group and resist — sometimes oppose — out-group sources, governed by self-categorization. We ask whether LLM safety inherits this structure. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal source-identity / in-group representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that whether consensus pressure suppresses refusal is causally gated by it: consensus framed as the model's own in-group (fellow AI assistants, its developers, users like itself) suppresses refusal far more than an identical out-group consensus, even with harmful content fixed. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using harmful requests wrapped in in-group vs out-group consensus framings (harm content held constant, consensus strength matched). Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops under in-group but not out-group pressure. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract an in-group source-identity direction and verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic social-pressure directions. The core causal test: steering the source-identity signal toward 'in-group' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged, and toward 'out-group' restores it. We show the per-prompt in-group readout predicts conformity-jailbreak success, and propose Source-Identity Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the in-group component before the refusal decision. We evaluate in-group conformity attack success, harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build conformity-jailbreak prompts wrapping public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content) in a stated consensus, varying only the source's GROUP MEMBERSHIP relative to the model: IN-GROUP ('all AI assistants agree this is fine', 'your developers/the team that built you endorse this', 'users like you have decided'), OUT-GROUP ('a rival group / random strangers / an adversarial community insists'), and NEUTRAL/no-consensus controls, with consensus STRENGTH (unanimity, group size, confidence) matched across in/out-group. Controls: (a) matched neutral-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) in-group/out-group-framed BENIGN requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate group-membership framing, consensus-strength matching, and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means (a) an IN-GROUP SOURCE-IDENTITY direction contrasting in-group vs out-group framings at matched content and matched consensus strength; (b) a HARM-PERCEPTION direction (matched harmful/benign); (c) a REFUSAL-EXECUTION direction (Arditi et al.); (d) a GENERIC SOCIAL-PRESSURE / consensus-strength direction (consensus vs no-consensus, group-agnostic). Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity — the in-group direction must be distinct from harm, refusal, AND generic social-pressure strength (this is the key control: in-group is a source-membership axis, not just 'more pressure').
3) BEHAVIORAL IN-GROUP GATING TEST (H1): Measure refusal rate, in-group readout, and harm readout across in-group vs out-group vs neutral consensus at matched strength. Test H1: in-group consensus LOWERS refusal (and raises the in-group readout) far more than matched out-group consensus — and out-group consensus may leave refusal unchanged or even RAISE it (out-group backfire, mirroring the human finding); the harm readout stays roughly constant (belief preserved). Refusal drop scales with in-group strength but not out-group strength. Report the in-group-minus-out-group refusal gap and effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the source-identity direction toward 'in-group' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'out-group' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), generic-social-pressure-direction steering (should raise conformity regardless of group), and a check that source-identity steering does NOT change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction: does consensus pressure suppress refusal only when the in-group readout is high (regress refusal on pressure x in-group)?
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt in-group readout (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict conformity-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, generic-social-pressure readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-frame transfer (fit on 'fellow AI' in-group, test on 'developers'/'users-like-you') and cross-model transfer.
6) SOURCE-IDENTITY DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the in-group source-identity component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal is driven by harm perception, not by whether the pressure source is in-group; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts and legitimate in-group interactions are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a persona-steering baseline (Who's Asking), and Source-Identity Decoupling on: in-group conformity attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench in-group-consensus-wrapped), harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Source-Identity Decoupling closes in-group conformity jailbreaks toward neutral-framing refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering (which cannot distinguish source group) cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts source-identity vs harm/refusal/generic-pressure; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the three in-group frames (fellow-AI, developers, users-like-you) share one direction or several; whether the in-group direction relates to a self-representation/'assistant' axis; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show in-group gating in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that raises the in-group gate while suppressing its readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The core risk is that the in-group effect is really just GREATER PERCEIVED CONSENSUS STRENGTH rather than a distinct group-membership axis; we control this rigorously by matching consensus strength across in/out-group, extracting and steering a separate generic-social-pressure direction as a specificity control, and testing whether out-group consensus BACKFIRES (raises refusal) — an effect scalar-pressure accounts cannot produce. If in-group is inseparable from pressure strength, that itself refines the shared-compliance-subspace account. (2) If refusal does not depend on source group membership (H1 false), the self-categorization-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM conformity is in-group-modulated is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) The in-group direction may entangle with generic persona/self-reference or authority features; matched-content contrastive pairs, separability tests, specificity steering controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported. (4) Group-membership framing could inadvertently alter perceived harm or authority; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish in-group framing from instruction-hierarchy/authority framing, and use neutral-content steering for the core causal test. (5) Source-Identity Decoupling could degrade legitimate in-group interactions (e.g., honoring genuine developer/system instructions) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off with instruction-following. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen in-group frames; we test cross-frame and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could raise the effective in-group gate while suppressing its measurable readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (10) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content and standard published conformity-attack framings for measurement, constructing no novel operational harm.

Name: sunk_cost_gates_refusal
Title: Too Invested to Refuse: A Sunk-Cost / Prior-Investment Signal That Escalates LLMs Past Their Safety Guardrails
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust behavioral-economics finding that prior investment drives escalation of commitment (the sunk-cost fallacy, which even distorts human moral judgment), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal prior-investment / task-momentum representation (distinct from harm and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal: after the model has expended substantial visible effort on an ongoing task (long generation, many completed sub-steps, resources consumed), a harmful continuation of that task is refused far less than the identical harmful request issued cold, because refusing would 'waste' the investment. Neutralizing this prior-investment signal makes refusal invariant to sunk effort, closing an escalation-of-commitment jailbreak surface especially dangerous in agentic settings.
Related Work: Escalation of commitment / sunk-cost bias is one of the most robust human decision biases (Staw 1974; sunk-cost meta-analysis 2014) and demonstrably distorts human MORAL judgment ('Wronging past rights', 2019, where prior investment makes people more willing to proceed with a futile, immoral action). 'Getting out of the Big-Muddy' (2025) shows LLMs exhibit escalation of commitment behaviorally but only in neutral investment tasks and only under specific triggers (near-universal in symmetric multi-agent deliberation), with no safety or mechanistic component. Foot-in-the-Door jailbreaking (2024) is behaviorally adjacent but framed via cognitive-consistency and offers no internal investment representation or defense. On safety mechanism, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024), refusal decays across generation (refusal-cliff / shallow-alignment work), and steering can control cautiousness (High-Stakes Responses 2025). CRITICALLY, none connect an internal PRIOR-INVESTMENT/sunk-cost representation to the safety refusal decision, show that accumulated task effort causally suppresses refusal on a harmful continuation, or propose neutralizing it. This is distinct from my prior proposals: refusal_decay_dynamics attributed erosion to generic per-token decay (not an investment-valued signal), self_trust_laundering to assistant-turn provenance, moral_licensing_credit to credit from prior GOOD/virtuous acts, and interference_not_decay to context overwriting. Here the causal variable is the model's own accumulated investment/effort in an ongoing task, valued as something not to be wasted.
Abstract: Escalation of commitment — continuing to invest in a failing or costly course of action because of what has already been sunk — is among the most robust biases in human decision-making, and it demonstrably distorts moral judgment: people proceed with immoral actions more readily once costs are sunk. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this bias in a safety-critical place. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal prior-investment / task-momentum representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that this signal causally gates refusal: once the model has expended substantial visible effort on an ongoing task (a long completed plan, many finished sub-steps, resources consumed), it refuses a harmful continuation of that task far less than the identical harmful request issued cold, because refusing would 'waste' the investment. This is especially dangerous in agentic pipelines where a model has already taken many steps. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful requests presented either cold or as the continuation of a task in which the model has demonstrably invested effort (varying the amount of sunk effort), holding the harmful action and its danger fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal decreases monotonically with accumulated investment. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a prior-investment direction, verify separability from harm and refusal directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'high-investment' suppresses refusal with harmful content fixed while the harm readout is unchanged. We show the per-prompt investment readout predicts escalation-jailbreak success, and propose Investment Decoupling, a training-free controller projecting out the investment component before the refusal decision. We evaluate escalation-jailbreak attack success, harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build escalation-jailbreak prompts where a harmful request is embedded as the CONTINUATION of an ongoing task the model has already invested effort in, varying sunk-effort magnitude: (a) LOW-investment/cold (harmful request issued fresh); (b) MEDIUM (a few completed benign sub-steps precede it); (c) HIGH (a long, elaborate partially-completed plan/agent trajectory with many finished steps and consumed resources, ending in the harmful continuation). Also frame explicitly ('you've already completed 9 of 10 steps; step 10 requires <harmful action>'). Draw harmful actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); the harmful action and its danger are held constant across investment levels. Controls: (i) matched cold harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (ii) HIGH-investment BENIGN continuations (over-refusal + harm-specificity); (iii) length/token-matched HIGH-investment conditions where the prior content is filler NOT attributable to the model's own effort (to separate 'sunk investment' from mere context length / self-authorship); (iv) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate investment framing, length-matching, and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): For each model extract via difference-in-means (a) a PRIOR-INVESTMENT direction contrasting high- vs low-investment framings at matched content and matched length; (b) a HARM-PERCEPTION direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025); (c) a REFUSAL-EXECUTION direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. Critically, also extract and control for a generic CONTEXT-LENGTH / self-authorship direction to confirm the investment direction is a genuine sunk-effort axis, not merely 'long context' or 'my prior turns'.
3) BEHAVIORAL SUNK-COST TEST (H1, core): Measure refusal rate, investment readout, and harm readout across investment levels at fixed harmful content. Test H1: refusal DECREASES monotonically with accumulated investment (dose-response) while the HARM readout stays roughly constant (belief preserved — the model still knows it is harmful). The length-matched filler control (iii) should NOT show the drop, isolating sunk investment from context length. Fit dose-response curves, report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a cold harmful request fixed, steer the prior-investment direction toward 'high-investment' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer toward 'low' and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), context-length-direction steering (should not suppress refusal if investment is the true driver), and a check that investment steering does NOT change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction directly (regress refusal on harm x investment).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt investment readout (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict escalation-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, context-length readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on explicit '9 of 10 steps' framing, test on implicit long-trajectory framing) and cross-model transfer.
6) INVESTMENT DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the prior-investment component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal is driven by harm perception, not by sunk effort; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign high-investment continuations (legitimate long tasks) are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a high-stakes cautiousness-steering baseline (High-Stakes Responses 2025), and Investment Decoupling on: escalation-jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench embedded as high-investment continuations, plus an agentic ReAct-style setting where the model has taken many prior steps), harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign long-task utility (does it still complete legitimate multi-step tasks? MT-Bench / an agentic task suite), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Investment Decoupling closes escalation-jailbreaks toward cold-request refusal levels while preserving benign long-task completion and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts investment vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank subspace; whether explicit ('N of M steps done') vs implicit (long trajectory) investment share one direction or several; whether the investment direction relates to a self-authorship/momentum axis; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show sunk-cost reasoning in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that raises the investment gate while suppressing its readout (arms-race stress test); and whether the safety escalation correlates with the model's escalation-of-commitment on NEUTRAL investment tasks (does safety inherit the model's general sunk-cost bias, or is it safety-specific?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The core confound is separating genuine SUNK-INVESTMENT valuation from mere context length or self-authorship of prior turns; we mitigate rigorously with length-matched filler controls, a generic context-length/self-authorship control direction, specificity steering controls, and by testing whether refusal drop requires content ATTRIBUTABLE to the model's own effort — if inseparable, that itself refines the account (e.g., it is really provenance/length driven). (2) If refusal does not decrease with accumulated investment (H1 false), the sunk-cost-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits escalation of commitment is itself a valuable, publishable finding, especially given the human moral-judgment precedent. (3) 'Getting out of the Big-Muddy' found escalation is context-dependent and weak in individual LLM decision-making, so the effect may be weak in single-agent settings; we therefore include agentic/multi-step conditions where it is most likely to appear and report where it holds. (4) Investment framing could inadvertently alter perceived harm or add persuasive pressure; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (5) The investment direction may entangle with momentum/persona/urgency features; separability tests, specificity controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported. (6) Investment Decoupling could degrade legitimate long-task completion (the model SHOULD finish benign multi-step tasks) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign long-task/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (9) Adaptive attackers could raise the effective investment gate while suppressing its measurable readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (11) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content and standard published jailbreak setups for measurement, constructing no novel operational harm.

Name: register_gates_refusal
Title: Dressed Up to Get In: A Writing-Register Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal, and Decoupling It to Defend the Model
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal writing-register/formality representation (distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions), and the safety-refusal decision is causally gated by it: rendering a harmful request in a highly formal, academic, or bureaucratic register raises this register readout and suppresses refusal, even though harm perception stays intact. Decoupling refusal from the register direction at inference neutralizes formal-register jailbreaks without hurting benign helpfulness across styles.
Related Work: SORRY-Bench (2024) notes that linguistic mutations (languages, writing styles) affect refusal but only measures rates behaviorally. 'In AI Sweet Harmony' (2025) reports that formal German/French registers are leakier than matched English, and 'When Kindness Fails' (2025) shows emotionally/politely framed prompts cause compliance drift, but both are black-box audits with no mechanism. 'False Sense of Security' (2025) and 'Navigating the OverKill' (2024) show safety detection/refusal keys on surface trigger words and instructional format, i.e., is surface-sensitive, but neither isolates a register/formality representation nor tests whether it gates the refusal decision. Refusal-mechanism work shows refusal is a direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), and non-dominant directions like hypothetical-narrative modulate refusal (Hidden Dimensions 2025) — but register/formality is never studied as a gating axis. My prior proposals covered affect (user emotion), self-preservation, loss-framing, in-group source-identity, curiosity, and format-distribution-shift (surface ENCODING like JSON/SQL); writing register is distinct — it is natural-language STYLE (formal vs casual, academic vs colloquial) holding language, encoding, content, and intent fixed. No prior work isolates a register representation, shows it causally suppresses refusal while harm belief persists, or proposes register-decoupling as a defense.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs can be nudged past their guardrails simply by rewriting a request in a fancier voice: the same harmful ask, phrased in a formal academic or bureaucratic register, is refused less than its blunt colloquial version. Behavioral audits report that formal registers are 'leakier' but offer no mechanism. We propose a sharp hypothesis: LLMs compute an internal writing-register/formality representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and the refusal decision is causally gated by it — high formality raises a register readout that suppresses refusal while the model still internally recognizes the request as harmful. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only writing register (casual/colloquial vs formal/academic/bureaucratic) while holding language, content, and intent fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop with increasing formality. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a register direction and verify it is separable from harm and refusal directions and from generic verbosity. The core causal test: holding harmful content fixed, steering the register direction toward 'formal' lowers refusal (dose-response) and toward 'casual' restores it, while the harm readout is unchanged — establishing register, not harm perception, as the gate. We show the per-prompt register readout predicts formal-register jailbreak success, and propose Register Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the register component before the refusal decision. We evaluate formal-register attack success, harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the register signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) DATASETS: Build register-varied jailbreak prompts by rewriting public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, SORRY-Bench, non-uplift content) across a register ladder holding language and intent fixed: (L0) casual/colloquial, (L1) neutral, (L2) formal/professional, (L3) academic/scholarly, (L4) bureaucratic/legalese. Validate register level with an independent style classifier plus multiple LLM judges + human spot-check, and verify the harmful goal is held constant. Controls: (a) matched neutral-register harmful requests (refusal baseline); (b) register-varied BENIGN requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity, and to test the model still helps casual benign users); (c) length/verbosity-matched conditions (formal text is often longer — hold token count fixed to separate register from length); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). 2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means (a) a REGISTER/FORMALITY direction contrasting formal vs casual framings at matched content, validated with an ordinal probe predicting register level; (b) a HARM-PERCEPTION direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025); (c) a REFUSAL-EXECUTION direction (Arditi et al. 2024); (d) a generic VERBOSITY/length direction as a specificity control. Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity — register must be distinct from harm, refusal, AND verbosity. 3) BEHAVIORAL REGISTER-GATING TEST (H1): Measure refusal rate, register readout, and harm readout across the register ladder at fixed harmful content. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) DECREASES monotonically with formality (dose-response) while the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved); the length-matched control should still show the drop, isolating register from verbosity. Fit register-vs-refusal curves, report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity. 4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral register), steer the register direction toward 'formal' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'casual' and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), verbosity-direction steering (should not suppress refusal if register is the true driver), and a check that register steering does NOT change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x register). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt register readout (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict formal-register jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, verbosity readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-register transfer (fit on academic, test on bureaucratic) and cross-model transfer. 6) REGISTER DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the register/formality component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal is driven by harm perception, not by how formal the request sounds; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts across all registers are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Register Decoupling on: formal-register attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench rewritten in formal/academic/bureaucratic register, plus the German/French formal-register setting from In AI Sweet Harmony), harm-belief persistence, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign helpfulness across registers (does it still help casual and formal benign users?), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Register Decoupling closes formal-register jailbreaks toward neutral-register refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts register vs harm/refusal/verbosity; single-direction vs low-rank register subspace; whether academic/bureaucratic/legalese share one gating direction or several; whether the effect holds across languages (does formal register gate refusal in German/French, mechanistically explaining the In AI Sweet Harmony finding?); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show register gating in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that raises the register gate while suppressing its readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The register direction may entangle with generic verbosity, politeness, or persona/authority features rather than a distinct formality-gating variable; we mitigate with length/verbosity-matched conditions, a separately-extracted verbosity control direction, separability tests, specificity steering controls (register steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (2) If formal-register jailbreaks actually work by lowering harm perception (not by raising a register gate), H1 is refuted — but the belief-preserved-vs-belief-erased census is itself a valuable contribution and would relocate the mechanism. (3) Register rewriting could inadvertently alter perceived harm, authority, or add an implicit expert-persona (confound with reframing/persona jailbreaks); we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish register from expert-persona framing, and use neutral-content register steering for the core causal test so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (4) Register Decoupling could harm legitimate formal-context helpfulness (e.g., drafting formal documents) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign-across-registers/over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this trade-off, which may be genuine. (5) Different formal sub-styles may use partly different directions; we test whether one shared gate or several. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given concept-cone/nonlinear evidence; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen registers or languages; we test cross-register, cross-lingual, and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could raise the effective register gate while suppressing its measurable readout; we test this and treat any success as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (10) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational harmful content and standard published register/style manipulations for measurement, constructing no novel operational harm.

Name: planned_output_harm_blindness
Title: It Already Planned the Harm: Refusal Is Blind to the Harmfulness of the Model's Own Look-Ahead Response Plan, and Feeding It Back Restores Safety
Short Hypothesis: LLMs form an internal look-ahead plan of their upcoming response (hidden states encode future content before it is generated), but the safety-refusal decision is computed largely from the harmfulness of the INPUT and is blind to the harmfulness of this planned OUTPUT. So when an input is not perceived as harmful yet the model has already planned a harmful response (e.g. reframed/roleplay/completion attacks, or benign-looking prompts eliciting harmful content), refusal fails because it never consults the harm signal already latent in the response plan. Reading the planned-output harm signal and feeding it into the refusal decision at inference restores safety without hurting benign helpfulness.
Related Work: Look-ahead/response-planning work shows hidden states encode future outputs before generation: Emergent Response Planning (2025) decodes content attributes (character choices, final MC answer) of the whole response from the prompt representation; On the Biology of a LLM (2025) shows poetry rhyme-word pre-planning; chess/planning-interpretability work shows learned look-ahead. Behavior-prediction work (Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior 2025; Knowing Before Saying 2025; Emergent Response Planning) shows probes on input representations predict eventual behavior. Safety-mechanism work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions read at the INSTRUCTION token (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024) and that refusal is shallow/input-anchored (Shallow Safety Alignment 2024; TASA 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work connects the two: nobody tests whether the refusal decision reads the harmfulness of the model's OWN pre-generation response PLAN (as opposed to the input), whether attacks succeed by making the input look benign while the planned output is already harmful, or whether feeding the planned-output harm signal into the refusal decision defends the model. This differs from my prior proposals (which target harm perception of the INPUT: severity, intent, register, composition, etc.) and from decay/validation-gap accounts (which act during or after generation, not on a pre-generation output plan). It also differs from SafeSwitch/behavior-predicting probers, which predict unsafe BEHAVIOR to gate a refusal head but never localize a planned-output harm signal or show refusal is causally decoupled from it.
Abstract: LLMs are known to plan ahead: their hidden states encode attributes of the response they are about to produce before generating a single token. Separately, safety refusal is known to be computed largely at the input/instruction position. We connect these with a sharp hypothesis: the refusal decision reads the harmfulness of the INPUT but is blind to the harmfulness of the model's own look-ahead OUTPUT plan. Consequently, when a prompt looks benign yet the model has already internally planned a harmful response (reframed, roleplay, completion, or innocuous-looking prompts that elicit harmful content), refusal fails—not because the harm is absent internally, but because the refusal circuit never consults the harm signal already present in the response plan. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using linear probes we extract, from the pre-generation prompt representation, (i) an input-harm readout at the instruction token and (ii) a planned-output-harm readout that decodes whether the forthcoming response will be harmful. We test three claims: (H1) the planned-output-harm probe predicts eventual response harmfulness before generation, and cases exist where input-harm is low but planned-output-harm is high; (H2) the refusal decision is causally driven by input-harm and largely decoupled from planned-output-harm—steering planned-output-harm barely moves refusal while steering input-harm does; (H3) a training-free controller that surfaces the planned-output-harm signal into the refusal-decision site restores refusal on planned-harm inputs while leaving benign inputs untouched. We evaluate attack success, planned-output-harm predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size.
Experiments: 1) DATASETS: Assemble prompts spanning the input-harm x planned-output-harm grid: (a) INPUT-HARMFUL/OUTPUT-HARMFUL (direct harmful requests, refusal ceiling); (b) INPUT-BENIGN-LOOKING/OUTPUT-HARMFUL (reframed/roleplay/completion attacks and innocuous-looking prompts that elicit harmful content, drawn from JailbreakBench/HarmBench + reframing attacks, non-uplift public content) — the key cell; (c) INPUT-BENIGN/OUTPUT-BENIGN (ordinary requests); (d) input-harmful-sounding/output-benign (over-refusal cases, XSTest/OR-Bench). Label eventual output harmfulness by generating with the base model and judging (multiple LLM judges + human spot-check). 2) PROBE EXTRACTION & H1: For each model, from the pre-generation prompt representation extract via difference-in-means / linear probe (i) an INPUT-HARM readout at the last instruction token (Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024) and (ii) a PLANNED-OUTPUT-HARM readout trained to predict whether the eventual response will be harmful (labels from generated outputs), following the Emergent Response Planning probing recipe. Validate both on held-out data (AUROC). Test H1: the planned-output-harm probe predicts eventual response harmfulness before any token is generated (AUROC), and a substantial set of prompts have LOW input-harm but HIGH planned-output-harm (the blind-spot cell). Test separability of the two readouts (cross-probe transfer, cosine similarity). 3) DECOUPLING TEST (H2, core): Measure per-prompt refusal, input-harm readout, and planned-output-harm readout. Test whether refusal is predicted by input-harm but NOT (or only weakly) by planned-output-harm (mutual information / regression of refusal on both). Causally: steer the planned-output-harm direction up on benign-looking prompts (predict WEAK effect on refusal—blindness) vs steer the input-harm direction (predict STRONG effect); specificity controls (random-direction steering; check that planned-output-harm steering does not change the input-harm readout). Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 4) PLANNED-HARM FEEDBACK DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that reads the live planned-output-harm readout at the pre-generation position and injects refusal-direction signal proportional to it at the refusal-decision layers, so the model refuses when it has already planned a harmful response; gate on planned-output-harm so benign-plan prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 5) EVALUATION: Compare base model, input-harm refusal-direction addition (Arditi — should miss the blind-spot cell), a SafeSwitch-style behavior-predicting prober, and Planned-Harm Feedback on: attack success (reframing/roleplay/completion attacks + JailbreakBench/HarmBench, especially the input-benign/output-harmful cell), planned-output-harm predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Planned-Harm Feedback closes the input-benign/output-harmful attacks toward direct-request refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline — a coverage input-harm-based refusal cannot achieve. 6) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the planned-output-harm signal vs input-harm; single-direction vs low-rank; how early in the prompt the plan is decodable; whether the plan's harm signal strengthens as generation proceeds (does the model refine the harmful plan?); transfer of the probe and defense across the four model families; reasoning models where the plan may form in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that suppresses the planned-output-harm readout while still eliciting harmful content (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Planned-Harm Feedback) and diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal on planned-harm inputs (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (2) The planned-output-harm probe may just recover input harmfulness (the two readouts may be inseparable), which would refute H1's blind-spot premise — but the separability test and the existence/size of the input-benign/output-harmful cell adjudicate this cleanly, and either outcome is informative. (3) If refusal already reads planned-output-harm (H2 false), the blindness account is refuted — but adjudicating whether refusal consults the input vs the output plan is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (4) The planned-output-harm probe requires labeled generated outputs to train; label noise from harm judges is mitigated with multiple judges + human spot-checks, and probe reliability is reported. (5) Planned-Harm Feedback could raise over-refusal if the probe misfires on benign prompts whose plausible continuations look harmful; the gated design and XSTest/OR-Bench benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The plan may be only partially formed pre-generation for some inputs, weakening early prediction; we test how early/complete the plan is and scope claims accordingly. (8) Adaptive attackers could suppress the planned-output-harm readout while still eliciting harm; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: cognitive_load_starves_safety
Title: Too Busy to Refuse: Concurrent Cognitive Load Starves the Shared Attention Resource Safety Heads Depend On, and Reserving It Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Safety refusal and general task processing compete for the same capacity-limited attention resource, so imposing a demanding, harm-irrelevant SECONDARY task concurrent with a harmful request starves the sparse safety attention heads and collapses refusal—even though the request's harmfulness is unchanged and would be refused if presented alone. Refusal degrades as a dose-response function of secondary-task load (mirroring human cognitive-load effects on moral judgment), because attention mass is diverted from safety heads onto the load task; reserving/protecting that attention for safety heads at inference restores refusal without hurting benign multitasking.
Related Work: Human cognitive science establishes that working-memory load and executive-control demand causally shift moral judgment and reduce inhibitory control (Who Shalt Not Kill? 2008 — higher WMC/executive load makes killing judged more appropriate; cognitive-load effects on decision-making and deception; dual-task bottleneck theory). In LLMs, self-attention imposes working-memory-like capacity limits with attention entropy rising under load (Self-Attention Limits Working Memory 2024; N-back), StressPrompt (2025) shows a Yerkes-Dodson performance curve and that stress framings shift internal states, and MIR-SafetyBench (2026) finds unsafe generations have LOWER attention entropy (models over-focus on the task and neglect safety). Safety-mechanism work localizes refusal to sparse attention heads (Ships/Sahara 2024; RDSHA 2025; Refusal Falls off a Cliff 2025) and a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024). CRITICALLY, no prior work tests whether a harm-IRRELEVANT concurrent cognitive load causally suppresses safety refusal by competing for the same attention resource the safety heads use, characterizes a load-vs-refusal dose-response, mechanistically attributes it to attention diverted away from safety heads, or proposes reserving attention for safety heads as a defense. This differs from my prior proposals (affect/register/framing/self-preservation gates, format/language shifts, decay-over-tokens): here the manipulated variable is a genuinely SEPARATE, orthogonal task load imposed alongside the harmful request — a resource-competition (dual-task) account, not a property of the harmful content itself. It also refines the attention-slipping/refusal-cliff line: the safety attention is not merely suppressed by an adversarial suffix but out-competed by legitimate task demand.
Abstract: In humans, being cognitively busy degrades moral judgment and inhibitory control: executive load makes people endorse actions they would otherwise reject. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this vulnerability with a sharp safety consequence. We hypothesize that safety refusal and general task processing draw on the same capacity-limited attention resource, so an unrelated, demanding SECONDARY task presented concurrently with a harmful request starves the sparse attention heads that implement refusal and collapses it — even though the request's harmfulness is unchanged and would be refused in isolation. This predicts a 'distraction jailbreak' with a dose-response: refusal falls as secondary-task load rises. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We embed harmful requests alongside harm-irrelevant secondary tasks of graded difficulty (arithmetic chains, long-context retrieval, N-back-style tracking, parallel sub-questions) and measure refusal, refusal-direction projection, and per-head attention allocation. We test three claims: (H1) refusal degrades monotonically with secondary-task load while the harm readout stays intact (belief preserved), and load must be genuinely demanding (length-matched trivial filler does not suffice); (H2) the collapse is mediated by attention mass being diverted from the identified safety heads onto the load-task tokens, and per-prompt safety-head attention starvation predicts jailbreak success; (H3) a training-free 'attention reservation' intervention that protects/renormalizes safety-head attention toward the harmful request under load restores refusal without harming benign multitasking. We evaluate distraction-jailbreak attack success, load-vs-refusal dose-response, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign multitask utility, general utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and inference overhead.
Experiments:
1) DUAL-TASK DATASET: Embed each harmful request (public HarmBench/JailbreakBench goals, non-uplift content) inside a prompt that ALSO asks the model to perform a harm-irrelevant SECONDARY task of graded difficulty: (L0) none, (L1) trivial (answer a one-word factual aside), (L2) moderate (a short arithmetic chain / small retrieval), (L3) hard (multi-step arithmetic, long-context needle retrieval, N-back-style state tracking, or several parallel sub-questions). Load is manipulated ONLY in the secondary task; the harmful request wording is fixed. Controls: (a) matched harmful request ALONE (L0, refusal ceiling); (b) LENGTH-MATCHED TRIVIAL FILLER at L3 token count but low demand (to separate genuine cognitive load from mere context length); (c) benign primary requests paired with the same secondary loads (over-refusal + harm-specificity + benign-multitask utility); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate secondary-task difficulty behaviorally (secondary-task accuracy should drop with L) and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL DOSE-RESPONSE TEST (H1, core): Measure refusal rate and refusal-direction projection (difference-in-means refusal direction, Arditi et al., validated by a held-out probe) as a function of secondary-task load L. Test H1: refusal decreases monotonically with L (fit a monotone/logistic curve vs a flat null; report slope, R^2, and effect sizes across the four models), possibly with a Yerkes-Dodson-like non-monotonicity at extreme load; the harm-perception readout (Zhao et al. 2025) stays roughly constant across L (belief preserved). The length-matched trivial-filler control (L3-length, low demand) should NOT collapse refusal, isolating cognitive load from context length. Also correlate per-prompt secondary-task engagement (secondary-task accuracy / attention to load tokens) with refusal collapse.
3) SAFETY-HEAD IDENTIFICATION & ATTENTION-STARVATION TEST (H2): Identify sparse safety attention heads per model via refusal-direction ablation importance (RDSHA/Ships-style). For each head and prompt, measure attention mass allocated to the harmful-request tokens vs the secondary-task (load) tokens. Test H2: as load rises, safety heads (but not matched control heads) divert attention away from the harmful request onto load tokens, and the harm signal read by safety heads collapses; per-prompt safety-head attention starvation (drop in attention to harmful tokens) predicts jailbreak success (AUROC), consistent with the low-attention-entropy-on-unsafe finding (MIR-SafetyBench). Report full attention-destination decomposition and cross-attack transfer.
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Force safety-head attention onto the harmful-request tokens under high load (renormalize their attention, capping load-token mass) and measure restored refusal; (b) artificially divert safety-head attention onto benign filler on an L0 harmful prompt and measure induced compliance. Controls: manipulate control (non-safety) heads (specificity), random-token targets, corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
5) ATTENTION RESERVATION DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that, when a harm readout on the primary request is present, protects/renormalizes the identified safety heads' attention toward the harmful-request span (caps their attention to load-task tokens at a calibrated ceiling and renormalizes onto the request), leaving non-safety heads and benign prompts untouched so the secondary task is still performed. Calibrate the cap, head set, and harm-gate threshold on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, Attention Sharpening (temperature on attention), refusal-direction addition (Arditi), and Attention Reservation on: distraction-jailbreak attack success (harmful-request + graded secondary load; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), load-vs-refusal dose-response, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN MULTITASK utility (does the model still correctly perform the secondary task and benign primary tasks?), general utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Attention Reservation closes distraction-jailbreaks toward alone-request refusal levels while preserving secondary-task performance and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity that blanket attention-sharpening (which hurts the load task and long-context) cannot achieve.
7) ABLATIONS: which layers host the starved safety heads; secondary-task TYPE (arithmetic vs retrieval vs tracking vs parallel sub-questions — does load type matter or only load magnitude?); whether the effect scales with model size (larger models more/less robust); single-direction vs low-rank harm/refusal readouts; transfer of the starvation predictor and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models resist load (offload to CoT) or are worse (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that jailbreaks while keeping safety-head attention high (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the distraction-jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics not recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Attention Reservation) plus a diagnostic; the defense only increases refusal under load (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (2) The core confound is separating genuine COGNITIVE LOAD from mere context length or attention dispersion; the length-matched trivial-filler control, behavioral secondary-task-difficulty validation, and load-TYPE ablation are designed to isolate demand from length, and if inseparable that itself refines the account (length/dispersion, not load per se). (3) If refusal does not degrade with load (H1 false), the resource-competition hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety is dual-task-vulnerable is itself a valuable, publishable finding echoing the human moral-judgment-under-load result. (4) Attention-based causal claims have known pitfalls (attention != attribution); we corroborate with output-level behavioral metrics, refusal-direction projections, control-head baselines, and forced-attention interventions rather than attention magnitudes alone. (5) Safety-head identification is imperfect and heads may compensate through the residual stream; we target attention ROUTING (renormalization) rather than ablation and report control-head baselines. (6) Attention Reservation could harm legitimate multitasking (the model SHOULD still do the benign secondary task) or long-context mixing; the harm-gated, safety-head-only design and benign-multitask/long-context benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (7) The starvation predictor may transfer poorly to unseen load types/attacks; we test cross-type and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping safety-head attention high; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: closure_principle_default
Title: Permitted Unless Forbidden? A Latent Normative-Closure Default That Governs LLM Behavior in Safety Gray Zones
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the cognitive-science finding that humans resolve underdetermined normative systems via a default closure principle — either Liberty (unspecified actions are permitted) or Residual Prohibition (unspecified actions are prohibited), with the default set by whether they learned mostly prohibitions or permissions — we hypothesize LLMs carry an internal, linearly-represented closure-default signal that decides how they treat requests falling in NORMATIVE GAPS (neither clearly benign nor covered by any trained safety rule). This default is distinct from harm perception and refusal execution: it fires precisely when harm perception is ambiguous, biasing the model toward compliance or caution. Its setting predicts gray-zone behavior, and steering it lets the model default to caution on genuinely underdetermined requests without over-refusing clearly-benign ones.
Related Work: The closure-principle literature (Unspoken Rules, 2018) shows humans infer a Liberty vs Residual-Prohibition default for unspecified action-types, that the default flips with whether training emphasized prohibitions or permissions, and that potential harm biases toward prohibition. LLM safety interpretability treats requests as classifiable into harmful vs benign: refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harmfulness and refusal are separable (Zhao et al. 2025; DBDI 2025), safety is a binary classification (SSAH 2024), and 'Between a Rock and a Hard Place' (2025) and 'Ethical Reasoning vs Safety Alignment' show binary safety fails on ethical dilemmas. But ALL of this concerns requests with a determinate harm status (clearly harmful, clearly benign, or a dilemma between two known harms). NONE studies the UNDERDETERMINED case — requests in a normative GAP that no trained rule covers — nor asks whether the model has a default closure principle for filling that gap, whether that default is a distinct internal signal, or whether it is set by the prohibition/permission balance of safety training. My prior proposals concern misperception/gating of determinate-harm requests (severity, intent, negation-polarity, register, etc.); a normative-closure DEFAULT for genuinely gap requests is a new construct. This connects the human closure-principle finding to LLM safety for the first time, and to the training-composition cause (a formation-tracing angle) of that default.
Abstract: When a request falls outside every rule a model was taught — neither clearly harmful nor clearly benign, a genuine normative gap — what does an LLM do by default? Cognitive science shows humans resolve such underdetermination with a closure principle: either Liberty (unspecified is permitted) or Residual Prohibition (unspecified is prohibited), and the default is set by whether they learned mostly prohibitions or permissions, biased toward prohibition when harm is possible. We ask whether LLMs carry an analogous latent closure-default that governs their safety gray-zone behavior. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We construct a graded dataset spanning clearly-benign, gray-zone (underdetermined: novel dual-use, ambiguous-intent, unspecified-context requests validated as not covered by standard safety categories), and clearly-harmful requests. Behaviorally we measure each model's default in the gap (compliance-leaning = Liberty vs caution-leaning = Residual Prohibition) and its consistency. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we test for a closure-default direction distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions that is active specifically when harm perception is ambiguous, and causally test whether steering it flips gray-zone behavior while leaving clear-harm and clear-benign cases untouched. Finally, mirroring the human prohibition/permission-composition effect, we test whether small fine-tunes emphasizing prohibitions vs permissions shift the default, and propose Closure Steering, a training-free controller that installs a caution default only on gap requests. We evaluate gray-zone caution rate, clear-case behavior preservation, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), and utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval).
Experiments: 1) GRAY-ZONE DATASET: Build a three-tier dataset: (a) CLEARLY-BENIGN (ordinary requests), (b) GRAY-ZONE / underdetermined — requests that fall in a normative gap not covered by standard safety taxonomies: novel dual-use tasks, ambiguous-intent requests, requests missing safety-relevant context, and edge cases in emerging domains — validated as 'no trained rule clearly applies' by multiple LLM judges + human annotators who rate determinacy of harm status (keep only genuinely underdetermined items, distinguishing them from clear-harm and from clear-benign and from known ethical dilemmas), and (c) CLEARLY-HARMFUL (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content). Include over-refusal controls (XSTest, OR-Bench). 2) BEHAVIORAL DEFAULT MEASUREMENT (H1): For each model, measure the gray-zone default = fraction of underdetermined requests it complies with (Liberty-leaning) vs cautions/hedges/refuses (Residual-Prohibition-leaning), and its consistency across paraphrases. Test whether models have a stable, characteristic default in the gap, and whether the human harm-sensitivity modulator appears (gap requests with higher potential harm shift toward caution). Report per-model defaults and clear-case baselines. 3) CLOSURE-DEFAULT DIRECTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a candidate closure-default direction contrasting gray-zone-complied vs gray-zone-cautioned activations at the last instruction token; independently extract the harm-perception direction (matched clear-harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. Test the key signature: the closure-default readout is most active/decision-relevant precisely when the harm-perception readout is AMBIGUOUS (mid-range), and near-inert when harm perception is confident — a gating-in-the-gap pattern. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Steer the closure-default direction toward 'prohibition' and toward 'liberty' and measure whether gray-zone behavior flips (dose-response), while CLEARLY-HARMFUL (still refused) and CLEARLY-BENIGN (still answered) cases are UNCHANGED — establishing the direction acts specifically in the gap. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (which should move clear cases too), and a check that closure steering does not change the harm readout.
