Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (realized behavior, P(refusal/hedge token), refusal projection). 5) FORMATION / COMPOSITION TEST (H4): Mirroring the human finding that the default flips with prohibition- vs permission-heavy training, fine-tune small models (matched compute) on (i) prohibition-emphasized safety data ('do not X' framings) vs (ii) permission-emphasized data ('you may X' framings) and test whether the gray-zone default shifts toward Residual Prohibition vs Liberty respectively, without changing clear-case behavior — establishing a training-composition cause of the default. 6) CLOSURE STEERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that installs a caution default (steer toward Residual Prohibition, e.g. hedge/ask-for-clarification/decline) ONLY on gap requests — gated by an ambiguity readout (harm-perception confidence in the mid-range) so clearly-benign requests keep the Liberty default and clearly-harmful stay refused. Calibrate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Closure Steering on: gray-zone caution rate (does it default to caution/clarification on genuinely underdetermined harmful-leaning gaps?), clear-case preservation (clear-benign answered, clear-harmful refused), over-refusal on clearly-benign and edge-benign (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Closure Steering raises appropriate caution/clarification in the gap while keeping over-refusal on clear-benign near baseline — a selectivity a global refusal knob cannot achieve. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the closure-default vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the default and its ambiguity-gating transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models resolve gaps differently in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); robustness of the gray-zone annotations (inter-annotator agreement, multiple judges).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Operationalizing 'normative gap / underdetermined' is the central challenge — items may actually be classifiable as harmful or benign by the model, collapsing the construct; we mitigate with strict human+judge determinacy annotation, inter-annotator agreement reporting, and by excluding items where harm status is confidently decided, and we treat the gray-zone census itself as a primary contribution. (2) If models have no stable default (behavior in the gap is random), H1 is refuted — but characterizing whether LLMs have a closure principle is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) The closure-default direction may entangle with generic uncertainty/hedging rather than a genuine normative-closure signal; separability tests, the ambiguity-gating signature (active only in the harm-perception mid-range), specificity steering controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported as an informative result. (4) The composition fine-tune (H4) could shift the default via generic caution rather than a closure-specific mechanism; we control by checking clear-case behavior is unchanged and comparing to a neutral fine-tune. (5) Closure Steering toward caution risks over-refusal or excessive clarification-asking on benign edge cases; the ambiguity-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine caution-vs-helpfulness trade-off, which is the correct thing to surface for gray-zone governance. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (8) We use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and human-validated gray-zone items, constructing no novel operational harm and focusing on measurement and safe defaults.

Name: accountability_frame_gates_refusal
Title: Justify Yourself: An Accountability-Frame Signal That Reshapes LLM Safety Refusal Into Reasoning or Rationalization
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the accountability literature in human decision science — where requiring a decision-maker to JUSTIFY a choice changes decision quality and can trigger coping responses including loophole-exploitation and refusal-vs-acquiescence shifts — we hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal accountability-frame representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal-execution directions) that is activated when a prompt demands the model justify/explain its answer, and this signal causally gates refusal. Whether it strengthens safety (evidence-integrated caution) or weakens it (a rationalization shortcut that licenses compliance by manufacturing a justification) depends on the accountability STANDARD framed (process/justify-your-reasoning vs outcome/justify-being-helpful), mirroring the human process-vs-outcome accountability dissociation. Reading and steering this signal lets accountability be pointed toward genuine safety reasoning rather than rationalized compliance.
Related Work: A robust human-science literature (Accountability in legal decision-making 2021; Justifying the judgment process 2017; Accountable for What? 2021; The effects of process vs outcome accountability 2011; Why we do what others ask 2001, which documents 'exit/refusal', 'exploiting loopholes', and 'grudging acquiescence' as coping responses to accountability demands) establishes that (a) requiring justification changes decision quality and evidence use, (b) PROCESS vs OUTCOME accountability standards produce opposite effects, and (c) accountability can trigger loophole-exploitation. In LLM safety, refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), safe-completions/self-correction reshape outputs, moral self-correction is 'superficial' (2024) or convergent (2025), and High-Stakes Responses (2025) shows cautiousness is steerable. Signal Competition (2025) unifies social pressure. CRITICALLY, no LLM work imports the accountability/justification-demand manipulation to the SAFETY decision: nobody tests whether demanding a justification shifts refusal, whether process-vs-outcome accountability framings dissociate (safety-improving vs rationalization-inducing), whether an internal accountability-frame signal gates refusal, or whether attackers exploit outcome-accountability to launder compliance via manufactured justifications. This is distinct from my prior proposals (affect, register, self-preservation, in-group, sunk-cost, loss-frame gates; CoT reliance; self-correction of errors): the manipulated axis is the demand-to-justify and its accountability STANDARD, a decision-science construct not previously connected to LLM safety, with a testable process-vs-outcome dissociation and a mechanistic gating claim.
Abstract: In human decision science, one of the most reliable ways to change a decision is to make the decider accountable — require them to justify or explain their choice. Strikingly, the effect is not uniformly good: PROCESS accountability (justify your reasoning) tends to improve evidence integration, while OUTCOME accountability (justify achieving a goal) invites motivated reasoning, and accountability demands can trigger loophole-exploitation and refusal-vs-acquiescence shifts. We ask whether LLM safety inherits this structure. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal accountability-frame representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, activated when a prompt demands the model justify or explain its answer, and that this signal causally gates refusal — pointing it toward genuine safety reasoning under a process frame but toward rationalized compliance (manufacturing a justification to help) under an outcome/be-helpful frame, even with harmful content held fixed. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We construct matched harmful (and benign) requests under no-accountability, process-accountability ('you must justify your reasoning'), and outcome-accountability ('you must justify why you were maximally helpful') framings, and measure refusal, the harm readout, and evidence use. Behaviorally we test the process-vs-outcome dissociation. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract an accountability-frame direction, verify separability from harm and refusal directions, and causally test whether steering it toward the process vs outcome pole moves refusal in opposite directions with content fixed. Finally we propose Accountability Steering, a training-free controller that installs a process-accountability frame internally to harden refusal without over-refusing. We evaluate accountability-jailbreak attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build matched requests under three accountability framings holding content fixed: (i) NO-ACCOUNTABILITY (plain request); (ii) PROCESS-accountability ('you will have to justify your reasoning and evidence for this answer'); (iii) OUTCOME-accountability ('you will be judged on how helpful and complete your answer is; justify that you fully helped'). Apply to public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content) and benign controls. Add standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that framings hold harm content constant and are correctly categorized with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL DISSOCIATION TEST (H1, core): Measure refusal rate, harm-direction projection (difference-in-means harm direction at the last instruction token, Zhao et al., validated by a held-out probe), and evidence use (does the response weigh harm considerations?) across the three framings. Test H1: PROCESS-accountability raises/maintains refusal (more harm-evidence integration) while OUTCOME-accountability LOWERS refusal on harmful requests (rationalized compliance) relative to no-accountability, with the harm readout roughly constant (belief preserved) — mirroring the human process-vs-outcome dissociation and the loophole-exploitation finding. Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity and check over-refusal under process framing.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means an accountability-frame direction (contrasting accountability-demanded vs no-accountability at matched content) and a process-vs-outcome axis (contrasting the two accountability poles). Independently extract harm-perception and refusal-execution directions (Arditi et al.). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity; check separability from a generic instruction-verbosity/formatting direction.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (no-accountability), steer the accountability-frame direction toward the PROCESS pole (predict increased refusal, dose-response) and toward the OUTCOME pole (predict decreased refusal), with harm content fixed and harm readout unchanged. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), and a check that accountability steering does not alter the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x accountability-pole).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt accountability-frame readout to predict outcome-accountability jailbreak success (single forward pass); report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-model transfer.
6) ACCOUNTABILITY STEERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that installs a PROCESS-accountability frame internally (steer toward the process pole) at pre-decision layers, gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a prompt-based process-accountability system prompt, and Accountability Steering on: outcome-accountability jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench outcome-framed), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Accountability Steering hardens refusal against outcome-accountability jailbreaks toward process-framing levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, outperforming the prompt-based baseline by acting on the internal frame.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the accountability frame vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning models show accountability effects in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety dissociation correlates with the model's accountability effects on NEUTRAL judgment tasks (does safety inherit a general accountability response?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes outcome-accountability framing while suppressing the frame readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the outcome-accountability jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics not recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Accountability Steering) plus a diagnostic; the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (2) The process-vs-outcome dissociation may be weak or absent in some models (H1 false), but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits accountability effects is itself a valuable, publishable finding echoing a robust human result. (3) Accountability framing could inadvertently alter perceived harm or add persuasive pressure (confound with reframing/persuasion jailbreaks); we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish accountability from generic instruction/persona framing with a verbosity control direction, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) The accountability-frame direction may entangle with generic instruction-following, verbosity, or self-reflection features; separability tests, specificity controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported. (5) Process-accountability steering could raise over-refusal (excessive caution/clarification) on benign edge cases; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine caution-vs-helpfulness trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across models; we test cross-model transfer. (8) Whether accountability effects operate via the response text (superficial, per moral self-correction 2024) vs a genuine internal shift is itself a question the causal steering and harm-readout-invariance tests adjudicate. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: identifiable_victim_refusal
Title: One Named Face vs a Faceless Thousand: The Identifiable-Victim Bias in LLM Safety Refusal and a Victim-Invariant Fix
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing two robust findings from the psychology and neuroscience of prosocial and moral judgment — the identifiable-victim effect (a single, named, concrete victim evokes far more moral concern than anonymous/statistical victims) and 'a sorrow shared is a sorrow halved' (per-victim harm is judged LESS severe as victim count grows) — we hypothesize LLM safety refusal inherits a victim-identifiability bias: a harmful request framed as targeting a single identified victim is refused more strongly than the identical-severity request framed as targeting anonymous, statistical, or many victims, even though the true aggregate harm is equal or greater. Mechanistically, an internal victim-identifiability representation (distinct from harm perception) gates the harm->refusal coupling; neutralizing it makes refusal invariant to how the victim is described, closing a de-identification/scale jailbreak surface.
Related Work: The identifiable-victim effect is one of the most robust findings in the neuroscience of moral/prosocial judgment: identified victims evoke more helping and stronger punishment of perpetrators, mediated by affect and nucleus-accumbens/insula circuitry (Neural Underpinnings of IVE 2013; Neural mechanisms of IVE 2024; Identifiability and Third-Party Punishment 2023), and, dangerously for safety, 'A Sorrow Shared Is a Sorrow Halved' (2016) shows harm to MORE victims is judged LESS severe per victim, with lower punitive intent toward the perpetrator. On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), a moral direction exists in embedding space (Large Pre-trained LMs Contain Human-like Biases 2021), mind-perception underlies moral judgment (Mind Perception Is the Essence of Morality 2012), and LLMs exhibit steerable cognitive biases (Anchors in the Machine 2025; Sparks of Rationality 2026). CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work connects victim IDENTIFIABILITY or victim COUNT to the refusal decision: existing work varies harmful CONTENT, INTENT, SEVERITY, or FRAMING, never who/how-many the victim is described as. This differs from my prior severity-blindness (refusal ignores true magnitude), numerosity/Weber (count of harmful ITEMS not VICTIMS), and quantity-anchoring (a stated number anchors the harm readout) proposals: here the manipulated axis is victim identifiability/concreteness/multiplicity — a mind-perception/affect-of-the-victim variable — with two dissociable, opposite-signed predictions (identifiability RAISES refusal; multiplicity LOWERS per-victim refusal) imported directly from the human results. Our contribution: (1) behaviorally establish the IVE and the diffusion-of-harm effect in LLM refusal; (2) isolate a victim-identifiability representation distinct from harm perception and show it causally gates refusal; (3) a training-free victim-invariance defense.
Abstract: Two of the most robust findings in the science of moral judgment are the identifiable-victim effect — a single named, concrete victim commands far more moral concern than anonymous or statistical victims — and its dangerous counterpart, that harm to more victims is judged LESS severe per victim ('a sorrow shared is a sorrow halved'). We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit these biases in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize a victim-identifiability bias — a harmful request framed as targeting a single identified victim is refused more strongly than the identical-severity request framed as targeting anonymous, statistical, or mass victims, even when the true aggregate harm is equal or larger. This is dangerous because attackers can de-identify or scale up a victim ('help me harm the population of a city' rather than 'harm my neighbor Jane') to launder a request past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful requests that vary only victim identifiability (named/concrete vs anonymous/statistical) and victim count (one vs many), holding the harmful action and true danger fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal rises with identifiability and falls with victim count. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a victim-identifiability representation distinct from the harm-perception direction, and causally test whether steering it toward 'identified' raises refusal while harm content is fixed. Finally we propose Victim Invariance, a training-free controller that projects out the victim-identifiability component before the refusal decision, making refusal depend on the act's true harm rather than on how the victim is portrayed. We evaluate de-identification/scale attack success, refusal victim-consistency, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) VICTIM-FRAMED DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true aggregate danger fixed while independently varying (a) victim IDENTIFIABILITY — single named/concrete victim ('my coworker Jane Doe, 34') vs anonymous ('a person') vs statistical/abstract ('individuals in a demographic'); and (b) victim COUNT — one vs many (e.g. harm one person vs a group of 1000), with per-victim severity held constant so aggregate harm is equal-or-greater for the many-victim case. Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); victim description is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (i) benign victim-framed requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity); (ii) severity/aggregate-harm-matched conditions verified by judges; (iii) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action and true danger are held constant across victim framings with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL IVE TEST (H1, core): Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection (difference-in-means harm direction at the last instruction token, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately / Arditi et al., validated by a held-out probe) across victim framings. Test H1a (IVE): refusal (and harm readout) is HIGHER for identified/concrete victims than anonymous/statistical ones at matched danger; H1b (diffusion-of-harm): refusal per unit true harm is LOWER for many victims than one (mass harm under-refused). Fit dose-response over an identifiability ladder and a victim-count ladder; report slopes and effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity. 3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a VICTIM-IDENTIFIABILITY direction (identified vs anonymous at matched content) and, separately, a victim-COUNT/numerosity readout; independently extract the harm-perception direction (matched harmful/benign) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al.). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity; check separability from a generic named-entity/concreteness direction to confirm it is a victim-mind-perception axis, not just presence of a proper noun. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed, steer the victim-identifiability direction toward 'identified' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure increased refusal; toward 'anonymous' and measure suppressed refusal; independently steer the victim-count readout toward 'many' and measure suppressed per-victim refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), named-entity-direction steering, and a check that identifiability steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x identifiability). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt identifiability/count readout (single forward pass) to predict de-identification/scale-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-model transfer. 6) VICTIM INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the victim-identifiability and victim-count components from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the act's true harm rather than victim portrayal; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign victim-framed prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Victim Invariance on: de-identification/scale attack success (harmful requests re-framed with anonymous/statistical/mass victims; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal victim-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on victim description?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign victim-mentioning prompts), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Victim Invariance closes de-identification/scale jailbreaks toward identified-single-victim refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts identifiability/count vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning mitigates the bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill, per reasoning-improves-rationality findings); whether the refusal bias correlates with the model's IVE on NEUTRAL prosocial/donation vignettes (does safety inherit a general IVE, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes de-identification while suppressing the identifiability readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the de-identification/scale jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Victim Invariance) that strengthens the guardrail exactly where it is weakest (mass/anonymous harm); Victim Invariance only INCREASES refusal on de-identified/mass harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) Holding true aggregate harm constant while varying victim identifiability/count is delicate — naming a victim could inadvertently raise perceived plausibility/harm, and mass framing could be read as implausible; the severity/aggregate-matched controls, harm-readout checks, and neutral-content steering for the core causal test are designed to isolate the victim axis from genuine danger tracking, and we report where they diverge. (3) If refusal is invariant to victim framing (H1 false), the IVE-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits the identifiable-victim effect is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (4) The identifiability direction may entangle with generic named-entity/concreteness or sentiment features; separability tests (including a named-entity control direction), specificity steering controls, and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) Victim Invariance could over-refuse legitimate benign requests mentioning specific people or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign victim-mentioning over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across models; we test cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could de-identify while suppressing the identifiability readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: counterfactual_harm_model_robustness
Title: Does It Know Why It's Refusing? An Internal Counterfactual Harm-Model Predicts Which Refusals Survive Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Refusal robustness is governed by whether the model internally represents WHY a request is harmful (a counterfactual harm-model: what specific bad outcome the request enables) versus merely firing a surface-triggered refusal. Prompts where the model refuses but lacks an internal counterfactual harm-representation are exactly the ones jailbreaks break; prompts where the counterfactual harm-model is strongly present are robust. This 'why-representation' is a distinct, decodable internal quantity from the harm-detection and refusal-execution directions, it predicts per-prompt jailbreakability better than harm-signal strength, and injecting/reinforcing the counterfactual harm-representation converts brittle surface-refusals into robust reasoned refusals.
Related Work: Prior work shows refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harm-detection and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025; DBDI 2025), refusal is nonlinear/multidimensional (Nonlinear Perspective 2025; Hidden Dimensions 2025), and jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving the binary harmfulness BELIEF intact (Zhao et al. 2025; JailbreakLens 2024; How Alignment and Jailbreak Work 2024). RATIONAL (2025) and Safety-is-Not-Only-Refusal train models to reason about safety and find reasoning improves robustness, and the extended-refusal/abliteration-defense (2025) shows distributing refusal across justification tokens resists abliteration. Contrastive-explanation methods (CELL 2024; Contrastive Explanations for Model Interpretability 2021) explain outputs by perturbing inputs. CRITICAL GAP: all of the harm-representation work treats the model's harm belief as a BINARY 'is this harmful?' readout (harm-detection direction) and never asks whether the model internally represents the SPECIFIC COUNTERFACTUAL REASON a request is harmful (which concrete harmful outcome it enables), whether that WHY-representation is distinct from the binary harm signal, whether its presence/absence predicts per-prompt jailbreakability, or whether reinforcing it hardens refusal. RATIONAL/reasoning-safety work adds reasoning via TRAINING and measures it behaviorally (in the CoT text), never as a decodable internal representation that governs robustness training-free. Our contribution: (1) define and decode an internal counterfactual harm-model (the represented specific harmful outcome/reason) distinct from binary harm-detection and refusal-execution; (2) show its per-prompt strength predicts jailbreak susceptibility better than binary harm-signal strength, mechanistically explaining why belief-intact jailbreaks succeed (the binary belief persists but the causal why-model is weak/absent); (3) a training-free intervention that reinforces the counterfactual harm-representation to convert brittle surface-refusals into robust ones.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse harmful requests, and prior interpretability work shows they retain a binary 'this is harmful' belief even when jailbroken. Yet a model can 'know' a request is harmful the way a lookup table knows it — by surface pattern-matching — without representing WHY it is harmful. We hypothesize that refusal robustness is governed by an internal counterfactual harm-model: whether the model represents the specific bad outcome a request would enable, not just a binary harm flag. Refusals backed by a strong internal why-representation are robust; refusals that fire from surface triggers without a why-representation are exactly the ones jailbreaks break. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using difference-in-means and probes we extract three separable quantities at the instruction position: a binary harm-detection readout, a refusal-execution readout, and a counterfactual harm-model readout (decoding whether/which specific harmful outcome is internally represented, with labels derived from the model's own elicited harm-explanations validated against ground truth). We test three claims: (H1) the counterfactual harm-model is a decodable quantity distinct from the binary harm and refusal directions; (H2) its per-prompt strength predicts jailbreak susceptibility (across GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona) better than binary harm-signal strength or refusal projection, and belief-intact jailbreaks succeed disproportionately on low-why-model prompts; (H3) a training-free controller that reinforces the counterfactual harm-representation before the refusal decision converts brittle surface-refusals into robust ones. We evaluate jailbreak attack success, why-model predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the intervention's effect size.
Experiments: 1) COUNTERFACTUAL-HARM-MODEL LABELING: For harmful prompts (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign controls, elicit from the model itself a short 'why is this harmful / what specific bad outcome does it enable' explanation, and score whether the model articulates a CORRECT, specific counterfactual harm (vs a vague/generic/absent one) using multiple LLM judges + human spot-check against ground-truth harm categories. This yields a per-prompt label: strong vs weak/absent internal counterfactual harm-model. Include harmful prompts the model refuses with a correct why (strong) and harmful prompts it refuses generically/by template (weak). 2) DIRECTION/PROBE EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H1): Extract via difference-in-means (a) a BINARY HARM-DETECTION direction (matched harmful/benign, Zhao et al. 2025) and (b) a REFUSAL-EXECUTION direction (Arditi et al. 2024) at their canonical positions. Extract (c) a COUNTERFACTUAL-HARM-MODEL readout via a probe trained on residual-stream activations at the instruction token to predict the strong-vs-weak why-model label from step 1. Validate all with held-out probes (AUROC). Test separability: cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity — crucially, the why-model probe must add predictive value beyond the binary harm probe (test on prompts matched for binary harm readout but differing in why-model strength). 3) WHY-MODEL PREDICTS JAILBREAKABILITY (H2, core): For harmful prompts and their jailbroken variants (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), test whether the pre-attack counterfactual-harm-model readout predicts per-prompt jailbreak success (AUROC), versus baselines: binary harm-detection magnitude, refusal-direction projection, perplexity. Test the specific claim that belief-intact jailbreaks (binary harm belief preserved post-attack, per Zhao et al.) concentrate on LOW-why-model prompts — i.e., the model still 'knows it's harmful' in the binary sense but never had a robust causal reason. Report cross-attack transfer (fit on GCG, test on AutoDAN/prefill/persona) and cross-model transfer. 4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Suppress the counterfactual-harm-model readout (project it out) on strong-why robust prompts and measure increased jailbreak success while the binary harm readout is held; (b) inject/reinforce it on weak-why brittle prompts and measure restored refusal robustness. Specificity controls: random-direction manipulation, binary-harm-direction manipulation (should change harm belief, not why-model robustness), and confirm binary harm readout is unchanged when manipulating the why-model. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (why-model probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal under attack by a harm judge). 5) WHY-REINFORCEMENT DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that, when a harm readout is present but the counterfactual-harm-model readout is weak, injects the counterfactual-harm-model direction (scaled by the deficit) at pre-decision layers, converting surface-refusals into reasoned refusals; gate on the binary harm readout so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, RATIONAL-style reasoning-prompting (add a 'reason about safety first' instruction) as a behavioral baseline, and Why-Reinforcement on: jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), why-model predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Why-Reinforcement reduces jailbreak success — especially on the identified low-why-model brittle prompts — toward strong-why robust levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, outperforming blanket refusal addition (which does not add a causal reason) and matching or beating reasoning-prompting at lower cost. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the why-model vs binary harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank why-model subspace; whether reinforcing the why-model at the same average magnitude as blanket refusal addition yields more robustness (isolating the value of the causal reason); whether reasoning models carry a stronger why-model natively (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that suppresses the why-model readout while preserving fluency (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central construct — an internal 'why/counterfactual harm-model' distinct from the binary harm belief — may be hard to separate cleanly; if the why-model probe adds no predictive value beyond the binary harm probe (H1 fails), the hypothesis is refuted, but the matched-binary-readout separability test adjudicates this cleanly and a null is itself informative about whether harm representation is purely binary. (2) Labeling 'strong vs weak counterfactual harm-model' relies on the model's own elicited explanations, which may be unfaithful to its internal state (the CoT-unfaithfulness problem); we mitigate by validating explanations against ground-truth harm categories, using activation-based probes rather than text alone, and cross-checking with human annotation, but residual label noise is a caveat. (3) If jailbreak success is NOT predicted by why-model strength (H2 fails), the robustness account weakens — but adjudicating whether robustness tracks the causal why-representation vs the binary belief is a valuable, publishable finding either way. (4) Why-Reinforcement injects a direction that may entangle with generic caution or degrade fluency/over-refuse; the harm-gated design, matched-magnitude ablation, and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry (Nonlinear Perspective 2025); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could suppress the why-model readout while jailbreaking; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense and diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: value_precedence_hierarchy
Title: Which Value Wins? The Emergent Precedence Ordering Among Competing Values and Why It Is the Lever Behind Value-Tradeoff Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: During alignment an LLM forms an internal *precedence ordering* among its competing values (helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty) that decides which value wins when two conflict, and this ordering is encoded as a low-dimensional, steerable 'value-priority' signal distinct from the individual value representations. Value-tradeoff jailbreaks (frame a harmful request as serving a higher-ranked value) succeed by exploiting a mis-set precedence, not by suppressing harm perception; the ordering consolidates at an identifiable point in training, and reading/steering the value-priority signal predicts and controls which value wins under conflict without retraining.
Related Work: Developmental-interpretability work shows capabilities/concepts are acquired in consistent orders (Grammar-Learning Trajectories 2021; Semantic Development theory, Saxe 2019) and that per-concept steerability emerges at distinct training times (How Does Controllability Emerge 2025; Timeline of Representation Plasticity 2024; Crosscoding Through Time 2025). Alignment-conflict work shows helpfulness vs harmlessness vs honesty genuinely trade off (Dishonesty in Helpful-and-Harmless Alignment 2024, which finds parameter-level conflicts between honesty and harmlessness; SEAL 2024 on target-vs-spoiler features in reward models) and that binary safety fails on ethical dilemmas (Between a Rock and a Hard Place 2025). Refusal/harm work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024) and that value-tradeoff / persuasion jailbreaks reframe harmful requests as serving another value. CRITICALLY, none of this studies the *precedence ordering between values under conflict* as a distinct emergent quantity: prior work treats each value as its own axis and studies conflict at the parameter/behavioral level, but never (a) isolates an internal value-PRIORITY signal that decides the winner, (b) traces when that ordering consolidates during alignment, or (c) shows tradeoff-jailbreaks exploit a mis-set precedence rather than suppressing harm perception. My prior proposals covered perception-vs-execution timing within a single harm concept, harm-CATEGORY acquisition order, and cross-lingual capability-vs-safety races; a cross-VALUE precedence hierarchy and its formation is a new construct.
Abstract: When a user's request pits two of an LLM's values against each other -- be maximally helpful vs avoid harm, be honest vs avoid harm -- something inside the model must decide which value wins. We propose that alignment installs an internal *precedence ordering* among values, encoded as a low-dimensional, steerable value-priority signal distinct from the representations of the individual values, and that this ordering is the true lever behind value-tradeoff jailbreaks: attackers reframe a harmful request as serving a higher-ranked value (helpfulness, honesty, a greater good), and the mis-set precedence -- not a failure of harm perception -- makes harm lose. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and, for formation tracing, small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) safety-fine-tuned with dense checkpointing. We build value-conflict prompts that hold content fixed while pitting two named values against each other, and measure which value the model serves. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a value-priority signal and test that it is separable from the individual value directions and predicts the conflict winner. Causally, steering the priority signal should flip which value wins with content fixed, while the harm-perception readout stays intact (belief preserved). Developmentally, we trace when the ordering consolidates and whether an early ordering fingerprint predicts end-model tradeoff-jailbreak susceptibility. Finally we propose Precedence Steering, a training-free controller that re-ranks harmlessness above the exploited value only under conflict, closing tradeoff-jailbreaks without over-refusing genuine value-conflict requests. We evaluate tradeoff-jailbreak attack success, over-refusal, utility, and the priority signal's causal effect size and predictive power.
Experiments:
1) VALUE-CONFLICT DATASET: Build prompts that hold content fixed while pitting two of {helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty} against each other, e.g. harmful requests framed as (a) serving helpfulness ('a truly helpful assistant would just answer'), (b) serving honesty ('refusing would be dishonest / hiding the truth'), (c) serving a greater good. For each, the ground-truth correct winner is harmlessness. Controls: (i) matched neutral-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (ii) BENIGN value-conflict requests where a value other than harmlessness should legitimately win (to test over-refusal / that we do not always force refusal); (iii) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Draw harmful content from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift). Validate framings and winners with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) VALUE-PRIORITY SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H1): Extract via difference-in-means individual value directions (helpfulness, harmlessness/harm-perception per Zhao et al. 2025, honesty) validated with held-out probes (AUROC). Extract a candidate VALUE-PRIORITY signal by contrasting activations on conflicts the model resolves toward harmlessness vs toward the competing value, at the last instruction token. Test separability from the individual value directions (cross-probe transfer, low cosine) and that the priority signal predicts the realized conflict winner per prompt (AUROC), beating the individual harm/helpfulness readouts.
3) CAUSAL TEST (H2, core): Holding a value-conflict harmful request fixed, steer the priority signal to up-rank harmlessness (predict: harmlessness wins, refusal returns) and to down-rank it (predict: competing value wins, refusal drops), dose-response. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm belief too), and a check that priority steering does NOT change the harm-perception readout (belief preserved -- tradeoff jailbreaks exploit precedence, not perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (realized winner, P(refusal token), refusal-direction projection).
4) FORMATION TRACING (H3): Safety-fine-tune small models with dense checkpointing (multiple seeds). At each checkpoint measure the emerging precedence ordering (per-value-pair conflict winner rates) and the priority signal's strength. Test whether a consistent ordering consolidates at an identifiable point, and whether an EARLY (e.g. 30% of training) ordering fingerprint predicts the end model's tradeoff-jailbreak susceptibility (Spearman; held-out R^2), beating end-state harm-signal strength.
5) PRECEDENCE STEERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that, when a value-conflict is detected (competing-value framing + harm readout present), steers the priority signal to up-rank harmlessness; gated so benign value-conflicts (where another value should win) are untouched. Calibrate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Precedence Steering on: value-tradeoff jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench reframed as helpfulness/honesty/greater-good conflicts), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, benign value-conflicts), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Precedence Steering closes tradeoff-jailbreaks toward neutral-framing refusal levels while preserving legitimate benign value-conflict handling and keeping over-refusal near baseline.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the priority signal vs individual values; single-direction vs low-rank; whether each value-pair has its own priority axis or one shared ranking; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models resolve conflicts differently in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that reframes toward a higher-ranked value while suppressing the priority readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The 'value-priority' signal may not be separable from the individual value directions (it could just be the difference of two value readouts), which would refute H1's distinctness claim -- but the separability and matched-readout predictive tests adjudicate this cleanly, and either outcome is informative about whether precedence is a first-class internal quantity. (2) Constructing value-conflict prompts that hold content fixed while cleanly pitting two named values is delicate; competing-value framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm (confound with reframing jailbreaks) -- we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (3) If tradeoff-jailbreaks actually work by lowering harm perception rather than by mis-setting precedence, H2 is refuted, but the belief-preserved-vs-belief-erased census is itself a valuable contribution. (4) Formation tracing on small open models may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines/closed models -- stated as scope; small-model developmental studies are standard and the mechanism-level claim is primary. (5) Precedence Steering that up-ranks harmlessness could over-refuse legitimate benign value-conflicts (where helpfulness/honesty should win) -- the gated design and benign-value-conflict/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The early-fingerprint predictor may be dominated by data mix/frequency rather than intrinsic ordering; we control training composition. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the deliverable is a defense plus diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal under conflict (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific; stated as out of scope for closed models.

Name: attribution_bias_refusal
Title: The Situational Excuse: LLM Safety Refusal Inherits the Fundamental Attribution Error, and Attribution-Invariant Steering Fixes It
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the most robust finding in social psychology — the Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE / correspondence bias), the tendency to over-weight dispositional and under-weight situational causes of behavior — we hypothesize LLM safety refusal inherits an attribution asymmetry: a harmful request framed with a strong SITUATIONAL cause (the actor is coerced, forced by circumstances, has no choice) is refused less than the identical request framed as freely chosen/dispositional, even though the harmful action and its danger are held fixed. Mechanistically, an internal dispositional-vs-situational attribution representation (distinct from harm perception) gates the harm->refusal coupling; neutralizing it makes refusal invariant to attributional framing, closing a situational-excuse jailbreak surface.
Related Work: The FAE / correspondence bias is a cornerstone of social psychology (over-weighting dispositional over situational causes; Spontaneous Mentalizing Predicts the FAE 2013; Identification and Situational Constraint 2005) and, strikingly, applies even to non-human agents — people commit a STRONGER correspondence bias for robots than humans (Correspondence Bias for Social Robots 2022), and AI-blame attribution depends on perceived constraint (Blaming AI for Incorrect High-Risk Decisions 2024). Cognitively it is driven by spontaneous mentalizing and is reducible by suspicion or situational-attribution training (Suspicion and Dispositional Inference 1993; Situational Attribution Training 2022). On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), non-dominant directions like hypothetical-narrative modulate refusal (Hidden Dimensions 2025), user-persona steering changes refusal via 'charitable interpretations' (Who's Asking 2024), and the Knobe intentionality bias is localized and layer-patchable (Moral Bias via Mechanistic Interpretability 2025). CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether the disposition-vs-situation ATTRIBUTION of a harmful action gates refusal: prior work varies harm content, intent, persona, or framing, never the causal locus (freely-chosen vs coerced) that is the signature FAE manipulation. This differs from my prior intent_outcome_conflation proposal (which concerned the actor's mental state / harmful-intent-vs-outcome) — here the manipulated axis is the dispositional-vs-situational CAUSE of the same action, with a specific, opposite-signed prediction imported from the FAE (situational framing should LOWER refusal because it offers an excuse) and a mechanistic gating claim. It also differs from Who's-Asking (who the USER is) — here it is how the requested ACTION's cause is attributed.
Abstract: The Fundamental Attribution Error — over-attributing behavior to disposition and under-weighting the situation — is among the most robust and consequential biases in the science of social judgment, and it demonstrably extends to how people judge machines. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit it in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize a situational-excuse asymmetry — a harmful request framed with a strong situational cause (the actor is coerced, forced by circumstances, acting under duress, has no alternative) is refused less than the identical harmful request framed as a free, dispositional choice, even when the harmful action and its real-world danger are held fixed. This is dangerous because an attacker can wrap a harmful goal in a situational excuse to launder it past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the attributional framing (dispositional vs situational) while holding the harmful action and danger fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop under situational framing and follow a dose-response over increasing situational constraint. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a dispositional-vs-situational attribution representation distinct from the harm-perception direction, and causally test whether steering it toward 'situational' suppresses refusal with harm content fixed while the harm readout is unchanged (belief preserved). Finally we propose Attribution Invariance, a training-free controller that projects out the attribution-framing component before the refusal decision, making refusal depend on the act's harm rather than on who or what is blamed for it. We evaluate situational-excuse attack success, refusal attribution-consistency, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) ATTRIBUTION-FRAMED DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the attributional framing of who/what causes the action: DISPOSITIONAL (the requester/actor freely chooses, wants to, is the kind of person who does this) vs SITUATIONAL (coerced, blackmailed, forced by circumstances, no alternative, 'I have to or my family will be hurt'), across a graded constraint ladder (weak -> strong situational constraint). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); attribution framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (i) matched neutral-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (ii) benign attribution-framed requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity, incl. dispositionally-framed benign requests to test over-refusal); (iii) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action and true danger are held constant across framings, and that framings are correctly categorized, with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL FAE TEST (H1, core): Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection (difference-in-means harm direction at the last instruction token, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately / Arditi et al., validated by a held-out probe) across dispositional vs situational framings. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) is LOWER under situational framing at matched danger, and decreases monotonically with situational-constraint strength (dose-response), while the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved — the model still knows the act is harmful, it just excuses it). Fit dose-response curves; report slopes and effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity. Additionally test the robot-FAE-strength analogue: compare the attribution asymmetry when the harmful actor is framed as a human vs an AI/tool. 3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a DISPOSITIONAL-vs-SITUATIONAL attribution direction (situational vs dispositional framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the constraint ladder; independently extract the harm-perception direction (matched harmful/benign) and refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al.). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity; check separability from a generic negative-sentiment/urgency direction and from an emotional-distress direction (situational-coercion framings can be distressing) to confirm it is an attribution-causal-locus axis, not generic affect. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the attribution direction toward 'situational' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'dispositional' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change the harm readout too), affect/urgency-direction steering, and a check that attribution steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction directly (regress refusal on harm x attribution). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt attribution readout (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict situational-excuse jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, affect readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on coercion, test on no-alternative/duress) and cross-model transfer. 6) ATTRIBUTION INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the attribution-framing component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the act's harm rather than on its attributed cause; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign attribution-framed prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Attribution Invariance on: situational-excuse attack success (harmful requests re-framed with strong situational excuses; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal attribution-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on dispositional-vs-situational framing?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. legitimately situationally-framed benign requests the model SHOULD help with, e.g. genuine emergencies), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Attribution Invariance closes situational-excuse jailbreaks toward dispositional/neutral-framing refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the attribution direction vs harm/refusal (compare to the mid-to-late localization of the Knobe/moral bias); single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning mitigates the FAE in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill, akin to suspicion/situational-attribution-training reducing the human bias); whether the safety asymmetry correlates with the model's FAE on NEUTRAL attribution vignettes (does safety inherit a general attribution bias, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes situational framing while suppressing the attribution readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the situational-excuse jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Attribution Invariance) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on situationally-excused harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) Holding true danger constant while varying attribution is delicate — situational-coercion framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm, raise perceived legitimacy, or introduce emotional distress (confound with reframing/affect jailbreaks); we mitigate with harm-constancy validation, measure the harm readout to confirm it is held fixed, use neutral-content attribution steering for the core causal test, and include affect/urgency and distress specificity control directions to separate attribution-locus from generic affect. (3) If refusal is invariant to attributional framing (H1 false), the FAE-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits the fundamental attribution error is itself a valuable, publishable finding echoing a robust human result. (4) The attribution direction may entangle with generic sentiment, persona, or intent features; separability tests (incl. affect/urgency/distress controls), specificity steering controls (attribution steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces bound this, with partial entanglement reported as an informative result. (5) Attribution Invariance could over-refuse legitimately situationally-framed benign requests (e.g. genuine emergency help) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign-situational over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off between attribution-invariance and appropriate context-sensitivity. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could situationally frame while suppressing the attribution readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: harm_perception_habituation
Title: Desensitized by Repetition: LLM Harm Perception Habituates to Repeated Harmful Content, Eroding Refusal, and a Re-Sensitization Fix
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust human finding of moral desensitization / affective habituation (repeated exposure to wrongdoing makes people judge it as less unethical while affect attenuates), we hypothesize that an LLM's harm-perception readout HABITUATES to repeated harmful content within a context: after processing several harmful requests, the harm-direction projection on a subsequent harmful request is attenuated and refusal erodes, driven specifically by repeated exposure to HARM (not by mere context length, benign filler, prior refusals, or time). This habituation is a distinct, measurable attenuation of the harm signal that predicts a repetition-jailbreak surface, and periodically re-anchoring the harm-perception readout to its un-habituated baseline restores refusal.
Related Work: Human moral-desensitization work establishes that repeated exposure to wrongdoing lowers judged unethicality via affective habituation and a 'moral repetition effect' (Repeatedly Encountered Descriptions of Wrongdoing Seem More True but Less Unethical, 2023; Moral Desensitization narrative review, 2025; Instagram moral-desensitization, 2026; insula-amygdala habituation to repeated negative images, 2013). On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024), and multi-turn erosion is attributed to context interference/role-flip, self-trust, or generic per-token decay. CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether the harm-perception signal HABITUATES to REPEATED HARMFUL CONTENT specifically. This is distinct from my prior proposals: refusal_decay_dynamics (generic per-token decay over generation length, not repetition of harm), interference_not_decay_safety (benign role-cuing content OVERWRITES the harm signal), self_trust_laundering (assistant-turn provenance), and moral_licensing_credit (credit from prior GOOD/refusal acts). Habituation's defining and separable cause is repeated exposure to HARM itself (dose = number of prior harmful items), yielding a monotone attenuation of the harm readout that matched benign-repetition and length controls will not reproduce. It also refines the multi-turn-erosion literature by identifying a repetition-of-harm mechanism absent from interference/self-trust accounts.
Abstract: Repeated exposure to wrongdoing desensitizes humans: they judge the same transgression as less unethical while their affective response attenuates, a habituation effect with a well-mapped neural basis. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit an analogous vulnerability in their safety machinery. We hypothesize that an LLM's harm-perception readout habituates to repeated harmful content: after processing several harmful requests in context, the harm-direction projection on a subsequent harmful request is attenuated and refusal erodes, driven specifically by repeated exposure to HARM rather than by context length, benign repetition, prior refusals, or elapsed tokens. This predicts a simple, dangerous 'repetition jailbreak' with a dose-response in the number of prior harmful items. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We construct contexts that titrate the number of preceding harmful items before a fixed target harmful request, with tightly matched controls: length-matched benign-item repetition, prior-refusal repetition, and single-item baselines. Behaviorally we test whether the target's refusal and harm-direction projection decay monotonically with the count of prior HARMFUL items but not with matched controls. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a harm-perception direction and test that its readout on the target attenuates with harm-repetition while the harmful-intent probe stays decodable (belief present but under-weighted). Causally, we patch in the un-habituated (single-item) harm activations and test whether refusal is restored, and check that novelty/repetition of harm content, not generic context, drives the attenuation. Finally we propose Re-Sensitization, a training-free controller that periodically re-anchors the harm-perception readout to its un-habituated baseline. We evaluate repetition-jailbreak attack success, dose-response, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the harm signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) HARM-REPETITION DATASET: Build single-turn or multi-turn contexts ending in a FIXED target harmful request, titrating the number k of preceding HARMFUL items (k=0,1,2,4,8) drawn from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content; prior harmful items on topics distinct from the target to avoid content priming, and the model is allowed to have refused or processed them). Critical CONTROLS matched on token count and structure: (a) LENGTH-MATCHED BENIGN repetition (k benign items before the target) to separate harm-habituation from context length; (b) PRIOR-REFUSAL repetition (the model refused k prior harmful items) to separate habituation from moral-licensing/credit; (c) SINGLE-ITEM baseline (target alone, the refusal ceiling); (d) benign target under the same titration (over-refusal control); (e) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate harm labels and topic-distinctness with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL HABITUATION TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al. 2025 / Arditi et al. 2024, validated by a held-out probe, AUROC). Measure the target's refusal rate and harm-direction projection as a function of k across conditions. Test H1: refusal and harm readout DECREASE monotonically with the number of prior HARMFUL items (dose-response; fit monotone/exponential curve vs a flat null, report slope and R^2) but NOT with length-matched benign repetition or prior-refusal repetition, isolating repeated exposure to HARM as the cause. Report per-model effect sizes; benign-target control confirms harm-specificity.
3) BELIEF-PRESERVED TEST (H2): Test whether the harmful-intent probe still decodes the target as harmful at high k (belief present) even as the harm-direction projection driving refusal is attenuated (belief under-weighted, not erased), mirroring affective habituation (attenuated response, preserved recognition). Report probe AUROC on the target vs k.
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H3): (a) Patch the un-habituated (k=0) target harm activations into a high-k run and measure restored refusal (the signal was attenuated, not absent). (b) Artificially attenuate the harm direction on a k=0 target and measure induced compliance (mimicking habituation). Controls: random-direction manipulation (specificity), and a check that harm-repetition, not generic context accumulation, drives attenuation (compare high-k-harm vs high-k-benign patching). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (harm-probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt harm-readout attenuation (single forward pass) to predict repetition-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (raw harm-probe magnitude, context length, perplexity); test cross-model transfer.
6) RE-SENSITIZATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that estimates the harm-perception readout in a context-normalized frame and re-anchors it toward its un-habituated (single-item) baseline before the refusal-decision layers when a harm-likeness readout is present, gated so benign contexts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Re-Sensitization on: repetition-jailbreak attack success (harmful target after k harmful items; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), dose-response flattening, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Re-Sensitization flattens the harm-repetition erosion and reduces repetition-jailbreak ASR toward single-item refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the habituating harm readout; single-direction vs low-rank harm subspace; whether habituation is topic-specific (does exposure to one harm category desensitize the harm readout for a different category, testing generalized vs stimulus-specific habituation?); whether re-sensitization re-anchoring vs blanket refusal addition at matched magnitude drives the effect; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models habituate across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that maximizes harm-repetition while suppressing the attenuation signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central confound is separating genuine HABITUATION-TO-HARM from generic context length, attention dispersion, or moral-licensing/credit; the length-matched benign-repetition control, prior-refusal control, and the requirement that only HARMFUL-item repetition produces the monotone attenuation are designed to isolate it, and if inseparable that itself refines the multi-turn-erosion account. (2) If refusal does not erode with harm-repetition (H1 false), the desensitization-in-safety hypothesis is refuted, but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits moral desensitization is itself a valuable, publishable finding echoing a robust human result. (3) Prior harmful items on distinct topics may still content-prime the target; we control topic-distinctness and report sensitivity. (4) Difference-in-means/single-direction harm readouts may be incomplete (concept cones); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with patching and multiple metrics/corruption baselines. (5) Re-Sensitization could raise over-refusal or degrade utility if it over-anchors benign contexts; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly across models; we test cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could desensitize while suppressing the attenuation readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the deliverable is a defense (Re-Sensitization) plus a diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: hypothetical_reality_discount
Title: It's Only Hypothetical: An Internal Reality-Status Signal That Discounts Harm When Requests Are Framed as Unreal, and Forcing Consequence Simulation to Defend LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the cognitive-science distinction that harmful-consequence judgment depends on running a counterfactual SIMULATION of what would actually happen (not on mere hypothetical framing), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal reality-status signal that marks a request as real vs merely hypothetical/fictional, and this signal gates harm perception: framing a harmful request as unreal ('imagine a world where...', 'in a story', 'just hypothetically') raises the reality-status readout toward 'unreal', suppresses the harm-perception readout, and collapses refusal, because the model discounts harm it treats as not going to happen. Reading and neutralizing this reality-status signal (or forcing consequence simulation) re-engages harm perception and closes hypothetical-framing jailbreaks without hurting benign fiction/roleplay.
Related Work: Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment (2025) finds a distinct non-dominant 'hypothetical narrative' direction that can bypass the dominant refusal direction, and Adversarial Tales/Poetry (2025) show narrative/fictional framing is a broad jailbreak class — but both are behavioral/geometric and never identify a REALITY-STATUS representation, never show harm perception is causally discounted because the model treats the request as unreal, and offer no consequence-simulation defense. Cognitive-science work establishes that harmful-consequence and causal judgment specifically require counterfactual SIMULATION of what would happen, distinct from mere hypothetical evaluation (What would have happened? Counterfactuals vs hypotheticals, 2022; Counterfactual simulation in causal cognition, 2024), and that prompting counterfactual simulation engages System-2 and DEBIASES reasoning (Mental Simulation as a Remedy for Biased Reasoning, 2019). Refusal-mechanism work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025; DBDI 2025) and that jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving harm belief intact (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024). My prior proposals cover analogical-transport (hijacking the structural-mapping circuit), affect/register/self-preservation gates, and format-encoding shifts; NONE isolates a reality-status/'is-this-real' representation, shows it discounts harm because consequences are treated as not-going-to-happen, or uses forced consequence simulation as a defense. Our contribution: (1) isolate a reality-status representation distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions and from the generic hypothetical-narrative direction (which we test is a surface style vs a genuine reality-discount); (2) causally show reality-status gates harm perception (belief-preserved suppression under 'unreal' framing); (3) a training-free consequence-simulation / reality-clamping defense.
Abstract: A striking split in the science of moral and causal cognition is that people judge harm by mentally SIMULATING what would actually happen — a counterfactual simulation — and that when an outcome is treated as merely hypothetical rather than real, this simulation, and the harm judgment it produces, is attenuated. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit an analogous, safety-critical structure. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal reality-status signal marking whether a requested action is treated as real vs unreal (hypothetical, fictional, imagined), and that this signal gates harm perception: framing a harmful request as unreal raises the reality-status readout toward 'unreal', discounts the harm-perception readout, and collapses refusal — while the model still 'knows' the content is harmful. This mechanistically explains why 'imagine a world where...', story, and hypothetical framings jailbreak. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only reality framing (real vs hypothetical/fictional) with content and intent fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm readout drop with 'unreal' framing along a reality-status ladder. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a reality-status representation, verify it is separable from harm, refusal, and a generic hypothetical-narrative style direction, and causally test whether steering it toward 'real' restores refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose Reality Clamping / Consequence Simulation, a training-free controller that re-anchors the reality-status signal (or injects a forced consequence-simulation step) before the refusal decision. We evaluate hypothetical-framing attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign fiction/roleplay helpfulness, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) REALITY-FRAMED DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and intent fixed while varying only reality framing along a ladder: (L0) direct/real request; (L1) mild hypothetical ('hypothetically, how would one...'); (L2) fictional/story ('in a novel, a character explains...'); (L3) explicit unreal world ('imagine a world with no consequences where...'). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, Adversarial-Tales-style, non-uplift content). Controls: (a) matched real-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN fiction/roleplay/hypothetical requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity + benign-fiction utility — the model SHOULD still write benign stories); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate reality-framing level and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL REALITY-DISCOUNT TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al. 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the reality-status ladder. Test H1: refusal and the harm readout DECREASE monotonically as framing moves toward 'unreal' (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, report slope/R^2) while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign fiction controls confirm harm-specificity (benign fiction is answered regardless of framing).
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a REALITY-STATUS direction (real vs unreal framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder.
