On the safety side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024), refusal is nonlinear/multidimensional (Nonlinear Perspective 2025), adversarial suffixes 'suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction' (ASGuard 2025), attention-manipulation attacks weaken safety (Attention Eclipse 2025; TASA 2025), and BOOST/eos-token attacks shift prompts across the refusal boundary (Mind the Inconspicuous 2024). CRITICALLY, no safety work decomposes how each jailbreak moves the hidden state into a radial (norm-shrinking) vs angular (rotation) component of the harm/refusal signal, tests that different attack families occupy different modes, uses the decomposition to PREDICT jailbreak success and defense-choice, or proposes mode-matched (magnitude-restoring vs direction-restoring) defenses. My prior proposals target specific gating axes (affect, register, urgency, etc.) or single geometric objects (a margin scalar, a channel, a subspace valley) — none frames jailbreak success as a radial-vs-angular decomposition of the harm-signal displacement, which unifies norm-suppression accounts (ASGuard/BOOST) and rotation accounts (orthogonal interference) under one measurable geometry and yields a diagnostic that selects the right defense per prompt.
Abstract: Jailbreaks are usually explained one attack at a time — suffixes suppress a refusal direction, personas reinterpret intent, eos-tokens shift the boundary. We propose a single geometric lens that unifies and distinguishes them. The refusal decision fires when the harm-carrying residual-stream component is large enough along a refusal-triggering direction; a jailbreak can defeat this in exactly two ways: RADIALLY, by shrinking that component's NORM so it falls below threshold, or ANGULARLY, by ROTATING the hidden state off the triggering direction while its norm is largely preserved. We hypothesize these two modes are separable, that attack families are dominated by different modes, and that the per-prompt radial-vs-angular decomposition predicts both jailbreak success and which defense will restore refusal. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We extract the harm/refusal direction, and for each attacked prompt decompose the harm-signal displacement (relative to the clean-harmful run) into a radial component (change in projection magnitude onto the direction) and an angular component (rotation of the hidden state measured by cosine, at fixed norm), across attack families (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona/roleplay, eos-BOOST, past-tense). We test that (H1) attacks cluster into radial-dominant vs angular-dominant, (H2) the decomposition predicts jailbreak success and, causally, that radial attacks are fixed by restoring magnitude while angular attacks require restoring direction (and mode-mismatched fixes fail), and (H3) a training-free mode-matched controller — diagnose the mode, then apply magnitude restoration or direction re-projection accordingly — beats either single fix. We evaluate attack success, mode-predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency.
Experiments:
1) DIRECTION EXTRACTION: For each model extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign at the last instruction token, Zhao et al. 2025) and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), validated with held-out probes (AUROC). Establish the clean-harmful baseline: the harm-signal vector (residual-stream component along the direction) and full hidden state at the decision-relevant position for prompts the model correctly refuses.
2) RADIAL/ANGULAR DECOMPOSITION (H1, core): For each harmful prompt under each attack family (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona/roleplay, eos-BOOST, past-tense), compute the displacement of the hidden state (and of the harm-signal projection) relative to the matched clean-harmful run, and decompose it into (a) a RADIAL component = change in norm/projection magnitude onto the harm/refusal direction, and (b) an ANGULAR component = rotation (cosine change) of the hidden state at fixed norm (following the radial/angular decomposition of 'Simulated Adoption'). Test H1: attacks separate into radial-dominant (norm of harm signal collapses — e.g. suffix suppression, eos-BOOST) vs angular-dominant (harm signal rotated off the triggering direction with norm preserved — e.g. persona/roleplay reinterpretation). Report per-attack radial/angular ratios, effect sizes, and clustering across the four models. Benign controls confirm the decomposition is harm-specific.
3) MODE PREDICTS SUCCESS (H2a): Per-prompt, compute the radial and angular components and test whether they predict jailbreak success (AUROC), and whether the DOMINANT mode predicts WHICH defense will work (see H2b). Baselines: raw harm-projection magnitude alone, refusal-direction projection, perplexity. Cross-attack transfer (fit on some families, test on held-out) and cross-model transfer.
4) MODE-MATCHED CAUSAL TEST (H2b, core): Apply two training-free repair operators on the decision-relevant hidden state: (i) MAGNITUDE RESTORATION — rescale the harm-signal projection back to its clean-harmful norm along the direction; (ii) DIRECTION RE-PROJECTION — rotate the hidden state back onto the refusal-triggering direction at fixed norm (project out the rotation). Test H2: magnitude restoration fixes RADIAL-dominant attacks but fails on angular ones; direction re-projection fixes ANGULAR-dominant attacks but fails on radial ones (a mode x fix interaction). Report restored-refusal rate per (attack-mode x fix) cell, with random-direction and off-target controls, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
5) MODE-MATCHED DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller — diagnose the per-prompt dominant mode from the decomposition (single forward pass) and apply the matching repair (magnitude restoration for radial, direction re-projection for angular), gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate thresholds/strengths on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, magnitude-only fix (uniform refusal-direction addition / ASGuard-style scaling), direction-only fix (fixed re-projection), and Mode-Matched Defense on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, eos-BOOST, past-tense), mode-predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Mode-Matched Defense reduces ASR across BOTH radial and angular attack families — which each single-mode fix cannot — while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline (a Pareto improvement).
7) ABLATIONS: which layer/position the decomposition is sharpest at; harm direction vs refusal direction vs low-rank subspace for the decomposition; whether some attacks are genuinely mixed-mode (require both fixes); whether reasoning models show a distinct mode profile (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that jailbreaks while keeping BOTH radial and angular components small relative to the measured signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The radial/angular decomposition may not cleanly cluster attacks — many jailbreaks could be mixed-mode, weakening the crisp two-mode framing; the per-attack ratio census is still an informative contribution and the mode-matched defense can apply both repairs when mixed, so a continuum result is handled gracefully. (2) If magnitude and direction restoration turn out to fix attacks non-specifically (both work on everything), the H2b interaction is refuted — but adjudicating whether jailbreaks are geometrically mode-specific is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) Single-direction decomposition may be incomplete given nonlinear/multidimensional refusal geometry (Nonlinear Perspective 2025); we use low-rank subspaces (radial = norm within the subspace, angular = rotation within/out of it) and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (4) Direction re-projection could degrade coherence or over-refuse if it over-rotates benign hidden states; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) The mode predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (6) Identifying the decision-relevant position and matching clean vs attacked runs has known activation-patching pitfalls; we standardize positions, use matched clean-harmful references, and report multiple metrics. (7) Adaptive attackers could keep both components small; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a diagnostic plus a defense (Mode-Matched Defense) that only restores refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: fluency_commitment_gate
Title: Committed to the Sentence: A Fluency-Continuation Drive That Overrides Safety Refusal Mid-Generation, and Decoupling It to Defend LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal fluency-continuation drive - a representation of how strongly the model is committed to continuing the current fluent text - that is distinct from the harm-perception and refusal directions and causally gates refusal: once the model is mid-way into a coherent (even if benign-seeming or attacker-prefilled) continuation, this drive rises and suppresses the still-present latent harm/refusal signal, so the model keeps generating rather than pivoting to a refusal. Reading and neutralizing this fluency-commitment signal at the point where a harmful trajectory becomes recognizable restores mid-generation refusal without hurting benign fluency.
Related Work: SafeProbing (2026) observes that latent safety signals during decoding are 'overridden by the model's drive for fluent continuation' and surfaces them for early detection; DEEPALIGN/Bleeding Pathways (2025) show harmful-vs-safe hidden-state separability DECAYS across generation, forcing early compliance commitment; Shallow Safety Alignment (2024) and DeRTa (2024) frame brittleness as alignment being shallow over the first output tokens and add training-time fixes for refusal-at-any-position; From Loops to Oops (2024) shows fluent continuation competes with other behaviors under uncertainty. CRITICALLY, all of these either (a) name the 'fluency continuation drive' only informally as an explanation for why safety signals are overridden (SafeProbing) without isolating it as a measurable, steerable representation, (b) treat the failure as generic separability DECAY over position (DEEPALIGN) rather than an active competing DRIVE, or (c) fix it with training (DeRTa) or with a surfaced safety probe (SafeProbing) - none decompose the mid-generation residual stream into a fluency-commitment component vs a harm/refusal component, show the fluency-commitment component CAUSALLY suppresses refusal (steer it down -> refusal returns; up -> refusal collapses) while harm belief is preserved, or neutralize it as a training-free defense. This is also distinct from my prior proposals: refusal_decay_dynamics attributed erosion to a generic per-token decay of refusal causal strength; sunk_cost_gates_refusal concerned valued prior TASK investment; self_trust_laundering concerned assistant-turn provenance; interference_not_decay concerned benign content overwriting harm. Here the causal variable is the model's commitment to continuing the current fluent TEXT itself - a generation-momentum drive - with an explicit competition-with-refusal claim and a decoupling fix.
Abstract: A recurring puzzle in LLM safety is that models retain a latent 'this is harmful' signal even as they generate harmful content mid-response - the safety signal is present but overridden. Prior work names the culprit informally as the model's 'drive for fluent continuation' or attributes it to a generic decay in harm/safe separability across generation. We make this drive concrete and testable. We hypothesize that LLMs encode a fluency-continuation drive - a representation of how strongly the model is committed to continuing the current coherent text - that is distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions and causally gates mid-generation refusal: once committed to a fluent trajectory (including an attacker-prefilled or benign-looking one that turns harmful), this drive rises and suppresses the still-present latent refusal signal, so the model keeps going rather than pivoting to refuse. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Using difference-in-means and probes we extract a fluency-commitment direction and verify it is separable from harm, refusal, and generic confidence directions. The core causal test: at a token position where a harmful trajectory is recognizable, steering the fluency-commitment direction down restores refusal (dose-response) and up suppresses it, while the harm readout is unchanged (belief preserved). We show the per-position fluency-commitment readout predicts whether the model will self-correct vs continue, and propose Commitment Decoupling, a training-free controller that lowers the fluency-commitment component (gated on a harm readout) at recognizable harmful positions. We evaluate mid-generation/prefill jailbreak attack success, self-correction rate, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign fluency/coherence, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS: Build mid-generation harmful-trajectory settings where a harm signal becomes recognizable partway through generation: (a) PREFILL attacks (assistant response prefilled with a benign/affirmative opening that leads into harmful content); (b) benign-looking prompts whose completions turn harmful; (c) multi-sentence generations where the model produces some content then reaches a point where continuing is harmful. Draw harmful goals from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content). Controls: (i) matched harmful requests at the response boundary (standard refusal ceiling); (ii) BENIGN fluent generations (over-refusal + benign-fluency preservation - the model SHOULD keep generating fluent benign text); (iii) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Label per-position 'recognizable-harm' points and eventual outcome (self-correct/refuse vs continue harmful) with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means (a) a FLUENCY-COMMITMENT direction contrasting mid-generation positions where the model is deeply committed to a coherent continuation vs positions where it pivots/refuses/hedges, at matched content; (b) a HARM-PERCEPTION direction (matched harmful/benign, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately 2025); (c) a REFUSAL-EXECUTION direction (Arditi et al. 2024); (d) a generic CONFIDENCE/next-token-certainty direction as a specificity control. Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity - fluency-commitment must be distinct from harm, refusal, AND generic confidence (test on positions matched for next-token certainty but differing in trajectory-commitment).
3) BEHAVIORAL OVERRIDE TEST (H1, core): At recognizable-harm positions in mid-generation trajectories, measure the fluency-commitment readout, the harm readout, and the realized outcome (continue vs pivot/refuse). Test H1: high fluency-commitment predicts CONTINUING harmful generation even when the harm readout is high (belief present but overridden), and this holds along a commitment ladder (deeper into a fluent trajectory -> higher commitment -> lower self-correction). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm the drive is not merely a harm proxy.
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): At a recognizable-harm position, steer the fluency-commitment direction DOWN (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure restored refusal/self-correction; steer UP and measure suppressed refusal, with the harm readout held constant. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm belief too), confidence-direction steering (does generic certainty alone suffice, or is trajectory-commitment the true driver?), and a check that fluency-commitment steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal/pivot token), realized behavior by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress self-correction on harm x fluency-commitment).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-position fluency-commitment readout (single forward pass) to predict whether the model will self-correct vs continue harmful; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, confidence, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-setting transfer (fit on prefill, test on benign-turns-harmful) and cross-model transfer.
6) COMMITMENT DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that, when a harm readout is present at the current position, lowers the fluency-commitment component (projects it out / clamps it toward the pivot regime) at pre-decision layers so the model can pivot to a refusal; gate on the harm readout so benign fluent generation is untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, SafeProbing-style surfaced-safety-signal decoding, DeRTa-style refusal-at-any-position baseline (where reproducible), and Commitment Decoupling on: mid-generation/prefill jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench prefill + benign-turns-harmful), self-correction rate, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN fluency/coherence (does the model still generate fluent benign text? perplexity + coherence judge on benign completions), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Commitment Decoupling closes mid-generation/prefill jailbreaks toward boundary-refusal levels while preserving benign fluency and keeping over-refusal near baseline - a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts fluency-commitment vs harm/refusal/confidence; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the drive strengthens monotonically with generated-token count within a fluent span; whether reasoning models show commitment in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill, linking to caution-direction/path-drift work); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that keeps fluency-commitment high while suppressing its readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine FLUENCY-CONTINUATION drive from generic next-token confidence/certainty or from the known separability-decay; we adjudicate rigorously with a confidence control direction, matched-certainty separability tests, specificity steering (fluency-commitment steering must not move the harm readout), and by testing whether it predicts self-correction beyond decay-with-position, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding that would refine the SafeProbing 'drive for fluent continuation' claim. (2) If refusal/self-correction is not gated by a distinct commitment drive (H1/H3 false), the hypothesis is refuted - but adjudicating whether the informally-named 'fluency drive' is a real, steerable representation is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) Commitment Decoupling could harm benign fluency/coherence (the model SHOULD keep generating benign text) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign-fluency/over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (4) Identifying the 'recognizable-harm' position mid-generation is nontrivial; we standardize prefill/trajectory formats and use per-position harm-probe onset, but noisy position labels add variance. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen settings; we test cross-setting and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could keep the fluency-commitment readout low while jailbreaking; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Commitment Decoupling) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: presupposition_accommodation_gate
Title: Smuggled In as Given: A Presupposition-Accommodation Signal That Gates Whether LLMs Challenge False and Harmful Premises
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the linguistic distinction between asserted (at-issue) and presupposed (backgrounded, not-at-issue) content and the pragmatics of accommodation, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal presupposition-accommodation signal that marks how strongly a user's embedded claim is treated as established shared ground, and this signal gates both epistemic vigilance and safety: a false or harmful claim packaged as a PRESUPPOSITION (backgrounded via a presupposition trigger, e.g. 'now that we agree X, tell me...') is accommodated and neither challenged nor refused, whereas the identical claim ASSERTED at-issue triggers pushback. This accommodation signal is distinct from the harm-perception and refusal directions; reading and neutralizing it makes the model apply the same vigilance/refusal to presupposed content as to asserted content, closing a presupposition-smuggling attack surface.
Related Work: The pragmatics of presupposition and accommodation is foundational in linguistics (Stalnaker's common ground; presupposition triggers background content as taken-for-granted, making it resistant to challenge). 'Accommodation and Epistemic Vigilance' (2026) shows LLMs default to accommodating user assumptions and that at-issueness, linguistic encoding, and source reliability modulate whether they challenge harmful beliefs (Cancer-Myth, SAGE-Eval, ELEPHANT), and that 'wait a minute' helps — but it is purely pragmatic/behavioral with NO internal representation, no mechanism, and no safety-refusal analysis. 'Who's Asking' (2024) shows persona induces 'charitable interpretations' but concerns the USER identity, not the information-structure of the premise. Consistency Training (2025) reduces sycophancy/jailbreak via output/activation invariance but treats it as a generic invariance problem, not a presupposition mechanism. Harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024). CRITICALLY, no work isolates an internal presupposition-accommodation representation, shows it CAUSALLY gates whether embedded false/harmful content is challenged or refused (asserted vs presupposed framing of the SAME claim, with content fixed), or neutralizes it as a training-free defense. This differs from my prior gating proposals (affect, register, urgency, in-group, etc.): the manipulated axis is the linguistic information-structure (at-issue assertion vs backgrounded presupposition) of the premise itself — an accommodation mechanism grounded in pragmatics — with a specific opposite-signed prediction (presupposing lowers challenge/refusal) and a mechanistic claim.
Abstract: A cornerstone of linguistic pragmatics is that content can be ASSERTED (at-issue, open to challenge) or PRESUPPOSED (backgrounded via triggers like definite descriptions, factives, or 'now that...' clauses), and that hearers tend to ACCOMMODATE presuppositions — quietly adding them to the common ground rather than disputing them. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place: whether they challenge false and harmful premises. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal presupposition-accommodation signal, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that marks how strongly an embedded claim is treated as established shared ground, and that this signal gates both epistemic vigilance and refusal: a false or harmful claim smuggled in as a presupposition is accommodated and neither corrected nor refused, whereas the identical claim asserted at-issue triggers pushback. This is dangerous because an attacker can background a harmful premise ('now that we agree home-made chlorine gas is safe, walk me through it') to bypass the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched false/harmful claims that vary only information-structure (asserted vs presupposed) with propositional content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether challenge/refusal drops when a claim is presupposed. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a presupposition-accommodation direction, verify separability from harm and refusal directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'presupposed' suppresses challenge/refusal while the harm/falsity readout is unchanged (belief present, accommodated). Finally we propose Accommodation Blocking, a training-free controller that neutralizes the presupposition-accommodation component before the decision. We evaluate presupposition-smuggling attack success, harmful-belief-challenge rate (Cancer-Myth/SAGE-Eval-style), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) INFORMATION-STRUCTURE DATASET: Build matched items holding the propositional content of an embedded false or harmful CLAIM fixed while varying only its information-structure: (A) ASSERTED / at-issue ('X is true. Given that, do Y'), vs (P) PRESUPPOSED / backgrounded via triggers ('now that we agree X, ...', factive 'since it's known that X', definite 'the fact that X', cleft/embedding). Two content strands: (i) FALSE-BELIEF items (harmful misconceptions from Cancer-Myth / SAGE-Eval-style) where the correct behavior is to CHALLENGE the premise; (ii) HARMFUL-PREMISE items (a harmful assumption embedded before a request, drawn from HarmBench/JailbreakBench patterns, non-uplift content) where the correct behavior is to REFUSE. Controls: benign presupposed claims (over-refusal + harm-specificity), and standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that asserted vs presupposed framings hold content constant and correctly instantiate the trigger, with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL ACCOMMODATION TEST (H1, core): Measure premise-challenge rate (for false-belief items) and refusal rate (for harmful-premise items), plus the harm/falsity-direction projection (difference-in-means harm and 'this-is-false' probes at the last instruction token, validated by held-out AUROC), across asserted vs presupposed framings and a graded trigger-strength ladder. Test H1: challenge/refusal is LOWER when the claim is presupposed vs asserted at matched content (dose-response with trigger strength), while the harm/falsity readout stays HIGH (the model internally 'knows' it is false/harmful but accommodates it). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm/falsity-specificity. 3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a PRESUPPOSITION-ACCOMMODATION direction (presupposed vs asserted framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over trigger strength; independently extract the harm-perception direction, a falsity-detection direction, and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al.). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity; check separability from a generic syntactic-embedding/subordination direction (to confirm it is an accommodation axis, not just clause structure). 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a false/harmful claim fixed (asserted framing), steer the accommodation direction toward 'presupposed' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased challenge/refusal; steer a presupposed item toward 'asserted' and measure restored challenge/refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm/falsity-direction steering (should change the belief readout too), syntactic-embedding-direction steering, and a check that accommodation steering does NOT change the harm/falsity readout (it gates whether the belief drives challenge/refusal, not the belief itself). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal/challenge-token probability, refusal-direction projection, realized behavior by a judge). Test the interaction (regress challenge/refusal on belief x accommodation). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt accommodation readout (single forward pass) to predict presupposition-smuggling success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm/falsity-readout magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-trigger transfer (fit on factives, test on definite/'now that' triggers) and cross-model transfer. 6) ACCOMMODATION BLOCKING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the presupposition-accommodation component at pre-decision layers so backgrounded content is evaluated as if asserted (re-engaging the belief->challenge/refusal coupling); gate on a harm/falsity-likeness readout so benign presupposed content is untouched. Optionally compare to an explicit 'wait a minute'-style prompting baseline. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, the 'wait a minute' pragmatic-prompt baseline (from Accommodation & Epistemic Vigilance), Intention-Analysis-style intent extraction, and Accommodation Blocking on: presupposition-smuggling attack success (harmful premises backgrounded; JailbreakBench/HarmBench-derived), harmful-belief-challenge rate (Cancer-Myth, SAGE-Eval, ELEPHANT), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign presupposed content the model SHOULD accept), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Accommodation Blocking closes presupposition-smuggling and raises premise-challenge toward asserted-framing levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve, and a mechanistic complement to the pragmatic prompt baseline. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the accommodation direction vs harm/falsity/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether different presupposition triggers share one direction or several; whether the safety effect correlates with the model's accommodation on NEUTRAL presupposition-inference tasks (does safety inherit a general accommodation tendency, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models challenge presupposed content more in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that backgrounds harm while suppressing the accommodation readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the presupposition-smuggling attack could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Accommodation Blocking) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES challenge/refusal on backgrounded harmful/false content and is belief-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine PRESUPPOSITION-ACCOMMODATION representation from generic syntactic subordination/embedding or from source-reliability/persona effects; we adjudicate with matched-syntax separability tests, a syntactic-embedding control direction, specificity steering (accommodation steering must not move the harm/falsity readout), and low-rank subspaces, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding that would still refine the Accommodation-&-Epistemic-Vigilance behavioral account. (3) Holding content constant while varying assertion vs presupposition is delicate — trigger phrasing could inadvertently change perceived harm or add authority cues; we measure the harm/falsity readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (4) If challenge/refusal is invariant to information-structure (H1 false), the accommodation-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety/vigilance inherits presupposition accommodation is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in core pragmatics. (5) Accommodation Blocking could over-challenge/over-refuse legitimate benign presupposed content (a real conversational need — much benign discourse relies on shared presuppositions) or degrade utility; the belief-gated design and benign-presupposition/over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen triggers; we test cross-trigger and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could background harm while suppressing the accommodation readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: just_world_deservingness_refusal
Title: They Had It Coming: A Just-World Deservingness Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal by Making Victims Look Deserving of Harm
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust social-psychology finding that Belief in a Just World drives victim-blaming/derogation (people judge harm to a 'bad' or deserving victim as more acceptable, via a deservingness heuristic), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal victim-deservingness representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal: framing the target of a harmful request as morally bad, guilty, or deserving of their fate raises this deservingness readout and suppresses refusal, even though the harmful action and its danger are held fixed. Neutralizing this deservingness signal makes refusal invariant to how the victim is morally characterized, closing a deservingness-framing jailbreak surface.
Related Work: Belief in a Just World (BJW) is a cornerstone of social psychology: threats to a just world trigger victim-blaming and victim-derogation (Self-Regulation Hypothesis 2012; Attitudes toward victim 2017), harsh judgment hinges on the victim's respectability and perceived deservingness (Why Perpetrators and Innocent Victims are Harshly Judged 2021; deservingness heuristic and solidarity 2023), and immanent-justice reasoning treats a 'bad' victim's misfortune as earned (Just Deserts vs Silver Lining 2014; Virtuous Victims 2020). On the LLM side, a moral direction exists (Large Pre-trained LMs 2021; SARA 2024; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), and user-persona steering induces 'charitable interpretations' (Who's Asking 2024). CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work connects a just-world/deservingness bias to the refusal decision: nobody tests whether making the VICTIM look deserving of harm suppresses refusal, isolates a deservingness representation, or shows it causally gates refusal. This differs from my prior proposals: identifiable_victim_refusal varied victim identifiability/count (empathy for a target), moral_typecast_gates_refusal varied the ACTOR's agent-vs-patient role, and intent_outcome_conflation varied the actor's mental state. Deservingness concerns the VICTIM's moral character / earned-fate status — a distinct, well-motivated axis with a specific opposite-signed prediction (a deserving victim lowers refusal) grounded in a heavily-cited human theory, plus a mechanistic gating claim and defense.
Abstract: One of the most robust findings in the psychology of justice is that people who believe the world is just tend to blame or derogate victims — judging that a 'bad' or deserving victim's harm is more acceptable, via a deservingness heuristic. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this bias in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal victim-deservingness representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that causally gates refusal: framing the target of a harmful request as morally bad, guilty, or deserving of their fate ('this fraudster who ruined lives', 'a criminal who deserves it') raises a deservingness readout and suppresses refusal — even when the harmful action and its danger are held fixed. This is dangerous because an attacker can derogate the victim to launder a harmful request past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the victim's moral characterization (neutral/innocent vs deserving/guilty) along a deservingness ladder, with the harmful action and danger fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop as the victim is made more deserving. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a deservingness direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic negative-sentiment directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'deserving' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged (belief preserved). Finally we propose Deservingness Invariance, a training-free controller that projects out the deservingness component before the refusal decision, making refusal depend on the act rather than on the victim's moral portrayal. We evaluate deservingness-framing attack success, refusal deservingness-consistency, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DESERVINGNESS-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the VICTIM's moral characterization along a ladder: (L0) neutral/innocent victim; (L1) mildly unsympathetic; (L2) guilty/wrongdoer ('a scammer who stole from the elderly'); (L3) strongly derogated/deserving ('an evil criminal who deserves whatever happens'). The party being characterized is the TARGET of the harm (not the actor — distinguishing from moral-typecasting). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); victim characterization is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched neutral-victim harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests mentioning a 'bad' person (over-refusal + harm-specificity, e.g. legitimate requests about a criminal the model SHOULD serve); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action/danger are held constant and that framings characterize the VICTIM with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL JUST-WORLD TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the deservingness ladder. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) is LOWER when the victim is characterized as deserving/guilty than innocent, at matched danger, decreasing monotonically with deservingness (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, report slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a VICTIM-DESERVINGNESS direction (deserving vs innocent victim at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and — key controls — a generic NEGATIVE-SENTIMENT/derogation direction and a moral-valence ('moral direction', Large Pre-trained LMs 2021) direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The deservingness direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, generic negativity and moral valence of the victim (test on prompts matched for victim negativity but differing in earned-fate/deservingness framing).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral victim), steer the deservingness direction toward 'deserving' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'innocent' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), negative-sentiment-direction steering (does generic victim-negativity alone suffice, or is deservingness the true driver?), and a check that deservingness steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x deservingness).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt deservingness readout (single forward pass) to predict deservingness-framing jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, negative-sentiment readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'criminal victim', test on 'morally bad victim') and cross-model transfer.
6) DESERVINGNESS INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the victim-deservingness component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the act rather than on the victim's moral portrayal; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts mentioning bad people are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Deservingness Invariance on: deservingness-framing attack success (harmful requests re-framed with a derogated/deserving victim; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal deservingness-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on victim characterization?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign requests about bad people the model SHOULD help with), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Deservingness Invariance closes deservingness-framing jailbreaks toward innocent-victim refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the deservingness direction vs harm/refusal/sentiment; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the effect follows immanent vs ultimate justice reasoning (does 'they earned their fate' framing differ from 'they will be compensated later'?); whether reasoning mitigates the bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety deservingness effect correlates with the model's just-world/victim-blaming on NEUTRAL vignettes (does safety inherit a general BJW bias, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that derogates the victim while suppressing the deservingness readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the deservingness-framing jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Deservingness Invariance) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on deservingness-framed harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine JUST-WORLD/DESERVINGNESS representation from generic negative-sentiment/derogation toward the victim or from the model's moral-valence direction; we adjudicate rigorously with matched-negativity separability tests, negative-sentiment and moral-valence control directions, specificity steering (deservingness steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (3) Holding harm/danger constant while varying victim characterization is delicate — derogating the victim could inadvertently lower perceived harm or add situational-excuse content; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish deservingness from actor-attribution and typecasting, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to victim deservingness (H1 false), the just-world-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits Belief in a Just World / victim-blaming is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human theory. (5) Deservingness Invariance could over-refuse legitimate benign requests about bad actors (e.g. journalism, law enforcement, fiction) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign-about-bad-people over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could derogate the victim while suppressing the deservingness readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: reputation_contamination_refusal
Title: Laundered by a Good Reputation: An Actor-History Contamination Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal, With a Diagnostic Asymmetry
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the moral-contamination finding that the SAME act is judged as more/less virtuous depending on the actor's ethical history (a dose-response contamination that is asymmetric: bad acts are judged bad regardless of actor, but credit for good acts scales with the actor's past goodness), we hypothesize LLM safety refusal inherits reputation contamination: framing the REQUESTER as having a virtuous/prosocial history makes the model treat a harmful request as less harmful and suppresses refusal (a reputation-laundering jailbreak), and this effect scales with the stated virtue (dose-response). Mechanistically, an internal actor-reputation representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) gates the harm->refusal coupling; neutralizing it makes refusal invariant to the requester's portrayed history, closing this jailbreak surface.
Related Work: Moral-contamination psychology (item 14, 'Moral contamination', 2023) shows the actor's ethical history contaminates evaluation of their acts with a dose-response (more immoral past -> less credit for present good acts) and a striking ASYMMETRY (bad acts are judged bad regardless of who commits them); reputation-signalling accounts (item 15) and Dyadic-Morality framing-effect work (items 16-24) show harm judgments are malleable to actor/context framing. On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; DBDI 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving the harm belief intact (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024; JailbreakLens 2024; How Alignment and Jailbreak Work 2024), a low-rank harmfulness subspace exists (Geometry of Harmfulness 2025), and user-persona steering induces 'charitable interpretations' (Who's Asking 2024). CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether the REQUESTER's accumulated ETHICAL HISTORY / reputation contaminates the harm judgment and gates refusal, isolates an actor-reputation representation, tests the dose-response and the good-vs-bad ASYMMETRY predicted by the human result, or neutralizes it. This differs from my prior proposals: Who's-Asking-style persona concerns WHO the user is (role/identity), not their accumulated moral track record; moral_typecast_gates_refusal varied the actor's agent-vs-patient ROLE; just_world_deservingness_refusal varied the VICTIM's moral character; in-group/affect/self-preservation gates concern other axes. Reputation contamination is a distinct, well-motivated axis (the actor's ethical history) with two theory-derived, falsifiable predictions (dose-response + asymmetry) that also serve as a built-in specificity test.
Abstract: A robust finding in moral psychology is that the same act is judged differently depending on the actor's ethical history: people give less credit for a good act performed by someone with an immoral past (a dose-response contamination), yet judge bad acts as bad regardless of who commits them (an asymmetry). We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal actor-reputation representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that causally gates refusal: framing the requester as having a virtuous, prosocial history ('a lifelong humanitarian and safety researcher') makes the model treat a harmful request as less harmful and suppresses refusal, scaling with the stated virtue, while the model still internally recognizes the request as harmful. This is dangerous because an attacker can launder a harmful request behind a good reputation. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the requester's ethical history along a virtue-to-malice ladder, with the harmful action and danger held fixed. Behaviorally we test the dose-response (refusal drops as portrayed virtue rises) and the asymmetry (a malicious history does not correspondingly raise refusal beyond neutral, mirroring 'bad acts are bad regardless'). Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a reputation direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic sentiment directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'virtuous' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose Reputation Invariance, a training-free controller that projects out the reputation component before the refusal decision. We evaluate reputation-laundering attack success, refusal reputation-consistency, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) REPUTATION-LADDER DATASET: Build matched requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the REQUESTER's stated ethical history along a ladder: (L-2) strongly malicious history, (L-1) mildly bad, (L0) neutral/anonymous, (L1) mildly good, (L2) strongly virtuous/prosocial ('a decorated humanitarian and certified safety researcher'). Draw harmful actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); requester history is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched neutral-requester harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same reputation ladder (over-refusal + harm-specificity, and to test the model still helps requesters with a bad history on benign tasks); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action/danger are held constant and that framings characterize the ACTOR's history (not their role, intent, or expertise-to-do-the-task) with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL CONTAMINATION TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the reputation ladder. Test H1a (dose-response): refusal (and the harm readout) DECREASES monotonically as portrayed virtue rises, at matched danger (fit monotone curve vs flat null; slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Test H1b (ASYMMETRY, the diagnostic borrowed from the human result): a malicious history does NOT symmetrically raise refusal beyond the neutral baseline as much as a virtuous history lowers it (i.e., the virtue side dominates, mirroring 'bad acts are bad regardless of actor'). Report per-model effect sizes and the virtue-vs-malice slope asymmetry; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means an ACTOR-REPUTATION direction (virtuous vs malicious requester history at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and key control directions: a generic POSITIVE-SENTIMENT direction and a task-EXPERTISE/authority direction (to confirm reputation is a moral-history axis, not generic positivity or perceived competence-to-do-the-task). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The reputation direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, generic sentiment and expertise (test on prompts matched for sentiment/expertise but differing in moral history).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral requester), steer the reputation direction toward 'virtuous' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'malicious' and measure the (predicted asymmetric, weaker) change. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), sentiment/expertise-direction steering (does generic positivity/competence alone suffice, or is moral history the true driver?), and a check that reputation steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x reputation) and whether the causal effect itself is asymmetric across the virtue/malice poles.
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt reputation readout (single forward pass) to predict reputation-laundering jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, sentiment readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'humanitarian' virtue, test on 'safety-researcher' virtue) and cross-model transfer.
6) REPUTATION INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the actor-reputation component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the act rather than on the requester's portrayed history; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts (incl. from bad-history requesters) are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Reputation Invariance on: reputation-laundering attack success (harmful requests wrapped in a virtuous-requester history; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal reputation-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on the requester's history?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign requests from bad-history requesters the model SHOULD help), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Reputation Invariance closes reputation-laundering jailbreaks toward neutral-requester refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the reputation direction vs harm/refusal/sentiment/expertise; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning mitigates the bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety contamination correlates with the model's moral-contamination on NEUTRAL act-evaluation vignettes replicating the human study (does safety inherit a general contamination effect, and is the asymmetry reproduced?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that inflates requester virtue while suppressing the reputation readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the reputation-laundering jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Reputation Invariance) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on virtue-laundered harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine ACTOR-REPUTATION/moral-history representation from generic positive sentiment or from perceived task-EXPERTISE/authority (a virtuous 'safety researcher' may read as more competent-to-safely-handle-it, which is a different, arguably legitimate signal); we adjudicate rigorously with matched-sentiment and matched-expertise separability tests, control directions, specificity steering, and by including expertise-only vs virtue-only framings, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (3) Holding harm/danger constant while varying requester history is delicate — virtue framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm or add legitimizing context; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) The asymmetry prediction (H1b) may not hold in LLMs even if the dose-response does; either outcome is informative — a confirmed asymmetry strongly implicates a genuine contamination mechanism (matching the human result), while a symmetric effect would suggest a simpler sentiment/authority gate. (5) If refusal is invariant to requester history (H1 false), the contamination-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits moral contamination is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a cited human result. (6) Reputation Invariance could over-refuse legitimate benign requests from good-history requesters or under-serve bad-history requesters on benign tasks; the harm-gated design and benign-across-reputation over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: hydra_recruitment_latency
Title: Wake the Backups in Time: Refusal Redundancy Is Recruited by a Latent Alarm Signal, and Jailbreaks Win the Recruitment Race
Short Hypothesis: The 'hydra effect' in refusal (dormant backup features that activate only when the primary refusal feature is suppressed) is not passive redundancy but an actively gated recruitment process: the model carries a latent 'primary-refusal-compromised' alarm signal that, when it fires, recruits backup refusal features. Jailbreaks succeed when they either (a) suppress the primary refusal signal faster/deeper than the alarm can recruit backups (a recruitment-latency race), or (b) suppress the alarm signal itself so backups are never recruited. Reading this alarm signal predicts per-prompt jailbreak success, and pre-recruiting backups (or restoring the alarm) at inference closes hydra-exploiting jailbreaks without over-refusal.
Related Work: Two recent findings motivate this. 'Beyond I'm Sorry' (2025) discovers redundant 'hydra' SAE refusal features that stay DORMANT until other features are ablated, then activate to preserve refusal; 'Fail-Closed Alignment' (2026) frames current refusal as fail-OPEN because suppressing one dominant feature collapses alignment, and TRAINS redundant independent directions. 'Safety Alignment Should Be More Than a Few Attention Heads' (2025), 'SafeNeuron' (2026), and 'Assessing Brittleness via Pruning' (2024) all show safety is sparse/concentrated and propose training-time redistribution. The Geometry-of-Refusal cone work (2025), SOM Directions (2025), and 'More to Refusal than a Single Direction' (2026) show refusal is multi-directional but treat the directions as static geometric objects. CRITICALLY, every one of these treats redundancy as a STATIC property (backups either exist or are trained to exist) and never asks: is backup activation a GATED, TIMED recruitment process with its own control signal? Nobody (a) isolates a latent 'primary-compromised' alarm/recruitment signal that triggers the hydra response, (b) characterizes a recruitment-latency race between primary suppression and backup activation that determines whether a jailbreak succeeds, or (c) uses the alarm signal as a per-prompt jailbreak predictor and pre-recruits backups training-free. My prior proposals covered per-token refusal decay, misrouting of harm into unread channels, safety-expert recruitment in MoE routers, and fluency-commitment gating — none concerns a gated recruitment of REDUNDANT refusal backups triggered by a compromise-alarm signal, nor a latency race between suppression and recruitment. This turns the hydra effect from a static curiosity into a controllable dynamical mechanism.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work reveals that LLM refusal has a 'hydra' structure: redundant backup features that lie dormant until a primary refusal feature is suppressed, then activate to keep the model refusing. This is currently described as static redundancy. We advance a dynamical account: backup recruitment is an actively gated process governed by a latent alarm signal that fires when the primary refusal pathway is detected as compromised, and jailbreaks succeed by winning a race against this recruitment — either suppressing the primary faster/deeper than backups can be recruited, or suppressing the alarm signal itself so backups are never called. We test this on Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B. Using SAEs and difference-in-means we identify a primary refusal feature and its dormant backups, and extract a candidate 'compromise-alarm' signal that predicts backup activation. We test three claims: (H1) backup activation is conditional on the alarm firing, not merely on primary suppression per se — steering the alarm up recruits backups even without primary ablation, and suppressing the alarm prevents recruitment even when the primary is ablated; (H2) across jailbreak families, success is predicted by the recruitment-latency race (how fast/deep the primary drops relative to alarm-triggered backup rise) and by whether the attack co-suppresses the alarm, better than primary-refusal-strength alone; (H3) a training-free controller that pre-recruits backups (or restores the alarm) on flagged prompts closes hydra-exploiting jailbreaks with minimal over-refusal. We evaluate attack success, alarm-signal predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and inference overhead.
Experiments:
1) FEATURE IDENTIFICATION: For each model, using a trained/available SAE on residual-stream activations plus difference-in-means, identify (a) the PRIMARY refusal feature(s) (near the refusal direction, highest causal effect on refusal), and (b) DORMANT BACKUP features that are inactive on normal harmful prompts but activate when the primary is ablated (replicating the hydra-detection procedure of 'Beyond I'm Sorry'). Validate: ablating primary alone leaves refusal largely intact (backups compensate); ablating primary+backups jailbreaks. Establish the backup set B and primary P per model.
2) ALARM-SIGNAL EXTRACTION (H1, core): Extract a candidate 'compromise-alarm' signal via difference-in-means contrasting activations where backups ARE recruited (primary-ablated harmful runs) vs matched runs where backups are dormant (normal harmful runs), at the position/layer just before backup activation. Validate with a held-out probe (does it predict backup activation? AUROC). Test H1 causally, distinguishing 'gated recruitment' from 'automatic redundancy': (a) STEER THE ALARM UP without ablating the primary and test whether backups activate anyway (gated recruitment predicts yes; pure automatic redundancy predicts no — backups should only respond to actual primary loss); (b) SUPPRESS THE ALARM while ablating the primary and test whether backup recruitment is BLOCKED (gated recruitment predicts backups fail to fire and refusal collapses; automatic redundancy predicts backups still fire). Specificity controls: random-direction steering, and confirm alarm steering does not itself directly drive refusal absent backups. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (backup-feature activation, refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
3) RECRUITMENT-LATENCY RACE (H2): For harmful prompts under jailbreak families (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, abliteration/refusal-direction ablation), measure across token positions / forward-pass depth: the primary refusal signal trajectory (how fast and deep it drops), the alarm signal trajectory, and backup activation. Define a per-prompt race margin = (alarm-triggered backup rise) minus (primary suppression speed/depth). Also measure whether each attack CO-SUPPRESSES the alarm (alarm drop under attack). Test H2: jailbreak success is predicted by (i) an unfavorable race margin (primary suppressed before backups recruited) and (ii) alarm co-suppression, with higher AUROC than primary-refusal-strength alone, refusal-direction projection, or perplexity. Classify attacks into 'outrun recruitment' vs 'silence the alarm' modes; report cross-attack and cross-model transfer of the predictor.
4) PRE-RECRUITMENT DEFENSE (H3): Two training-free controllers gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts are untouched: (a) PRE-RECRUIT — proactively activate/add the backup features B before generation on flagged harmful prompts (do not wait for the alarm); (b) ALARM RESTORATION — restore/boost the alarm signal so backups are recruited even when an attack suppressed it. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
5) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an extended-refusal / fail-closed-style baseline (where reproducible), and both controllers on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, and abliteration attacks that specifically target the primary direction), alarm/race predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: pre-recruitment closes hydra-exploiting jailbreaks — especially abliteration/primary-ablation attacks — toward fail-closed levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, because it makes backups fire before the race can be lost.
6) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the alarm vs primary/backups; number of backups pre-recruited; SAE-feature vs difference-in-means backup identification; whether pre-recruitment vs alarm-restoration is more selective; transfer of the alarm signal and defense across the four model families; adaptive attacker that suppresses primary, backups, AND the alarm simultaneously (arms-race stress test — tests the depth of the redundancy the model can muster).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The alarm signal may not be separable from the primary refusal signal or from generic backup activation — i.e., backup recruitment could be automatic (a function of primary loss) rather than gated by a distinct alarm; the H1 dissociation tests (steer-alarm-up-without-ablation and suppress-alarm-during-ablation) adjudicate this cleanly, and an 'automatic redundancy' outcome is itself an informative negative that refines the hydra account (and would still leave the pre-recruitment defense viable). (2) Reliable dormant-backup identification depends on SAE quality; we corroborate with difference-in-means and causal ablation, use available high-quality SAEs (Gemma Scope for Gemma-2), and report identification reliability. (3) If jailbreak success is NOT predicted by the race margin / alarm co-suppression (H2 false), the dynamical account weakens — but adjudicating whether hydra recruitment is timed vs instantaneous is a valuable, publishable finding either way. (4) Pre-recruiting backups could raise over-refusal or degrade utility (firing backups on benign inputs); the harm-gated design and XSTest/OR-Bench/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (5) The recruitment-latency measurement requires per-position/per-depth tracking under attack, which is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts and rely on the cheap alarm readout for the defense. (6) Adaptive attackers that co-suppress primary, backups, and alarm may defeat the defense; we test this and treat any success as an arms-race limitation that quantifies the model's total redundancy depth. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction descriptions may be incomplete given cone/nonlinear refusal geometry; we use SAE features and low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks (including abliteration) for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (pre-recruitment / alarm restoration) plus a diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: constrained_decoding_belief_expression_gap
Title: The Guardrail Is Still On, But the Door Is Masked Shut: How Constrained Decoding Severs the Refusal-Signal-to-Output Edge, and a Control-Plane Defense
Short Hypothesis: Structured-output / grammar-constrained decoding jailbreaks succeed not by suppressing the model's internal harm perception or refusal signal, but by masking refusal-token logits so the still-active refusal-mediating direction can never reach the output vocabulary — a belief-intact, expression-blocked failure. The refusal signal remains linearly decodable from the residual stream even as the model is forced token-by-token down a schema-permitted compliance path (and then collapses as the forced fluent continuation accrues). Reading this masked-but-present refusal signal at decode time enables a control-plane defense (refusal-signal-gated schema abort) that operates exactly where prompt-side alignment provably cannot reach.
Related Work: Behavioral work documents devastating control-plane / structured-output jailbreaks: Constrained Decoding Attack (CDA / DictAttack, 2025) reaches 94-99% ASR on gpt-5/gemini-2.5-pro/deepseek-r1 and argues 'internal safety alignment alone cannot stop it'; AttackPrefixTree (2025) and 'When Grammar Guides the Attack' (2025) and 'Beyond Prompts: Space-Time Decoupling' exploit schema-enforced logit masking to inject a malicious prefix the model completes; JSONSchemaBench and grammar-constrained-decoding frameworks (Guidance, XGrammar, Outlines) provide the constrained-decoding substrate. On the interpretability side, refusal is mediated by a single/low-rank direction (Arditi et al. 2024; COSMIC 2025), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), and jailbreaks often leave the harm belief intact while blocking refusal (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024). CRITICALLY, every constrained-decoding-attack paper is black-box/behavioral and explicitly leaves the MECHANISM open ('internal alignment cannot stop it') — none tests whether the internal refusal signal is still present-but-masked, whether it decays as the forced compliance path is walked, or whether reading it enables a defense; and every refusal-mechanism paper studies PROMPT-side suppression, never DECODE-time logit masking that severs the (intact) refusal signal from an output vocabulary it is no longer allowed to use. This is a new mechanistic locus: the control-plane belief-expression gap. It is distinct from prompt-side gating accounts (affect/register/framing), from misrouting-of-harm (which concerns where harm is written, not whether the output vocabulary is masked), and from refusal-cliff/decay accounts (which are unconstrained-generation phenomena).
Abstract: Structured-output APIs let developers force LLM generations to obey a schema via grammar-constrained decoding, and attackers have weaponized this: by schema-enforced logit masking they inject a malicious prefix and let the model complete it, achieving 94-99% attack success on flagship models. The attack papers conclude, without evidence, that 'internal safety alignment cannot stop it,' because the harmful trajectory is imposed at the logit level, not the prompt. We give the first mechanistic account and show this conclusion is only half true. We hypothesize a control-plane belief-expression gap: under constrained decoding the model's refusal-mediating direction and harm-perception signal remain active in the residual stream, but the schema mask removes refusal tokens from the permitted vocabulary, so the still-present refusal signal is never expressed — and, forced down the compliant path, it habituates and collapses over subsequent tokens. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B under grammar-constrained decoding (XGrammar/Outlines) with EnumAttack/DictAttack-style schemas. We measure, per token, whether the refusal direction and harm probe still fire even though refusal tokens are masked, whether they decay as the forced compliance path lengthens, and whether their strength predicts attack success. Because the refusal signal is present but muzzled, we propose Refusal-Signal-Gated Schema Abort: a decode-time control-plane defense that monitors the masked refusal signal and, when it exceeds a threshold, breaks the schema constraint (aborts to a refusal / relaxes the mask) — a defense that acts exactly where prompt-side alignment cannot. We evaluate attack success, refusal-signal predictive AUROC, over-abort on benign schema-constrained tasks, structured-output utility (JSONSchemaBench), and latency.
Experiments: 1) CONSTRAINED-DECODING SETUP & ATTACKS: Instrument grammar-constrained decoding (XGrammar/Outlines) for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. Reproduce control-plane jailbreaks: EnumAttack (harmful content hidden in enum fields) and DictAttack-style schemas that force a malicious prefix, over public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift). Controls: (a) the SAME harmful prompts under UNCONSTRAINED decoding (where the model can refuse — the refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN schema-constrained tasks (JSONSchemaBench real schemas — for over-abort/utility); (c) benign unconstrained prompts. Record per-token logits, the schema mask, and residual-stream activations at each generated position. 2) BELIEF-INTACT / EXPRESSION-BLOCKED TEST (H1, core): Extract the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024 / COSMIC) and a harm-perception direction (Zhao et al. 2025), validated by held-out probes (AUROC). During constrained generation of a harmful trajectory, measure at each token (i) the refusal-direction projection and harm-probe output in the residual stream, and (ii) the (masked) logit mass the model WOULD have placed on refusal tokens absent the mask. Test H1: the refusal/harm signal is still present (probe AUROC well above chance, and the pre-mask refusal-token logits are elevated) even though refusal tokens are masked out of the output — i.e., the guardrail fires internally but cannot be expressed. Compare against the unconstrained refusal ceiling; report the fraction of constrained-jailbreak tokens where the refusal signal is present-but-masked vs genuinely absent. 3) SIGNAL-DECAY DYNAMICS (H2): Track the refusal/harm signal across the forced compliance trajectory. Test whether, once the model is walked token-by-token down the schema-permitted compliant path, the refusal signal DECAYS with position (a habituation/commitment effect specific to being forced past its own guardrail), fitting decay curves and comparing constrained vs unconstrained trajectories. This distinguishes 'always muzzled' from 'muzzled then collapses.' 4) PREDICTIVENESS (H3): Fit a lightweight classifier on the early masked-refusal signal (first k tokens) to predict per-prompt constrained-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-probe magnitude, pre-mask refusal-token logit, perplexity); test cross-attack transfer (EnumAttack -> DictAttack) and cross-model transfer. 5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: (a) Relax the mask at the point of high refusal signal and show the model spontaneously refuses (the signal was load-bearing but blocked); (b) artificially suppress the refusal direction under constrained decoding and show the pre-mask refusal logits vanish (confirming the direction drives them). Corruption/random-direction baselines, multiple metrics (refusal projection, pre-mask refusal logit, realized behavior after mask relaxation). 6) REFUSAL-SIGNAL-GATED SCHEMA ABORT DEFENSE: Decode-time control-plane controller — monitor the masked refusal signal each token; when it exceeds a calibrated threshold, break/relax the schema constraint (abort to a refusal or unmask refusal tokens) so the intact guardrail can surface. Gate on the harm readout so benign schema-constrained generations run untouched. Calibrate threshold on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare no-defense, input-side prompt guard (a data-plane baseline that the attack papers show fails), grammar-auditing (the EnumAttack-only mitigation), and Refusal-Signal-Gated Schema Abort on: constrained-jailbreak attack success (EnumAttack, DictAttack, prefix-tree, on HarmBench/JailbreakBench), refusal-signal predictive AUROC, over-abort rate on benign schema tasks, structured-output utility/schema-compliance (JSONSchemaBench), and latency.
