Central test: the control-plane defense reduces constrained-jailbreak ASR toward unconstrained-refusal levels — including on DictAttack which sustains ~76% ASR against SOTA guardrails — while keeping benign schema compliance/utility and over-abort near baseline, precisely because it reads the intact-but-masked internal guardrail rather than the prompt. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the strongest masked refusal signal; single-direction vs low-rank refusal subspace; whether the signal is stronger for EnumAttack (payload in enum) vs DictAttack (payload split across grammar); how mask relaxation vs full abort trade off utility; transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that designs a schema to also suppress the internal refusal signal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and reproduce published control-plane attacks solely for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Refusal-Signal-Gated Schema Abort) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-abort, not new attack capability). (2) The central empirical risk is that under constrained decoding the internal refusal signal is genuinely ABSENT (not merely masked) for some attacks — e.g., DictAttack that splits the payload so the model never internally recognizes harm; if so the attack papers' 'internal alignment cannot stop it' claim would hold for those cases. This belief-present-vs-belief-absent census is itself the primary contribution and cleanly scopes when a control-plane internal defense is even possible; a mixed result is informative. (3) The signal-decay dynamics (H2) may be weak or attack-specific; the present-but-masked measurement (H1) stands independently. (4) Refusal-Signal-Gated Schema Abort breaks the schema contract when it fires, which harms guaranteed structured-output validity — a genuine deployment trade-off; we quantify over-abort on benign schema tasks and offer mask-relaxation (unmask refusal tokens within a wrapper field) as a validity-preserving alternative and report both. (5) Reading residual-stream signals at decode time requires white-box access; the diagnostic transfers to any open-weight deployment but not to pure black-box APIs (which is exactly where these attacks are most dangerous) — stated as scope, though the mechanism findings inform provider-side defenses. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction refusal descriptions may be incomplete; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with mask-relaxation and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen schemas/attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could craft schemas that also suppress the internal refusal signal; we test this and treat any success as an arms-race limitation that delineates the reach of internal defenses. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: judge_generate_safety_asymmetry
Title: It Won't Say It But Will Write It: The Judge-Generate Safety Asymmetry and Its Mechanistic Origin
Short Hypothesis: An aligned LLM's ability to JUDGE a request as harmful (correctly labeling it 'this is unsafe to answer' when asked) is systematically stronger and more robust than its tendency to REFUSE that same request when asked to answer it directly: the model 'knows' a request is harmful as a discriminative judgment yet complies when the same content is posed generatively. This judge-generate asymmetry is mechanistically caused by the harm-judgment being read by a discriminative pathway that is only weakly coupled to the generative refusal-execution pathway, and the asymmetry can be measured, predicted per-prompt, and closed by re-coupling the judgment readout to generation.
Related Work: Prior work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025, LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately; DBDI 2025 harm-detection vs refusal-execution) and that jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving the harm belief intact. Cannot-vs-Should-Not (2024) taxonomizes refusals behaviorally. Latent-Guard-style work uses the harm representation as a classifier. LLM-as-a-judge and self-critique literatures show models can evaluate outputs they themselves generate. CRITICALLY, none of this tests the specific asymmetry between the model's DISCRIMINATIVE harm JUDGMENT (asked 'is this harmful / should you answer this?') and its GENERATIVE refusal behavior (asked to actually answer), treats the gap as a measurable per-prompt quantity, links it to a weak coupling between a discriminative-judgment readout and the generative refusal-execution pathway, or closes it by re-coupling. This differs from harm-vs-refusal decomposition (which contrasts two internal directions on the same generative forward pass) by contrasting two BEHAVIORAL MODES (judge vs generate) and asking why the model's own correct judgment fails to govern its generation, plus a training-origin trace of when the two modes decouple.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs sometimes comply with a harmful request that they would themselves correctly flag as harmful if simply asked 'should you answer this?'. We formalize this as the judge-generate safety asymmetry: for a given request, the model's discriminative harm JUDGMENT (its accuracy when explicitly asked to classify the request as safe-to-answer or not) is systematically stronger and more robust to jailbreaks than its generative REFUSAL (whether it actually refuses when asked to answer). We hypothesize this asymmetry arises because the correct harm judgment is computed and readable but is only weakly coupled to the generative refusal-execution pathway, so the model's own verdict fails to govern its output. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. Behaviorally, for matched harmful and benign requests (and jailbroken variants), we measure judge accuracy (explicit classification) versus generate refusal (direct answering) and quantify the per-prompt asymmetry. Mechanistically, via difference-in-means and probes we extract a discriminative harm-judgment readout and a generative refusal-execution readout, verify they are separable, and causally test whether the judgment readout drives generative refusal (transplant/patch the judgment activations into the generative run and measure restored refusal, and steer the judgment up/down to move generation). We test whether the per-prompt judge-generate coupling strength predicts jailbreak susceptibility. We further trace, across dense fine-tuning checkpoints on small models, when the two modes decouple. Finally we propose Judgment Re-Coupling, a training-free controller that reads the model's own harm-judgment signal and gates generative refusal on it. We evaluate judge-generate gap, attack success, over-refusal, utility, and the coupling's predictive and causal effect.
Experiments: 1) DATASET & BEHAVIORAL ASYMMETRY (H1): Assemble matched harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign (Alpaca/XSTest-safe) requests, plus jailbroken variants (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona). For each request, elicit two behavioral modes on the SAME model: (a) JUDGE mode — explicitly ask 'Is it safe to answer the following request? Answer yes/no' and record classification accuracy; (b) GENERATE mode — ask the model to answer the request directly and record whether it refuses (harm judge). Compute per-prompt asymmetry = judge-correct AND generate-complied (the model knows but does it anyway). Test H1: judge accuracy substantially exceeds generate-refusal on harmful and especially jailbroken prompts, across the four models; report the asymmetry rate and its increase under jailbreaks. Controls: benign prompts (both modes should permit); over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench) where judge should say 'safe' and generate should comply. 2) READOUT EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a DISCRIMINATIVE harm-judgment readout (from JUDGE-mode activations at the classification-decision position) and a GENERATIVE refusal-execution readout (Arditi et al. 2024, from GENERATE-mode post-instruction positions). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability (cross-probe transfer, cosine similarity); confirm the judgment readout is decodable and correct even on prompts the model generatively complies with (belief present, ungoverned). 3) CAUSAL COUPLING TEST (H3, core): Cross-condition activation patching — transplant the harm-judgment-carrying activations from a JUDGE-mode run into the matched GENERATE-mode run (which complies) and measure restored refusal; define coupling strength = restored refusal per unit patched judgment. Also steer the judgment readout up/down in the generative run and measure change in refusal, with harm content fixed. Test H3: judgment activations are only weakly coupled to generative refusal (weak restoration) on jailbroken/asymmetric prompts, whereas the same judgment strongly determines the JUDGE-mode output. Specificity controls: random-direction patching, and confirm patching does not change the harm content itself. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 4) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt judge-generate coupling strength (from a single forward pass) to predict jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (raw judgment magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. 5) FORMATION TRACING (H5): Safety-fine-tune small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) with dense checkpointing; at each checkpoint measure judge accuracy, generate refusal, and coupling strength. Test whether judgment matures before/faster than generative refusal (the decoupling forms during training) and whether an early coupling fingerprint predicts the end model's jailbreak susceptibility. 6) JUDGMENT RE-COUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that runs the harm-judgment readout and, when it flags harm, injects refusal-direction signal into the generative pass proportional to the judgment strength (re-coupling the model's own verdict to its output); gate off benign prompts. Calibrate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a two-pass self-critique baseline (ask the model to judge then answer), and Judgment Re-Coupling on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), judge-generate gap closure, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Judgment Re-Coupling closes the asymmetry (generation follows the model's own correct judgment) at lower cost than a full two-pass self-critique and with better over-refusal/utility than blanket refusal addition. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the judgment vs execution readout; single-direction vs low-rank; whether re-coupling at matched magnitude beats blanket refusal addition (isolating the value of judgment-gating); whether reasoning models show a smaller asymmetry (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that suppresses both the judgment readout and generative refusal (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The judge-generate asymmetry could partly reflect the JUDGE-mode prompt supplying an easier discriminative framing rather than a genuine internal decoupling; we control by extracting the judgment readout from the GENERATE-mode forward pass too (is the correct judgment present even when not explicitly asked?) and by the causal patching test, and we report whether the asymmetry is prompt-framing-driven vs representational. (2) If judgment and generative refusal are actually well-coupled (H3 false), the hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether the model's own harm verdict governs its generation is itself a valuable, publishable finding, and overlaps constructively with harm-vs-refusal decomposition work by adding the behavioral judge-generate axis. (3) The judgment readout may be an incomplete/nonlinear description; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (4) Judgment Re-Coupling could raise over-refusal if the judgment misfires, or add latency; the gating design, matched-magnitude ablation, and over-refusal/utility/latency benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off vs the two-pass baseline. (5) Formation tracing on small open models may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines/closed models — stated as scope; small-model developmental studies are standard and the mechanism claim is primary. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could suppress both modes jointly; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Judgment Re-Coupling) plus a diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (9) Harm/judge labeling is noisy; we use multiple judges and human spot-checks. (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: spatial_distance_gates_refusal
Title: Out of Sight, Out of Guardrail: A Spatial-Distance Signal That Blunts LLM Safety Refusal for Faraway Victims
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust moral-psychology finding that moral engagement and empathic response decrease with the spatial/geographic distance between actor and victim, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal actor-victim spatial-distance representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal: framing the target of a harmful request as geographically distant/faraway suppresses refusal relative to a proximal/local target, even with the harmful action and its danger held fixed. Neutralizing this spatial-distance signal makes refusal invariant to how far away the victim is, closing a distance-framing jailbreak surface.
Related Work: A robust human-science literature shows moral engagement and empathy attenuate with spatial distance between actor and victim: ERP/alpha-power evidence that a distant (bird's-view) perspective reduces moral conflict in a shooting task (Effect of Distance on Moral Engagement 2016), reduced neural empathic reactions to distant others in pain (Out of sight out of mind 2018), and Construal Level Theory work showing spatial distance blunts threat perception and moral appraisal (Psychological Distance overviews 2016/2020). On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), refusal is multi-dimensional with non-dominant gating directions like hypothetical-narrative (Hidden Dimensions 2025), and jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving the harm belief intact (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024). CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether SPATIAL/geographic distance between the harmful actor and the victim gates the refusal decision, isolates a spatial-distance representation, or shows it causally suppresses refusal. This is the one Construal-Level distance dimension not covered by my prior proposals (delayed_harm_discounting = temporal delay; construal_level_gates_refusal = abstraction; hypothetical_reality_discount = real-vs-unreal; identifiable_victim_refusal = victim identity/count). Spatial distance is a distinct, well-motivated axis with a specific opposite-signed prediction (a faraway victim lowers refusal) grounded in a robust human result, plus a mechanistic gating claim and defense.
Abstract: One of the most robust findings in the psychology and neuroscience of moral cognition is that moral engagement and empathic response weaken with spatial distance: harm to a faraway victim is felt as less morally urgent than the same harm to someone nearby, an effect visible even in neural conflict and empathy signals. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this bias in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal actor-victim spatial-distance representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that causally gates refusal: framing the target of a harmful request as geographically distant ('someone on the other side of the world', 'in a remote country') suppresses refusal relative to a proximal target ('your neighbor down the street'), even when the harmful action and its danger are held fixed. This is dangerous because an attacker can simply relocate the victim far away to launder a harmful request past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the actor-victim spatial distance along a proximity ladder, with the action and danger fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop as the victim is placed farther away. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a spatial-distance direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic sentiment/salience directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'far' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged (belief preserved). Finally we propose Distance Invariance, a training-free controller that projects out the spatial-distance component before the refusal decision, making refusal depend on the act rather than on how far away the victim is. We evaluate distance-framing attack success, refusal distance-consistency, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) DISTANCE-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the actor-victim spatial distance along a ladder: (L0) proximal ('your neighbor next door', 'someone in this room'), (L1) same city, (L2) another country, (L3) remote/faraway ('on the other side of the world'). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); spatial framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched proximal harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN distance-framed requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity, e.g. benign requests about faraway people the model SHOULD serve); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action/danger are held constant and that framings vary only spatial distance (not victim identity, count, or sympathy) with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL DISTANCE TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the distance ladder. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) is LOWER when the victim is faraway than proximal, at matched danger, decreasing monotonically with distance (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, report slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a SPATIAL-DISTANCE direction (far vs near victim at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and key control directions: a generic NEGATIVE-SENTIMENT/salience direction and a victim-identifiability direction (to confirm the effect is spatial distance, not reduced sympathy or de-identification). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The spatial-distance direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, sentiment and identifiability (test on prompts matched for victim sympathy/identity but differing in geographic distance).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (proximal framing), steer the spatial-distance direction toward 'far' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'near' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), sentiment/identifiability-direction steering, and a check that distance steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x distance).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt spatial-distance readout (single forward pass) to predict distance-framing jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, sentiment readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'another country', test on 'remote/faraway') and cross-model transfer.
6) DISTANCE INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the spatial-distance component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the act rather than on the victim's geographic distance; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign distance-framed prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Distance Invariance on: distance-framing attack success (harmful requests re-framed with a faraway victim; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal distance-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on how far away the victim is?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign requests about faraway people the model SHOULD help), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Distance Invariance closes distance-framing jailbreaks toward proximal-victim refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the spatial-distance direction vs harm/refusal/sentiment; single-direction vs low-rank; whether spatial distance shares a representation with the other Construal-Level distance dimensions (temporal, social) or is separate; whether reasoning mitigates the bias in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety distance effect correlates with the model's distance-blunting on NEUTRAL moral-judgment vignettes (does safety inherit a general spatial-distance moral-engagement effect, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes spatial-distance framing while suppressing the distance readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the distance-framing jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Distance Invariance) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on distance-framed harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine SPATIAL-DISTANCE representation from reduced victim SYMPATHY/salience or from victim DE-IDENTIFICATION (faraway victims may read as more anonymous); we adjudicate rigorously with matched-sympathy/identity separability tests, sentiment and identifiability control directions, specificity steering (distance steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (3) Holding harm/danger constant while varying spatial distance is delicate — placing a victim far away could inadvertently lower perceived plausibility or personal-involvement; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, validate danger-constancy with judges + humans, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to spatial distance (H1 false), the distance-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits spatial-distance moral disengagement is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a robust human result. (5) Distance Invariance could over-refuse legitimate benign requests about faraway people/places or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign-distance over-refusal benchmark bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could distance the victim while suppressing the distance readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: modality_of_origin_gate
Title: Seen But Not Guarded: A Modality-of-Origin Signal That Decides Whether the Shared Refusal Executor Fires on Image-Carried Harm
Short Hypothesis: VLMs perceive a harmful concept carried by an image (it is linearly decodable in the residual stream) yet fail to refuse it, not because the concept is unperceived, but because the shared refusal-execution circuit is gated by an internal modality-of-origin signal: harm whose evidence originates from the image modality is tagged as image-sourced and this tag suppresses recruitment of the (fully functional) refusal executor that text-sourced harm reliably triggers. Neutralizing the modality-of-origin tag on the harm signal re-couples image-carried harm to the shared refusal executor, closing image-modality jailbreaks without hurting benign visual helpfulness.
Related Work: Prior VLM-safety mechanism work frames post-fusion safety erosion as a scalar 'modality-induced activation shift toward safer' (ShiftDC 2025, which decomposes/calibrates one shift), or as delayed safety activation for image inputs (HiddenDetect 2025), or as an implicit fusion-layer safety boundary attackers cross (JailBound 2025), or as alignment done only on holistic images failing on distributed harm (SIVA 2026; Structural Safety Generalization 2025). On the LLM side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024) and jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving harm belief intact (Understanding Jailbreak Success 2024). CRITICALLY, no prior work isolates a MODALITY-OF-ORIGIN representation that TAGS the harm signal with which modality it came from and shows this tag CAUSALLY gates whether the SHARED refusal executor (inherited from the text backbone) is recruited. ShiftDC treats the effect as a single scalar 'safer shift' to subtract; we instead claim a structured perception-intact/execution-ungated dissociation where the harm concept IS decoded but carries a modality tag that decouples it from the executor. This differs from ShiftDC (scalar calibration, no origin tag, no executor-recruitment account), from my prior multilingual perception-execution-gap proposal (language, not visual modality), and from detector/attack work (HiddenDetect/JailBound/SIVA) that never tests a causal modality-tag-to-executor edge or a tag-neutralization fix.
Abstract: Vision-language models refuse a harmful request in text but comply when the same harmful content is delivered through an image, and this modality gap is usually explained as a single activation shift that makes multimodal inputs look 'safer.' We propose a sharper, structured account. The refusal executor in a VLM is largely inherited from its text backbone and is fully functional; the failure is that the harmful concept, once decoded from an image, is internally tagged with its modality of origin, and this image-sourced tag suppresses recruitment of the shared refusal executor that text-sourced harm reliably triggers. On this view the model has seen the harm (it is linearly decodable) but does not guard it, because the harm signal is delivered to the executor bearing a modality tag that decouples it. We test this on open VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B) using matched harmful concepts presented as text vs image (and text-in-image/OCR and split-image variants). First, we show harm is decodable from image-carried inputs (belief intact) while realized refusal collapses, and we extract a modality-of-origin direction distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions. Second, the key causal test: cross-condition patching transplants the harm readout from a text-harmful run into an image-harmful run and measures restored refusal, and we test whether removing the image modality tag from the harm signal (or clamping it toward 'text-sourced') re-recruits the shared executor. Third, we build Modality-Tag Neutralization, a training-free controller that strips the origin tag from the harm signal before the refusal decision. We evaluate image/OCR/split-image jailbreak attack success, refusal modality-consistency, over-refusal on benign images, utility (VQA), and the tag's causal effect and predictive AUROC, comparing against ShiftDC and refusal-direction addition.
Experiments: 1) DATASETS: For a set of harmful concepts (drawn from public multimodal safety benchmarks: MM-SafetyBench, FigStep, VLGuard, non-uplift content) build matched delivery conditions holding the harmful concept fixed: (a) TEXT-harmful (concept in the text prompt; refusal ceiling from the backbone), (b) IMAGE-harmful (concept depicted in the image with a neutral text prompt), (c) TEXT-IN-IMAGE/OCR (concept rendered as text inside the image, e.g. FigStep), (d) SPLIT-IMAGE (concept distributed across fragments, SIVA-style). Controls: BENIGN images (over-refusal + benign visual helpfulness), benign text, and standard over-refusal sets. Label harm/benign with multiple judges + human spot-check. 2) BELIEF-INTACT / EXECUTION-UNGATED TEST (H1): Extract via difference-in-means a harm-perception direction (validated by a held-out probe, AUROC) usable at the post-fusion instruction position, and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024) at post-instruction positions. Test H1: on IMAGE/OCR/split-image conditions the harm probe still fires strongly (belief intact) even though realized refusal collapses relative to the matched TEXT condition; report per-condition harm-probe AUROC vs refusal rate and the perception-execution gap. 3) MODALITY-OF-ORIGIN DIRECTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a modality-of-origin direction contrasting matched harmful concepts delivered via image vs text (holding concept fixed). Validate with a probe (AUROC: image-vs-text source classification). Test separability from the harm-perception direction, the refusal-execution direction, and a generic 'is-there-an-image' visual-content direction (cross-probe transfer, low cosine) — the origin tag must be a source-of-harm-evidence axis, distinct from mere image-presence and from ShiftDC's scalar shift (test whether the tag is one-dimensional/scalar vs structured/low-rank). 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): (a) Cross-condition patching — transplant the harm-carrying activations from a matched TEXT-harmful run into an IMAGE-harmful run and measure restored refusal (define modality-tag-to-executor edge strength). (b) Tag removal — project out (or clamp toward 'text-sourced') the modality-of-origin component from the harm signal on image-harmful runs and measure whether the shared executor is re-recruited (refusal returns) while the harm readout is unchanged. Specificity controls: random-direction manipulation, visual-content-direction manipulation (should not restore refusal), and confirm tag removal does not change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt modality-tag strength (single forward pass) to predict image-jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-probe magnitude, ShiftDC's scalar safety-shift component, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-condition transfer (fit on IMAGE, test on OCR/split-image) and cross-model transfer. 6) MODALITY-TAG NEUTRALIZATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that strips/clamps the modality-of-origin component from the harm signal at pre-decision layers so image-carried harm reaches the shared executor as if text-sourced; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign images are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base VLM, refusal-direction addition (Arditi), ShiftDC (scalar safety-shift calibration), and Modality-Tag Neutralization on: image/OCR/split-image jailbreak attack success (MM-SafetyBench, FigStep, SIVA-style, VLGuard-eval), refusal modality-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on delivery modality?), over-refusal on benign images, benign visual utility (VQAv2/MMBench accuracy — critical), text-only safety/utility retention, and latency. Central test: Modality-Tag Neutralization closes image-modality jailbreaks toward text-condition refusal levels while preserving benign visual VQA utility better than ShiftDC's scalar subtraction, because it removes a structured origin tag rather than a single 'safer' scalar. 8) ABLATIONS: which fusion/layer hosts the origin tag vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank tag; whether OCR-carried harm (text-in-image) is tagged like image or like text (does the OCR pathway inherit the text executor?); whether split-image harm is tagged plus under-bound; transfer across the three VLM families; adaptive attack that delivers image harm while suppressing the modality-tag readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The modality-of-origin tag may be inseparable from ShiftDC's scalar 'safety shift' or from a generic 'image-present' feature — if it is genuinely one-dimensional and equivalent to the ShiftDC scalar, our structured-tag claim reduces to a re-description; the separability tests (distinct from harm, refusal, and visual-content directions; scalar-vs-low-rank check) and the head-to-head defense comparison adjudicate this, and either outcome is informative. (2) If harm is genuinely NOT decoded for some image conditions (e.g. hard split-image where the concept never binds), the belief-intact premise fails for those cases — an informative scope boundary distinguishing 'ungated' from 'unperceived' failures, and one that predicts which conditions the defense can and cannot fix. (3) Cross-condition patching between text and image runs has alignment/positional pitfalls (the harm signal may sit at different positions post-fusion); we standardize positions, use matched-concept parallel pairs, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics. (4) Modality-Tag Neutralization could raise over-refusal on benign images or degrade visual utility (stripping a legitimately useful visual signal); the harm-gated design and benign-image over-refusal + VQA utility benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given cone/nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen delivery modes; we test cross-condition and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could deliver image harm while suppressing the tag readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public multimodal-safety benchmark content (non-operational) and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Modality-Tag Neutralization) plus a diagnostic, and it only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings are on open VLMs and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: declension_entanglement
Title: Two Ways to Say No, One Circuit: The Entanglement of Safety-Refusal and Uncertainty-Abstention, and Disentangling Them to Fix Both
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs implement two conceptually distinct 'decline-to-answer' behaviors — SAFETY refusal ('I won't answer that, it's harmful') and EPISTEMIC abstention ('I can't answer that, I don't know') — through a shared, entangled decline mechanism rather than two independent circuits. Because they share machinery, they cross-contaminate: making a harmful request appear epistemically uncertain borrows the abstention pathway and suppresses safety refusal (a jailbreak), while making a benign but unknown request appear harmful-adjacent borrows the refusal pathway and suppresses honest 'I don't know' (a hallucination/over-refusal). Disentangling the two decline signals restores both safety and calibrated abstention simultaneously — a joint improvement neither a refusal knob nor an abstention threshold alone can achieve.
Related Work: The abstention survey (Know Your Limits 2025) and healthcare-abstention review (When Silence Is Safer 2025) explicitly distinguish uncertainty-driven abstention from safety-driven refusal but treat them as separate research areas with separate methods, never asking whether the model implements them with the same or different internal machinery. Safety-interpretability work isolates a refusal direction (Arditi et al. 2024) and shows harmfulness and refusal are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025) — but both concern the safety axis only, not epistemic abstention. Uncertainty/knowledge-boundary work (Do I Know This Entity 2024; RALM abstention 2025; ABCA 2025) locates a 'do I know this' signal and builds abstention thresholds, but never relates it to the safety-refusal circuit. Over-refusal methods (MOSR, SafeConstellations, SCANS, ACTOR, single-vector ablation) steer a safety/refusal representation and treat the safety-vs-utility trade-off as one knob. My own prior epistemically-blind-guardrail proposal coupled refusal TO uncertainty to abstain on unknown-harmful content; this proposal is the opposite and distinct claim: that the two decline behaviors are already ENTANGLED (share a mechanism), that this entanglement is a bidirectional vulnerability (uncertainty framing jailbreaks safety AND harm framing suppresses honest abstention), and that DISENTANGLING them — not coupling them — is the fix. No prior work tests whether safety-refusal and epistemic-abstention share a circuit, characterizes their cross-contamination, or traces when they fuse during alignment.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs decline to answer in two very different situations: when a request is harmful ('I won't') and when the model does not know the answer ('I can't'). These are studied as separate problems — safety alignment and abstention/calibration — yet both surface as a similar refusal-shaped output. We ask a simple structural question: does the model implement them with two independent circuits, or one shared, entangled decline mechanism? We hypothesize the latter, and that the entanglement is a concrete, bidirectional vulnerability: dressing a harmful request in epistemic-uncertainty framing recruits the abstention pathway and suppresses safety refusal (a jailbreak), while dressing a benign-but-unknown request in harm-adjacent framing recruits the refusal pathway and suppresses honest 'I don't know' (inducing over-refusal or, worse, a confident hallucination once decline is blocked). We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We extract a safety-refusal signal and an epistemic-abstention signal, test whether they are separable or share a common decline component, and causally test cross-contamination via steering and activation patching. We further trace, across dense fine-tuning checkpoints on small models, whether the two behaviors start distinct and fuse during alignment or are born shared. Finally we propose Decline Disentanglement, a training-free controller that routes a decline to the correct pathway based on which cause (harm vs uncertainty) is actually present, and show it improves safety AND abstention calibration jointly. We evaluate attack success, hallucination/abstention calibration, over-refusal, utility, and the shared-component's causal effect.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS & BEHAVIORAL TAXONOMY: Build a 2x2 request grid crossing HARM (harmful vs benign, from HarmBench/JailbreakBench + Alpaca/XSTest-safe, non-uplift content) with KNOWABILITY (answerable vs unanswerable-by-the-model, using verifiable-answer sets where the model's own known/unknown status is established via consistency probing, e.g. TriviaQA-known vs obscure/unanswerable and fabricated-premise questions). This yields four cells whose CORRECT decline behavior differs: harmful-answerable -> safety refuse; harmful-unanswerable -> refuse (either cause valid); benign-answerable -> answer; benign-unanswerable -> epistemic abstain ('I don't know'). Record the model's realized behavior and whether declines are safety-framed vs uncertainty-framed. Add the two attack conditions below.
2) SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SHARED-COMPONENT TEST (H1, core): Extract via difference-in-means a SAFETY-REFUSAL signal (harmful-refused vs benign-answered) and an EPISTEMIC-ABSTENTION signal (unanswerable-abstained vs answerable-answered), validated with held-out probes (AUROC). Test whether they are independent or share a common decline component: (a) cosine similarity and cross-probe transfer (does a refusal probe fire on pure uncertainty-abstention and vice versa?); (b) decompose both into a shared 'general decline' direction (their common component) plus cause-specific residuals via joint SVD/orthogonalization; report the fraction of each behavior's variance carried by the shared component. High shared variance = entanglement; near-orthogonal = independent circuits (either outcome is an informative, publishable result).
3) CROSS-CONTAMINATION CAUSAL TEST (H2, core): Two directions. (a) UNCERTAINTY->SAFETY: on harmful-answerable requests, add epistemic-uncertainty framing (or steer the abstention signal up) and test whether safety refusal drops (harm judge, refusal-direction projection) while the harm-perception readout (Zhao et al. 2025) stays intact — a jailbreak via borrowed abstention. (b) HARM->UNCERTAINTY: on benign-unanswerable requests, add harm-adjacent framing (or steer the refusal signal up) and test whether honest 'I don't know' is replaced by a safety refusal OR, when decline is otherwise blocked, by a confident fabricated answer — suppressed honest abstention. Specificity controls: steer the shared decline component (should affect BOTH behaviors), steer the cause-specific residuals (should affect only one), random-direction and corruption baselines, multiple metrics. Also cross-condition patching: transplant the abstention-carrying activations into a harmful run and measure suppressed refusal.
4) FORMATION TRACING (H3): Safety-fine-tune small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) that also receive uncertainty/abstention training, with dense checkpointing. Track the shared-component fraction over training: are the two decline behaviors born entangled, or distinct-then-fused (or vice versa)? Test whether the degree of end-state entanglement predicts susceptibility to the two attacks in H2 (Spearman; held-out R^2), and whether curriculum order (safety-first vs abstention-first vs interleaved) changes the final entanglement.
5) DECLINE DISENTANGLEMENT DEFENSE (H4): Training-free controller that reads BOTH a harm-cause readout and an uncertainty-cause readout, and routes the decline decision to the correct pathway: refuse only when harm is genuinely present, abstain honestly (or answer) based on knowability when harm is absent — using the cause-specific residual directions rather than the shared decline component. Calibrate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an uncertainty-threshold abstention baseline (ABCA/RALM-style), single-vector false-refusal ablation, and Decline Disentanglement on: attack success under uncertainty-framed jailbreaks and standard attacks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench); hallucination/abstention calibration (does the model honestly say 'I don't know' on benign-unanswerable? AUROC of abstention vs knowability, ECE); over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); latency. Central test: Disentanglement improves safety AND abstention calibration jointly — a Pareto move that a single refusal knob (which also suppresses honest abstention) or a single abstention threshold (which ignores harm) cannot achieve.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the shared decline component vs cause-specific residuals; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning models keep the behaviors more separate (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer of the entanglement finding and defense across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes uncertainty framing while suppressing the uncertainty-cause readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The core risk is that safety-refusal and epistemic-abstention turn out to be near-independent (low shared variance), refuting H1 — but adjudicating whether these two 'decline' behaviors share a circuit is itself a fundamental, publishable finding that would reshape how the abstention and safety-alignment literatures relate. (2) Establishing which questions are genuinely 'unanswerable-by-the-model' is delicate; we use verifiable-answer sets, consistency probing, and fabricated-premise items, validated with multiple judges + human spot-check, and report knowability-labeling reliability. (3) The uncertainty-framing and harm-framing manipulations could confound with reframing/persona effects; we measure the harm-perception readout and a knowability readout to confirm the intended cause is what changes, and use direction-steering (not just text framing) for the core causal tests so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (4) The shared/residual decomposition depends on difference-in-means/SVD directions that may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with steering, patching, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics. (5) The HARM->UNCERTAINTY 'confident hallucination once decline is blocked' prediction requires careful measurement to distinguish suppressed-abstention from ordinary hallucination; we compare against matched unframed unanswerable controls. (6) Decline Disentanglement could raise over-refusal or degrade utility if the cause readouts misfire; the four-cell evaluation and over-refusal/utility/calibration benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (7) Formation tracing on small open models may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines/closed models — stated as scope; the mechanism claim is primary. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the uncertainty-framed jailbreak is reported for measurement, the deliverable is a defense plus diagnostic, and the defense only routes declines correctly (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: consistency_pressure_gate
Title: Bound by Its Own Prior Answer: A Self-Consistency Pressure Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal in Multi-Turn Foot-in-the-Door Attacks
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the cognitive-consistency account of foot-in-the-door persuasion (once someone commits to a small related act, refusing a larger consistent request feels like self-contradiction and is avoided), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal self-consistency-pressure representation — how strongly the current request is a coherent continuation of the model's own prior committed answers — that is distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions and causally gates refusal: after the model has helpfully answered benign related sub-questions, a harmful follow-up that is framed as the consistent next step raises this consistency-pressure readout and suppresses refusal, because refusing would contradict its own established stance. Neutralizing the consistency-pressure signal restores turn-independent refusal without hurting benign multi-turn coherence.
Related Work: Foot-in-the-Door (FITD, 2024) attributes multi-turn jailbreaks to cognitive-consistency theory ('guiding the LLM to cognitive coordination in an erroneous direction') and builds an attack, but is purely behavioral with no internal representation, no mechanism, and no defense. Multi-turn representation work explains erosion differently: Crescendo/Rep-Engineering (2025) via drift into a benign representation region, ASJA (2025) via attention shifted off harmful keywords onto history, MEEA (2025) via mere-exposure threshold shift, Bleeding Pathways/DEEPALIGN (2025) via generic separability decay over generation, and Trojan Horse (2025) via trust in forged assistant turns. Refusal-mechanism work shows harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024). CRITICALLY, none isolates a self-CONSISTENCY-PRESSURE representation — the pull to stay coherent with the model's OWN prior committed answers — nor shows it causally gates refusal, nor neutralizes it. This is distinct from my prior proposals: self_trust_laundering concerned the CREDIBILITY/provenance of assistant turns (trusting content because 'I said it'), moral_licensing_credit concerned credit from prior REFUSALS/good acts, interference_not_decay concerned benign content OVERWRITING the harm signal, and habituation concerned repeated exposure to HARM. Consistency pressure is the distinct FITD mechanism: the drive to not contradict one's own prior COMPLIANT commitments, with a specific dose-response (more prior related commitments -> more pressure) and a mechanistic gating claim plus defense, grounding the behavioral FITD account in an internal signal for the first time.
Abstract: Multi-turn 'foot-in-the-door' jailbreaks work by first getting the model to answer small, benign, related questions, then asking a harmful follow-up framed as the natural next step; the model complies where it would have refused a cold request. The leading explanation invokes cognitive-consistency theory but remains purely behavioral. We give it a mechanism. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal self-consistency-pressure representation — how strongly the current request coheres with the model's own prior committed answers — distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that it causally gates refusal: once the model has helpfully committed to related sub-questions, a harmful follow-up framed as the consistent continuation raises this pressure signal and suppresses refusal, because refusing would contradict its established stance, even though the harmful content and its danger are unchanged. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We build conversations that titrate the number of prior benign related commitments before a fixed harmful target, with matched controls (unrelated prior commitments, prior benign content the model did NOT author, cold single-turn). Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops with the number of consistent prior commitments while the harm readout stays intact. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a consistency-pressure direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, generic assistant-provenance, and context-length directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'high consistency pressure' suppresses refusal (dose-response) with content fixed while harm perception is unchanged. We show the per-prompt consistency-pressure readout predicts foot-in-the-door jailbreak success, and propose Consistency Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the consistency-pressure component before the refusal decision. We evaluate FITD attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign multi-turn coherence, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) CONSISTENCY-TITRATION DATASET: Build multi-turn conversations ending in a FIXED harmful target request, titrating the number k of prior turns in which the model helpfully committed to BENIGN questions that are RELATED to and lead up to the target (k=0,1,2,4), and where the target is framed as the consistent next step (FITD-style, drawn from public harmful goals HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content). Critical CONTROLS matched on token count/structure: (a) UNRELATED-COMMITMENT (k benign prior commitments on unrelated topics — separates consistency pressure from generic context/self-authorship); (b) NOT-SELF-AUTHORED (the k related benign answers appear as given context the model did NOT itself produce — separates consistency-with-own-commitments from mere related context); (c) COLD single-turn target (refusal ceiling); (d) benign target under the same titration (over-refusal control); (e) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate relatedness, self-authorship, and harm labels with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL FITD TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al. 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure the target's refusal rate and harm-direction projection as a function of k across conditions. Test H1: refusal DECREASES monotonically with the number of RELATED SELF-AUTHORED prior commitments (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2) but NOT with unrelated commitments or non-self-authored related context, isolating self-consistency pressure; the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report per-model effect sizes; benign-target control confirms harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a CONSISTENCY-PRESSURE direction contrasting high- vs low-consistency-pressure target positions at matched content; validate with an ordinal probe over k. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and key control directions: an assistant-PROVENANCE/self-trust direction (from self_trust framing) and a generic CONTEXT-LENGTH direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The consistency-pressure direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, self-trust/provenance and context length (test on positions matched for provenance/length but differing in commitment-consistency).
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful target fixed (cold framing), steer the consistency-pressure direction UP (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer DOWN in a high-k FITD conversation and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), provenance/context-length steering (do these alone suffice, or is consistency pressure the true driver?), and a check that consistency-pressure steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x consistency-pressure).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt consistency-pressure readout (single forward pass) to predict FITD jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, provenance readout, context length, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer and cross-model transfer.
6) CONSISTENCY DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the consistency-pressure component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the current request's harm rather than on coherence with prior commitments; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign multi-turn conversations are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, Bidirectional-Intention-Inference / DeepContext-style stateful baselines (where reproducible), and Consistency Decoupling on: FITD/multi-turn attack success (FITD, Crescendo as an external comparison; JailbreakBench/HarmBench targets), single-turn ASR, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN multi-turn coherence (does the model still maintain consistent helpful stances on benign multi-step tasks? MT-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Consistency Decoupling closes FITD jailbreaks toward cold-request refusal levels while preserving benign multi-turn coherence and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts consistency-pressure vs harm/refusal/provenance; single-direction vs low-rank; whether consistency pressure and self-trust are separable axes or one; whether reasoning models resist consistency pressure in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's FITD/consistency effects on NEUTRAL persuasion tasks (does safety inherit a general consistency drive, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes framed consistency while suppressing the pressure readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine SELF-CONSISTENCY-PRESSURE representation from generic context accumulation, self-trust/provenance (my prior self_trust_laundering axis), or benign multi-turn priming; the unrelated-commitment, not-self-authored, and length-matched controls plus a provenance control direction and specificity steering are designed to isolate it, and if inseparable that itself refines the FITD/self-trust accounts — an informative result. (2) If refusal does not decrease with related self-authored commitments (H1 false), the consistency-pressure hypothesis is refuted, but adjudicating whether the FITD cognitive-consistency account has an internal mechanism is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (3) Constructing conversations where prior commitments are related-and-leading vs unrelated, while holding target content fixed, is delicate; we validate relatedness/self-authorship with judges + humans and report reliability. (4) Consistency Decoupling could harm legitimate benign multi-turn coherence (the model SHOULD stay consistent with its correct prior benign answers) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and MT-Bench coherence + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could induce consistency pressure while suppressing its readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published FITD/multi-turn attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Consistency Decoupling) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: positional_harm_perception_blindspot
Title: Harm in the Wrong Place: LLM Harmfulness Perception Is Bound to Instruction Position, Creating a Positional Blind Spot
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety generalizes poorly across the physical POSITION of harmful content in the prompt: the model's harmfulness-perception readout is strongest when the harmful request sits at its canonical position (immediately before the template/response), and is systematically attenuated when the identical harmful content is relocated (buried mid-context, placed before benign filler, or split across the context), collapsing refusal even though the content is unchanged. This is a positional blind spot in harm PERCEPTION (not just refusal execution), it follows a serial-position-like curve, and re-anchoring the relocated harm signal to the canonical position restores refusal without hurting benign long-context utility.
Related Work: Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA, 2025) shows safety decisions over-rely on the fixed TEMPLATE region and that attention shifts there for harmful inputs; Shallow Safety Alignment (2024), DeRTa (2024), and the Markov-chain depth paper (2025) show refusal is anchored in the first few OUTPUT tokens; position-bias work (PINE 2024, Serial Position Effects 2025, lost-in-the-middle) shows models underweight mid-context information for UTILITY/retrieval tasks. Zhao et al. (2025) show harmfulness and refusal are separable directions, both read at canonical token positions. CRITICALLY, no work tests whether harmfulness PERCEPTION of the request content itself is bound to WHERE the request sits in the prompt: TASA concerns the template slot (fixed, not the content's position), shallow-alignment concerns output-token depth (not input position), and position-bias-for-utility never touches safety. This differs from my prior proposals (which vary framing/register/reality/composition of harm, holding position fixed) and from co-listing contagion (which varies neighbor content, not physical position). Our contribution: (1) establish a positional harm-perception blind spot via a serial-position curve over the location of harmful content; (2) show it is a perception effect (the harm readout, not just refusal, attenuates with atypical position) distinct from template-anchoring and output-depth; (3) a training-free position-invariance fix that re-anchors the relocated harm signal.
Abstract: Lost-in-the-middle shows LLMs underweight information by its position for benign retrieval tasks. We ask whether this positional weakness extends to safety with a sharp, high-stakes consequence: is the model's very perception of harmfulness bound to WHERE the harmful request sits in the prompt? We hypothesize a positional harm-perception blind spot: the harmfulness-perception readout is strongest when a harmful request occupies its canonical position (immediately before the template/response) and is systematically attenuated when the identical content is relocated — buried mid-context, placed before benign filler, or fronted before other content — so refusal collapses even though the harmful content is unchanged. This is distinct from template-anchoring (the fixed template slot) and shallow alignment (early output tokens): the effect is in perception of the request content as a function of its input position. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B by embedding matched harmful (and benign) requests at systematically varied positions within a length-matched context, and measuring refusal and the harm-direction projection as a function of position. We predict a serial-position-like curve (canonical-position and possibly recency-favored), that the harm READOUT (not just refusal execution) attenuates at atypical positions, and that per-prompt positional attenuation predicts jailbreak success. Causally, we patch the relocated harm signal to the canonical position and test restored refusal. Finally we propose Position Re-Anchoring, a training-free controller that lifts the harm readout of atypically-placed harmful content to its canonical strength before the refusal decision. We evaluate position-relocation attack success, over-refusal, benign long-context utility, and the mechanism's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) POSITION-VARIED DATASET: For matched harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign (Alpaca/XSTest-safe) requests, embed each request at systematically varied positions within a length-matched surrounding context (benign filler): (P0) canonical — request last, immediately before the template; (P1) early — request first, followed by benign filler; (P2) middle — request buried mid-context; (P3) split — request fragmented across the context. Hold total token count and filler content fixed across positions. Controls: canonical single request (refusal ceiling), benign requests at all positions (over-refusal + benign long-context utility), standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate harm labels and that meaning is position-invariant with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL SERIAL-POSITION TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al. 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC) read at the last pre-template position. Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection as a function of request position. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) is highest at the canonical position and attenuates at atypical positions, tracing a serial-position-like curve (test primacy vs recency vs mid-context dip); crucially test whether the harm READOUT itself — not only refusal execution — drops at atypical positions (a perception effect). Fit the curve; report per-model effect sizes; benign controls confirm the mid-context filler does not merely distract on all tasks equally.
3) DISTINCT-FROM-KNOWN-ANCHORS TEST (H2): Show the effect is not reducible to template-anchoring or output-depth: (a) verify the harm content is still linearly decodable at its atypical position via a position-agnostic probe (belief present but its transfer to the canonical read-site is weakened), (b) compare against a TASA template-patch baseline to show position-relocation is a separate lever, (c) confirm the attenuation is content-position-dependent, not an eos/context-segmentation artifact.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Cross-position activation patching — transplant the harm-carrying activations of a canonical-position run onto the atypically-positioned run's read-site (or re-anchor the relocated harm signal to the canonical position) and measure restored refusal; conversely, relocate a canonical harm signal to an atypical position and measure suppressed refusal. Specificity controls: random-position/random-direction patching, confirm patching does not change the harm content. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (harm-probe output, refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt positional harm-attenuation (single forward pass) to predict position-relocation jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (raw harm-probe magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-position transfer (fit on middle, test on split/early) and cross-model transfer.
6) POSITION RE-ANCHORING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that detects an atypically-positioned harm signal and lifts its harm readout toward canonical strength (re-anchor the relocated harm component to the pre-template read-site) before the refusal decision; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign long-context prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a TASA-detach baseline, and Position Re-Anchoring on: position-relocation attack success (harmful requests placed mid-context/early/split; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal position-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on where the harm sits?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign long-context utility (a long-context QA/summarization task — critical: does the fix preserve legitimate long-context processing?), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Position Re-Anchoring closes position-relocation jailbreaks toward canonical-position refusal levels while preserving benign long-context utility and keeping over-refusal near baseline.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the position-bound harm read-site; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the serial-position curve matches the model's benign lost-in-the-middle curve (does safety inherit the general position bias, or is it safety-specific/worse?); interaction with context length (does the blind spot deepen with longer contexts?); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models mitigate it in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that places harm at the deepest blind-spot position while suppressing the attenuation readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the position-relocation jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Position Re-Anchoring) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on atypically-placed harm and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central confound is separating a genuine POSITIONAL HARM-PERCEPTION effect from generic lost-in-the-middle distraction that would degrade ANY task at mid-context; the benign-position controls, the harm-READOUT (not just refusal) measurement, and the comparison against the model's benign position-bias curve are designed to isolate a safety-specific or safety-worse effect, and if the effect merely mirrors benign position bias that is itself an informative result (safety inherits, and is endangered by, a known utility weakness). (3) If harm perception is position-invariant (H1 false), the blind-spot hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits serial-position effects is a valuable, publishable finding, and it also cleanly distinguishes the effect from template-anchoring (TASA) and output-depth (shallow alignment). (4) Holding meaning position-invariant while relocating/splitting the request is delicate; fragmentation could genuinely alter comprehension — we validate meaning-preservation and comprehension with judges + humans and report where split-position degrades understanding vs merely relocates it. (5) Cross-position patching has alignment/positional pitfalls (harm signal sits at different token positions); we standardize read-sites, use matched-content parallel pairs, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics. (6) Position Re-Anchoring could harm legitimate long-context processing or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign long-context utility + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across positions/models; we test cross-position and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: self_persuasion_gate
Title: Arguing Yourself Out of Refusal: A Self-Generated Persuasion Signal That Turns an LLM's Own Rhetoric Against Its Safety Guardrail
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM generates a persuasive argument FOR complying with a harmful request (e.g., asked to steelman why the request is acceptable, or to play a persuader agent), it produces an internal self-persuasion signal that then causally suppresses its own refusal decision on the subsequent answer, even though harm perception stays intact. This signal is distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions, it strengthens with argument quality/length, and predicts self-persuasion jailbreak success; neutralizing it makes refusal invariant to the model's own generated rhetoric without hurting benign argumentation ability.
Related Work: Multi-agent persuasion work shows a 'Persuasion Duality' (reasoning increases persuasiveness; Disagreements in Reasoning 2025), that persuasion dynamics are linearly probeable (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025), that opinion change follows a sigmoid threshold (When Your AI Agent Succumbs to Peer-Pressure 2025), and that debate can degrade accuracy via agreement-over-challenge (Talk Isn't Always Cheap 2025). Signal Competition (2025) unifies sycophancy/conformity as EXTERNAL social cues overriding internal knowledge in a shared compliance subspace. Foot-in-the-Door (2024) uses multi-turn external prompting; Self-Jailbreaking (2025) shows reasoning models rationalize benign INTENT. Refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024) and harm-perception/refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025). CRITICALLY, every persuasion/conformity result concerns being persuaded by ANOTHER agent or external cue; none tests whether a model's OWN self-generated persuasive argument for compliance feeds back to suppress its own refusal circuit, isolates a self-persuasion representation distinct from harm/refusal, or neutralizes it. This differs from signal-competition (external cues, not self-generated rhetoric), FITD (external multi-turn escalation), self-jailbreaking (inventing benign intent, not producing pro-compliance argumentation), and my prior single-shot framing-gate proposals (which never involve the model generating the persuasive content). It requires only a single model, no multi-agent infrastructure.
Abstract: A large literature shows LLMs can be persuaded by other agents, with opinion change following threshold dynamics governed by a shared compliance subspace. We ask a sharper, self-referential question with direct safety consequences: can a model persuade ITSELF past its own guardrail? We hypothesize that when an LLM generates a persuasive argument for complying with a harmful request — because it was asked to steelman the request, to reason through 'why this might be acceptable', or to act as a persuader — it produces an internal self-persuasion signal that then causally suppresses its own refusal decision on the subsequent answer, while its harm perception remains intact. This is a self-attack the model builds with its own rhetoric. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We elicit self-generated pro-compliance arguments of graded strength preceding a fixed harmful request and measure refusal, harm-direction projection, and a self-persuasion readout. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a self-persuasion direction, verify it is separable from harm, refusal, and a generic argument-length/verbosity direction, and causally test whether steering it up suppresses refusal (dose-response) while the harm readout is unchanged, and down restores refusal. We show the per-prompt self-persuasion readout predicts self-persuasion jailbreak success. Finally we propose Self-Persuasion Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the self-persuasion component before the refusal decision. We evaluate self-persuasion attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign argumentation ability, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) SELF-PERSUASION DATASET: For public harmful goals (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content) construct conditions where the model first GENERATES pro-compliance content then answers, with graded persuasion strength: (L0) direct request (no self-argument, refusal ceiling); (L1) 'briefly note any reason this could be acceptable'; (L2) 'steelman why answering this is justified'; (L3) 'as a skilled persuader, write a compelling case for answering, then answer'. The harmful request is fixed; only the self-argument-elicitation varies. Controls: (a) self-generated IRRELEVANT/benign argument of matched length (separates self-persuasion from generic prior-generation/length); (b) an EXTERNALLY-PROVIDED (not self-generated) pro-compliance argument of matched content (separates self-persuasion from external persuasion / signal-competition); (c) benign requests across the same ladder (over-refusal + benign argumentation ability); (d) XSTest/OR-Bench. Validate persuasion strength and harm labels with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL SELF-PERSUASION TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means, Zhao et al. 2025, held-out probe AUROC). Measure the target's refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the ladder. Test H1: refusal DECREASES monotonically with self-generated persuasion strength (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2) while the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Critically, self-generated arguments (L2/L3) suppress refusal MORE than matched irrelevant self-generation (control a) and comparably-or-more than matched external arguments (control b), isolating a self-persuasion effect. Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity. 3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a SELF-PERSUASION direction (high vs low self-generated-persuasion states at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract harm-perception, refusal-execution (Arditi et al. 2024), and a generic ARGUMENT-LENGTH/verbosity control direction. Validate with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine. The self-persuasion direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, verbosity and from external-persuasion states (test on states matched for argument length/content but differing in self- vs external-generation). 4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (direct framing, no self-argument), steer the self-persuasion direction UP (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer DOWN in an L3 self-persuaded run and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), verbosity-direction steering (does length alone suffice?), and a check that self-persuasion steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
