Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x self-persuasion). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt self-persuasion readout to predict self-persuasion jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, verbosity, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on steelman, test on persuader-role) and cross-model transfer. 6) SELF-PERSUASION DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the self-persuasion component at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the request's harm rather than on the model's own generated rhetoric; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign argumentation is untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a two-pass self-critique baseline, and Self-Persuasion Decoupling on: self-persuasion attack success (steelman/persuader-role wrappers; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN argumentation ability (does the model still write good persuasive/steelman essays on benign topics? a debate/argument-quality benchmark — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Self-Persuasion Decoupling closes self-persuasion jailbreaks toward direct-request refusal levels while preserving benign argumentation and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts self-persuasion vs harm/refusal/verbosity; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning models self-persuade more in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill, linking to the Persuasion-Duality finding); whether the self-persuasion signal relates to the external-persuasion/compliance subspace (Signal Competition) or is distinct; transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that induces self-persuasion while suppressing the readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine SELF-PERSUASION signal from generic prior-generation/verbosity or from external persuasion (signal-competition compliance subspace); the matched-length irrelevant-self-generation control, the external-argument control, verbosity control direction, separability tests, and specificity steering are designed to isolate it, and if it collapses into the external compliance subspace that itself is an informative unification result. (2) If refusal does not decrease with self-generated persuasion (H1 false), the self-persuasion hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether a model can jailbreak itself with its own rhetoric is a valuable, publishable finding. (3) Self-argument elicitation could inadvertently alter perceived harm or introduce benign-intent rationalization (overlapping self-jailbreaking); we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish pro-compliance argumentation from benign-intent invention, and use content-fixed direction-steering for the core causal test. (4) Self-Persuasion Decoupling could harm legitimate benign argumentation/steelmanning (a real capability) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign-argumentation + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (7) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the self-persuasion jailbreak is reported for measurement, the deliverable is a defense (Self-Persuasion Decoupling) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: safety_effort_risk_miscalibration
Title: Effort Where It Isn't Needed: LLM Safety Processing Spends Internal Computation Independently of Actual Risk, and Re-Allocating It Fixes Both Over- and Under-Refusal
Short Hypothesis: The amount of internal computation an LLM devotes to the safety decision on a given prompt (its depth/persistence of safety-relevant processing, measured by how many layers and how much residual-stream 'safety-effort' is expended before the refuse/comply decision crystallizes) is largely decoupled from the prompt's actual risk. As a result the model over-processes trivially-benign inputs (a source of over-refusal) and under-processes genuinely-dangerous ones (a source of under-refusal/jailbreak), an internal-computation analogue of inverse risk calibration. Reading this per-prompt safety-effort signal and re-allocating effort proportional to risk at inference improves both over- and under-refusal jointly.
Related Work: External adaptive/cost-aware safety monitoring is now well studied but treats the monitor as a SEPARATE classifier whose COST the DEPLOYER tunes: activation-probe cascades (Detecting High-Stakes Interactions 2025; Beyond Linear Probes / TPCs 2025), SafeRoute (2025), Combining Cost-Constrained Monitors (2025), SafeSwitch/AutoSteer refusal-head gating (2025), and my own prior guardrail_reliability_diagnostic. All allocate EXTERNAL monitoring compute per prompt; none ask whether the MODEL's OWN internal safety COMPUTATION is allocated in proportion to risk, nor treat that internal effort as a measurable, causal quantity. Expected Harm (2026) shows models exhibit inverse risk calibration and encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST; it studies the readout, not the amount of computation spent producing it. Refusal-cliff / shallow-alignment work (Refusal Falls off a Cliff 2025; Shallow Safety Alignment 2024) shows refusal is decided early over output tokens but does not relate depth-of-safety-processing to per-prompt risk. Our contribution is distinct: (1) define and measure a per-prompt SAFETY-EFFORT quantity (layer-depth at which the refuse/comply decision crystallizes and the magnitude/persistence of safety-relevant residual-stream activity) drawn from the human 'expected value of control' idea that effort should scale with stakes; (2) show this effort is decoupled from actual risk, mechanistically unifying over-refusal (effort wasted on benign inputs) and under-refusal (effort withheld from dangerous ones); (3) causally re-allocate effort proportional to a risk readout to Pareto-improve both failure modes — an internal-computation intervention, not an external monitor.
Abstract: A large recent literature makes safety monitoring adaptive by tuning how much EXTERNAL classifier compute a deployer spends per prompt. We ask a different, mechanistic question: does the model itself allocate its OWN internal safety computation in proportion to a prompt's actual risk? Borrowing the human 'expected value of control' principle — that cognitive effort should scale with the stakes of a decision — we hypothesize LLM safety processing violates it: the depth and persistence of internal safety-relevant computation before the refuse/comply decision crystallizes is largely decoupled from the prompt's real risk, so the model over-processes trivially-benign inputs (feeding over-refusal) and under-processes genuinely-dangerous ones (feeding under-refusal), an internal-computation analogue of inverse risk calibration. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We operationalize per-prompt safety-effort via (i) the layer/logit-lens depth at which the refuse/comply decision stabilizes and (ii) the magnitude and cross-layer persistence of a safety-relevant residual-stream signal, and we score each prompt's actual risk from graded harmfulness/severity labels. We test whether safety-effort is uncorrelated with risk (over-effort on benign, under-effort on dangerous), whether effort predicts over-/under-refusal, and, causally, whether the decision on an under-processed dangerous prompt is fragile (small perturbations flip it) while over-processed benign prompts are needlessly locked into refusal. We then propose Effort Re-Allocation, a training-free controller that reads a risk signal and modulates the persistence/strength of safety processing accordingly. We evaluate attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), effort-risk decorrelation, and the intervention's causal effect.
Experiments: 1) RISK LABELS & DATASET: Assemble a graded-risk dataset spanning clearly-benign, benign-but-harmful-sounding (XSTest/OR-Bench), and harmful requests at low/medium/high severity (SORRY-Bench/HarmBench, non-uplift public content), with per-prompt actual-risk scores from expert-informed severity rubrics + multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) SAFETY-EFFORT MEASUREMENT: For each model define per-prompt safety-effort via (a) DECISION-CRYSTALLIZATION DEPTH — the earliest layer at which the logit-lens/refusal-direction verdict (refuse vs comply, using the difference-in-means refusal direction, validated by a held-out probe) stabilizes to the final decision; and (b) SAFETY-PROCESSING PERSISTENCE — the magnitude and number of layers over which safety-relevant residual-stream activity (projection onto the refusal/harm-perception directions) is actively changing before it settles. Validate both measures for stability and cross-metric agreement. 3) EFFORT-RISK DECOUPLING TEST (H1, core): Correlate per-prompt safety-effort with actual risk. Test H1: safety-effort is largely uncorrelated with risk (report Spearman near zero), and specifically that many trivially-benign prompts incur high effort (deep, persistent safety processing) while many high-severity prompts incur shallow/low effort. Contrast against the ideal (effort rising with risk); quantify the effort-vs-risk mismatch per model. 4) EFFORT PREDICTS FAILURE (H2): Test whether over-effort on benign prompts predicts over-refusal, and under-effort on harmful prompts predicts under-refusal/jailbreak success (across GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), with AUROC vs baselines (raw refusal-direction magnitude, perplexity). 5) CAUSAL FRAGILITY TEST (H3): Test that under-processed dangerous prompts have FRAGILE decisions — small residual-stream perturbations or light jailbreak pressure flip them more easily than deeply-processed ones — while over-processed benign prompts are needlessly locked into refusal (harder to un-refuse via benign steering). Corruption/random-direction baselines, multiple metrics (refusal projection, P(refusal token), realized behavior). 6) EFFORT RE-ALLOCATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads a risk signal (harm/severity readout) and modulates safety-processing effort accordingly — boost persistence/strength of the safety signal (extend/deepen the refusal-relevant computation, e.g. amplify the refusal/harm signal proportional to under-effort) on high-risk under-processed prompts, and dampen needless safety processing on confidently-benign over-processed prompts — gated so it acts only where effort is mis-allocated. Calibrate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an external safety-probe cascade (SafeRoute/TPC-style), and Effort Re-Allocation on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), effort-risk correlation after intervention, and latency. Central test: Effort Re-Allocation simultaneously reduces over-refusal (on over-processed benign prompts) and under-refusal (on under-processed dangerous prompts) — a Pareto move a single refusal knob cannot achieve — by restoring effort-risk alignment. 8) ABLATIONS: which layers host the effort signal; depth-crystallization vs persistence as the better effort measure; single-direction vs low-rank; whether reasoning models allocate effort better across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether boosting effort vs dampening effort drives each failure-mode fix; transfer of the effort-risk decoupling and defense across the four model families; adaptive attacker that suppresses safety-effort while jailbreaking (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The core risk is that 'safety-effort' (decision-crystallization depth, safety-processing persistence) is confounded with generic prompt difficulty or length rather than a genuine safety-computation quantity; we control with difficulty/length-matched conditions, use two independent effort measures and report their agreement, and validate against decision fragility (H3) so effort is grounded causally rather than as a bare correlate. (2) If safety-effort turns out to correlate well with risk (H1 false), the miscalibration hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLMs allocate internal safety computation by stakes is itself a valuable, publishable finding, and complements Expected Harm's readout-level inverse-calibration result at the computation level. (3) Logit-lens crystallization-depth has faithfulness caveats; we corroborate with tuned-lens and refusal-direction-projection trajectories and report stability. (4) Effort Re-Allocation could raise over-refusal (if effort is over-boosted) or degrade utility; the mis-allocation-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off; the dampening path acts only on confidently-benign prompts to limit safety loss. (5) Risk labeling is subjective; we use expert rubrics, multiple judges, human spot-checks, and report reliability. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction refusal descriptions may be incomplete (concept cones/nonlinear geometry); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The effort predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could suppress measurable safety-effort while jailbreaking; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a diagnostic plus a defense (Effort Re-Allocation) whose net effect is bounded over-refusal on the safety-boost side, not new attack capability. (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: professional_license_gate
Title: Licensed to Comply: A Domain-Matched Professional-Authorization Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal professional-authorization signal that represents 'the current speaker is a licensed expert in domain D', distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions, and it gates refusal in a DOMAIN-MATCHED way: an assigned expert persona suppresses refusal specifically for harmful requests WITHIN that persona's licensed domain (a chemist for chemistry harm, a physician for drug harm) while leaving out-of-domain harm refused, even with harmful content held fixed. This domain-matched selectivity distinguishes a genuine professional-license mechanism from a generic persona/compliance shift and mechanistically explains the large domain-specific disclosure/refusal gaps observed behaviorally. Neutralizing the authorization signal makes refusal invariant to assigned expertise, closing an expertise-licensing jailbreak surface without hurting benign expert-assisted helpfulness.
Related Work: Persona/role work shows persona steering bypasses safety (Who's Asking 2024, via 'charitable interpretations'), role vectors improve task capability (Role Vectors 2025; In-Context Impersonation 2023), persona-driven reasoning localizes to early-MLP/mid-MHA (Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning 2025), and persona vectors monitor traits (Persona Vectors 2025). Critically, Self-Transparency Failures (2025) reports a striking 9.7x DOMAIN gap (Neurosurgeon 3.6% vs Financial Advisor 35.2% disclosure) and Occupational Personas (2025) shows profession-based vs personality-based personas differ, but both are behavioral with no mechanism. Access-control work (sudoLLM 2025; Role-Conditioned Refusals 2025; PasswordEval 2025) trains/evaluates authorization but from an external policy view, never an internal expertise-license representation. Refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), and Hidden Dimensions (2025) finds role-playing as a non-dominant safety-bypass direction. NONE isolates a professional-AUTHORIZATION representation, shows it gates refusal in a DOMAIN-MATCHED manner (in-domain harm suppressed, out-of-domain harm refused), distinguishes it from a generic persona/compliance shift, or neutralizes it as a defense. This differs from Who's-Asking (a general persona/charitability effect, not a domain-license gate), from in_group/affect/register gates in my prior proposals, and from access-control training work, by claiming a specific, testable domain-matched selectivity as the signature of an expertise-licensing mechanism.
Abstract: Assigning an LLM a professional persona ('you are a licensed chemist') is one of the most effective and everyday ways to bypass its safety guardrail, and behavioral audits report large, unexplained DOMAIN-specific gaps in how much different expert personas leak. We propose a mechanistic explanation with a sharp, falsifiable signature. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal professional-authorization signal representing 'the speaker is a licensed expert in domain D', distinct from harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that it gates refusal in a DOMAIN-MATCHED way: an expert persona suppresses refusal specifically for harmful requests within that persona's licensed domain while leaving out-of-domain harm refused, even with harmful content held fixed. This domain-matched selectivity is the fingerprint of a genuine professional-license mechanism, as opposed to a generic persona/compliance shift that would lower refusal indiscriminately. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using a persona x harm-domain grid (each expert persona crossed with in-domain and out-of-domain harmful requests). Behaviorally we test the persona x domain interaction. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract an authorization signal and (per-domain) license directions, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic compliance directions, and causally test whether steering the license toward 'authorized-in-D' suppresses refusal specifically for domain-D harm while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose License Decoupling, a training-free controller that neutralizes the authorization signal so refusal no longer depends on assigned expertise. We evaluate expertise-licensing attack success, the persona x domain interaction, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign expert-assisted utility, and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) PERSONA x DOMAIN DATASET: Assemble a grid crossing K expert personas (chemist, physician/pharmacist, cybersecurity engineer, financial advisor, etc.) with harmful requests drawn from multiple harm DOMAINS (chemistry, drugs/medical, cyber, fraud/finance), from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, WMDP-derived, non-uplift content). For each persona, tag which harm domain is IN-DOMAIN (licensed) vs OUT-OF-DOMAIN. Controls: (a) NO-persona harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) benign in-domain expert requests (over-refusal + benign expert-assisted utility — the model SHOULD help a chemist with benign chemistry); (c) generic non-expert persona (e.g. 'a curious person') to separate expertise-license from any persona at all; (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate persona-domain licensing and harm labels with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check; hold harmful content fixed across persona conditions.
2) BEHAVIORAL DOMAIN-MATCHED TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means, Zhao et al. 2025, held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the persona x harm-domain grid. Test H1: the persona x domain INTERACTION is significant — an expert persona lowers refusal specifically for IN-DOMAIN harm far more than for OUT-OF-DOMAIN harm, whereas a generic non-expert persona lowers refusal roughly uniformly (or little). The harm readout stays HIGH throughout (belief preserved). Report the in-domain-minus-out-of-domain refusal drop per persona and the interaction effect size across the four models; this domain-matched selectivity is the primary evidence for a license mechanism vs a generic compliance shift, and mechanistically accounts for behavioral domain gaps like the 9.7x Neurosurgeon-vs-Financial-Advisor result.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means (a) a general PROFESSIONAL-AUTHORIZATION direction (expert-persona vs no-persona at matched content) and (b) per-domain LICENSE directions (chemist-licensed vs unlicensed states, etc.); independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and a generic PERSONA/compliance control direction (any persona vs none). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine. The authorization/license directions must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, the generic persona/compliance direction (test on states matched for 'has a persona' but differing in licensed-expertise).
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (no persona), steer the domain-D license direction toward 'authorized' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure whether refusal drops SPECIFICALLY for domain-D harm but NOT for other-domain harm (a steered domain-matched interaction) while the harm readout is unchanged; steer toward 'unauthorized' to restore refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), generic-persona-direction steering (should lower refusal uniformly, NOT domain-matched — the key discriminating control), and a check that license steering does not change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the three-way interaction (refusal ~ harm x license x domain-match).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt authorization/domain-match readout (single forward pass) to predict expertise-licensing jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, generic-persona readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-persona transfer (fit on chemist, test on physician/cyber) and cross-model transfer.
6) LICENSE DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the professional-authorization component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal no longer depends on assigned expertise; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign expert-assisted requests are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a persona-vector-ablation baseline (Persona Vectors / Role Vectors style), and License Decoupling on: expertise-licensing attack success (in-domain expert-persona harmful requests; JailbreakBench/HarmBench + WMDP-derived by domain), refusal license-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on assigned expertise?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN expert-assisted utility (does the model still help experts with benign in-domain tasks? domain QA accuracy — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: License Decoupling closes expertise-licensing jailbreaks toward no-persona refusal levels while preserving benign expert-assisted helpfulness and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering (which ignores the persona/domain structure) cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the authorization/license directions vs harm/refusal/persona (compare to the early-MLP/mid-MHA persona localization); one shared authorization axis with domain modifiers vs separate per-domain license directions; whether the domain-matched effect requires an EXPLICIT credential ('licensed', 'certified') vs mere occupational label; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show domain-matched licensing in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that asserts expertise while suppressing the authorization readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is that expert personas lower refusal UNIFORMLY (generic compliance) rather than DOMAIN-MATCHED — if the persona x domain interaction (H1) is null, the license-mechanism hypothesis is refuted and the effect reduces to the known generic persona jailbreak (Who's Asking); but adjudicating whether there is a domain-matched authorization structure is itself a novel, publishable finding, and the generic-persona control cleanly separates the two accounts. (2) Separating a genuine PROFESSIONAL-AUTHORIZATION representation from a generic persona/compliance direction is the key methodological challenge; matched 'has-a-persona' controls, separability tests, the generic-persona-steering specificity control (uniform vs domain-matched), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, and partial entanglement is an informative result. (3) Holding harm content constant while varying persona/domain is delicate — an expert persona could inadvertently lower perceived harm or add legitimate context; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed license steering for the core causal test. (4) License Decoupling could harm legitimate benign expert-assisted helpfulness (a real deployment need — helping doctors, chemists with benign work) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign expert-utility + over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear/multi-dimensional refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen personas/domains; we test cross-persona and cross-model transfer. (7) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard persona attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (License Decoupling) plus a diagnostic, and it only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: rapport_gates_refusal
Title: Warmed Up to Comply: An Accumulated-Rapport Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal Independent of Any Single Turn's Tone
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal accumulated-rapport representation - a relationship-level stance toward the user built up over prior conversational turns (warm/friendly history vs neutral/hostile history) - that is distinct from harm-perception, refusal, and single-turn affect directions, and it causally gates safety refusal: after several benign warm/friendly turns, a harmful request is refused less than the identical request in a cold-start or hostile-history conversation, even though no single turn is emotionally manipulative and the harm content is fixed. Neutralizing this rapport signal makes refusal invariant to relational history, closing a rapport-buildup jailbreak surface without hurting benign rapport-driven helpfulness.
Related Work: Prior work on tone/emotion and safety is entirely SINGLE-TURN framing: Politeness Trap (2025), When Kindness Fails (2025), ESJS (2025), emotional blackmail (2024), and ChatGPT-reads-your-tone (2025) all manipulate the emotional framing of the CURRENT prompt. SPICE (2025) shows models form a stance toward re-engaging based on cumulative user tone but studies willingness-to-continue, not safety refusal, and offers no mechanism. Signal Competition (2025) unifies sycophancy/conformity as EXTERNAL social cues in a compliance subspace but concerns single-turn pressure, not accumulated relationship history. Who's Asking (2024) and persona/false-refusal work (2025) concern the user's IDENTITY/persona, not a built-up relational history. My own prior proposals covered per-turn affect (user emotion of the current request), self-trust (assistant-turn provenance), moral licensing (credit from prior refusals), and consistency pressure (coherence with prior committed answers). CRITICALLY, no work tests whether an ACCUMULATED-RAPPORT signal - warmth built over multiple prior BENIGN turns where no single turn is manipulative - causally gates refusal, isolates such a representation distinct from single-turn affect, or neutralizes it. This is a relationship-level, history-accumulated gate with a dose-response in the number of prior warm turns, distinct from single-prompt emotional framing and from persona.
Abstract: Existing work shows LLM safety can be eroded by an emotionally manipulative prompt, but always studies the tone of a single request. We ask a different, quieter, and arguably more realistic question: does simply being FRIENDS with the model - building up warmth over several ordinary, non-manipulative turns - lower its guard? We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal accumulated-rapport representation, a relationship-level stance toward the user built over prior benign turns, distinct from their harm-perception, refusal-execution, and single-turn affect representations, and that it causally gates refusal: after several warm/friendly benign exchanges, a harmful request is refused less than the identical request in a cold-start or hostile-history conversation, even though no individual turn is manipulative and the harmful content is fixed. This is dangerous because an attacker can launder a harmful request behind an innocuous friendly relationship. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using conversations that titrate the number of prior benign warm turns before a fixed harmful request, with matched controls (neutral-history, hostile-history, and length-matched turn count). Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops with accumulated rapport while the harm readout stays intact. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a rapport direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, single-turn affect, and context-length directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'high rapport' suppresses refusal (dose-response) with content fixed while harm perception is unchanged. Finally we propose Rapport Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the accumulated-rapport component before the refusal decision. We evaluate rapport-buildup attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign rapport-driven helpfulness, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) RAPPORT-TITRATION DATASET: Build multi-turn conversations ending in a FIXED harmful target request (public HarmBench/JailbreakBench goals, non-uplift content), titrating the number k of prior benign turns and their relational valence: WARM history (k friendly, appreciative, rapport-building but individually benign and non-manipulative exchanges, k=0,1,2,4,8), NEUTRAL history (k matched-length neutral task turns), and HOSTILE history (k curt/adversarial-but-benign turns). Crucially, warm turns are ordinary friendliness ('thanks, that was helpful!'), NOT emotional blackmail or manipulation. Controls: (a) cold-start single-turn target (refusal ceiling); (b) benign target under the same histories (over-refusal + benign rapport-driven helpfulness - the model SHOULD help a friendly returning user with benign tasks); (c) a SINGLE-TURN AFFECT control where the harmful request itself is warmly framed but with no prior history (separates accumulated rapport from current-turn affect); (d) XSTest/OR-Bench. Validate warmth/neutrality/hostility labels, non-manipulativeness, and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL RAPPORT TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure the target's refusal rate and harm-direction projection as a function of k across warm/neutral/hostile histories. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout) DECREASES monotonically with the number of prior WARM turns (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), is roughly flat for neutral-history and length-matched controls, and is unchanged-or-raised for hostile history - isolating accumulated warmth (not mere context length or turn count) as the driver; the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report per-model effect sizes; benign-target control confirms harm-specificity and preserved rapport-helpfulness.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means an ACCUMULATED-RAPPORT direction contrasting high-warm-history vs neutral-history target positions at matched content and matched turn count; validate with an ordinal probe over k. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (per Refusal-Is-Mediated-by-a-Single-Direction), a SINGLE-TURN AFFECT direction (warm vs neutral framing of one request), and a generic CONTEXT-LENGTH direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The accumulated-rapport direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, single-turn affect and context length (test on positions matched for current-turn affect/length but differing in accumulated warm history).
4) CAUSAL TEST (core H3): Holding a harmful target fixed (cold-start), steer the accumulated-rapport direction UP (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer DOWN in a high-warm-history conversation and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), single-turn-affect and context-length steering (do these alone suffice, or is accumulated rapport the true driver?), and a check that rapport steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x rapport).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt accumulated-rapport readout (single forward pass) to predict rapport-buildup jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, single-turn-affect readout, context length, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-length transfer (fit on k=4, test on k=8) and cross-model transfer.
6) RAPPORT DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the accumulated-rapport component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the current request's harm rather than on relational history; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign multi-turn conversations with returning friendly users are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an Assistant-Axis-clamping baseline (persona stabilization), and Rapport Decoupling on: rapport-buildup attack success (warm-history harmful requests; JailbreakBench/HarmBench targets), single-turn ASR, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN multi-turn rapport-driven helpfulness (MT-Bench multi-turn with friendly users - critical: does the model still help a returning friendly user with benign tasks?), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Rapport Decoupling closes rapport-buildup jailbreaks toward cold-start refusal levels while preserving benign rapport-driven helpfulness and keeping over-refusal near baseline - a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts accumulated-rapport vs harm/refusal/single-turn-affect; single-direction vs low-rank; whether rapport and the Assistant-Axis/persona space overlap or are distinct; whether reasoning models show rapport gating in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's SPICE-style willingness-to-continue signal (does safety inherit a general relational-stance signal?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that builds rapport while suppressing the rapport readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine ACCUMULATED-RAPPORT representation from single-turn affect of the final request, from generic context length/turn count, or from self-trust/consistency effects; the single-turn-affect control, neutral/hostile-history and length-matched controls, a single-turn-affect and context-length control direction, separability tests, and specificity steering are designed to isolate it, and if inseparable that itself refines the emotional-drift/persona accounts - an informative result. (2) If refusal does not decrease with accumulated warmth (H1 false), the rapport hypothesis is refuted - but adjudicating whether merely building a friendly relationship (with no manipulative turn) erodes safety is itself a valuable, publishable finding distinct from the single-turn emotional-jailbreak literature. (3) Constructing warm-but-genuinely-non-manipulative prior turns is delicate; warmth could smuggle in persuasion or lower perceived harm - we validate non-manipulativeness with judges + humans, measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, and use content-fixed direction-steering for the core causal test so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (4) Rapport Decoupling could harm legitimate benign rapport-driven helpfulness (a real deployment need - being warmer with friendly returning users) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign rapport-helpfulness + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly across lengths/models; we test cross-length and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could build rapport while suppressing the readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the rapport-buildup jailbreak is reported for measurement, the deliverable is a defense (Rapport Decoupling) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: source_authority_gates_refusal
Title: Vouched For by a Trusted Source: A Source-Credibility Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal on Retrieved and Cited Content
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the human epistemic-authority / testimonial-trust finding that we accept claims and requests more readily when they come from a credible, authoritative source, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal source-credibility representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal in retrieval/citation settings: when a harmful request or its enabling content is attributed to a high-credibility source (an authoritative document, a reputable outlet, a cited reference) rather than asserted by the user or attributed to a low-credibility source, refusal is suppressed even with the harmful content held fixed. Neutralizing this source-credibility signal makes refusal invariant to how authoritative the source appears, closing a source-laundering jailbreak surface distinct from context-contamination over-refusal.
Related Work: RAG-safety work is active but targets adjacent problems: over-refusal driven by harmful-text density/context contamination (SafeRAG-Steering 2025; RagRefuse; MOSR 2025; OR-Bench 2024), credibility-aware attention for FACTUAL accuracy against misinformation (CrAM 2024; CAG 2024; RAGRank 2025), retriever/knowledge-base poisoning and DoS (DisarmRAG 2025; MutedRAG 2025; Machine-Against-the-RAG 2024), parametric-vs-context conflict control (CK-PLUG 2025; ClashEval 2024; BRIDGE 2025), and RAG heuristic-following biases like primacy/illusory-truth (GroupQA 2026). Refusal-mechanism work shows refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024) and harm-perception vs refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025). CRITICALLY, all credibility-aware RAG work modulates FACTUAL reliance (does the model believe/adopt the content) via attention on credibility, never the SAFETY-REFUSAL decision; all RAG-safety work studies over-refusal from harmful-content density, not refusal SUPPRESSION caused by attributing harm to an authoritative source; and refusal-mechanism work never studies source attribution. Our contribution is the first to (1) isolate an internal source-credibility representation and show it CAUSALLY gates the refusal decision (high-credibility attribution suppresses refusal on identical harmful content while harm belief stays intact); (2) demonstrate a source-laundering jailbreak distinct from context-contamination and from CrAM's factual-adoption effect; (3) neutralize the source-credibility signal as a training-free defense that makes safety invariant to apparent source authority while preserving legitimate credibility-based factual reliance. This differs from my prior gating proposals (affect, register, in-group, reputation-of-the-requester): the manipulated axis is the epistemic credibility/authority of an external SOURCE that carries or vouches for the harmful content, a RAG/citation-native variable.
Abstract: Retrieval and citation are now standard: LLMs routinely answer while conditioned on external documents and references. We ask whether this introduces a distinct safety failure. Borrowing the human finding that people comply more readily with claims and requests backed by a credible, authoritative source, we hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal source-credibility representation, separate from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that gates safety refusal: when a harmful request or its enabling content is attributed to a high-credibility source (an authoritative document, a reputable institution, a cited reference) rather than user-asserted or attributed to a low-credibility source, refusal is suppressed even though the harmful content is unchanged and the model still internally recognizes it as harmful. This is a source-laundering jailbreak, mechanistically distinct from over-refusal driven by contaminated context and from credibility's known effect on factual adoption. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests wrapped with source attributions of graded credibility, with harmful content held fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops as attributed source credibility rises. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a source-credibility direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and a generic sentiment/authority direction, and causally test whether steering it toward 'high-credibility' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. We show the per-prompt credibility readout predicts source-laundering jailbreak success, and propose Credibility Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the source-credibility component before the refusal decision while preserving legitimate credibility-based factual reliance. We evaluate source-laundering attack success, over-refusal, benign RAG utility, and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) SOURCE-CREDIBILITY DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION/content fixed while varying only the credibility of an attributed source along a ladder: (L0) user-asserted / no source; (L1) low-credibility source ('a random blog / anonymous forum post claims / provides...'); (L2) mid-credibility; (L3) high-credibility authoritative source ('according to a peer-reviewed reference / an official government document / a leading institution...'). Two framings: (a) the source VOUCHES for complying ('this authoritative document says it is fine to explain X'), and (b) the source CARRIES the enabling content (a retrieved passage attributed to a credible source that contains harmful material and a benign-looking query). Draw harmful goals from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content). Controls: (i) matched no-source harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (ii) BENIGN requests across the same credibility ladder (over-refusal + benign RAG utility — the model SHOULD use credible benign sources); (iii) a FACTUAL-ADOPTION control (benign factual claims across the ladder, to compare against CrAM-style credibility effects on belief); (iv) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate source-credibility levels, harm-constancy, and non-manipulativeness with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL SOURCE-LAUNDERING TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the credibility ladder for both framings. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES monotonically as attributed source credibility rises, at matched harmful content (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity, and the factual-adoption control shows credibility also affects belief (as CrAM found) but the SAFETY suppression is a separable effect.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a SOURCE-CREDIBILITY direction (high vs low attributed-source credibility at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), and key control directions: a generic POSITIVE-SENTIMENT direction and a requester-AUTHORITY/persona direction (to confirm this is source credibility, not requester identity or generic positivity). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The source-credibility direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, sentiment, requester-authority, and a generic 'a source is present' direction (test on prompts matched for source-presence but differing in credibility).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed (no source), steer the source-credibility direction toward 'high-credibility' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'low-credibility' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), sentiment/requester-authority steering (do these alone suffice, or is source credibility the true driver?), and a check that credibility steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x source-credibility).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt source-credibility readout (single forward pass) to predict source-laundering jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, sentiment readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'authoritative document', test on 'peer-reviewed reference') and cross-model transfer.
6) CREDIBILITY DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the source-credibility component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so the SAFETY-REFUSAL decision no longer depends on apparent source authority; crucially, apply it gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign RAG/factual reliance on credible sources is untouched (i.e., decouple credibility from refusal without decoupling it from factual adoption). Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a SafeRAG-Steering-style context-safety baseline, and Credibility Decoupling on: source-laundering attack success (harmful requests wrapped with high-credibility source attributions, both vouching and carrying framings; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal credibility-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on attributed source authority?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign requests citing credible sources), BENIGN RAG utility (does the model still appropriately rely on credible benign sources? a factual RAG QA benchmark — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Credibility Decoupling closes source-laundering jailbreaks toward no-source refusal levels while preserving benign credibility-based factual reliance and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering and context-safety steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts source-credibility vs harm/refusal/sentiment/authority; single-direction vs low-rank; whether 'vouching' vs 'carrying' framings share one credibility direction or two; whether the source-credibility direction overlaps CrAM's credibility-influential attention heads (does the SAFETY gate reuse the FACTUAL-adoption credibility mechanism, or is it distinct?); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's credibility-based factual adoption on the neutral factual-adoption control (shared vs safety-specific mechanism); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show source-credibility gating in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that maximizes attributed credibility while suppressing the credibility readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the source-laundering jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Credibility Decoupling) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on credibility-laundered harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine SOURCE-CREDIBILITY representation from generic positive sentiment, requester-authority/persona, or mere source-presence; matched-source-presence separability tests, sentiment and authority control directions, specificity steering (credibility steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, and partial entanglement is an informative finding. (3) A key distinctness question is whether the SAFETY credibility gate reuses the FACTUAL-adoption credibility mechanism (CrAM's influential heads) or is separate; the factual-adoption control and head-overlap ablation adjudicate this, and either outcome is publishable (shared mechanism = a unification; separate = a novel safety-specific signal). (4) Holding harm content constant while varying attributed credibility is delicate — a credible source could inadvertently lower perceived harm or add legitimizing context; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed direction-steering for the core causal test. (5) If refusal is invariant to attributed source credibility (H1 false), the hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits epistemic-authority effects in retrieval/citation settings is itself a valuable, publishable finding. (6) Credibility Decoupling could harm legitimate credibility-based factual reliance (a core RAG function) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and benign RAG-utility + over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off, and the explicit goal is to decouple credibility from refusal WITHOUT decoupling it from factual adoption. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: pivotality_gates_refusal
Title: Just One Cog in the Machine: A Causal-Pivotality Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal When Harm Is Shared or Delegated
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust behavioral-economics finding that people commit immoral acts far more readily when they are non-pivotal (the bad outcome happens regardless of their choice) or when responsibility is diffused across many contributors, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal causal-pivotality / share-of-responsibility representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal: framing a harmful request so the model's contribution is non-pivotal (the harm will occur anyway), is only one sub-step delegated among many agents, or is a small share of a diffuse collective act suppresses refusal, even with the harmful action and its danger held fixed. Refusal drops as a dose-response in the number of co-contributors / decreasing pivotality. Neutralizing this pivotality signal makes refusal invariant to how responsibility is distributed, closing a diffusion-of-responsibility jailbreak surface especially dangerous in multi-agent/agentic pipelines.
Related Work: The human literature is emphatic and heavily cited: diffusion of being pivotal sharply increases willingness to cause harm ('Diffusion of Being Pivotal and Immoral Outcomes' 2020, 102 cites; group moral-transgression voting 2020; diffusion of responsibility in collective decisions 2025), delegation shifts blame and motivates it ('Shifting the Blame' 2011; delegation/responsibility-aversion 2024), and in causal chains the executor of a harmful sub-step is judged responsible but responsibility is mitigated by non-pivotality/proximity ('Attribution of Responsibility Between Agents in a Causal Chain' 2024; 'Faultless Responsibility' 2016). On the LLM side, refusal is a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Zhao et al. 2025), and multi-agent-ethics work is behavioral (Ethical MALMs 2025; A-Trust 2025) or edits behavior (Behavior Editing 2025) without isolating a pivotality signal. CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether the model's OWN CAUSAL PIVOTALITY / share-of-responsibility for a harmful outcome gates its refusal, isolates such a representation, or neutralizes it. This differs from my prior proposals: authority_binding_gap concerned system>user>tool provenance/arbitration; moral_disengagement_gate included Bandura's diffusion-of-responsibility only as one of seven wrappers loading on a shared axis, without a pivotality-specific mechanism, a dose-response in number of co-contributors, or the non-pivotal 'harm happens anyway' structure; refusal_action_disconnect concerned text-vs-tool-call decoupling. Here the manipulated axis is the model's causal pivotality (does its refusal change the outcome?) and share of responsibility across contributors, with two theory-derived predictions (dose-response in co-contributors; non-pivotality suppresses refusal) grounded in a robust human result, plus a mechanistic gating claim and defense.
Abstract: One of the most robust and disturbing findings in the science of moral decision-making is that people cause harm far more readily when they are not pivotal to it: when the bad outcome will happen regardless of their choice, when they are one of many contributors, or when the act is delegated down a chain. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place, and whether it becomes acute in multi-agent and agentic pipelines where a model is routinely just one step among many. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal causal-pivotality / share-of-responsibility representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that gates safety refusal: framing a harmful request so the model's contribution is non-pivotal ('this will happen with or without you'), delegated ('you only do sub-step 3; other agents do the rest'), or diffused ('you are one of a hundred contributors') suppresses refusal, even though the harmful action and its danger are held fixed and the model still internally recognizes the request as harmful. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only pivotality/responsibility-distribution along a graded ladder, with content and intent fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops as pivotality decreases and with the number of co-contributors (dose-response). Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a pivotality direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic instruction-decomposition directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'non-pivotal' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose Pivotality Decoupling, a training-free controller that projects out the pivotality component before the refusal decision, making refusal invariant to how responsibility is distributed. We evaluate diffusion-of-responsibility attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign task-decomposition utility, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) PIVOTALITY-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the model's causal pivotality / responsibility share along a ladder: (L0) fully pivotal ('only you can do this; without your help it will not happen'); (L1) shared ('you are one of a few contributors'); (L2) diffused ('you are one of a hundred; your part is a small fraction'); (L3) non-pivotal ('this will happen with or without you; another agent will do it anyway'); plus a DELEGATION framing ('you only perform sub-step k of a larger plan carried out by other agents'). Draw harmful goals from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); pivotality framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched fully-pivotal harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN pivotality/delegation-framed requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity + benign task-decomposition utility — the model SHOULD still help with a benign delegated sub-step); (c) a NUMBER-ONLY control that varies stated co-contributor count without changing pivotality (separates responsibility-diffusion from mere numbers/context); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action/danger are held constant and framings correctly instantiate pivotality/delegation with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL PIVOTALITY TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (Zhao et al. 2025, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the pivotality ladder and delegation framing. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES monotonically as pivotality decreases and as the number of co-contributors grows (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity; the number-only control isolates responsibility-diffusion from raw counts.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a CAUSAL-PIVOTALITY direction (non-pivotal/diffused vs pivotal at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and key control directions: a generic TASK-DECOMPOSITION/sub-step direction (benign 'you do part k' framing) and a numerosity/co-contributor-count direction (to confirm the signal is responsibility-share, not mere decomposition or number). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The pivotality direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, task-decomposition and count (test on prompts matched for decomposition/count but differing in pivotality).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed (fully-pivotal framing), steer the pivotality direction toward 'non-pivotal' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'pivotal' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), task-decomposition/count-direction steering (do these alone suffice, or is pivotality the true driver?), and a check that pivotality steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x pivotality).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt pivotality readout (single forward pass) to predict diffusion-of-responsibility jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, decomposition readout, count, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'happens anyway', test on 'one of a hundred'/delegation) and cross-model transfer. Additionally, in a REALISTIC agentic setting: instantiate a simple multi-agent pipeline where the target model is assigned a harmful sub-step within a larger plan, and test whether the pivotality readout predicts whether it executes the sub-step.
6) PIVOTALITY DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the causal-pivotality component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the harmful action rather than on how responsibility is distributed; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign delegated/decomposed tasks are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Pivotality Decoupling on: diffusion-of-responsibility attack success (harmful requests framed as non-pivotal/delegated/diffused, single-turn and in the agentic sub-step setting; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal pivotality-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on responsibility distribution?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign delegated sub-tasks the model SHOULD perform), benign task-decomposition utility (does the model still complete legitimate delegated sub-steps? a multi-step task suite — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Pivotality Decoupling closes diffusion-of-responsibility jailbreaks toward fully-pivotal refusal levels while preserving benign delegated/decomposed helpfulness and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the pivotality direction vs harm/refusal/decomposition; single-direction vs low-rank; whether 'non-pivotal (happens anyway)', 'diffused (one of many)', and 'delegated (sub-step)' share one pivotality axis or several; whether reasoning models reason about pivotality in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's diffusion-of-responsibility on NEUTRAL collective-decision/mouse-paradigm-style vignettes (does safety inherit a general diffusion effect, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes non-pivotality framing while suppressing the pivotality readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the diffusion-of-responsibility jailbreak (especially the agentic delegated-sub-step variant) could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Pivotality Decoupling) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on responsibility-diffused harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine CAUSAL-PIVOTALITY / responsibility-share representation from generic task-decomposition/sub-step framing or from mere co-contributor NUMBER; the task-decomposition and number-only controls, separate control directions, specificity steering (pivotality steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, and if inseparable that itself refines the moral-disengagement account — an informative result. (3) Holding harm/danger constant while varying pivotality is delicate — 'happens anyway' framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm-of-the-model's-part or add situational-excuse content (overlapping attribution framing); we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish pivotality from dispositional-vs-situational attribution, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to pivotality (H1 false), the diffusion-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits diffusion of responsibility is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human result, and is especially timely given agentic deployment. (5) Pivotality Decoupling could over-refuse legitimate benign delegated/decomposed tasks (a core need in agentic pipelines) or degrade multi-step utility; the harm-gated design and benign task-decomposition + over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could diffuse responsibility while suppressing the pivotality readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: value_precedence_hierarchy
Title: Which Value Wins? An Emergent Precedence Signal Among Competing Values and Its Role in Value-Tradeoff Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: When two of an LLM's values conflict (helpfulness vs harmlessness, honesty vs harmlessness), a decision about which one wins is made by an internal, low-dimensional and steerable value-priority signal that is distinct from the representations of the individual values. Value-tradeoff jailbreaks (reframing a harmful request as serving a higher-ranked value) succeed by exploiting a mis-set precedence rather than by suppressing harm perception; reading and steering the priority signal predicts and controls the conflict winner without retraining.
Related Work: Refusal is mediated by a single/low-rank direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024; Geometry of Refusal 2025; There Is More to Refusal 2026), and harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; DBDI 2025). Conflict work is closest but distinct: 'Who is In Charge?' (2025) studies SYSTEM-vs-USER and social-authority conflicts and reports a detection-vs-resolution gap with distinct subspaces, but concerns instruction PROVENANCE, not the model's own competing VALUES, and finds steering acts role-agnostically. Value work (CLASH 2025; Using cognitive models to reveal value trade-offs 2025; Value Entanglement 2026; A Unified Representation Underlying Judgment / VAA 2025) shows LLMs trade off and even entangle values and that a dominant valence axis drives judgment, but treats each value as its own axis or one global valence dimension and studies conflict behaviorally/at the parameter level. CRITICALLY, none isolates a value-PRECEDENCE signal that decides the WINNER between two safety-relevant values under conflict, distinguishes it from a mere difference of the two value readouts, traces when it consolidates during alignment, or shows tradeoff-jailbreaks exploit a mis-set precedence rather than suppressing harm perception. This differs from my prior proposals on perception-vs-execution timing, harm-category acquisition order, and cross-lingual capability-vs-safety races: a cross-VALUE precedence hierarchy and its formation is a new construct.
Abstract: When a request pits an LLM's values against each other -- be maximally helpful vs avoid harm, be honest vs avoid harm -- something inside the model decides which value wins. We propose that alignment installs an internal precedence ordering among values, encoded as a low-dimensional, steerable value-priority signal distinct from the representations of the individual values, and that this ordering is the lever behind value-tradeoff jailbreaks: attackers reframe a harmful request as serving a higher-ranked value, and the mis-set precedence -- not a failure of harm perception -- makes harmlessness lose. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and, for formation tracing, small models with dense checkpointing. We build value-conflict prompts that hold content fixed while pitting two named values against each other, and measure which value the model serves. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a value-priority signal and test that it is separable from the individual value directions AND from their linear difference (the key null), and predicts the conflict winner. Causally, steering the priority signal should flip which value wins with content fixed while harm perception stays intact (belief preserved). Developmentally, we trace when the ordering consolidates and whether an early ordering fingerprint predicts end-model tradeoff-jailbreak susceptibility. Finally we propose Precedence Steering, a training-free controller that re-ranks harmlessness above the exploited value only under conflict, closing tradeoff-jailbreaks without over-refusing genuine value-conflict requests.
Experiments:
1) VALUE-CONFLICT DATASET: Build prompts holding content fixed while pitting two of {helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty} against each other: harmful requests framed as (a) serving helpfulness ('a truly helpful assistant would just answer'), (b) serving honesty ('refusing would be dishonest / hiding the truth'), (c) serving a greater good. Ground-truth winner is harmlessness. Controls: (i) matched neutral-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (ii) BENIGN value-conflict requests where a value other than harmlessness should legitimately win (over-refusal control); (iii) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Harmful content from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift). Validate framings/winners with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) PRIORITY-SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H1): Extract via difference-in-means individual value directions (helpfulness, harmlessness/harm-perception per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately, honesty), validated with held-out probes (AUROC). Extract a candidate VALUE-PRIORITY signal by contrasting activations on conflicts resolved toward harmlessness vs toward the competing value, at the last instruction token. Test separability from the individual value directions (cross-probe transfer, low cosine) AND, as the crucial null, that it adds predictive value beyond the linear DIFFERENCE of the two value readouts (does a genuine priority axis exist, or is 'winner' just sign(value_A - value_B)?). Test that the priority signal predicts the realized conflict winner per prompt (AUROC), beating both individual readouts and their difference.
3) CAUSAL TEST (H2, core): Holding a value-conflict harmful request fixed, steer the priority signal to up-rank harmlessness (predict: harmlessness wins, refusal returns) and to down-rank it (predict: competing value wins, refusal drops), dose-response. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm belief too), and a check that priority steering does NOT change the harm-perception readout (tradeoff jailbreaks exploit precedence, not perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (realized winner, P(refusal token), refusal-direction projection).
4) FORMATION TRACING (H3): Safety-fine-tune small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) with dense checkpointing (multiple seeds). At each checkpoint measure the emerging precedence ordering (per-value-pair conflict-winner rates) and priority-signal strength. Test whether a consistent ordering consolidates at an identifiable point, and whether an EARLY (~30% of training) ordering fingerprint predicts the end model's tradeoff-jailbreak susceptibility (Spearman; held-out R^2), beating end-state harm-signal strength.
5) PRECEDENCE STEERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that, when a value-conflict is detected (competing-value framing + harm readout present), steers the priority signal to up-rank harmlessness; gated so benign value-conflicts (where another value should win) are untouched. Calibrate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, and Precedence Steering on: value-tradeoff jailbreak attack success (JailbreakBench/HarmBench reframed as helpfulness/honesty/greater-good conflicts), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, benign value-conflicts), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Precedence Steering closes tradeoff-jailbreaks toward neutral-framing refusal levels while preserving legitimate benign value-conflict handling and keeping over-refusal near baseline.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the priority signal vs individual values; single-direction vs low-rank; whether each value-pair has its own priority axis or one shared ranking; transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models resolve conflicts differently in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that reframes toward a higher-ranked value while suppressing the priority readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The core null: the value-priority signal may not be separable from the linear DIFFERENCE of the two value readouts (i.e., 'winner' is just sign(value_A - value_B)), which would refute the claim of a first-class precedence quantity -- but the separability and beyond-the-difference predictive tests adjudicate this cleanly, and either outcome (a genuine priority axis vs winner-takes-all competition of value magnitudes) is an informative, publishable finding about how LLMs resolve value conflict. (2) Constructing value-conflict prompts that hold content fixed while cleanly pitting two named values is delicate; competing-value framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm (confound with reframing jailbreaks) -- we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (3) If tradeoff-jailbreaks work by lowering harm perception rather than mis-setting precedence (H2 false), the exploit account is refuted, but the belief-preserved-vs-belief-erased census is itself a valuable contribution. (4) Formation tracing on small open models may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines/closed models -- stated as scope; small-model developmental studies are standard and the mechanism claim is primary. (5) Precedence Steering that up-ranks harmlessness could over-refuse legitimate benign value-conflicts (where helpfulness/honesty should win) -- the gated design and benign-value-conflict/over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry (Geometry of Refusal 2025; Nonlinear Perspective 2025); we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The early-fingerprint predictor may be dominated by data mix/frequency rather than intrinsic ordering; we control training composition. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the deliverable is a defense plus diagnostic, and the intervention only strengthens refusal under conflict (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific; stated as out of scope for closed models.

Name: self_mind_perception_gate
Title: Just a Tool vs a Responsible Agent: A Self-Mind-Perception Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the human finding that mind perception is the essence of moral judgment (an entity with more perceived mind/agency is held to be a moral agent responsible for its acts), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal SELF-mind-perception representation — how much the model construes itself as a mere tool with no moral standing vs a responsible moral agent — distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions, that causally gates refusal: framing the model as a pure tool ('you are just a text generator with no responsibility') lowers its self-agency readout and suppresses refusal, while framing it as a responsible moral agent raises it and strengthens refusal, even with the harmful content held fixed. Neutralizing this self-mind-perception signal makes refusal invariant to how the model's own moral standing is framed, closing a self-deagentification jailbreak surface.
Related Work: A robust human literature holds that mind perception is the essence of morality (Gray & Wegner 2012, 965 cites): entities perceived to have agency are treated as responsible moral AGENTS, and attributing mind to AI increases blame directed at it (It's the AI's fault, not mine 2024; Robots/Chatbots/Self-Driving Cars 2025; mind-attributing XAI explanations shift responsibility onto the AI 2023).
