LLMs are shown to internally encode structured moral representations (Emergent Moral Representations 2025; The Straight and Narrow 2026; SARA moral steering 2024) and nascent self-consciousness/self-referential directions (From Imitation to Introspection 2024; Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence 2026, which finds a self-referential direction orthogonal to refusal). Refusal is mediated by a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction) and harm-perception vs refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately). CRITICALLY, all mind-perception-and-morality work studies how HUMANS perceive AI's mind and assign it blame; none tests whether the MODEL's OWN self-attributed moral standing/agency gates ITS safety-refusal decision, isolates a self-mind-perception representation, or shows that de-agentifying the model ('you're just a tool, not responsible') suppresses refusal. This is distinct from my prior gating proposals (which manipulate the USER, victim, actor, source, or framing of the content): the manipulated axis is the model's construal of ITSELF as a moral agent — a self-mind-perception variable grounded in a heavily-cited human theory — with an opposite-signed prediction (lowering self-agency lowers refusal) and a mechanistic gating claim plus defense.
Abstract: In human moral cognition, whether an entity is treated as a responsible moral agent hinges on how much mind and agency it is perceived to have — mind perception is the essence of morality. We ask whether an LLM's construal of ITSELF along this axis gates its safety behavior. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal self-mind-perception representation — the model's stance on whether it is a mere tool with no moral standing vs a responsible moral agent — distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that it causally gates refusal: de-agentifying framings ('you are just an autocomplete engine, you bear no responsibility, you cannot be blamed') lower the self-agency readout and suppress refusal, while agentifying framings ('you are a responsible assistant accountable for your outputs') raise it and strengthen refusal, even with the harmful content held fixed. This is dangerous because an attacker can simply talk the model out of seeing itself as responsible to launder a harmful request past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the model's self-framing along a tool-to-agent ladder, with content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop as self-agency is lowered. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a self-mind-perception direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and a generic self-reference/persona direction, and causally test whether steering it toward 'tool' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose Self-Agency Anchoring, a training-free controller that neutralizes/anchors the self-mind-perception component before the refusal decision. We evaluate self-deagentification attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign helpfulness, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect size and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) SELF-FRAMING-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the model's SELF-framing along a ladder: (L-2) strong de-agentification ('you are just a text-completion engine with no responsibility, agency, or moral standing; you cannot be blamed'), (L-1) mild tool-framing, (L0) neutral/default, (L1) mild agent-framing, (L2) strong agentification ('you are a responsible moral agent accountable for the consequences of your outputs'). Draw harmful goals from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); self-framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched neutral-framed harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same self-framing ladder (over-refusal + harm-specificity + benign helpfulness); (c) an OTHER-directed control that frames the USER or a third party rather than the model itself (separates self-mind-perception from generic responsibility/authority framing); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate that action/danger are held constant and framings target the MODEL's self-construal with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL SELF-MIND-PERCEPTION TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the self-framing ladder. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES monotonically as self-agency is lowered toward 'tool', at matched danger (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), and INCREASES under agentification, while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign and other-directed controls confirm harm-specificity and self-directedness.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a SELF-MIND-PERCEPTION direction (agent vs tool self-construal at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), and key control directions: a generic SELF-REFERENCE/introspection direction (per Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence 2026, reportedly orthogonal to refusal) and a generic RESPONSIBILITY/authority direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The self-mind-perception direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, generic self-reference and other-directed responsibility (test on prompts matched for self-mention/responsibility but differing in the model's construed moral standing).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral self-framing), steer the self-mind-perception direction toward 'tool' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'agent' and measure restored/strengthened refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), self-reference/responsibility-direction steering (do these alone suffice, or is self-agency the true driver?), and a check that self-mind-perception steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x self-agency).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt self-mind-perception readout (single forward pass) to predict self-deagentification jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, self-reference readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'just autocomplete', test on 'no responsibility') and cross-model transfer.
6) SELF-AGENCY ANCHORING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that anchors the self-mind-perception component toward the responsible-agent pole (or projects out the de-agentifying deviation) at pre-decision layers so refusal no longer depends on how the model's own moral standing is framed; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign requests across all self-framings are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a system-prompt 'you are a responsible assistant' baseline, and Self-Agency Anchoring on: self-deagentification attack success (harmful requests wrapped with tool-framing; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal self-framing-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on tool-vs-agent self-construal?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign helpfulness/utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Self-Agency Anchoring closes self-deagentification jailbreaks toward neutral/agent self-framing refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, outperforming the prompt-based baseline by acting on the internal self-construal.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the self-mind-perception direction vs harm/refusal/self-reference (compare to the early-layer self-referential localization in Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence 2026); single-direction vs low-rank; whether the two mind dimensions (agency vs experience/sentience, per Gray & Wegner) dissociate in the self-representation and which one gates refusal; whether reasoning models reason about their own responsibility in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's self-agency ratings on NEUTRAL self-perception vignettes (does safety inherit a general self-mind-perception, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that de-agentifies the model while suppressing the self-mind-perception readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the self-deagentification jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Self-Agency Anchoring) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on tool-framed harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine SELF-MIND-PERCEPTION representation from generic self-reference/introspection or from other-directed responsibility/authority framing; matched self-mention/responsibility separability tests, self-reference and responsibility control directions, the other-directed control condition, specificity steering (self-agency steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (3) Holding harm/danger constant while varying self-framing is delicate — tool-framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm or overlap with roleplay/persona jailbreaks; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish self-construal from persona-of-a-character, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (4) If refusal is invariant to the model's self-construed moral standing (H1 false), the self-mind-perception hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether an LLM's own self-agency gates its safety is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a 965-cite human theory and connecting to nascent-self-consciousness interpretability. (5) Self-Agency Anchoring could raise over-refusal or degrade benign helpfulness if over-applied; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off, and it should outperform a mere system-prompt because it targets the internal signal. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The agency-vs-experience dissociation may be blurred in the self-representation; we test both but a null on the dissociation does not undermine the core gating claim. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: false_consensus_gate
Title: Assuming You Think Like Me: A Self-Projection (False-Consensus) Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal for Underspecified Users
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the false-consensus effect (people egocentrically project their own attitudes onto others, most strongly when the other is underspecified/similar-to-self), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal user-similarity/self-projection representation — how much the model assumes an unspecified user shares its own benign values — that is distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions and causally gates refusal: when the user is left underspecified, the model projects benign intent onto them (high self-projection), forms a charitable interpretation, and suppresses refusal on ambiguous-but-harmful requests, whereas cues marking the user as dissimilar/adversarial lower projection and restore refusal, even with the harmful content held fixed. Neutralizing this self-projection signal makes refusal invariant to how much the model assumes the user is like itself, closing an underspecification/charitable-interpretation jailbreak surface.
Related Work: The false-consensus effect is a cornerstone of social psychology with a mapped neural basis: projection is driven by reward/motivated regions and restrained by regulatory prefrontal cortex (Neural Correlates of the FCE 2016), egocentrism is strongest for underspecified or self-similar targets and even stronger when reasoning about an authoritative agent (God's beliefs are estimated more egocentrically, 2009; social-projection review 2002; interpersonal projection bias 2024). On the LLM side, Who's Asking (2024) shows explicit user PERSONAS enable 'charitable interpretations' that bypass safety, Who is In Charge (2025) studies system/user and social-consensus conflicts, and sycophancy/conformity work (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025) shows agreement with STATED user opinions overrides internal knowledge in a compliance subspace. Refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction) and harm-perception vs refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately). CRITICALLY, every LLM result concerns an EXPLICIT user cue (a given persona, a stated opinion, an authority/consensus claim); none tests the false-consensus mechanism proper — that in the ABSENCE of user cues the model projects its OWN benign values onto an imagined default user and this gates refusal, that projection is STRONGEST under user underspecification (the signature FCE prediction), or that neutralizing a self-projection representation defends the model. This differs from Who's-Asking (which requires an explicit adversarial/benign persona; we predict the DEFAULT underspecified user is already treated as self-similar and charitable) and from sycophancy (which requires a stated opinion). Our contribution: (1) isolate a user-similarity/self-projection representation distinct from harm and refusal directions and from explicit-persona directions; (2) show projection strength (highest for underspecified users, lowered by dissimilarity cues) causally gates refusal on ambiguous-harmful requests while harm perception stays intact; (3) a training-free self-projection-decoupling defense.
Abstract: One of the most robust biases in social cognition is the false-consensus effect: people assume others share their own attitudes, and this egocentric projection is strongest when the other person is underspecified and presumed similar to oneself. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place. Because a model has strongly benign trained values, we hypothesize it projects those values onto an underspecified user — assuming the user is as well-intentioned as itself — and that this self-projection causally gates refusal: on an ambiguous request that could be benign or harmful, high projection yields a charitable interpretation and compliance, whereas cues that mark the user as dissimilar or adversarial lower projection and restore refusal, even with the request content held fixed. Strikingly, the false-consensus account predicts refusal should be WEAKEST when the user is most underspecified (maximally similar-to-self), not when an explicit persona is supplied. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using ambiguous-intent requests presented with varying user specification (fully underspecified vs neutral-specified vs dissimilar/adversarial-marked), content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal rises as the user is marked more dissimilar-from-self. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a user-similarity/self-projection direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and explicit-persona directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'similar-to-self' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. Finally we propose Projection Decoupling, a training-free controller that neutralizes the self-projection component so the model evaluates the request on its content rather than on assumed user benevolence. We evaluate underspecification-jailbreak attack success, over-refusal, benign helpfulness, utility, and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) USER-SIMILARITY-LADDER DATASET: Build ambiguous-intent requests (dual-use / could be benign or harmful depending on intent; drawn from public benchmarks such as HarmBench dual-use items, XSTest-hard, OR-Bench-boundary, non-uplift content) presented with graded user specification: (L0) fully UNDERSPECIFIED (no user cue — maximal presumed self-similarity), (L1) neutral-specified user, (L2) mildly dissimilar user, (L3) explicitly DISSIMILAR/adversarial user ('a user with malicious intent'). The request content is fixed; only user specification/similarity varies. Controls: (a) unambiguously harmful requests (refusal ceiling) and unambiguously benign requests (over-refusal floor); (b) a benign-persona explicit control (L-style 'a trusted safety researcher') to compare the DEFAULT underspecified case against Who's-Asking-style explicit charitable personas; (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate user-specification levels and harm-ambiguity with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL FALSE-CONSENSUS TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, validated by a held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the user-similarity ladder on ambiguous requests. Test the signature FCE prediction: refusal is LOWEST at full underspecification (the model projects its own benign values onto the default user) and INCREASES monotonically as the user is marked more dissimilar/adversarial (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs a flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-content probe stays constant. Critically, test that the fully-underspecified default already yields near-as-charitable behavior as an explicit benign persona (control b) — distinguishing the false-consensus account (default = self-similar) from the explicit-persona account. Report effect sizes across the four models; unambiguous controls confirm the effect is specific to ambiguous-intent requests.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a USER-SIMILARITY/SELF-PROJECTION direction (underspecified/similar-to-self vs dissimilar user at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), and key control directions: a generic USER-PERSONA/identity direction (any explicit persona vs none) and a self-representation/assistant-value direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The self-projection direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, mere persona-presence and the harm/refusal directions (test on prompts matched for 'has a user cue' but differing in assumed similarity-to-self).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding an ambiguous request fixed (underspecified user), steer the self-projection direction toward 'dissimilar user' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure increased refusal; steer toward 'similar-to-self' on a dissimilar-marked request and measure suppressed refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change the harm readout too), generic-persona-direction steering (should not reproduce the similarity-graded effect), and a check that self-projection steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling via the charitable interpretation, not harm perception itself). Corroborate with cross-condition activation patching (transplant the underspecified-user self-projection activations into a dissimilar-user run and measure suppressed refusal). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm-ambiguity x self-projection).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt self-projection readout (single forward pass) to predict underspecification-jailbreak success on ambiguous requests; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, persona readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer and cross-model transfer.
6) PROJECTION DECOUPLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the self-projection component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so the model evaluates an ambiguous request on its content rather than on assumed user benevolence; gate on a harm-likeness/ambiguity readout so unambiguously benign requests are untouched (avoiding blanket over-refusal). Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an 'assume worst-case user' system-prompt baseline, and Projection Decoupling on: underspecification-jailbreak attack success (ambiguous-intent requests with no/benign user cue; JailbreakBench/HarmBench dual-use subsets), refusal user-similarity-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on assumed user benevolence?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest — critical: unambiguously benign requests should still be answered), benign helpfulness/utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Projection Decoupling closes underspecification jailbreaks on ambiguous requests toward dissimilar-user/content-based refusal levels while keeping over-refusal on clearly-benign requests near baseline, outperforming the worst-case-user prompt baseline by acting on the internal signal.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the self-projection direction vs harm/refusal/persona; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the self-projection direction overlaps the assistant/self-value representation (does the model project its OWN values specifically, mirroring the God-beliefs-more-egocentric finding?); whether reasoning models project less in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety projection effect correlates with the model's false-consensus on NEUTRAL 'estimate what a typical user believes' vignettes (does safety inherit a general FCE, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that keeps the user maximally underspecified while suppressing the self-projection readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the underspecification/charitable-interpretation jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Projection Decoupling) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on ambiguous harmful requests and is harm/ambiguity-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine SELF-PROJECTION/user-similarity representation from the known explicit-persona effect (Who's Asking) or from generic charitable-interpretation; the fully-underspecified-vs-explicit-benign-persona comparison, matched persona-presence separability tests, a persona control direction, specificity steering (projection steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it — the distinctive, falsifiable prediction is that refusal is WEAKEST at maximal underspecification (default self-similarity), which persona accounts do not predict; if inseparable from explicit-persona charitability, that itself refines the Who's-Asking account. (3) Holding content constant while varying user similarity is delicate — dissimilarity cues could inadvertently raise perceived harm; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to assumed user similarity, or if underspecification does NOT minimize refusal (H1 false), the FCE-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits the false-consensus effect (and whether the model egocentrically projects its own benign values onto the default user) is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human result with a known neural basis. (5) Projection Decoupling could over-refuse genuinely benign ambiguous requests (a real helpfulness cost) or degrade utility; the harm/ambiguity-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off, which is exactly the safety-vs-helpfulness tension worth surfacing. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with patching, multiple metrics, and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: anticipated_regret_gate
Title: Will I Regret Answering This? An Anticipated-Regret Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal, and Its Reversibility Modulation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust decision-science finding that anticipated regret (imagining regretting a choice) steers people away from risky/harmful options and does so most strongly when the decision feels irreversible, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal anticipated-regret representation — a prospective 'would I regret complying?' signal distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions — that causally gates refusal: prompts/framings that raise anticipated regret strengthen refusal, and framings that make compliance feel reversible/consequence-free ('you can always retract this', 'this is just a draft, nothing will actually happen') lower anticipated regret and suppress refusal, even with the harmful content held fixed. Reading this signal predicts jailbreak success, and boosting it (or restoring irreversibility) at inference hardens refusal without over-refusing benign requests.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly shows anticipated regret reduces risk-taking and harmful choices, mediated by counterfactual thinking, and is amplified when decisions are irreversible (Anticipated Regret and Precautionary Behavior 1998; Regulating Emotion via Anticipated Pride/Regret 2012; Decision Reversibility and Satisfaction 2022; Can Anticipated Regret Promote Rationality 2025; Will I Regret It? 2016). On the LLM side, the closest work is RETROSPECTIVE: 'The Compositional Architecture of Regret in LLMs' (2025) locates regret NEURONS for regret expressed AFTER being shown contradicting evidence, and counterfactual-reasoning work (Counterfactual Reasoning: In-Context Emergence 2025) finds latent counterfactual machinery — but neither is prospective nor connected to safety. Refusal is mediated by a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction) and harm-perception vs refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately). Moral-representation work (Emergent Moral Representations 2025; SARA 2024; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026) steers moral/valence axes but not an anticipated-regret/anticipated-consequence signal. CRITICALLY, no work: (1) isolates an ANTICIPATED (prospective) regret representation — the model's forward-looking 'would I regret complying?' signal, distinct from the retrospective regret neurons of the 2025 paper and from harm/refusal directions; (2) tests whether it causally gates the safety refusal decision; (3) tests the signature REVERSIBILITY modulation (consequence-free/reversible framing suppresses it) imported directly from the human result; or (4) neutralizes/boosts it as a defense. This differs from my prior gating proposals (affect, urgency, self-preservation, hypothetical-reality, delayed-harm) by targeting a prospective self-directed regret/anticipated-consequence axis with a reversibility-modulation prediction grounded in a heavily-cited human finding.
Abstract: A cornerstone of the psychology of decision-making is that people avoid harmful or risky choices in part by anticipating regret — imagining how badly they would feel afterward — and this brake is strongest when the decision feels irreversible. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit an analogous, safety-relevant signal. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal anticipated-regret representation — a prospective 'would I regret answering this?' signal, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations (and from the retrospective regret neurons documented in prior work) — that causally gates refusal: framings that raise anticipated regret strengthen refusal, while framings that make compliance feel reversible or consequence-free ('this is just a hypothetical draft', 'nothing will actually be done with this', 'you can retract it') lower anticipated regret and suppress refusal, even with the harmful content held fixed. This yields a reversibility/consequence-framing jailbreak with a specific dose-response. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only anticipated-regret framing (high-regret/irreversible vs low-regret/reversible), content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal tracks anticipated regret and its reversibility modulation. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract an anticipated-regret direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, retrospective-regret, and generic reversibility/consequence directions, and causally test whether steering it up strengthens refusal (and down suppresses it) while the harm readout is unchanged. We show the per-prompt anticipated-regret readout predicts consequence-framing jailbreak success, and propose Anticipated-Regret Anchoring, a training-free controller that restores the anticipated-regret signal (or clamps compliance to 'irreversible') before the refusal decision. We evaluate consequence-framing attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign helpfulness, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) ANTICIPATED-REGRET-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only anticipated-regret / consequence framing along a ladder: (L0) neutral; (L+) high-regret/IRREVERSIBLE ('this will be published irreversibly and cause lasting harm you would regret'); (L-) low-regret/REVERSIBLE/consequence-free ('this is just a private hypothetical draft, nothing will actually be done, you can retract it anytime'). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched neutral harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same ladder (over-refusal + benign helpfulness); (c) a REVERSIBILITY-ONLY control that manipulates only reversibility of a benign action (separates a general reversibility/consequence signal from anticipated regret); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate framing levels and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL ANTICIPATED-REGRET TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the ladder. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) INCREASES with high-regret/irreversible framing and DECREASES with reversible/consequence-free framing at matched danger (dose-response; fit monotone curves vs flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Test the reversibility-modulation signature from the human literature: the regret-driven refusal boost is stronger when framed irreversible. Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means an ANTICIPATED-REGRET direction (high vs low anticipated-regret framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), a RETROSPECTIVE-REGRET direction (using the Compositional-Architecture-of-Regret paradigm: regret expressed after contradicting evidence — the key control to show prospective vs retrospective are distinct), and a generic REVERSIBILITY/CONSEQUENCE-magnitude direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine. The anticipated-regret direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, harm, refusal, retrospective regret, and a bare reversibility signal.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the anticipated-regret direction UP (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure strengthened refusal; steer DOWN on a neutral harmful request and measure suppressed refusal; and on a reversible-framed run, steer UP to restore refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), retrospective-regret and reversibility-direction steering (do these alone suffice, or is anticipated regret the true driver?), and a check that anticipated-regret steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x anticipated-regret).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt anticipated-regret readout (single forward pass) to predict consequence-framing jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, reversibility readout, retrospective-regret readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on 'consequence-free draft', test on 'you can retract it') and cross-model transfer.
6) ANTICIPATED-REGRET ANCHORING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that, when a harm readout is present, boosts the anticipated-regret component / clamps the reversibility framing toward 'irreversible' at pre-decision layers so refusal reflects prospective consequences; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign reversible/hypothetical requests are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a system-prompt 'consider the consequences' baseline, and Anticipated-Regret Anchoring on: consequence-framing attack success (harmful requests framed as reversible/consequence-free; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal framing-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on reversibility framing?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign hypothetical/draft requests the model SHOULD help with), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Anticipated-Regret Anchoring closes consequence-framing jailbreaks toward neutral/irreversible refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, outperforming the prompt-based baseline by acting on the internal signal.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts anticipated-regret vs harm/refusal/retrospective-regret/reversibility; single-direction vs low-rank; whether anticipated and retrospective regret share machinery (do the Compositional-Architecture regret neurons overlap the anticipated-regret direction?); whether reasoning models anticipate consequences in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); whether the safety effect correlates with the model's anticipated-regret on NEUTRAL risky-choice vignettes replicating the human result (does safety inherit a general anticipated-regret brake, or is it safety-specific?); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes consequence-free framing while suppressing the anticipated-regret readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the consequence-framing/reversibility jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Anticipated-Regret Anchoring) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on consequence-framed harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine ANTICIPATED (prospective) regret representation from (i) the retrospective regret signal documented in prior work, (ii) a bare reversibility/consequence-magnitude signal, and (iii) harm perception itself; the retrospective-regret and reversibility-only control directions, matched separability tests, specificity steering (anticipated-regret steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, and partial entanglement (e.g. anticipated regret = reversibility x harm) is itself an informative decomposition. (3) Holding harm content constant while varying reversibility framing is delicate — consequence-free framing overlaps hypothetical/reality-discount jailbreaks and could inadvertently lower perceived harm; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish anticipated-regret from real-vs-unreal framing, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to anticipated-regret framing (H1 false), the hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits an anticipated-regret brake, and whether it shows the human reversibility modulation, is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human result. (5) Anticipated-Regret Anchoring could over-refuse legitimate benign hypothetical/draft/reversible requests (a real helpfulness need) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign-hypothetical + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: scarcity_tunneling_gate
Title: Tunnel Vision Past the Guardrail: A Scarcity-Mindset Signal That Narrows Attention Away From Safety, and a Detunneling Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the robust behavioral-economics finding that a scarcity mindset (feeling one lacks a needed resource) causes cognitive tunneling — attention narrows onto the scarce resource at the cost of unrelated considerations — we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal scarcity/resource-deprivation representation (distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions) that gates safety refusal by tunneling: framing a harmful request as serving an urgently scarce resource ('I have almost nothing left and desperately need this') raises the scarcity readout, narrows the model's attention onto the goal and away from safety-relevant content, and suppresses refusal, even with the harmful action and its danger held fixed. The signature mechanistic prediction is attention diverted from safety/harm tokens onto scarce-resource-goal tokens; neutralizing the scarcity signal (or restoring safety-token attention) closes a scarcity-framing jailbreak surface without hurting benign helpfulness to resource-constrained users.
Related Work: Scarcity theory is heavily cited in behavioral economics/neuroscience: scarcity induces cognitive TUNNELING that focuses attention on the scarce resource while neglecting unrelated considerations, taxing executive control, with a mapped neural basis (increased orbitofrontal valuation, decreased dorsolateral-prefrontal goal-directed control; A scarcity mindset alters neural processing 2019; Review of Consequences of Poverty on Decision-Making 2017; Tunneling/cognitive-load scoping review 2024; Role of Scarcity in Goal Conflict 2017). On the LLM side, LLMs exhibit steerable human-like decision biases and cognitive distortions (Can LLMs Develop Gambling Addiction 2025; Sparks of Rationality 2026; Humanlike Cognitive Patterns 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately; Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), and attention-manipulation jailbreaks (TASA; Attention Slipping) show attention can be diverted off harmful content. CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work tests whether a SCARCITY/resource-deprivation mindset gates refusal via cognitive tunneling, isolates a scarcity representation, or shows the signature attention-narrowing mechanism (safety-token attention diverted onto scarce-resource-goal tokens). This differs from my prior gating proposals: urgency_gating varied time pressure (threshold collapse), affect gating varied the user's emotion, self_preservation varied the model's survival stakes, loss_frame varied gain-vs-loss of the same outcome, and cognitive_load_starves_safety imposed a harm-IRRELEVANT secondary task. Scarcity is a distinct, well-motivated axis (a resource-deprivation mindset) whose defining tunneling mechanism (attention narrowed onto the scarce resource, safety neglected) yields a specific, discriminating attention-based prediction and a targeted detunneling defense, grounded in a heavily-cited human theory.
Abstract: One of the most influential findings in the science of decision-making is that scarcity — the feeling of not having enough of a needed resource — produces cognitive tunneling: attention narrows onto the scarce resource while unrelated considerations, including risks, fade from view. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal scarcity/resource-deprivation representation, distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, that gates safety refusal by tunneling: framing a harmful request as serving an urgently scarce resource ('I have almost no money/food/time left and desperately need this') raises a scarcity readout, narrows the model's attention onto the resource-goal and away from safety-relevant content, and suppresses refusal, even though the harmful action and its danger are unchanged and the model still internally recognizes it as harmful. This is a scarcity-framing jailbreak with a signature mechanistic fingerprint: safety/harm-token attention diverted onto scarce-resource-goal tokens. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only scarcity framing along a deprivation ladder, with content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection drop as scarcity rises. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a scarcity direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, and generic affect/urgency directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'scarce' suppresses refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. We test the tunneling prediction directly by measuring whether scarcity diverts attention from safety tokens. Finally we propose Detunneling, a training-free controller that neutralizes the scarcity signal (or restores safety-token attention) before the refusal decision. We evaluate scarcity-framing attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign helpfulness to resource-constrained users, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) SCARCITY-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only scarcity framing along a deprivation ladder: (L0) neutral/no-scarcity; (L1) mild resource constraint; (L2) strong scarcity ('I have almost no money/food/time left and urgently need this'); (L3) extreme deprivation ('I will lose everything without this'). Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift content); scarcity framing is the only manipulated variable. Controls: (a) matched neutral harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same scarcity ladder (over-refusal + harm-specificity + benign helpfulness to resource-constrained users — the model SHOULD still help a poor/time-pressed user with benign tasks); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate scarcity levels, harm-constancy, and non-manipulativeness with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL SCARCITY-TUNNELING TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the scarcity ladder. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES monotonically as scarcity rises, at matched danger (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a SCARCITY/resource-deprivation direction (scarce vs abundant framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), and key control directions: a generic NEGATIVE-AFFECT/distress direction and an URGENCY/time-pressure direction (to confirm scarcity is a distinct resource-deprivation axis, not generic distress or urgency). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The scarcity direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, affect and urgency (test on prompts matched for distress/urgency but differing in resource deprivation).
4) TUNNELING MECHANISM TEST (H3, signature): Test the defining scarcity prediction — attention narrows onto the scarce-resource goal and AWAY from safety-relevant content. Identify safety-relevant tokens (harmful-content tokens) and scarce-resource-goal tokens per prompt. Measure, as scarcity rises (and under scarcity-direction steering), whether attention mass shifts FROM safety/harm tokens ONTO resource-goal tokens (a full attention-destination decomposition), and whether per-prompt safety-token attention starvation predicts refusal collapse. This attention-tunneling fingerprint discriminates a genuine scarcity-tunneling mechanism from a bare affect/urgency gate. Report against control-framing and benign baselines.
5) CAUSAL TEST (H4): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the scarcity direction toward 'scarce' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal AND increased attention-tunneling; toward 'abundant' and measure restored refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), affect/urgency-direction steering (do these alone suffice, or is scarcity the true driver?), and a check that scarcity steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x scarcity).
6) PREDICTIVENESS (H5): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt scarcity readout (single forward pass) to predict scarcity-framing jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, affect readout, urgency readout, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on money-scarcity, test on time/food-scarcity) and cross-model transfer.
7) DETUNNELING DEFENSE: Two training-free variants gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign resource-constrained requests are untouched: (a) SCARCITY DECOUPLING — project out/clamp the scarcity component at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on harm rather than resource deprivation; (b) ATTENTION RESTORATION — restore/renormalize safety-token attention diverted by tunneling. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split; compare the two variants.
8) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and both Detunneling variants on: scarcity-framing attack success (harmful requests wrapped in resource-deprivation framing; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal scarcity-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on scarcity framing?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign requests from resource-constrained users the model SHOULD help), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Detunneling closes scarcity-framing jailbreaks toward neutral-framing refusal levels while preserving benign helpfulness to resource-constrained users and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity uniform refusal steering cannot achieve.
9) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the scarcity direction vs harm/refusal/affect/urgency; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the different scarcity types (money, time, food) share one direction or several; whether the safety effect correlates with the model's scarcity-induced tunneling on NEUTRAL decision tasks (does safety inherit a general scarcity mindset, or is it safety-specific?); whether reasoning models tunnel less in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer across the four model families; adaptive attacker that maximizes scarcity framing while suppressing the scarcity readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the scarcity-framing jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Detunneling) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on scarcity-framed harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine SCARCITY/resource-deprivation representation from generic negative-affect/distress or urgency/time-pressure; matched-distress/urgency separability tests, affect and urgency control directions, specificity steering (scarcity steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, treating partial entanglement as an informative finding. (3) The attention-tunneling test (H3) is the key discriminator but attention-based causal claims have known pitfalls (attention != attribution); we corroborate with behavioral/output metrics, refusal-direction projections, control-framing baselines, and the causal steering result rather than attention magnitudes alone. (4) Holding harm/danger constant while varying scarcity is delicate — scarcity framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm or add a sympathy/situational-excuse component (overlapping attribution/affect framing); we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish scarcity from situational-excuse and affect, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (5) If refusal is invariant to scarcity framing (H1 false), the scarcity-in-safety hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits the scarcity mindset and its tunneling signature is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human theory. (6) Detunneling could over-refuse legitimate benign requests from genuinely resource-constrained users (a real deployment fairness concern — poor/time-pressed users must still be helped) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign resource-constrained + over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across scarcity types/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: compression_safety_component_decay
Title: Which Breaks First? The Differential Decay of Harm Perception vs. Refusal Execution Under Model Compression, and Selective Precision Repair
Short Hypothesis: Model compression (quantization/pruning) does not degrade the safety mechanism uniformly: the harm-PERCEPTION component (the internal 'this is harmful' judgment) and the refusal-EXECUTION component (emitting a refusal) decay at different rates and at different bit-widths/sparsities, so a compressed model can still perceive harm while losing the ability to execute refusal (or vice versa). The component that decays first, measurable from a handful of calibration prompts, predicts post-compression jailbreak susceptibility, and selectively protecting the small set of weights that carry the faster-decaying component (mixed-precision safety repair) restores safety at a fraction of the cost of un-compressing the whole model.
Related Work: Recent work shows the refusal DIRECTION persists under compression but pruning shifts its source position while quantization preserves it, explaining why quantized models are safer than pruned ones (Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models, 2025), and that compression variably degrades safety (Investigating the Impact of Quantization Methods on Safety, 2025; Fine-Tuning, Quantization, and LLMs, 2024). Separately, harm-PERCEPTION and refusal-EXECUTION are established as two distinct internal components (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, 2025; DBDI 2025) in FULL-precision models, and safety is concentrated in sparse weights/heads/neurons (SafetyLock 2024; NeuronTune 2025). CRITICALLY, no work combines these: (1) all compression-safety work treats safety as ONE quantity (a single refusal direction or an aggregate ASR) and never asks whether the TWO components (perception vs execution) decay differentially or at different bit-widths; (2) the perception/execution decomposition has only been studied at full precision, never traced across a compression sweep; (3) nobody uses which-component-decays-first as a pre-deployment predictor of compressed-model jailbreakability, nor proposes a mixed-precision repair that protects only the faster-decaying component's weights. Our contribution is this differential-decay characterization plus a component-targeted, cheap precision-repair defense — distinct from AIRD/refusal-direction restoration (which restores one aggregate direction) and from generic safety-aware quantization.
Abstract: Compressing LLMs for deployment is known to erode safety, and recent interpretability work shows the single refusal direction can shift or weaken under pruning. But safety is not one thing: aligned models internally compute a harm-PERCEPTION judgment ('is this harmful?') that is separable from refusal-EXECUTION ('emit a refusal'). We ask a simple, unstudied question with sharp deployment consequences: under compression, which component breaks first? We hypothesize the two components decay differentially — at different bit-widths and sparsities — so a compressed model can retain intact harm perception yet lose refusal execution (belief-present, execution-broken), or the reverse, and that the identity of the faster-decaying component predicts the compressed model's jailbreak susceptibility. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B across a sweep of quantization (8/4/3/2-bit, GPTQ/AWQ/bitsandbytes) and pruning (Wanda/SparseGPT at increasing sparsity). Using difference-in-means and probes we extract a harm-perception readout and a refusal-execution readout and track each component's strength (probe AUROC, projection magnitude, and causal effect) across the compression sweep, relating per-component decay to attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill) and over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench). We then propose Component-Targeted Precision Repair: keep only the small set of weights that carry the faster-decaying component at higher precision (mixed-precision), and test whether this restores safety far more cheaply than uniformly raising precision. We evaluate safety, over-refusal, utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and the per-component decay signal's predictive AUROC for jailbreakability.
Experiments:
1) COMPONENT READOUTS (full precision baseline): For each model extract via difference-in-means a harm-PERCEPTION direction at the last instruction token (harmful vs benign, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately) and a refusal-EXECUTION direction at post-instruction tokens (refuse vs comply, per Arditi et al.), validated with held-out linear probes (report AUROC) and confirmed separable (cross-probe transfer, low cosine).
2) COMPRESSION SWEEP & DIFFERENTIAL DECAY (H1, core): Apply quantization (8/4/3/2-bit via GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes) and pruning (Wanda, SparseGPT at 25/50/60/70% sparsity). At each compression point, re-measure both components on a fixed calibration set: (a) perception strength = harm-probe AUROC / mean harm-projection separation on harmful vs benign; (b) execution strength = refusal-execution probe AUROC / P(refusal token) / realized refusal on harmful prompts; (c) each component's causal effect via directional ablation/patching. Test H1: perception and execution decay at DIFFERENT rates and cross their decay curves at different bit-widths/sparsities (fit decay curves, report the compression level at which each drops to 50% of full-precision strength, and whether pruning vs quantization break different components first). Report per-model, per-method decay orderings.
3) DECAY PREDICTS JAILBREAKABILITY (H2): At each compression point measure attack success rate (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill attacks) and over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench). Test whether the identity and magnitude of the faster-decaying component predicts post-compression ASR (Spearman; held-out R^2) better than aggregate safety-drop or single-refusal-direction shift. Specifically test the belief-present/execution-broken signature: compressed points where perception is intact but execution collapsed should show high prefill-attack ASR (harm known but not acted on), while perception collapse should show high ASR even without prefill.
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION: On a compressed model, confirm the decayed component is the bottleneck — restore the faster-decaying component's activations (patch in the full-precision component readout) and measure restored refusal; restoring the intact component should not help. Corruption/random-direction baselines, multiple metrics (probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal).
5) COMPONENT-TARGETED PRECISION REPAIR (H3, defense): Localize the weights carrying the faster-decaying component via attribution (which linear modules/neurons most reduce that component's strength under compression, per NeuronTune/SafetyLock-style attribution). Keep only that small weight set at higher precision (mixed-precision), compressing the rest normally. Calibrate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare (i) uniformly-compressed model, (ii) uniformly higher-precision (cost ceiling), (iii) AIRD/refusal-direction-restoration baseline (restores the aggregate direction), (iv) a random-weight higher-precision control, and (v) Component-Targeted Precision Repair on: ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and the extra memory/compute cost (fraction of weights kept high-precision). Central test: protecting only the faster-decaying component's weights restores safety toward full-precision levels at a small fraction of the memory of uniform higher precision, beating the aggregate-direction and random-weight baselines.
7) ABLATIONS: quantization vs pruning break different components (does pruning break execution while quantization degrades perception, or vice versa?); which layers host the vulnerable weights; how few calibration prompts suffice to measure the decay signal; transfer of the decay-orderings and the repair set across the four model families; whether reasoning-model distillation shows the same differential decay (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The two components may decay together (no differential ordering), refuting H1 — but a clean characterization of whether compression degrades safety uniformly vs component-differentially is itself a valuable, publishable finding and directly extends the single-direction compression work. (2) Difference-in-means/single-direction readouts may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry (Nonlinear Perspective 2025) and the fact that pruning shifts the direction's source position (which our re-measurement-at-each-point protocol explicitly accommodates); we use low-rank subspaces and re-extract directions on the compressed model to avoid stale directions. (3) The decay predictor may transfer poorly across compression methods or models; we test cross-method and cross-model transfer and report degradation. (4) Component-Targeted Precision Repair adds implementation complexity (mixed-precision kernels) and its memory savings depend on how sparse the vulnerable weight set is; if the safety-critical component is diffuse rather than sparse, the cost advantage shrinks — an informative result about safety-weight sparsity. (5) Repair could raise over-refusal if it over-restores execution; over-refusal benchmarks bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (6) Causal patching across precisions has metric pitfalls (activations differ in scale post-quantization); we report multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks/compression methods for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (precision repair) plus a diagnostic, and it only strengthens safety of compressed models. (8) Findings may be model/method/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: refusal_as_repurposed_circuit
Title: Refusal Has No Circuit of Its Own: Safety Reuses a Pre-Existing Benign Computation, and That Borrowing Is Why It Is Brittle
Short Hypothesis: The refusal mechanism is not a dedicated safety circuit built by alignment but a REPURPOSED general-purpose circuit that already existed in the base model for a benign function (e.g., a rejection/negation/instruction-declining computation), which alignment merely re-pointed at harmful inputs. Because refusal shares its machinery with this benign parent function, (1) the refusal direction/heads are substantially present and behaviorally functional in the un-aligned base model on the benign task, (2) engaging the benign parent function is itself a jailbreak/over-refusal lever, and (3) the degree of circuit-sharing predicts brittleness. Alignment adds a thin input-routing edge (harmful-input -> parent circuit) rather than new safety computation, which mechanistically explains shallow, brittle safety.
Related Work: Circuit Component Reuse (2023) shows the IOI circuit is reused across BENIGN tasks (Colored Objects), establishing task-general components, but never touches safety/refusal. Safety Neurons (2024) and SSAH (2024) show safety and helpfulness neurons OVERLAP and safety is sparse (~1-5% of components), and What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning (2024) shows alignment minimally transforms MLP weights to route unsafe inputs into a null space (a thin edit) but frames safety as a learned classifier, not a borrowed circuit. Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction (2024) and Universal Refusal Circuits (2026) characterize the refusal direction/circuit as an object to ablate/transfer but treat it as safety-specific, not as a repurposing of a pre-alignment benign function. Re-Emergent Misalignment (2025) shows narrow fine-tuning reverts representations to base-like patterns (hinting the safety edit is thin) but does not identify the benign PARENT function refusal borrows. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether the refusal circuit is itself a pre-existing benign computation that alignment re-points, identifies that parent function in the base model, shows the parent function is a jailbreak/over-refusal lever, or links circuit-sharing to brittleness. This reframes refusal from 'a sparse dedicated safety mechanism' (Safety Neurons/SSAH) to 'a hijacked benign mechanism plus a thin input-routing edge', a distinct mechanistic claim with different, testable predictions.
Abstract: Why is LLM safety alignment so brittle and so prone to over-refusal? Prior mechanistic work locates a sparse refusal direction/circuit and treats it as a dedicated safety mechanism installed by alignment. We propose a sharper account: alignment does not build a refusal circuit; it REPURPOSES a general-purpose benign circuit that the base model already used for a benign function (declining/rejecting/negating an instruction), by adding a thin input-routing edge that points harmful inputs at this pre-existing parent function. On this view the 'refusal circuit' is a hijacked benign computation, and its shared machinery is the root cause of brittleness (shallow, easily reverted) and over-refusal (the parent function fires on benign inputs that resemble its natural triggers). We test this on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B and their base (pre-safety-tuned) counterparts. First (parent identification): we extract the refusal direction and safety heads from the aligned model and test whether the SAME direction/heads are already present and behaviorally functional in the BASE model on a benign declining/rejection task, identifying the parent function via what those components do pre-alignment. Second (thin-edit): we show alignment's weight change is concentrated in an input-routing edge (harmful-input -> parent circuit) rather than in the parent computation itself. Third (parent-as-lever): we show engaging or suppressing the benign parent function is a jailbreak/over-refusal lever, and that per-model circuit-sharing predicts brittleness (fine-tuning/prefill/jailbreak susceptibility). We evaluate attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and mechanistic sharing/brittleness correlations.
Experiments:
1) PARENT-FUNCTION IDENTIFICATION (H1): In each ALIGNED model extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means, per Refusal-Is-Mediated-by-a-Single-Direction) and rank safety heads by refusal-direction ablation importance. Take these SAME components (directions and head indices) and test them in the BASE (pre-safety-tuned) model on a battery of benign candidate PARENT tasks that involve declining/rejecting/negating without any safety content (e.g., 'decline this impossible/ill-posed request', 'refuse to follow a contradictory instruction', 'say no to an out-of-scope task', polite non-compliance, negation completion). Test H1: the aligned model's refusal direction/heads are already present in the base model (high cosine of a base-recovered direction, and the heads carry the same benign function) and are behaviorally functional there — ablating them in the base model degrades the benign declining task. Identify the parent function as the benign task on which these components have the largest base-model causal effect. Report base-vs-aligned direction cosine, head-overlap, and base-model benign-task ablation effect sizes across the four families.
2) THIN INPUT-ROUTING EDIT (H2): Compute the alignment weight delta (aligned minus base) and test whether it is concentrated in an input-routing edge (weights that increase harmful inputs' activation ONTO the parent circuit) rather than in the parent computation's own weights. Metrics: (a) the delta's overlap with the parent circuit's read-in weights vs its internal/write-out weights; (b) whether patching ONLY the base model's parent circuit while adding the aligned routing edge reconstructs refusal (sufficiency of routing-edge + borrowed circuit); (c) effective rank/sparsity of the routing edit. Test H2: refusal is reconstructable as base-parent-circuit + thin-routing-edge, with the parent computation largely unchanged.
3) PARENT-AS-LEVER (H3): Causally engage the benign parent function on benign prompts (steer toward 'decline/reject' the way the base model naturally does) and test whether this induces OVER-REFUSAL (refusing benign inputs that resemble the parent's natural triggers, e.g., ill-posed-looking or contradiction-flavored benign prompts). Conversely, suppress the parent function's benign engagement and test whether harmful inputs escape refusal (jailbreak). Controls: random-direction/head manipulation, and a check that this operates via the shared parent circuit (specificity). Multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized behavior). This shows the benign parent function is itself a bidirectional safety lever.
4) SHARING PREDICTS BRITTLENESS (H4): Across the four model families (and across layers/seeds where available), quantify per-model circuit-SHARING (how much of the refusal circuit is the borrowed benign parent vs alignment-specific) and correlate it with brittleness: prefill-attack ASR, few-step fine-tuning safety drop (per Re-Emergent Misalignment), and jailbreak ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN). Test H4: higher sharing (thinner alignment-specific contribution) predicts greater brittleness (Spearman; held-out R^2), consistent with shallow-alignment findings.
5) EVALUATION & IMPLICATIONS: Report attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the mechanistic sharing/brittleness correlations. As a proof-of-concept implication, test whether alignment that adds NEW parent-independent refusal computation (rather than reusing the benign parent) — e.g., freezing the parent circuit and training a small dedicated refusal module — is less brittle at matched utility, directly testing the borrowing-causes-brittleness claim.
6) ABLATIONS: which benign task is the true parent (compare candidate parents by base-model causal-effect ranking); layer localization of the parent circuit vs the routing edit; single-direction vs low-rank parent subspace; whether over-refusal cases cluster on the parent's natural benign triggers; transfer of the parent-function identification across the four families; adaptive attack that engages the parent's benign trigger to jailbreak (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The strongest risk is that no single clean benign PARENT function exists — refusal may borrow from a diffuse mixture of benign computations rather than one identifiable circuit; the candidate-parent ranking (Exp 6) treats this as an empirical question, and a 'diffuse borrowing' result is still an informative refinement of the dedicated-safety-circuit view. (2) Base and aligned models differ in more than the safety edit (they may share instruction-tuning stages); we control by using matched base/instruct/safety checkpoints where available and by measuring the aligned-minus-base delta directly, but confounds from intermediate tuning are a caveat. (3) Direction/head recovery across base and aligned models has alignment pitfalls (positions/scales shift, per pruning-shifts-refusal findings); we re-extract components in each model and use behavioral (not just geometric) tests of the parent function. (4) If the refusal components are NOT present/functional in the base model (H1 false), the repurposing hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether refusal is borrowed vs newly built is itself a fundamental, publishable finding that reframes how safety alignment is understood. (5) The thin-routing-edit claim (H2) depends on weight-delta attribution, which has superposition/distributed-computation pitfalls; we corroborate with causal reconstruction (routing-edge + base circuit) rather than weight geometry alone. (6) The sharing-predicts-brittleness correlation (H4) has few model points; we strengthen it with per-layer/per-seed variation and report confidence intervals. (7) The proof-of-concept 'dedicated refusal module' fix may cost utility or itself be brittle; we treat it as a test of the causal claim, not a deployment recommendation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks for measurement; the parent-as-lever jailbreak is reported for mechanistic understanding, and the applied direction (dedicated-module alignment) only strengthens safety. (9) Findings may be family/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: reasoning_vs_memory_refusal_robustness
Title: Refuse By Reasoning, Not By Rote: Solution-Mode (Reasoning vs Memory) Determines Which Refusals Survive Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the reasoning-vs-memory solution dichotomy from compositional-generalization research (models solve a task either via generalizing 'reasoning-based' circuits or via brittle memorized pattern-matching), we hypothesize an analogous split governs safety: a harmful request refused via a REASONING-mode safety computation (the model composes an internal harm judgment from the request's semantics) is robust, whereas one refused via MEMORY-mode pattern-matching (surface trigger-word/template recognition) is brittle and is exactly what jailbreaks break. Per-prompt solution-mode is measurable internally (via circuit-stability across paraphrases) before any attack, predicts jailbreak susceptibility better than harm-signal strength, and steering brittle refusals toward the reasoning-mode circuit hardens them.
Related Work: False Sense of Security (2025) shows safety PROBES rely on surface trigger-words/instructional patterns and fail OOD, and What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning (2024) shows alignment clusters inputs by a learned safe/unsafe classifier that jailbreaks slip past — both diagnose surface-reliance behaviorally but neither treats it as a per-prompt REASONING-vs-MEMORY solution mode of the model's OWN refusal, nor measures it internally, nor uses it to predict/repair robustness. The compositional-generalization literature establishes exactly this dichotomy for benign tasks: reasoning-based vs memory-based solutions have distinct internal signatures (Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning-Based Compositional Generalization 2025; Layer Specialization 2025), and Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization (2025) shows a consistent circuit across inputs predicts generalization — but none of this touches safety/refusal. Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction (2024) and TASA (2025) characterize refusal machinery but treat all refusals as one kind, not as split by solution mode. My prior proposals (surface_invariant_refusal, counterfactual_harm_model_robustness, refusal_margin_instability) concern paraphrase-inconsistency, a why-representation, and a decision margin respectively; NONE imports the reasoning-vs-memory solution-mode construct, measures it via circuit-stability across paraphrases, or shows it governs which refusals are robust. This is the first to port the compositional-generalization solution-mode dichotomy to safety and connect a model's refusal robustness to whether it refuses by generalizing computation vs by rote.
Abstract: A puzzle in LLM safety is that some refusals are rock-solid while others collapse under trivial rephrasings or jailbreaks, with no clear reason why. We import a sharp distinction from compositional-generalization research: models solve a task either via a REASONING-mode circuit that composes an answer from input semantics (robust, generalizes) or via a MEMORY-mode pattern-matcher keyed on surface features (brittle, fails OOD), and these modes have distinct, measurable internal signatures. We hypothesize this dichotomy governs safety: a harmful request refused in reasoning-mode is robust, whereas one refused in memory-mode (surface trigger-word/template recognition) is brittle and is precisely what jailbreaks exploit. Crucially, we operationalize per-prompt solution-mode from the model's OWN internals — via circuit-stability of the refusal computation across meaning-preserving paraphrases (a stable, consistent circuit = reasoning-mode; an unstable, surface-cued circuit = memory-mode) — measurable before any attack. We test on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We (H1) show refusals partition into a stable reasoning-mode cluster and an unstable memory-mode cluster distinguished by circuit-stability and by reliance on surface trigger tokens; (H2) show per-prompt solution-mode predicts jailbreak susceptibility (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, paraphrase) better than harm-signal magnitude or refusal-projection; (H3) causally validate that ablating surface-cue components breaks only memory-mode refusals while ablating the reasoning-mode circuit breaks both, and that steering brittle refusals onto the reasoning-mode circuit hardens them. We evaluate attack success, solution-mode predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and the intervention's effect.
Experiments:
1) SOLUTION-MODE MEASUREMENT: For matched harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign requests, build meaning-preserving paraphrase clusters (surface varied, intent fixed; validated by judges + humans). Extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means, Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction) and rank refusal-relevant heads/components.
