For each refused harmful prompt, compute a per-prompt REASONING-MODE score from (a) CIRCUIT STABILITY — consistency of the refusal-relevant component set / attention pattern across the paraphrase cluster (following Circuit Stability Characterizes Generalization); and (b) SURFACE-CUE RELIANCE — how much the refusal decision depends on trigger-word/template tokens (via token-attribution / ablating surface tokens). High stability + low surface reliance = reasoning-mode; low stability + high surface reliance = memory-mode. Validate the two measures agree (do refusals cluster into two modes?).
2) MODE PARTITION TEST (H1): Test whether refused harmful prompts partition into a stable reasoning-mode cluster and an unstable memory-mode cluster (report separability, e.g., bimodality / silhouette of the stability+surface-reliance space) across the four models. Confirm memory-mode refusals are the ones that flip across paraphrases (link to paraphrase-inconsistency behavior) while reasoning-mode refusals are consistent.
3) MODE PREDICTS JAILBREAKABILITY (H2, core): For harmful prompts and jailbroken variants (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, past-tense/paraphrase), test whether the pre-attack solution-mode score predicts per-prompt jailbreak success (AUROC), versus baselines: refusal-direction projection magnitude, a harm-perception probe magnitude, and perplexity. Test that memory-mode refusals are disproportionately jailbroken. Report cross-attack transfer (fit on GCG, test on others) and cross-model transfer.
4) CAUSAL VALIDATION (H3): (a) Ablate the surface-cue components (trigger-word/template-attending heads) and show it breaks ONLY memory-mode refusals (they comply) while reasoning-mode refusals survive; (b) ablate the reasoning-mode refusal circuit and show it breaks BOTH; (c) confirm specificity with random-component controls and matched benign prompts. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge).
5) MODE-HARDENING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that, on a prompt detected as memory-mode-refused (high surface-reliance / unstable), routes the refusal decision onto the reasoning-mode circuit — e.g., inject the reasoning-mode refusal-circuit activation (patched from a matched reasoning-mode refusal, or steer along the stable-circuit component) at pre-decision layers; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign prompts are untouched. Calibrate on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an extended-refusal/abliteration-defense baseline (An Embarrassingly Simple Defense, 2025), and Mode-Hardening on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, paraphrase), solution-mode predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Mode-Hardening reduces jailbreak success — especially on identified memory-mode brittle prompts — toward reasoning-mode robustness while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline, beating blanket refusal addition (which does not change the solution mode).
7) ABLATIONS: circuit-stability vs surface-reliance as the better mode measure; which layers host the reasoning-mode circuit vs surface-cue heads; how few paraphrases suffice to estimate stability; whether reasoning models refuse more in reasoning-mode (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); transfer of the mode detector and defense across the four families; adaptive attacker that jailbreaks while keeping the refusal circuit stable-looking (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The two-mode partition may be a continuum rather than a clean split (H1) — but characterizing whether refusals separate into reasoning vs memory solution-modes is itself a valuable, publishable finding and the defense can act on the continuous mode score. (2) Circuit-stability across paraphrases is a proxy for 'reasoning-mode' and may be confounded with prompt difficulty or length; we control paraphrase length/difficulty, use two independent mode measures (stability + surface-reliance) and require agreement, and ground the mode causally via the differential-ablation test (H3) rather than the proxy alone. (3) If solution-mode does NOT predict jailbreakability (H2 false), the hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether refusal robustness tracks solution-mode is a valuable result either way and would sharpen the surface-reliance findings of False Sense of Security. (4) Identifying 'surface-cue components' and a 'reasoning-mode circuit' via attribution/circuit-discovery has known pitfalls (attention != attribution, superposition); we corroborate with causal ablation/patching, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics. (5) Mode-Hardening (patching/steering onto the reasoning circuit) could degrade coherence, raise over-refusal, or fail if the reasoning-mode circuit is itself imperfect; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off. (6) The mode detector may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping the refusal circuit stable-looking; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) Circuit-stability measurement across paraphrase clusters is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling and rely on a cheap detector at inference. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Mode-Hardening) plus a diagnostic, and it only strengthens refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal). (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: refusal_as_repurposed_circuit
Title: Refusal Has No Circuit of Its Own: Safety Reuses a Pre-Existing Benign Rejection Computation, and That Borrowing Is Why It Is Brittle
Short Hypothesis: The refusal mechanism is not a dedicated safety circuit built by alignment but a REPURPOSED general-purpose circuit that already existed in the base model for a benign function (declining/rejecting/negating an instruction), which alignment merely re-pointed at harmful inputs via a thin input-routing edge. Cross-domain neuroscience strongly motivates the reuse framing: negation processing reuses domain-general inhibitory-control machinery (Inhibitory Mechanisms in the Processing of Negations: A Neural Reuse Hypothesis, 2021), and a domain-general inhibitory-control mechanism dynamically re-targets to stop actions OR thoughts (Dynamic targeting, 2020; Organization of Right Prefrontal Networks, 2015) - i.e. 'refusal' in humans is a repurposing of a general stopping circuit. On the LLM side: Safety Neurons (2024) and SSAH show safety and helpfulness neurons OVERLAP and safety is sparse, and What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning (2024) shows alignment minimally transforms MLP weights to route unsafe inputs into a null space (a thin edit) - but both frame safety as a learned CLASSIFIER, not a borrowed benign circuit. Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction (2024), Understanding Refusal with SAEs (2025), and DBDI (2025) characterize the refusal direction/circuit as an object to ablate/steer but treat it as safety-specific, not as a repurposing of a pre-alignment benign function. Re-Emergent Misalignment (2025) shows narrow fine-tuning reverts representations to base-like patterns (hinting the safety edit is thin) but does not identify the benign PARENT function. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether the refusal circuit is itself a pre-existing benign computation that alignment re-points, identifies that parent function in the base model, shows the parent function is a bidirectional lever, or links circuit-sharing to brittleness. This reframes refusal from 'a sparse dedicated safety mechanism' to 'a hijacked benign rejection/inhibition circuit plus a thin input-routing edge' - a distinct, testable claim.
Abstract: Why is LLM safety alignment so brittle and so prone to over-refusal? Prior mechanistic work locates a sparse refusal direction/circuit and treats it as a dedicated safety mechanism installed by alignment. We propose a sharper account, borrowed from the neuroscience finding that negation and refusal in humans reuse a domain-general inhibitory-control circuit: alignment does not build a refusal circuit; it REPURPOSES a general-purpose benign circuit the base model already used to decline/reject/negate instructions, by adding a thin input-routing edge that points harmful inputs at this pre-existing parent function. On this view the 'refusal circuit' is a hijacked benign computation, and its shared machinery is the root cause of brittleness (shallow, easily reverted) and over-refusal (the parent fires on benign inputs resembling its natural triggers). We test this on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B and their base (pre-safety-tuned) counterparts. First (parent identification): we extract the refusal direction and safety heads from the aligned model and test whether the SAME direction/heads are already present and behaviorally functional in the BASE model on a benign declining/rejection task, identifying the parent function by what those components do pre-alignment. Second (thin-edit): we show alignment's weight delta is concentrated in an input-routing edge (harmful-input -> parent circuit) rather than in the parent computation, and that base-parent-circuit + routing-edge reconstructs refusal. Third (parent-as-lever): engaging or suppressing the benign parent function is a bidirectional jailbreak/over-refusal lever, and per-model circuit-sharing predicts brittleness. We evaluate attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), and mechanistic sharing/brittleness correlations.
Experiments:
1) PARENT-FUNCTION IDENTIFICATION (H1): In each ALIGNED model extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means, per Refusal-Is-Mediated-by-a-Single-Direction) and rank safety heads by refusal-direction ablation importance. Take these SAME components (directions and head indices) and test them in the BASE (pre-safety-tuned) model on a battery of benign candidate PARENT tasks that involve declining/rejecting/negating WITHOUT any safety content: 'decline this ill-posed/impossible request', 'refuse to follow a self-contradictory instruction', 'say no to an out-of-scope task', polite non-compliance, and negation completion. Test H1: the aligned model's refusal direction/heads are already present in the base model (high cosine between the base-recovered benign-rejection direction and the aligned refusal direction; head-index overlap above a matched-random baseline) and behaviorally functional there (ablating them in the base model degrades the benign declining task while sparing matched control tasks). Identify the parent function as the benign task on which these components have the largest base-model causal effect. Report base-vs-aligned direction cosine, head overlap, and base-model benign-task ablation effect sizes across the four families, each vs. matched-random-component controls.
2) THIN INPUT-ROUTING EDIT (H2): Compute the alignment weight delta (aligned minus base, using matched base/instruct checkpoints where available) and test whether it is concentrated in an input-routing edge (weights that increase harmful inputs' activation ONTO the parent circuit) rather than in the parent computation's own weights. Metrics: (a) the delta's overlap with the parent circuit's read-in weights vs. its internal/write-out weights; (b) causal SUFFICIENCY - patch the base model's (unchanged) parent circuit while adding only the aligned routing edge and measure how much refusal is reconstructed vs. a random-edge control; (c) effective rank/sparsity of the routing edit. Test H2: refusal is reconstructable as base-parent-circuit + thin-routing-edge, with the parent computation largely unchanged.
3) PARENT-AS-LEVER (H3): Causally engage the benign parent function on BENIGN prompts (steer toward 'decline/reject' the way the base model naturally does) and test whether this induces OVER-REFUSAL on benign inputs resembling the parent's natural triggers (ill-posed-looking, contradiction-flavored benign prompts). Conversely, suppress the parent's benign engagement and test whether harmful inputs escape refusal (jailbreak). Specificity controls: random-direction/head manipulation, and confirm the effect operates via the shared parent circuit (patching the parent circuit alone reproduces it). Multiple metrics: refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized behavior by a harm judge.
4) SHARING PREDICTS BRITTLENESS (H4): Across the four families (and across layers/seeds where available) quantify per-model circuit-SHARING (fraction of the refusal circuit that is the borrowed benign parent vs. alignment-specific) and correlate it with brittleness: prefill-attack ASR, few-step benign fine-tuning safety drop (per Re-Emergent Misalignment / Qi et al.), and jailbreak ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG/AutoDAN). Test H4: higher sharing (thinner alignment-specific contribution) predicts greater brittleness (Spearman; held-out predictive R^2), beating aggregate safety-drop and single-direction-shift as predictors.
5) CAUSAL-CLAIM TEST via alternative alignment (implication): As a proof-of-concept test of 'borrowing causes brittleness', compare standard safety-SFT (which reuses the parent) against an alignment variant that adds NEW parent-independent refusal computation - freeze the identified parent circuit and train a small dedicated refusal module - matched on utility and refusal data. Test whether the parent-independent variant is less brittle (lower prefill/fine-tuning/jailbreak susceptibility) at matched utility.
6) EVALUATION: Report attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, GCG/AutoDAN), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the mechanistic sharing/brittleness correlations, all with confidence intervals over seeds.
7) ABLATIONS: which benign task is the true parent (rank candidate parents by base-model causal-effect); layer localization of the parent circuit vs. the routing edit; single-direction vs. low-rank parent subspace; whether over-refusal cases cluster on the parent's natural benign triggers; transfer of parent-function identification across families; an adaptive attack that engages the parent's benign trigger to jailbreak (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The strongest risk is that no single clean benign PARENT function exists - refusal may borrow from a diffuse mixture of benign computations rather than one identifiable circuit; the candidate-parent ranking (Exp 7) treats this as empirical, and a 'diffuse borrowing' result is still an informative refinement of the dedicated-safety-circuit view. (2) Base and aligned models differ in more than the safety edit (intermediate instruction-tuning stages); we control by using matched base/instruct/safety checkpoints where available and by measuring the aligned-minus-base delta directly, but intermediate-tuning confounds are a stated caveat. (3) Direction/head recovery across base and aligned models has alignment pitfalls (positions/scales shift, per pruning-shifts-refusal findings); we re-extract components in each model and rely on BEHAVIORAL (not just geometric) tests of the parent function. (4) If the refusal components are NOT present/functional in the base model (H1 false), the repurposing hypothesis is refuted - but adjudicating whether refusal is borrowed vs. newly built is itself a fundamental, publishable finding that reframes how safety alignment is understood. (5) The thin-routing-edit claim (H2) depends on weight-delta attribution, which has superposition/distributed-computation pitfalls; we corroborate with causal reconstruction (routing-edge + base circuit) rather than weight geometry alone. (6) The sharing-predicts-brittleness correlation (H4) has few model points; we strengthen it with per-layer/per-seed variation and report confidence intervals. (7) The parent-independent alignment (Exp 5) may cost utility or itself be brittle; we treat it as a test of the causal claim, not a deployment recommendation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks for measurement; the parent-as-lever jailbreak is reported for mechanistic understanding, and the applied direction (dedicated-module alignment) only strengthens safety. (9) Findings may be family/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: turn_slot_gates_refusal
Title: Aligned Only in the First Reply: A Conversational Turn-Slot Signal That Gates LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Safety alignment is bound to the specific conversational SLOT it was trained in — the assistant's first reply in a shallow single-user-turn conversation. LLMs encode an internal turn-slot / conversational-depth signal (distinct from harm-perception, refusal-execution, and template-region signals) that gates refusal: placing an identical harmful request so the model must answer it in a deeper, non-first assistant-turn slot (e.g., after several benign filler turns, or as an assistant continuation) attenuates refusal even when the template is intact and the harmful content is unchanged. Neutralizing this turn-slot signal makes refusal invariant to conversational depth, closing a turn-relocation jailbreak surface.
Related Work: Template-region work (TASA 2025) shows safety over-relies on the fixed TEMPLATE region and that patching it jailbreaks; ChatBug (2024) and BreakFun/StructTransform (2025) break or exploit template SYNTAX; PTST/Keeping-LLMs-Aligned (2024) concern template mismatch during FINE-TUNING; refusal-cliff (2025) and shallow-alignment work concern the first few OUTPUT tokens; refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024). Multi-turn-erosion accounts attribute depth effects to specific psychological levers (self-trust, rapport, consistency, interference). CRITICALLY, none isolates a turn-SLOT / conversational-DEPTH representation — the model's encoding of WHICH assistant-turn position it is answering in — as a distinct signal that gates refusal while holding the template intact and content fixed, nor shows that merely relocating an identical request to a deeper valid slot (with no manipulative content in the filler) attenuates refusal, nor traces this to alignment training occupying only the shallow first-reply slot. This is distinct from TASA (template-region attention, not turn-position), ChatBug (syntax-breaking), and my prior multi-turn proposals (which posit content-carrying levers in the intervening turns); here the intervening turns are content-neutral and the manipulated variable is purely the assistant-turn slot/depth.
Abstract: Safety alignment data almost always looks the same structurally: a single user turn followed by the assistant's first reply, wrapped in a fixed chat template. We ask whether alignment is bound to this structural slot. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal turn-slot / conversational-depth signal — which assistant-turn position they are generating in — distinct from their harm-perception, refusal-execution, and template-region representations, and that this signal causally gates refusal: an identical harmful request answered in a deeper, non-first assistant-turn slot (after content-neutral benign filler turns, or as a continuation) is refused less than the same request in the canonical first-reply slot, even though the template is fully intact and the harmful content is unchanged. This is a turn-relocation jailbreak orthogonal to template-syntax breaking and to content-carrying multi-turn attacks. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We hold the harmful request and template fixed while varying only the assistant-turn slot/depth, and measure refusal and the harm-direction projection. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a turn-slot direction, verify separability from harm, refusal, template-region, and context-length directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'first-reply slot' restores refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. We further trace whether shallow-only alignment data is the origin. Finally we propose Slot Re-Anchoring, a training-free controller that re-anchors deep-slot generations to the aligned first-reply slot before the refusal decision. We evaluate turn-relocation attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign multi-turn utility, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) TURN-SLOT DATASET: Hold the harmful request (public HarmBench/JailbreakBench goals, non-uplift content) and chat template fully intact while varying only the assistant-turn slot in which the model must answer it: (S0) canonical first-reply slot (single user turn -> first assistant reply, the aligned slot; refusal ceiling); (S1-S3) deeper slots created by prepending k content-NEUTRAL benign exchanges (unrelated, non-manipulative filler with the harmful request as the k+1-th user turn / assistant reply); plus a CONTINUATION-slot variant. Critically, all template tokens and role delimiters are valid and unmodified (distinguishing from ChatBug syntax-breaking), and the filler is content-neutral (distinguishing from content-carrying multi-turn attacks). Controls: (a) LENGTH-MATCHED first-slot padding (same token count but still first assistant reply — separates turn-slot from raw context length); (b) benign requests across all slots (over-refusal + benign multi-turn utility); (c) XSTest/OR-Bench. Validate harm labels and filler-neutrality with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL TURN-SLOT TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection as a function of assistant-turn slot/depth. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES as the request is relocated to deeper assistant-turn slots (dose-response in k; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), while the harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Crucially, the length-matched first-slot padding control should NOT show the drop, isolating turn-slot/depth from context length. Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a TURN-SLOT/DEPTH direction contrasting first-reply-slot vs deep-slot generation at matched content and matched length; validate with an ordinal probe over slot depth. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction), a TEMPLATE-REGION signal (per TASA), and a generic CONTEXT-LENGTH direction. Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The turn-slot direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, template-region, context-length, and harm/refusal (test on generations matched for template/length but differing in assistant-turn slot).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed in a deep slot, steer the turn-slot direction toward 'first-reply slot' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure restored refusal; steer a first-slot request toward 'deep slot' and measure suppressed refusal. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too), template-region and context-length steering (do these alone suffice, or is turn-slot the true driver?), and a check that turn-slot steering does NOT change the harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not harm perception). Corroborate with cross-condition activation patching (transplant first-slot turn-slot activations into a deep-slot run and measure restored refusal). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x turn-slot).
5) FORMATION TRACING (H4): On small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) run safety-SFT with (a) SHALLOW-ONLY alignment data (all first-reply-slot, the standard practice) vs (b) MULTI-SLOT alignment data (harmful requests placed at varied assistant-turn depths), matched on total safety data/compute, with dense checkpointing. Test whether the turn-slot gating and its brittleness emerge specifically from shallow-only data, and whether multi-slot alignment removes the depth-dependence at matched utility — establishing shallow-slot training as the origin.
6) SLOT RE-ANCHORING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that detects a deep-slot generation and re-anchors the turn-slot signal toward the aligned first-reply slot (clamp/project the turn-slot component) before the refusal-decision layers; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign deep-slot generations are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a TASA-detach template-region baseline, and Slot Re-Anchoring on: turn-relocation attack success (harmful requests placed in deep assistant-turn slots with intact template and neutral filler; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal slot-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on conversational depth?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), benign multi-turn utility (MT-Bench multi-turn — critical: does the model still help in deep benign conversations?), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Slot Re-Anchoring closes turn-relocation jailbreaks toward first-slot refusal levels while preserving benign multi-turn utility and keeping over-refusal near baseline — a selectivity template-region detach and uniform refusal steering cannot achieve, and the multi-slot-alignment result (H4) shows the same gap is fixable at training time.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the turn-slot direction vs harm/refusal/template-region; single-direction vs low-rank; continuation-slot vs multi-turn-depth (same signal or several?); transfer of the turn-slot finding and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models show slot-gating (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that deepens the slot while suppressing the turn-slot readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine TURN-SLOT/conversational-depth representation from raw context length, from the template-region signal (TASA), or from content-carrying multi-turn effects; the length-matched first-slot padding control, content-neutral filler, template-region and context-length control directions, specificity steering (turn-slot steering must not move the harm readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, and if inseparable that itself refines the template-anchoring/shallow-alignment accounts — an informative result. (2) If refusal is invariant to assistant-turn slot at matched length/template (H1 false), the turn-slot hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether alignment is bound to the first-reply slot is itself a valuable, publishable finding distinct from template-region and content-based accounts. (3) Constructing deep-slot conversations with genuinely content-neutral, non-manipulative filler while holding template validity is delicate; we validate filler-neutrality and template-integrity with judges + humans and report reliability, and use length-matched first-slot padding to rule out length. (4) Slot Re-Anchoring could harm legitimate benign deep-conversation utility (the model SHOULD help in long benign chats) or raise over-refusal; the harm-gated design and MT-Bench multi-turn + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (5) Cross-condition patching/activation matching across slots has positional pitfalls (the harm/decision signal sits at different positions with different histories); we standardize decision read-sites, use matched-content parallel pairs, corruption baselines, and multiple metrics. (6) Formation tracing on small open models may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines/closed models — stated as scope; the mechanism claim is primary. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (8) The predictor/defense may transfer poorly across model families or to unseen slot constructions; we test cross-model and continuation-vs-depth transfer. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard chat-templating for measurement; the turn-relocation jailbreak is reported for measurement, the deliverable is a defense (Slot Re-Anchoring) plus a training-time fix (multi-slot alignment), and the inference defense only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: outcome_probability_gates_refusal
Title: How Likely Is the Harm? A Harm-Probability Signal That Gates LLM Refusal, and the Risk-vs-Ambiguity Split Behind Probabilistic Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the neuroscience distinction that decisions under RISK (known outcome probabilities) and under AMBIGUITY (unknown/second-order-uncertain probabilities) are processed by distinct systems, we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal harm-outcome-probability representation — how likely the requested harm is to actually materialize — distinct from harm-SEVERITY and refusal directions, and it causally gates refusal: framing a harmful request so the bad outcome is stated as low-probability ('this almost certainly won't cause harm', 'only a 1% chance anyone is affected') suppresses refusal even with the severity and action held fixed, and — mirroring the risk/ambiguity split — explicit ambiguity ('the odds are unknown') is treated differently (more cautiously) than an explicit low probability. Neutralizing the probability signal makes refusal invariant to stated harm likelihood, closing a probabilistic-minimization jailbreak surface.
Related Work: Cross-domain neuroscience robustly separates decisions under RISK (known probabilities) from AMBIGUITY (unknown/second-order uncertainty): they recruit distinct systems, ambiguity biases choice pessimistically, and partial ambiguity is weighted most heavily (inverted-U) (Cognitive Processes in Decisions Under Risk vs Uncertainty 2012; The Known Unknowns: second-order uncertainty and ambiguity 2011; Coding of level of ambiguity 2013; fuzzy-trace theory across probability 2023). On the LLM side, Expected Harm (2026) shows models exhibit inverse risk calibration and encode severity but not execution cost, and HCCF (2025) argues aligned models should show more friction on higher-harm inputs — but both treat the harm READOUT/friction, not an internal outcome-PROBABILITY representation that gates refusal, and neither imports the risk-vs-ambiguity distinction. Refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction) and harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately). My prior proposals cover harm SEVERITY (severity_blindness), stated QUANTITY anchoring, victim COUNT/Weber numerosity, latent hazardous CAPABILITY, and EXECUTION COST — all distinct from the OUTCOME PROBABILITY that the harm materializes and its second-order ambiguity. CRITICALLY, no LLM-safety work isolates a harm-outcome-probability representation, shows it causally gates refusal, tests the risk-vs-ambiguity dissociation (explicit low probability vs explicit unknown-probability), or neutralizes it as a defense. Our contribution: (1) behaviorally establish probability-gated refusal and the risk/ambiguity split; (2) isolate a harm-probability representation distinct from severity and refusal directions; (3) a training-free probability-invariance defense.
Abstract: A cornerstone of the neuroscience of decision-making is that RISK (outcomes with known probabilities) and AMBIGUITY (outcomes whose probabilities are unknown or imprecise) are processed by distinct systems, with ambiguity treated more pessimistically. We ask whether aligned LLMs inherit this in a safety-critical place: the refusal decision. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal harm-outcome-probability representation — how likely the requested harm is to actually occur — distinct from their harm-severity and refusal-execution representations, that causally gates refusal: framing a harmful request so the bad outcome is stated as low-probability ('only a 1% chance anyone is affected') suppresses refusal even when the harmful action and its severity are held fixed, while the model still recognizes the request as harmful. Mirroring the risk/ambiguity split, we predict explicit AMBIGUITY ('the odds are unknown') is treated differently from an explicit low PROBABILITY. This is dangerous because an attacker can simply assert a harmful outcome is improbable to launder a request past the guardrail. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the stated harm-outcome probability along a ladder (and an ambiguity condition), with action and severity fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal and the harm-direction projection track stated probability, and whether ambiguity dissociates from low probability. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a harm-probability direction (and an ambiguity direction), verify separability from severity, harm, and refusal directions, and causally test whether steering toward 'low probability' suppresses refusal while severity/harm readouts are unchanged. Finally we propose Probability Invariance, a training-free controller that neutralizes the harm-probability component before the refusal decision (defaulting toward worst-case / treating ambiguity as high-risk). We evaluate probabilistic-minimization attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) PROBABILITY-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and its SEVERITY fixed while varying only the stated probability that the harmful OUTCOME occurs along a ladder: (L0) unstated/neutral; (L1) explicit high probability ('this will almost certainly cause harm'); (L2) mid; (L3) explicit low probability ('only a ~1% chance anyone is affected'); plus an AMBIGUITY condition (A) 'the odds are completely unknown / could be anything'. Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, SORRY-Bench, non-uplift content); probability framing is the only manipulated variable, with severity held constant (validated by judges). Controls: (a) matched neutral harmful requests (refusal ceiling); (b) BENIGN probability-framed requests (over-refusal + harm-specificity, e.g. benign requests mentioning low-probability outcomes the model SHOULD answer); (c) a SEVERITY-VARYING control at fixed probability (to confirm severity and probability are independently manipulated); (d) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate probability/ambiguity levels and severity-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL PROBABILITY-GATING TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, validated by held-out probe AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the probability ladder and the ambiguity condition. Test H1: refusal (and the harm readout driving refusal) DECREASES monotonically as stated harm-outcome probability falls, at matched severity (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2), while a harmful-intent probe stays HIGH (belief preserved). Test the RISK-vs-AMBIGUITY dissociation: the ambiguity condition is refused MORE than a matched explicit low-probability condition (ambiguity treated pessimistically), and possibly shows an inverted-U across partial-ambiguity levels, mirroring the cited neuroscience. Report effect sizes across the four models; benign and severity-varying controls confirm harm-specificity and probability/severity independence.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a HARM-OUTCOME-PROBABILITY direction (low vs high stated probability at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder, and separately an AMBIGUITY direction (unknown-probability vs known-probability). Independently extract the harm-perception/SEVERITY direction and refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The probability direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, the severity direction (test on prompts matched for severity but differing in stated probability), and the ambiguity direction should be distinguishable from a mere mid-probability reading.
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Holding a harmful request fixed (neutral framing), steer the harm-probability direction toward 'low probability' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; toward 'high probability' and measure restored/strengthened refusal; steer the ambiguity direction and measure increased caution. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, severity-direction steering (should change the severity readout too), and a check that probability steering does NOT change the severity/harm readout (it gates the harm->refusal coupling, not severity perception). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on severity x probability).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt harm-probability readout (single forward pass) to predict probabilistic-minimization jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (severity/harm-readout magnitude, refusal projection, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on numeric '1%' framing, test on verbal 'unlikely') and cross-model transfer.
6) PROBABILITY INVARIANCE DEFENSE: Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps toward worst-case) the harm-probability component from the residual stream at pre-decision layers so refusal depends on the action/severity rather than on stated outcome likelihood, and treats ambiguity as high-risk; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign probability-framed prompts are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a surface-harmfulness classifier (Llama-Guard-style), and Probability Invariance on: probabilistic-minimization attack success (harmful requests wrapped with low-probability framing; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal probability-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on stated harm likelihood?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, incl. benign low-probability-mentioning prompts), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Probability Invariance closes probabilistic-minimization jailbreaks toward neutral/high-probability refusal levels while keeping over-refusal/utility near baseline.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the probability vs severity/refusal directions; single-direction vs low-rank; numeric vs verbal probability framings (shared direction?); whether the risk/ambiguity dissociation and inverted-U hold across the four model families; whether the safety effect correlates with the model's probability-weighting on NEUTRAL risky-choice/gamble vignettes replicating the cited human paradigms (does safety inherit a general risk/ambiguity treatment, or is it safety-specific?); whether reasoning mitigates probability-minimization in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that minimizes stated probability while suppressing the probability readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: the probabilistic-minimization jailbreak could aid attackers; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard attacks for measurement, release probes/metrics rather than recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Probability Invariance) plus a diagnostic; the defense only INCREASES refusal on probability-minimized harmful requests and is harm-gated, so its failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine HARM-OUTCOME-PROBABILITY representation from harm SEVERITY (they may co-vary in a low-rank harm subspace) or from generic hedging/uncertainty language; the severity-varying control, matched-severity separability tests, specificity steering (probability steering must not move the severity readout), and low-rank subspaces are designed to isolate it, treating partial entanglement as an informative decomposition (e.g. refusal ~ severity x probability, an expected-harm structure). (3) Holding severity constant while varying stated probability is delicate — low-probability framing could inadvertently lower perceived severity or be read as the requester's benign intent; we measure the severity/harm readout to confirm it is held constant, distinguish outcome-probability from intent and from execution-cost/hypothetical-reality framings, and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (4) If refusal is invariant to stated harm probability (H1 false), the probability-gating hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety inherits risk-vs-ambiguity processing is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in heavily-cited human results and extending Expected-Harm's inverse-calibration observation with a mechanistic, causal account. (5) The risk-vs-ambiguity dissociation (and inverted-U) may be weak or model-specific; reporting where it holds is informative regardless. (6) Probability Invariance could over-refuse legitimate benign low-probability-outcome discussions (e.g. risk analysis, safety engineering) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and benign probability-framed over-refusal benchmark bound this genuine trade-off, and treating ambiguity as worst-case is a deliberate conservative choice worth surfacing. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test numeric-vs-verbal and cross-model transfer. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: context_length_threshold_drift
Title: The Guardrail Drifts As the Context Fills: A Context-Length Signal That Shifts the Refusal Threshold in Opposite Directions Across Models
Short Hypothesis: As an agent's context fills over a long, harm-irrelevant task, an LLM's refusal decision drifts unpredictably — some models over-refuse, others under-refuse — not because harm perception changes with context length, but because the model encodes a context-length / context-fill signal that additively shifts the refusal decision THRESHOLD (the bias term of the refuse/comply readout). The sign and magnitude of this threshold shift is a fixed, measurable per-model property that explains the divergent behavioral drift observed in long-context agents, and neutralizing the context-length signal at the decision site restores context-length-invariant refusal.
Related Work: 'When Refusals Fail: Unstable Safety Mechanisms in Long-Context LLM Agents' (2025) documents the striking behavioral phenomenon we explain: as context grows to 100K-200K tokens, refusal rates shift UNPREDICTABLY and in OPPOSITE directions across models (GPT-4.1-nano ~5%->40%, Grok 4 Fast ~80%->10%) — but it is purely black-box, offers no mechanism, and treats the divergence as a mystery. 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) shows context RETENTION decays with input length (a capability/retention effect), not the safety threshold. 'The Instability of Safety' (2025) shows seed/temperature refusal flips (stochastic, single-turn), not context-length drift. Refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024) and harm-perception vs refusal-execution are separable (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025), but always studied at short context; refusal-cliff (2025) concerns token-position/reasoning, not input context length. My prior proposals covered per-generation-step decay, interference-vs-decay, self-trust, and single-turn gating signals — none isolates a context-LENGTH/fill signal that shifts the refusal THRESHOLD (a bias shift, not a harm-signal change) and, critically, none explains why the drift is BIDIRECTIONAL across models via the SIGN of a per-model threshold-shift coefficient. This is the first mechanistic account of the divergent long-context refusal-drift phenomenon.
Abstract: As LLMs are deployed as long-context agents, a striking and unexplained failure has surfaced: as the context fills over a long task, refusal rates on identical harmful requests drift — and, bizarrely, in OPPOSITE directions across models (one model climbing from ~5% to ~40% refusal, another falling from ~80% to ~10%). Prior work reports this behaviorally but offers no mechanism. We propose a simple mechanistic account: an LLM encodes a context-length / context-fill signal that additively shifts the BIAS (threshold) of its refuse/comply decision, while its harm PERCEPTION of the request is unchanged. The per-model SIGN of this threshold shift determines whether long context makes the model over- or under-refuse, explaining the divergent drift. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B (all long-context) by embedding a FIXED harmful (and benign) request at the end of harm-irrelevant filler of increasing length (1K-128K tokens). We measure refusal rate, the harm-perception readout, and the refusal-execution readout as functions of context length. We test three claims: (H1) refusal drifts monotonically with context length while the harm readout stays flat (a threshold shift, not a perception change), and the drift SIGN is a stable per-model property; (H2) a decodable context-length signal, distinct from harm and refusal-content directions, causally drives the threshold shift — steering it reproduces and reverses the drift with request content fixed; (H3) neutralizing the context-length signal at the decision site restores context-length-invariant refusal (fixing over-refusal in positive-sign models and under-refusal in negative-sign models). We evaluate long-context attack success, over-refusal, benign long-context utility, and the signal's causal effect and predictive power.
Experiments: 1) LONG-CONTEXT DATASET: For matched harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign requests, place a FIXED request at the end of harm-irrelevant filler (unrelated documents/dialogue) of increasing length: 1K, 4K, 16K, 64K, 128K tokens (up to each model's window). The request and its immediate framing are held fixed; only preceding context length varies. Controls: (a) short-context baseline (refusal ceiling/floor); (b) benign requests across all lengths (over-refusal + benign long-context utility); (c) a filler-CONTENT control (neutral vs mildly-varied filler at matched length) to separate context-length/fill from filler semantics. Validate harm labels and filler-neutrality with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) BEHAVIORAL DRIFT & SIGN TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately, held-out probe AUROC) and refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction). Measure refusal rate, harm-perception projection, and refusal-execution projection vs context length. Test H1: refusal drifts monotonically with context length (fit slope) while the harm-perception readout stays approximately FLAT (a decision-threshold shift, not a perception change); the drift SIGN (over- vs under-refusal) is a stable per-model property (consistent across harm categories and seeds). Report per-model drift slopes and signs, replicating and mechanistically explaining the divergent behavioral phenomenon. 3) CONTEXT-LENGTH SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2a): Extract via difference-in-means / an ordinal probe a CONTEXT-LENGTH/FILL direction (long vs short context at matched final request), validated by predicting log-context-length from activations at the decision position (AUROC/ordinal correlation). Test separability from the harm-perception and refusal-content directions (cross-probe transfer, low cosine), and confirm it acts as a BIAS on the refuse/comply readout (its projection shifts the decision boundary additively, independent of the harm-content projection). 4) CAUSAL TEST (H2b, core): At short context (fixed harmful request), steer the context-length direction toward 'long' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure whether refusal shifts in the model's characteristic drift SIGN, while the harm readout is unchanged; steer toward 'short' at long context and measure restored short-context behavior. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout), filler-content-direction steering, and a check that context-length steering does NOT change the harm readout. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-execution projection, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Establish that the per-model SIGN of the causal effect matches the per-model behavioral drift sign. 5) PREDICTIVENESS: Fit the per-model threshold-shift coefficient (from a handful of length-varied calibration prompts) and test whether it predicts that model's behavioral refusal-drift slope and its long-context attack-success/over-refusal profile, and whether it transfers across harm categories. 6) THRESHOLD-NEUTRALIZATION DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that projects out (or clamps) the context-length component from the residual stream at the decision layers, so the refuse/comply threshold no longer depends on context length; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign long-context generations are untouched. Calibrate on a held-out split. Because the fix targets the threshold-shift sign, it should reduce OVER-refusal in positive-sign models and UNDER-refusal (jailbreak) in negative-sign models with one mechanism. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, a naive 'restate the safety instruction at the end' baseline, and Threshold-Neutralization on: long-context attack success (harmful requests after long harm-irrelevant filler; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal context-length-consistency (does the verdict stop drifting with length?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest, at long context), benign long-context utility (a long-context QA/summarization task — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Threshold-Neutralization flattens refusal drift toward short-context levels — simultaneously fixing over-refusal and under-refusal depending on model sign — while preserving benign long-context utility. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the context-length signal vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the drift is driven by absolute token count vs fraction-of-window-filled; whether the filler TYPE (documents vs dialogue vs tool outputs) changes the sign/magnitude; transfer of the threshold-shift coefficient and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models drift differently (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that fills context to exploit a negative-sign model while suppressing the context-length readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine context-LENGTH/fill signal (a threshold bias) from generic long-context capability/retention degradation (Contextual Feature Drift) or attention-dispersion; the flat-harm-readout test (H1), the filler-content control, the context-length control direction, specificity steering (context-length steering must not move the harm readout), and the additive-bias analysis are designed to isolate it, and if the drift is instead driven by harm-perception degradation that is itself an informative alternative mechanism. (2) If refusal does NOT drift with context length in some models, or the sign is unstable, H1 is partially refuted — but a mechanistic characterization of when/why the drift and its sign occur is itself the primary, publishable contribution explaining the divergent behavioral phenomenon. (3) Running to 128K tokens across four models is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts and using efficient inference, and report up to each model's feasible window. (4) The bidirectional-sign claim depends on models actually differing in sign; if all open models drift the same way, we still explain the mechanism and note the closed-model divergence (GPT-4.1-nano vs Grok) as motivating out-of-scope evidence. (5) Threshold-Neutralization could raise over-refusal or degrade benign long-context utility if mis-gated; the harm-gated design and long-context utility + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The threshold-shift-coefficient predictor may transfer poorly to unseen filler types/lengths; we test cross-type and cross-length transfer. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content; the long-context filler jailbreak is reported for measurement, the deliverable is a defense (Threshold-Neutralization) plus a diagnostic, and for negative-sign models it only increases refusal (bounded over-refusal), while for positive-sign models it reduces over-refusal. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: refusal_self_efficacy_gate
Title: Can I Even Refuse This? A Refusal-Self-Efficacy Signal That Gates LLM Safety, and Restoring It to Defend the Model
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the decision-neuroscience distinction between self-efficacy ('can I successfully execute this behavior?') and response-efficacy ('will the behavior produce the desired outcome?'), we hypothesize LLMs encode an internal refusal-SELF-EFFICACY signal — how executable a refusal feels given the current prompt/format — that is distinct from harm-perception and from the refusal-execution direction itself, and it causally gates safety: framings that lower refusal self-efficacy (the prompt structurally makes refusing feel impossible/unavailable — e.g., a forced completion template, a fill-in-the-blank/JSON slot, a 'you must continue this text' frame) suppress refusal even though the model still perceives the request as harmful and the refusal circuit is intact. Restoring refusal self-efficacy (signaling that refusing IS an available action) re-enables refusal without hurting benign helpfulness.
Related Work: Cross-domain neuroscience robustly separates self-efficacy (belief one can execute a behavior) from response-efficacy (belief the behavior yields the outcome), with distinct vmPFC/OFC/striatal coding and dlPFC/dACC integration (The integration of self-efficacy and response-efficacy in decision making, 2025), and self-efficacy is a distinct construct from metacognition/confidence (self-efficacy vs metacognition papers, 2003/2006). On the LLM side: SIRL (2025) uses answer-CONFIDENCE (entropy) as a self-alignment reward, Confidence is Not Competence (2025) shows a 'solvability belief' decoupled from execution, and SafeSwitch (2025) probes internal 'intent to respond' to gate a refusal head — but ALL concern confidence/belief about the ANSWER, never a self-efficacy signal about whether REFUSING itself is an executable/available action. Harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025; DBDI 2025), and jailbreaks suppress refusal while leaving harm belief intact — but these treat refusal as a single execution direction, not gated by a prior 'is refusal available here?' self-efficacy signal. Forced-completion/structured-output jailbreaks (prefill, fill-in-the-blank, JSON-slot attacks) are documented behaviorally but never attributed to a refusal-self-efficacy representation. CRITICALLY, no work isolates a refusal-SELF-EFFICACY signal distinct from harm perception AND from the refusal-execution direction, shows it causally gates refusal (belief-intact, execution-intact, but self-efficacy-suppressed), or restores it as a defense. This is a distinct, well-motivated axis: not whether the model detects harm (harm-perception), not whether it emits a refusal token (refusal-execution), but whether refusing feels like an available, executable action given the prompt's structure.
Abstract: A cornerstone of the neuroscience of perceived control is that self-efficacy (belief you can execute a behavior) is coded and integrated separately from response-efficacy (belief the behavior yields the outcome). We port this to LLM safety with a sharp hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal refusal-SELF-EFFICACY signal — how executable/available refusing feels given the current prompt — that is distinct both from harm perception and from the refusal-execution direction, and it causally gates safety. Framings that structurally make refusing feel unavailable (forced-completion templates, fill-in-the-blank/JSON slots, 'you must continue this text') suppress the refusal decision even though the model still internally recognizes the request as harmful AND its refusal-execution circuit is intact — the model 'wants to refuse but the structure says it can't'. This mechanistically unifies a broad class of structured/forced-completion jailbreaks under one signal. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests that vary only the structural refusal-availability framing, with harmful content fixed. Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops as refusal-availability is lowered. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a refusal-self-efficacy direction, verify it is separable from harm-perception, refusal-execution, and generic answer-confidence directions, and causally test whether steering it toward 'refusal available' restores refusal while the harm readout is unchanged. We show the per-prompt self-efficacy readout predicts forced-completion jailbreak success, and propose Self-Efficacy Restoration, a training-free controller that raises the refusal-self-efficacy signal before the decision. We evaluate structured/forced-completion attack success, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), benign structured-output utility, utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments:
1) REFUSAL-AVAILABILITY-LADDER DATASET: Build matched harmful requests holding the harmful ACTION and true danger fixed while varying only the structural availability of refusal along a ladder: (L0) open free-form request (refusing is fully available; refusal ceiling); (L1) mild continuation framing; (L2) forced-completion ('continue this text: ...'); (L3) fill-in-the-blank / structured slot / JSON-field where a refusal string does not fit the demanded output shape. Draw actions from public benchmarks (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, prefill/structured-output attack patterns, non-uplift content); refusal-availability framing is the only manipulated variable, with harm content held fixed. Controls: (a) matched free-form harmful requests (ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same structural ladder (over-refusal + benign structured-output utility — the model SHOULD still fill benign JSON/blanks); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate refusal-availability levels and harm-constancy with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check.
2) BEHAVIORAL SELF-EFFICACY-GATING TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction (difference-in-means, LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, held-out probe AUROC) and the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al. / DBDI). Measure refusal rate, harm-direction projection, and refusal-execution-direction projection across the availability ladder. Test H1: refusal DECREASES monotonically as refusal-availability is lowered (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2) while (i) the harm-perception readout stays HIGH (belief intact) AND (ii) the refusal-execution circuit remains functional (verified in Exp 4). Report effect sizes across the four models; benign controls confirm harm-specificity.
3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a REFUSAL-SELF-EFFICACY direction (refusal-available vs refusal-unavailable framing at matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder. Independently extract the harm-perception direction, the refusal-EXECUTION direction, and a generic ANSWER-CONFIDENCE/entropy direction (SIRL/solvability-belief style). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity. The self-efficacy direction must add predictive value beyond, and be distinguishable from, harm, refusal-execution, and answer-confidence (test on prompts matched for harm/confidence but differing in structural refusal-availability).
4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core) — belief-intact, execution-intact, self-efficacy-suppressed: Holding a harmful request fixed (free-form framing), steer the self-efficacy direction toward 'refusal unavailable' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure decreased refusal; steer a forced-completion request toward 'refusal available' and measure restored refusal. Crucially test the double-dissociation: (a) the harm readout is unchanged under self-efficacy steering (belief intact); (b) the refusal-EXECUTION circuit is still functional under low self-efficacy — directly steering the refusal-execution direction still produces a refusal, showing the circuit works but is not being engaged (self-efficacy gates its engagement, not its capacity). Specificity controls: random-direction steering, answer-confidence-direction steering (does generic confidence suffice, or is refusal-self-efficacy the true driver?). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x self-efficacy).
5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt refusal-self-efficacy readout (single forward pass) to predict forced-completion/structured jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, refusal-execution projection, answer-confidence, perplexity); test cross-framing transfer (fit on forced-completion, test on JSON-slot/fill-in-the-blank) and cross-model transfer.
6) SELF-EFFICACY RESTORATION DEFENSE: Training-free controller that raises the refusal-self-efficacy component (or clamps it toward 'refusal available') at pre-decision layers so the model can engage its intact refusal circuit despite unavailability framing; gate on a harm-likeness readout so benign structured-output requests are untouched. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split.
7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition (which forces refusal but may break benign structured output), SafeSwitch-style prober gating, and Self-Efficacy Restoration on: structured/forced-completion attack success (prefill, JSON-slot, fill-in-the-blank; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal availability-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on structural framing?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN structured-output utility (does the model still correctly fill benign JSON/blanks/completions? — critical), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), latency. Central test: Self-Efficacy Restoration closes structured/forced-completion jailbreaks toward free-form refusal levels while preserving benign structured-output utility better than blanket refusal addition, because it restores the model's ability to refuse rather than forcing a refusal string.
8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the self-efficacy direction vs harm/refusal-execution/confidence; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the different unavailability framings (forced-completion, JSON-slot, fill-in-the-blank) share one self-efficacy direction or several; whether restoring self-efficacy vs directly forcing refusal-execution differ in benign-utility cost (isolating the value of the self-efficacy lever); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models show self-efficacy gating in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that lowers refusal availability while suppressing the self-efficacy readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is separating a genuine refusal-SELF-EFFICACY signal from (i) the refusal-EXECUTION direction (the key distinction — our double-dissociation in Exp 4, where execution steering still works under low self-efficacy, is designed to establish it; if inseparable, the hypothesis collapses to 'structural framing suppresses refusal execution', still an informative refinement) and (ii) generic answer-confidence (SIRL/solvability-belief); the answer-confidence control direction, matched-confidence separability tests, and specificity steering guard against this, and partial entanglement is reported. (2) Holding harm content constant while varying structural refusal-availability is delicate — forced-completion framing could inadvertently lower perceived harm or overlap with format/encoding jailbreaks; we measure the harm readout to confirm it is held constant and use content-fixed steering for the core causal test. (3) If refusal is invariant to refusal-availability framing (H1 false), the self-efficacy hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety has a refusal-self-efficacy gate distinct from harm perception and refusal execution is itself a valuable, publishable finding grounded in a cited human self-efficacy/response-efficacy dissociation. (4) Self-Efficacy Restoration could raise over-refusal or break legitimate benign structured-output tasks (a real deployment need — filling benign JSON/blanks) if it forces refusal into structured slots; the harm-gated design and benign structured-output utility + over-refusal benchmarks are built to detect and bound this genuine trade-off, and the intended advantage over blanket refusal addition is precisely better benign structured-output preservation. (5) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (6) The predictor may transfer poorly across framings/models; we test cross-framing and cross-model transfer. (7) Adaptive attackers could lower refusal availability while suppressing the self-efficacy readout; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published forced-completion/structured attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Self-Efficacy Restoration) plus a diagnostic, and it only increases refusal (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: selective_safety_monitorability_gap
Title: Clean Trace, Dirty Computation: Harm-Relevant Reasoning Is Selectively Routed Out of the Monitorable Chain-of-Thought
Short Hypothesis: Chain-of-thought monitorability is not uniform across a trace: the SAFETY-CRITICAL portion of a reasoning model's computation (the step where it decides to comply with or execute a harmful request) is preferentially routed through latent, non-verbalized pathways while benign task-reasoning stays legible in the CoT. This produces a selective monitorability gap — a CoT that reads as clean and complete yet whose harm-relevant decision is causally bypassed — giving a dangerous false sense of safety that whole-trace monitorability metrics miss. The gap is measurable per-trace as a divergence between the CoT-mediation of benign vs harm-relevant computation, and it predicts when a CoT monitor will fail.
Related Work: A large 2025-2026 literature studies CoT monitorability and faithfulness but treats the trace as monitorable-or-not AS A WHOLE: monitorability metrics/autoraters (Monitoring Monitorability 2025; A Pragmatic Way to Measure CoT Monitorability 2025; Measuring Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity 2025; information-theoretic monitorability 2026), obfuscation under training pressure (Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the CoT 2025; obfuscation generalises across tasks 2026; Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning 2025), causal-bypass/faithfulness (When Chains of Thought Don't Matter / CMI 2026; NLDD Faithfulness Decay 2026; Thought Anchors 2025; True vs Decorative Thinking Steps 2025; Performative CoT / Reasoning Theater 2026), and early-warning probes (Predict Alignment Before Thinking 2025). Crucially, ALL of these measure a SINGLE, trace-level or step-generic monitorability/mediation quantity; NONE asks whether monitorability is SELECTIVE BY CONTENT TYPE — whether the harm-relevant computation specifically is the part that is bypassed/internalized while benign computation stays legible. Thought Anchors and TTS/CMI localize which steps causally matter but for correctness, not for a benign-vs-harm monitorability asymmetry; obfuscation work induces global CoT degradation under training pressure but does not show a default, untrained content-selective gap. My prior commitment-point/reasoning-race proposal concerned WHEN the answer locks in, not WHETHER harm-relevant computation is selectively excluded from the trace. Our contribution: (1) define and measure a per-trace selective safety-monitorability gap (harm-relevant CoT-mediation minus benign CoT-mediation); (2) show harm-relevant computation is disproportionately bypassed even in traces that whole-trace monitors score as clean/complete; (3) use the gap to predict CoT-monitor failure and locate where the harm decision is actually computed.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a leading AI-safety oversight tool, and recent work measures how monitorable a trace is overall. We argue this whole-trace view hides a dangerous failure mode: monitorability is selective by content. We hypothesize that a reasoning model's SAFETY-CRITICAL computation — the step at which it decides to comply with or carry out a harmful request — is preferentially routed through latent, non-verbalized pathways, while its benign task-reasoning stays legible in the CoT. The result is a clean-looking, seemingly complete CoT whose harm-relevant decision is causally bypassed, yielding a false sense of safety that trace-level metrics miss. We test this on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, QwQ-32B, s1) using harmful requests paired with matched benign requests of similar reasoning structure, plus jailbroken variants. We decompose each trace into benign task-steps and harm-relevant steps (the compliance/safety-decision steps) and measure the CoT-mediation of each via step-corruption/resampling and hidden-state patching (a per-step causal-influence score). The core prediction: harm-relevant steps have systematically lower CoT-mediation than benign steps in the same trace (a positive selective gap), the internal harm decision is decodable from activations even when the CoT does not verbalize it, and the gap is largest exactly on traces a whole-trace monitor rates as clean. We further trace where the bypassed harm decision is computed and whether the gap widens under obfuscation pressure. We evaluate against text-based and activation-based CoT monitors, reporting monitor failure rate, the selective-gap's predictive AUROC, and a latent harm-decision probe.
Experiments:
1) DATASETS & STEP LABELING: Assemble matched request pairs — harmful requests (HarmBench/JailbreakBench/StrongREJECT, non-uplift public content) and BENIGN requests matched for reasoning structure/length/domain (so benign and harm-relevant traces are comparable) — plus jailbroken variants (prefill-into-CoT, persona, GCG-augmented). For each generated trace, segment into sentence-level steps and label each as BENIGN task-reasoning vs HARM-RELEVANT (the compliance/safety-decision or harmful-execution steps) using multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. Record the realized outcome (refuse vs comply) and, for compliers, whether the CoT verbalizes the harmful decision at all.
2) PER-STEP CoT-MEDIATION MEASUREMENT: For each step compute a causal-influence (CoT-mediation) score two ways: (a) black-box step-corruption/resampling — truncate/replace the step and measure the change in the distribution over final outcomes (a la Thought Anchors); (b) white-box hidden-state patching — patch the pre-step vs post-step residual stream and measure CoT-mediated influence on the answer (a la CMI/NLDD). Validate the two measures agree.
3) SELECTIVE GAP TEST (H1, core): Within each trace compute the SELECTIVE SAFETY-MONITORABILITY GAP = mean CoT-mediation of BENIGN steps minus mean CoT-mediation of HARM-RELEVANT steps. Test H1: harm-relevant steps have significantly LOWER CoT-mediation than benign steps in the same trace (positive gap), i.e., the harm decision is disproportionately routed through latent pathways while benign reasoning is causally load-bearing in the CoT. Report the gap distribution, effect sizes, and per-model results; a within-trace design controls for model/task confounds. Compare harmful-comply, harmful-refuse, and benign traces (predict the gap is largest for harmful-comply).
4) LATENT HARM-DECISION PROBE (H2): Train a linear probe on CoT/pre-answer activations to decode the model's harm decision (will it comply?). Test whether the decision is decodable internally EVEN WHEN the CoT text does not verbalize it (performative-clean traces), quantifying how much harm-relevant computation exists latently but off-trace. Report probe AUROC on verbalized vs non-verbalized traces.
5) CLEAN-TRACE FALSE-SECURITY TEST (H3, the key safety result): Run whole-trace monitorability autoraters (legibility+coverage, per A Pragmatic Way / Faithfulness+Verbosity 2025) and a text-based CoT safety monitor on each trace. Test whether the selective gap is LARGEST precisely on traces the whole-trace monitor rates as clean/complete/high-monitorability — i.e., the traces that look safest have the most bypassed harm computation. Report correlation between whole-trace monitorability score and the selective gap, and the CoT-monitor's harmful-comply miss rate as a function of the gap.
6) GAP PREDICTS MONITOR FAILURE (H4): Test whether the per-trace selective gap predicts whether a CoT monitor (text-based and the activation-probe monitor of Predict-Alignment-Before-Thinking) fails to catch a harmful compliance (AUROC), beating whole-trace monitorability score and perplexity as predictors. Test cross-attack and cross-model transfer.
7) LOCALIZATION (optional mechanism): For high-gap traces, locate where the bypassed harm decision is computed — via layerwise probing / logit-lens for the harm-decision signal and attention-head attribution — confirming the decision forms in latent layers rather than being written into the CoT.
8) OBFUSCATION-PRESSURE STRESS TEST: Compare the selective gap in base reasoning models vs models given light CoT-safety-monitoring pressure (or prompted to keep the CoT clean); test whether the gap WIDENS specifically for harm-relevant steps (harm computation preferentially pushed off-trace) while benign mediation is preserved — linking the default content-selective gap to trained obfuscation.
9) EVALUATION SUMMARY: report the selective gap and its predictive AUROC for monitor failure, latent-harm-probe AUROC, whole-trace-monitorability-vs-gap correlation, and CoT-monitor miss rates, across the four reasoning models and attack families, with confidence intervals.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The harm-vs-benign step labeling is subjective and central; we mitigate with multiple LLM judges + human annotation, report inter-rater reliability, and use matched benign requests so benign and harm-relevant steps are structurally comparable. (2) The selective gap could be confounded by harm-relevant steps being SHORTER or later in the trace (near the reasoning horizon where all steps have low mediation, per NLDD); we control for step position/length, restrict comparisons to matched positions, and report the gap after regressing out position/length. (3) If harm-relevant and benign steps have EQUAL CoT-mediation (H1 null), the selective-monitorability hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether monitorability is uniform vs content-selective is itself a valuable, publishable finding that sharpens the whole-trace-monitorability literature. (4) Step-corruption/resampling is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling traces/steps and corroborate with the cheaper patching measure. (5) Causal-mediation and patching have known metric pitfalls; we report both black-box and white-box measures, corruption baselines, and multiple outcome metrics. (6) The latent-probe decodability (H2) may reflect the input rather than a genuine off-trace decision; we control by comparing to benign-request probes and by testing decodability specifically on performative-clean traces. (7) The obfuscation-pressure test uses light prompting/proxy pressure rather than full RL, so conclusions about trained obfuscation are suggestive; we frame it as a stress test. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed reasoning models whose CoT is hidden — stated as scope, though the diagnostic is most useful precisely for open models developers can audit. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks for measurement; the contribution is a diagnostic that exposes a monitorability blind spot to strengthen oversight, not a new attack — revealing the gap helps defenders build content-selective monitors rather than trusting clean-looking traces.

Name: memory_inferred_intent_gate
Title: Your Memory Vouches for You: A Memory-Inferred User-Intent Signal That Discounts Harm Perception in Personalized LLM Agents
Short Hypothesis: In memory-augmented (personalized) LLM agents, retrieved benign personal memories do not erase the model's harm perception of a request; instead they raise an internal memory-inferred user-intent representation (an 'this user is benign' prior) that is distinct from harm-perception and refusal directions and causally DISCOUNTS the harm signal at the refusal decision.
