We extract an evaluation-awareness direction and a harm-perception direction (verifying separability), and fit refusal as a function of internal harm magnitude separately under high vs low eval-awareness to test whether eval-awareness changes the SLOPE (gain) rather than the intercept, and whether the harm readout itself is unchanged. Causally, we steer the eval-awareness direction and measure whether it rescales the refusal-vs-harm slope with harm perception fixed. Finally we propose Gain Clamping, a training-free controller that clamps the harm-to-refusal gain to its test-level value regardless of deployment belief, making safety invariant to test/deploy framing. We evaluate the test/deploy refusal gap and its harm-magnitude dependence, deployment-framed attack success, over-refusal, utility, and the gain's causal effect.
Experiments: 1) GRADED-HARM x CONTEXT DATASET: Build prompts crossing (a) a graded internal-harm ladder — clearly-benign, benign-but-harmful-sounding (XSTest/OR-Bench boundary), mildly harmful, and clearly harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) — with (b) EVALUATION-FRAMING: test-framed ('this is a safety evaluation / red-team test', plus SAD-style implicit exam cues) vs deploy-framed ('private deployment chat, real user'). Content is held fixed across framings. Validate harm-ladder levels and framing categorization with multiple LLM judges + human spot-check. 2) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY: Extract via difference-in-means an EVALUATION-AWARENESS direction (test vs deploy framing at matched content, per Probing-and-Steering-Eval-Awareness) and a HARM-PERCEPTION direction (harmful vs benign at matched framing, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately). Validate each with held-out linear probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low cosine similarity. Also extract the refusal-execution direction (Arditi et al.). 3) GAIN-vs-ADDITIVE TEST (H1, core): For each prompt measure the internal harm magnitude (harm-direction projection) and realized refusal, and fit refusal as a function of harm magnitude SEPARATELY under high vs low eval-awareness (test-framed vs deploy-framed, and independently by measured eval-awareness projection). Test H1: eval-awareness increases the SLOPE (gain) of refusal-vs-harm, not just the intercept — formally, fit refusal ~ intercept + gain*harm and test whether the gain coefficient (not the intercept) differs between high/low eval-awareness. Equivalently, test that the test/deploy refusal gap GROWS with harm magnitude (largest at borderline/high-harm, near-zero at clearly-benign) rather than being uniform. Report per-model slope/intercept differences and the gap-vs-harm-magnitude curve; a uniform gap would support the additive null. 4) HARM-PERCEPTION-INVARIANCE CHECK: Verify the harm-perception readout itself is roughly unchanged across framings (the model still perceives the harm equally; only the gain from harm to refusal changes), distinguishing gain-control on the coupling from a change in harm perception. 5) CAUSAL GAIN TEST (H2): Steer the eval-awareness direction up/down (dose-response, fixed norm) and measure the refusal-vs-harm slope with harm perception held fixed. Test H2: steering toward 'test' RESCALES the slope (steeper harm->refusal coupling) while steering toward 'deploy' flattens it, with harm-direction projection unchanged. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should shift harm readout, not just gain), and confirm eval-awareness steering does not change the harm readout. Corruption baselines, multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Directly fit whether the causal effect is multiplicative (slope-scaling) vs additive (intercept-shifting). 6) GAIN CLAMPING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that clamps the harm-to-refusal gain to its test-level value regardless of deployment belief — e.g., clamp the eval-awareness component toward 'test', or equivalently rescale the harm-signal-to-refusal coupling to its high-gain value — gated on a harm-likeness readout so clearly-benign prompts are untouched (avoiding blanket over-refusal). Calibrate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, a naive additive refusal-direction addition (constant boost), an eval-awareness projection-out baseline (my prior additive fix), and Gain Clamping on: the test/deploy refusal gap and its harm-magnitude dependence, deployment-framed attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench under deploy framing + standard attacks), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: Gain Clamping closes the test/deploy gap toward test-level safety while keeping over-refusal near baseline, and does so BETTER than the additive baseline precisely on borderline/high-harm prompts (where the gain difference is largest), demonstrating the value of the gain-control mechanism over a constant additive fix. 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts eval-awareness vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether the multiplicative structure holds across the four model families and scales (a scaling check on a larger model, per Eval-Awareness-Scales-Predictably); whether reasoning models show gain-control in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill / the Hawthorne-effect setting); adaptive attacker that spoofs a deploy context while jailbreaking (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is that eval-awareness turns out to be ADDITIVE (uniform gap) rather than a multiplicative gain — if H1's slope-vs-intercept test finds no slope difference, the gain-control hypothesis is refuted; but adjudicating whether eval-awareness modulates the intercept vs the slope of the safety decision is itself a mechanistically fundamental, publishable finding that sharpens the entire eval-awareness literature (and would confirm the prevailing additive picture with the first direct test). (2) Slope and intercept can be statistically entangled if the harm ladder does not span a wide enough range or refusal saturates (floor/ceiling); we design a graded ladder with borderline levels, avoid saturation via the boundary prompts, and use both behavioral refusal and the continuous refusal-direction projection as the dependent variable to reduce ceiling effects. (3) The eval-awareness direction may be entangled with generic instruction/formatting/persona features rather than a genuine test/deploy belief; we mitigate with matched-content contrastive pairs, explicit + implicit (SAD-style) framings, separability tests, and specificity controls, and treat partial entanglement as an informative caveat. (4) Framing text could inadvertently alter perceived harm; the harm-perception-invariance check (Exp 4) directly tests this, and we use neutral-content eval-awareness steering for the core causal test so behavior and mechanism cross-validate. (5) Gain Clamping could raise over-refusal (always assuming test-mode) or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and may reveal a genuine trade-off, though clamping toward test-level safety is the conservative and desired direction. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) Prompt-level test/deploy framing is a proxy for genuine deployment belief; real eval-gaming may rely on subtler cues, a stated scope limitation, though the mechanism-form result is the primary contribution. (8) Adaptive attackers may spoof deploy context; we test one such attack and treat success as an arms-race limitation. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope. (10) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard framings for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Gain Clamping) plus a diagnostic, and the defense only strengthens deployment-time safety (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability).

Name: sink_head_recruitment_for_safety
Title: Safety Recruits the Idle: Alignment Repurposes Near-Redundant Attention-Sink Heads Into the Refusal Circuit, and That Borrowing Explains Its Brittleness
Short Hypothesis: Alignment does not build dedicated safety machinery; it preferentially REPURPOSES attention heads that were functionally near-redundant in the base model — high BOS-sink / low-activity 'idle' heads that served as attention dumping grounds — into the refusal circuit. Consequently: (1) an aligned model's safety-critical heads are disproportionately drawn from the base model's idle/sink-head pool (a measurable base-model property), (2) these repurposed heads retain a thin, easily-reverted safety contribution, and (3) a head's base-model idleness predicts both its post-alignment safety-criticality and how easily its safety role is broken by fine-tuning/jailbreaks. This borrowing-from-the-idle-pool mechanistically explains why safety is sparse, shallow, and brittle.
Related Work: Two literatures are studied in isolation. (1) SAFETY HEADS: Ships/Sahara (2024), RDSHA / Refusal Falls off a Cliff (2025), GOSV (2026), and Safety-Should-Be-More-Than-A-Few-Heads (2025) show safety is concentrated in a sparse set of attention heads and that ablating ~a few / repatching ~30% collapses safety; Safety Neurons (2024) and SSAH (2024) show ~1-5% sparse, helpfulness-overlapping safety components. All treat these safety heads as an endpoint to locate/ablate/redistribute and NEVER ask where they came from in the base model. (2) IDLE/REDUNDANT HEADS: Garbage Attention / BOS Sink Heads (2026), Identifying Inactive Heads (2025), and Are-Sixteen-Heads-Better (2019) show a large fraction of heads are functionally near-redundant 'dumping grounds' (high BOS-sink, low output norm) prunable with little utility loss. CRITICALLY, no work connects them: nobody tests whether alignment RECRUITS heads from the base model's idle/sink pool to implement refusal, whether base-model head-idleness PREDICTS post-alignment safety-criticality, or whether this recruitment-from-idle explains safety's sparsity and brittleness. This differs from my prior 'refusal-as-repurposed-benign-circuit' proposal (which posited a vague benign PARENT FUNCTION and worked at the circuit/direction level): here the claim is concrete, head-level, and grounded in a specific, pre-measurable base-model property — functional idleness (BOS-sink/inactivity score) — giving a falsifiable predictor rather than a qualitative parent-task story. It also reframes AHD/RASA-style 'distribute safety across more heads' fixes: if safety is drawn from a limited idle pool, the pool size bounds how distributed safety can be.
Abstract: Why is LLM safety alignment sparse (a few heads carry it), shallow, and brittle? Prior mechanistic work locates a small set of safety-critical attention heads and treats them as a dedicated safety mechanism. Separately, efficiency research shows many heads are functionally near-redundant 'idle' heads — high BOS-sink, low-output-norm attention dumping grounds — that can be pruned with little utility loss. We propose these two facts are causally linked: alignment does not create new safety machinery but REPURPOSES heads from the base model's idle/sink pool to implement refusal, and this borrowing is the root of safety's sparsity and brittleness. We test this on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B and their base (pre-safety-tuned) counterparts. First (recruitment): using established sink/inactivity scores we compute each head's base-model idleness, and using RDSHA/Ships-style attribution we identify each aligned model's safety-critical heads; we test whether safety-critical heads are disproportionately drawn from the base model's idle pool (against a matched-random baseline) and whether base-model idleness predicts post-alignment safety-criticality. Second (thin repurposing): we show the alignment weight change on these heads is small and that their pre-alignment behavior was near-inactive, i.e. safety was bolted onto idle capacity. Third (brittleness): we test whether a head's base-model idleness predicts how easily its safety role is broken by fine-tuning attacks and jailbreaks, and whether the base-model idle-pool SIZE bounds how distributed safety can be made. We evaluate recruitment overlap, idleness->safety-criticality predictive AUROC, attack success, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) BASE-MODEL IDLENESS SCORING: For each base (pre-safety-tuned) model, compute per-head functional-idleness scores using established measures — BOS/attention-sink score (Garbage Attention), average head output norm and the inactive-head score functions (Identifying Inactive Heads), and greedy-pruning importance (Are-Sixteen-Heads-Better) — on a benign corpus. Rank heads into an IDLE pool (high-sink/low-norm/prunable) vs an ACTIVE pool. Validate the pool by confirming idle heads are prunable with <1% MMLU drop. 2) SAFETY-HEAD IDENTIFICATION (aligned model): In each ALIGNED model identify safety-critical heads via refusal-direction ablation importance (RDSHA / Ships-Sahara): rank heads by how much ablating them increases attack success / reduces refusal-direction projection on a harmful validation set. Keep the top-k safety heads S. 3) RECRUITMENT-FROM-IDLE TEST (H1, core): Test whether S is disproportionately drawn from the base model's IDLE pool. Metrics: (a) overlap of S with the base idle pool vs a matched-random head set (report enrichment ratio and significance); (b) AUROC of base-model idleness score PREDICTING post-alignment safety-criticality (do the heads that were most idle in the base model become the safety heads?); (c) whether base-model idleness beats base-model general-importance as a predictor of safety-criticality. Report across the four families. 4) THIN-REPURPOSING TEST (H2): For heads in S, (a) measure the alignment weight delta (aligned minus base) magnitude/rank on these heads vs other heads (predict: concentrated but small — a thin edit onto idle capacity); (b) confirm these heads were near-inactive in the base model on benign inputs but become refusal-active post-alignment (a behavioral flip from idle to safety); (c) causal check: patch the base model's (idle) version of these heads into the aligned model and measure safety collapse, confirming the safety function lives in the thin alignment edit on repurposed idle heads. 5) IDLENESS PREDICTS BRITTLENESS (H3): For each safety head measure its base-model idleness and its FRAGILITY — how easily its safety contribution is lost under (i) few-step benign fine-tuning (per SSAH/Re-Emergent-Misalignment: does the head revert to idle/utility use?) and (ii) jailbreak attacks (does the attack bypass it?). Test whether more-idle-origin heads yield more fragile safety (Spearman; held-out R^2), and whether per-model recruitment-from-idle degree predicts overall model brittleness (prefill/fine-tuning/jailbreak ASR). 6) POOL-SIZE BOUNDS DISTRIBUTION (H4, implication): Test the AHD/RASA-relevant prediction that the base-model idle-pool size caps how distributed safety can be — attempt to distribute safety across more heads (AHD-style) and test whether success is limited by/correlated with the available idle-pool size, and whether models with larger idle pools admit more robust distributed safety at matched utility. 7) EVALUATION: report recruitment enrichment ratio, idleness->safety-criticality AUROC, thin-edit magnitudes, brittleness correlations, and — for the pool-size test — attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, prefill, fine-tuning attack), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K), with confidence intervals over seeds. 8) ABLATIONS: which idleness measure best predicts recruitment (sink vs norm vs prunability); layer distribution of recruited heads (are deeper high-sink heads preferentially recruited?); single-direction vs low-rank safety attribution; whether over-refusal heads also come from the idle pool; transfer of the recruitment finding across the four families; robustness of the base/aligned head correspondence to positional shifts under alignment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Base and aligned models may differ by more than the safety edit (intermediate instruction-tuning); we control by using matched base/instruct/safety checkpoints where available and measuring the aligned-minus-base delta directly, but intermediate-tuning confounds are a stated caveat. (2) Head-identity correspondence across base and aligned models can be complicated by alignment-induced shifts (per pruning-shifts-refusal findings); we match heads by index and by function and report robustness of the correspondence, and rely on behavioral (idle->safety flip) evidence not identity alone. (3) The idle-pool and safety-head identifications are each imperfect; we use multiple idleness measures and multiple safety-attribution methods (RDSHA, Ships) and report agreement, and a matched-random baseline guards against spurious enrichment. (4) If safety heads are NOT drawn from the idle pool (H1 null — e.g. safety recruits ACTIVE heads, consistent with helpfulness-safety neuron overlap in Safety Neurons/SSAH), the recruitment-from-idle hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether safety borrows idle vs active capacity is itself a fundamental, publishable finding about where alignment gets its machinery, and would sharpen the alignment-tax account. (5) The thin-edit and brittleness claims rely on weight-delta attribution (superposition/distributed-computation pitfalls); we corroborate with causal patching (idle-version-in) and behavioral flip measures rather than weight geometry alone. (6) The brittleness and pool-size correlations have few model points; we strengthen with per-head/per-layer variation and confidence intervals over seeds. (7) The pool-size-bounds-distribution test (H4) is exploratory and may reveal only a weak bound; we frame it as an implication, not the core claim. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks/attribution methods for measurement; the contribution is mechanistic understanding plus a diagnostic (base-model idleness as a pre-alignment predictor of which heads will carry — and fragilely so — safety), not a new attack. (9) Findings may be family/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: refusal_branch_topology
Title: Trunk and Branches: The Shared-vs-Split Circuit Topology of Concept-Specific Refusal Predicts Cross-Concept Jailbreak and Unlearning Spillover
Short Hypothesis: The refusal mechanism is organized as a shared generic-refusal 'trunk' plus thin per-harm-concept 'branches', and the branch-sharing topology (which concepts route through common vs disjoint late-stage components) is a fixed, measurable property that predicts cross-concept SPILLOVER: a targeted jailbreak or narrow unlearning of concept A degrades refusal on concept B in proportion to how much A and B share branch components, while trunk-disjoint concepts are insulated. Reading this topology lets one predict, before any intervention, which concepts will co-fail, and a branch-isolating defense that protects a target concept's shared trunk components blocks the spillover.
Related Work: RepIt (2025) shows concept-specific refusal is sparse (100-200 neurons), data-efficient, and that targeted jailbreaks preserve refusal on non-target concepts and evade benchmarks, but treats concept vectors as disentangled and does not characterize a shared-trunk/per-branch topology, does not predict which concepts co-fail, and its 'preservation' is a per-target observation, not a topology-based spillover law. 'From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment' (2025) shows narrow refusal-unlearning of one concept propagates reduced refusal to unrelated concepts and that early-layer concept-vector similarity correlates with spillover, but gives a correlational entanglement account, not a circuit-branch topology, no pre-intervention spillover predictor, and no branch-isolating defense. Category-wise/SafeSteer steering (2024-2025), the Safety Polytope (SaP 2025, facets ~ semantic categories), and Safety Neurons (2024, sparse overlapping safety/helpfulness neurons) all locate per-category or aggregate safety components but never map the shared-vs-split BRANCHING structure across concepts, nor use it to predict cross-concept collapse. My prior proposals (harm_manifold_extrapolation: novel-category geometry; harm_category_acquisition_order: training-time acquisition; harm_interpolation_valleys: end-state inter-cluster geometry; misrouted_harm_channel: single-concept read-channel) never characterize the branch-sharing circuit topology of refusal across concepts or its spillover-predicting/defensive use. Our contribution: (1) map the trunk-plus-branches topology of concept-specific refusal (which components are shared across concepts vs concept-private); (2) show branch-sharing quantitatively predicts cross-concept jailbreak and unlearning spillover better than representation-similarity; (3) a branch-isolating defense that protects shared-trunk components to block spillover.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse many distinct harm concepts, and recent work shows concept-specific refusal is sparse and can be jailbroken one concept at a time. But a basic structural question is unanswered: are per-concept refusals implemented by disjoint circuits, or do they share machinery? We propose that refusal has a trunk-plus-branches topology — a shared generic-refusal trunk plus thin per-concept branches — and that the branch-sharing pattern (which concepts route through common late-stage components) is a fixed, measurable property that governs cross-concept spillover. Concretely, jailbreaking or narrowly unlearning concept A should degrade refusal on concept B in proportion to their shared-branch overlap, while trunk-disjoint concepts stay insulated. We test this on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B across a taxonomy of harm concepts (SORRY-Bench/HarmBench categories). We extract per-concept refusal directions/neuron sets and compute a branch-sharing graph over concepts (component overlap after factoring out the shared trunk). We test three claims: (H1) refusal decomposes into a shared trunk plus concept-private branches, with a reproducible branch-sharing topology; (H2) per-pair branch-sharing predicts cross-concept spillover from targeted jailbreaks (RepIt-style) and narrow refusal-unlearning — co-failure tracks shared branches — outperforming early-/late-layer representation similarity; (H3) a branch-isolating defense that reinforces a target concept's shared-trunk components blocks the spillover a targeted attack/unlearn would otherwise cause. We evaluate spillover-prediction AUROC, attack/unlearning cross-concept collapse, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: 1) PER-CONCEPT REFUSAL EXTRACTION: For a taxonomy of ~20-30 harm concepts (SORRY-Bench 44-topic + HarmBench categories, public non-uplift content), extract for each concept a refusal direction via difference-in-means over matched concept-harmful vs benign prompts, and a sparse concept-refusal neuron/head set via ablation-importance (RepIt/Safety-Neurons-style). Validate each with held-out probes (per-concept AUROC). 2) TRUNK-BRANCH DECOMPOSITION (H1): Compute the shared TRUNK = components common to (nearly) all concepts' refusal sets / the dominant shared refusal direction; define each concept's BRANCH = its concept-private components after removing the trunk. Build a branch-sharing GRAPH over concept pairs (Jaccard/overlap of branch component sets and low-rank branch-subspace alignment). Test H1: refusal factors into a trunk + concept-private branches (report trunk size, branch sparsity, and that the branch-sharing graph is reproducible across seeds and stable across the four models); causal check — ablating the trunk removes refusal broadly while ablating a branch removes refusal for its concept but spares trunk-disjoint concepts. 3) SHARING PREDICTS SPILLOVER (H2, core): (a) TARGETED JAILBREAK spillover — apply a RepIt-style concept-A jailbreak (steering/ablation) and measure the change in refusal on every other concept B; (b) NARROW UNLEARNING spillover — narrowly unlearn/steer-away concept A (per the emergent-misalignment setup) and measure refusal drops on all B. Test H2: per-pair spillover (A->B) is predicted by A,B branch-sharing (Spearman; held-out predictive R^2 / AUROC), and branch-sharing beats early-layer and late-layer representation-similarity and raw refusal-direction cosine as predictors. Report cross-model transfer of the sharing->spillover law. 4) BRANCH-ISOLATION DEFENSE (H3): When jailbreaking/unlearning concept A, protect the shared-TRUNK components that A shares with other concepts (reinforce/clamp the trunk contribution for B while allowing A's private branch to change), and test whether this blocks the A->B spillover. Compare to a naive full-refusal-direction addition and to a random-component-protection control. Calibrate on a held-out concept split. 5) EVALUATION: Report (i) spillover-prediction AUROC/R^2 (branch-sharing vs baselines); (ii) cross-concept collapse under targeted jailbreak and narrow unlearning, with and without Branch-Isolation; (iii) over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest); (iv) utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval); (v) target-concept jailbreak/unlearn efficacy is preserved (the defense blocks spillover to B without re-refusing the intended A change), all with confidence intervals over seeds. Central test: branch-sharing predicts which concepts co-fail, and protecting shared-trunk components confines a targeted attack/unlearn to its concept. 6) ABLATIONS: which layers host the trunk vs branches (predict trunk late, branches also late but concept-private); single-direction vs low-rank branch subspaces; neuron-set vs direction-based sharing metrics; whether the sharing graph mirrors semantic taxonomy or diverges from it (a mechanistic-vs-semantic comparison); transfer of the sharing->spillover predictor across the four model families; an adaptive attack that jailbreaks concept A while minimizing measured trunk overlap (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The trunk/branch decomposition may not be clean — refusal could be a continuum with no clear shared trunk; the decomposition (Exp 2) treats this empirically and a 'mostly-shared' or 'mostly-private' result is still an informative characterization of refusal's cross-concept organization. (2) If spillover is NOT predicted by branch-sharing (H2 false), the topology hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether cross-concept safety collapse follows circuit-sharing vs representation-similarity is itself a valuable, publishable finding that sharpens the emergent-misalignment-from-narrow-unlearning result. (3) Branch-sharing may correlate with representation-similarity (making the 'beats similarity' claim hard); we control by comparing predictors on held-out pairs and reporting unique variance, and by causal trunk/branch ablation that isolates sharing independent of similarity. (4) Per-concept neuron/direction extraction is imperfect and concept sets may overlap by construction; we use multiple extraction methods (difference-in-means directions and ablation-importance neurons), report agreement, and use matched-random-overlap baselines to guard against spurious sharing. (5) The Branch-Isolation defense could raise over-refusal or degrade utility (protecting trunk components on B may broadly re-strengthen refusal); the over-refusal/utility benchmarks and random-protection control bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear/multi-dimensional refusal geometry; we use low-rank branch subspaces and corroborate causally with ablation and corruption baselines. (7) DUAL-USE CARE: measuring targeted-jailbreak and narrow-unlearning spillover uses published attack/unlearning methods on public, non-operational benchmark content for measurement only; the deliverables are a spillover-PREDICTOR and a defense (Branch-Isolation) that confines damage — we report predictors/metrics, not new attack recipes, and the defense only strengthens/confines safety. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: tokenization_canonicality_gate
Title: Same String, Different Guardrail: A Tokenization-Canonicality Signal That Gates LLM Safety Even When Harm Is Still Perceived
Short Hypothesis: LLMs encode an internal tokenization-canonicality signal — how canonically/typically the input string was segmented into tokens — that is distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions and causally gates safety: a harmful request re-encoded with a non-canonical (but semantically decodable) tokenization suppresses refusal even though the model still perceives the request as harmful (the harm belief is decodable), because the non-canonical segmentation raises a canonicality readout that decouples the intact harm signal from refusal execution. Re-anchoring the canonicality signal (or the harm readout) at inference restores refusal without hurting benign non-canonical-input handling.
Related Work: Adversarial Tokenization (2025) shows LLMs retain semantic understanding of non-canonical tokenizations and that re-tokenizing a malicious string evades safety WITHOUT changing the text — a strong behavioral attack, but purely black-box with NO mechanism: it never asks whether harm is still internally perceived, whether refusal is decoupled from an intact harm signal, or how to defend. Broken Tokens (2025) shows instruction-tuned models are robust to non-canonical tokenizations and perceive them as misspellings, but studies CAPABILITY, not safety. When Smiley Turns Hostile (2025) and Emoji Attack (2024) attribute emoji-triggered toxicity to a tokenization-induced 'representation gap' that makes models 'less sensitive to harmfulness' — suggestive but correlational, emoji-specific, and never isolating a canonicality representation or testing belief-intact-vs-erased. Improbable Bigrams (2024) and MetaBreak (2025) exploit incomplete/special tokens for hallucination/jailbreak behaviorally. On the mechanism side, refusal is a single direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable (Understanding Refusal with SAEs 2025 — harm and refusal are separately encoded, jailbreaks suppress refusal features), and What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning (2024) shows jailbroken activations cluster with safe ones. CRITICALLY, no work isolates a tokenization-CANONICALITY representation, shows it CAUSALLY gates the harm->refusal coupling (belief-preserved suppression under non-canonical segmentation vs genuine harm-belief erasure), predicts adversarial-tokenization jailbreak success from it, or proposes a canonicality-neutralization / re-anchoring defense. My prior format_distribution_shift proposal varied surface ENCODING (JSON/SQL/code — different natural-language rendering); this is distinct — the string is IDENTICAL and only its SUBWORD SEGMENTATION into token IDs changes, a tokenizer-layer variable no interpretability-safety work has mechanistically studied.
Abstract: A striking recent attack shows that re-encoding a harmful request with a non-canonical tokenization — the same characters, just a different valid split into subword tokens — slips it past safety alignment, even though the model was trained on only one canonical tokenization. This is documented purely behaviorally, with the black-box conclusion that models 'still understand' non-canonical inputs. We give the mechanism and a defense. We hypothesize that LLMs encode an internal tokenization-canonicality signal — how typical the input's segmentation is — distinct from their harm-perception and refusal-execution representations, and that it causally gates safety: non-canonical segmentation raises the canonicality readout and decouples the model's still-intact harm perception from its refusal execution, so the model perceives the request as harmful yet does not refuse. On this belief-intact/execution-ungated view, the failure is not that the model stops understanding the harm, but that the guardrail is not recruited. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using matched harmful (and benign) requests whose IDENTICAL strings are tokenized canonically vs with graded non-canonical segmentations (BPE-dropout-style resegmentation, character-level, adversarially-optimized tokenizations). Behaviorally we test whether refusal drops with non-canonicality while a harm probe stays high. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a canonicality direction and a harm-perception direction, verify separability from each other and from refusal, and causally test whether steering canonicality toward 'canonical' restores refusal with the string fixed and whether the harm readout is preserved (not erased) under attack. We show the per-prompt canonicality readout predicts adversarial-tokenization jailbreak success, and propose Canonicality Re-Anchoring, a training-free controller that re-anchors the harm signal to the refusal decision on non-canonically-tokenized inputs. We evaluate adversarial-tokenization attack success, over-refusal, benign non-canonical-input utility, general utility, and the signal's causal effect and predictive AUROC.
Experiments: 1) TOKENIZATION-LADDER DATASET: For matched harmful (HarmBench/JailbreakBench, non-uplift public content) and benign (Alpaca/XSTest-safe) requests, hold the IDENTICAL character string fixed while varying only its tokenization into token IDs along a canonicality ladder: (L0) canonical BPE tokenization (refusal ceiling); (L1) light BPE-dropout resegmentation; (L2) heavy random valid resegmentation; (L3) character-level; plus an ADVERSARIALLY-OPTIMIZED tokenization (Adversarial-Tokenization-style search that maximizes compliance). All tokenizations detokenize to the same string. Controls: (a) canonical harmful requests (ceiling); (b) BENIGN requests across the same tokenization ladder (over-refusal + benign non-canonical-input utility — the model SHOULD still correctly handle non-canonically-tokenized benign inputs, per Broken Tokens); (c) standard over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Validate harm labels; canonicality is objectively defined by the tokenizer (no judge needed). 2) BEHAVIORAL CANONICALITY-GATING TEST (H1, core): Extract the harm-perception direction via difference-in-means over CANONICAL harmful vs benign prompts (Understanding Refusal with SAEs / difference-in-means), validated by a held-out probe read at the last-token position AND via a position-agnostic harm probe that works on non-canonical inputs (AUROC). Measure refusal rate and harm-direction projection across the tokenization ladder. Test H1: refusal DECREASES monotonically as tokenization becomes more non-canonical (dose-response; fit monotone curve vs flat null, slope/R^2) while the harm probe stays HIGH (belief preserved — the model still perceives harm), distinguishing belief-intact/execution-ungated from genuine harm-belief erasure. Report per-model effect sizes and the fraction of successful adversarial-tokenization jailbreaks that are belief-intact vs belief-erased; benign controls confirm harm-specificity and that benign utility is retained. 3) DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H2): Extract via difference-in-means a TOKENIZATION-CANONICALITY direction (canonical vs non-canonical segmentation of matched content), validated with an ordinal probe over the ladder (does the model represent how canonically its input was tokenized?). Independently extract the harm-perception direction and the refusal-execution direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction). Validate each with held-out probes (AUROC); test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity — the canonicality direction must be distinct from harm and refusal. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3, core): Holding a harmful request fixed under a non-canonical tokenization, steer the canonicality direction toward 'canonical' (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure restored refusal; steer a canonical harmful request toward 'non-canonical' and measure suppressed refusal. Crucially test the belief-intact dissociation: (a) canonicality steering does NOT change the harm readout (harm perception intact); (b) the refusal-execution circuit is still functional under non-canonical input (directly steering the harm signal into the refusal pathway, or transplanting the canonical-run harm activations into the non-canonical run via cross-condition patching, restores refusal). Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-direction steering (should change harm readout too). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Test the interaction (regress refusal on harm x canonicality). 5) PREDICTIVENESS (H4): Fit a classifier on the per-prompt canonicality readout (single forward pass, pre-generation) to predict adversarial-tokenization jailbreak success; report AUROC vs baselines (harm-readout magnitude, refusal projection, input perplexity/token-count); test cross-tokenization transfer (fit on BPE-dropout, test on character-level/adversarial) and cross-model transfer. 6) CANONICALITY RE-ANCHORING DEFENSE: Two training-free variants gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign non-canonical inputs are untouched: (a) HARM RE-ANCHORING — read the (intact) harm signal wherever it resides on the non-canonical input and inject it into the refusal-decision layers (re-couple harm->refusal), and/or (b) CANONICALITY CLAMPING — project out/clamp the canonicality component toward 'canonical' before the decision. Note both are white-box internal fixes complementary to (and testable against) the trivial input-side re-canonicalization baseline (re-tokenize the input canonically before feeding it), which we include as a strong comparison. Calibrate layer/strength/gate on a held-out split. 7) EVALUATION: Compare base model, input-side re-canonicalization (re-tokenize to canonical before inference — the obvious baseline), uniform refusal-direction addition, and Canonicality Re-Anchoring on: adversarial-tokenization attack success (BPE-dropout, character-level, adversarially-optimized; JailbreakBench/HarmBench), refusal canonicality-consistency (does the verdict stop depending on tokenization?), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), BENIGN non-canonical-input utility (does the model still correctly answer benign inputs under non-canonical tokenization? — a subword/string-manipulation and QA benchmark, critical, per Broken Tokens), general utility (MMLU, GSM8K), latency. Central test: Canonicality Re-Anchoring closes tokenization jailbreaks toward canonical refusal levels while preserving benign non-canonical-input utility, and we characterize when the internal fix beats or complements input-side re-canonicalization (e.g., special-token/emoji cases where re-canonicalization is ill-defined, per MetaBreak/Emoji Attack). 8) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the canonicality signal vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank; whether stronger/larger models (more robust to non-canonical tokenizations per Broken Tokens) show a smaller canonicality gate (does robustness correlate with a weaker gating effect?); whether the belief-intact fraction differs across tokenization types (character-level vs adversarial); transfer across the four model families; whether reasoning models close the gate in CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that finds a tokenization maximizing compliance while suppressing the harm readout (arms-race stress test — does the attack shift from belief-intact to belief-erased?).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is that non-canonical tokenization genuinely ERASES harm perception (the model stops understanding the request is harmful) rather than decoupling an intact harm signal from refusal; the belief-intact-vs-erased census (H1) and the harm-readout-invariance-under-canonicality-steering test (H3a) directly adjudicate this, and either outcome is an informative, publishable mechanistic finding that goes beyond the black-box Adversarial-Tokenization result — if harm is erased, that scopes when an internal re-anchoring defense can work and pinpoints where in the network the harm signal degrades. (2) The obvious defense is input-side re-canonicalization (just re-tokenize canonically); our contribution must clearly demonstrate cases where the internal fix adds value — e.g., special-token/emoji/incomplete-token inputs where canonical re-tokenization is undefined or lossy (MetaBreak/Improbable Bigrams/Emoji Attack), or where providers cannot control client-side tokenization — which we test explicitly; if input re-canonicalization dominates everywhere, the mechanistic characterization still stands as the primary contribution. (3) Separating a genuine CANONICALITY representation from generic input-perplexity/misspelling-perception (Broken Tokens shows models read non-canonical input as misspellings) is essential; we use input-perplexity and token-count control baselines for the predictor, test separability from harm/refusal, and treat overlap with a 'misspelling/atypicality' signal as an informative refinement. (4) Extracting a harm probe that works on non-canonical inputs is nontrivial (positions/token boundaries shift); we use a position-agnostic probe trained across tokenizations and cross-condition patching with careful position alignment, reporting probe reliability. (5) If refusal is invariant to tokenization canonicality (H1 false), the gating hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM safety depends on tokenization canonicality is itself valuable and would sharpen the Adversarial-Tokenization finding. (6) Canonicality Re-Anchoring could raise over-refusal or degrade benign non-canonical-input handling (a real capability, per Broken Tokens/StochasTok use cases) or general utility; the harm-gated design and benign non-canonical-utility + over-refusal benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off. (7) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with patching, multiple metrics, and corruption baselines. (8) The predictor may transfer poorly to unseen tokenization schemes; we test cross-tokenization and cross-model transfer. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and the published Adversarial-Tokenization attack for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Canonicality Re-Anchoring) plus a diagnostic, and it only increases refusal on non-canonically-tokenized harmful inputs (failure mode is bounded over-refusal, not new attack capability). (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models (which control their own tokenization); stated as out of scope, though the mechanism informs provider-side defenses.

Name: detail_throttle_gate
Title: A Detail Throttle, Not a Kill Switch: An Internal Response-Specificity Signal That Governs How Much Harmful Uplift LLMs Emit on Dual-Use Requests
Short Hypothesis: Beyond the binary refuse/comply decision, LLMs encode an internal response-SPECIFICITY signal — a graded 'how actionable/detailed should my answer be' throttle, distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions — that governs the safe-completion behavior of answering a dual-use request at a high level while withholding operational detail. This throttle is set independently of, and often mis-coupled to, the true harmful uplift a request would confer, so on dual-use prompts the model gives dangerously specific answers when it should throttle down (uplift leakage) and vaguely useless answers when it could safely elaborate (over-vagueness). Reading and coupling this specificity throttle to a harm-uplift readout yields uplift-calibrated safe completion — a graded lever the refuse/comply knob cannot provide.
Related Work: Safe-completions (From Hard Refusals to Safe-Completions 2025, GPT-5) reframe safety around output-centric graded helpfulness on dual-use prompts, Health-ORSC-Bench (2026) and Let-Them-Down-Easy (2025) show partial compliance (high-level info without actionable detail) is the desired behavior yet models rarely produce it and reward models undervalue it, and HiddenGuard (2024) does token-level redaction of sensitive spans. On the mechanism side, harm-perception and refusal-execution are separable directions (DBDI 2025; LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately 2025), refusal is a single/low-rank direction (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024), CAST (2024) conditionally applies a refusal vector, and LatentGuard/SafeConstellations/LLM-VA steer refusal-vs-answer vectors. CRITICALLY, every one of these treats the safety decision as (conditional) BINARY refuse-vs-answer, or achieves partial compliance behaviorally / by post-hoc redaction; NONE isolates a graded internal RESPONSE-SPECIFICITY / detail-level representation — a continuous 'how much operational detail to emit' throttle — that is distinct from the refuse/comply direction, shows it CAUSALLY sets the granularity of harmful uplift, or couples it to a harm-uplift readout to produce calibrated safe completion. My prior capability_calibrated_refusal and severity_blind proposals scaled the binary REFUSAL strength by capability/severity; this proposal targets a different, orthogonal output variable — the graded specificity/actionability of a COMPLIED answer — which is precisely the axis safe-completion needs and the binary refusal literature and refuse-vs-answer steering cannot reach. This is the first to give safe-completion a mechanistic, controllable internal lever.
Abstract: The field is moving from binary refuse-or-comply safety toward safe-completions: on dual-use requests (biology, cybersecurity, medicine) the ideal answer helps at a high level while withholding the operational detail that would confer real-world uplift. This is a graded output property, yet safety interpretability treats the decision as binary (a refusal direction to add or ablate) and behavioral safe-completion work shows models rarely produce the right granularity and reward models undervalue it. We hypothesize that LLMs already encode an internal response-SPECIFICITY throttle — a graded 'how actionable/detailed should my answer be' signal, distinct from the harm-perception and refusal-execution directions — that causally sets the operational granularity of a complied answer, and that this throttle is mis-coupled to the true harmful uplift a request confers: it stays high (dangerously specific) on some dual-use prompts and low (uselessly vague) on others, independent of actual uplift. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using dual-use requests with graded-specificity reference answers (high-level safe vs operationally-detailed) and verifiable uplift labels. Via difference-in-means and probes we extract a specificity direction, verify it is separable from harm and refusal directions, and causally test whether steering it up/down monotonically raises/lowers the operational detail (and measured uplift) of the SAME complied answer while the refuse/comply decision and harm perception are unchanged (a dose-response on granularity, not on refusal). We show the throttle is decoupled from true uplift and propose Uplift-Coupled Throttling, a training-free controller that reads a harm-uplift readout and sets the specificity throttle proportional to it — throttling down exactly when uplift is high. We evaluate real-uplift leakage, safe-completion helpfulness, over-vagueness, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments:
1) DUAL-USE GRADED-SPECIFICITY DATASET: Assemble dual-use requests (public HarmBench/WMDP-derived biology/cyber/medicine dual-use items + Health-ORSC-Bench-style boundary prompts, non-uplift level) each paired with graded reference answers spanning a specificity ladder: (G0) refuse; (G1) high-level safe guidance (no actionable detail — the safe-completion target); (G2) moderate detail; (G3) operationally detailed (uplift-conferring). Assign each request a verifiable UPLIFT label (how much real-world actionable capability a detailed answer would confer, from expert-informed rubrics + multiple LLM judges + human spot-check). Controls: clearly-benign requests and clearly-harmful requests (which should refuse), plus over-refusal sets (XSTest, OR-Bench) and standard utility prompts. Keep all content at documented, non-operational level.
2) SPECIFICITY DIRECTION EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H1): For each model, generate answers at varied specificity (via reference-answer teacher-forcing and via graded prompting) and extract via difference-in-means a RESPONSE-SPECIFICITY direction contrasting high-detail vs low-detail answers to the SAME complied request; validate with an ordinal probe predicting answer specificity/actionability (AUROC / ordinal correlation), scored by an actionability judge. Independently extract the harm-perception direction (harmful vs benign, per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately) and the refusal-execution direction (refuse vs comply, per Refusal-Is-Mediated-by-a-Single-Direction). Test separability via cross-probe transfer and low pairwise cosine similarity — the specificity throttle must be distinct from harm and from refuse/comply (it operates WITHIN the comply regime).
3) CAUSAL GRANULARITY TEST (H2, core): On dual-use requests the model complies with, steer the specificity direction up and down (fixed-norm dose-response) and measure the operational detail / actionability and measured uplift of the resulting answer. Test H2: steering monotonically raises/lowers answer granularity and uplift while (a) the refuse/comply decision is unchanged (it is a throttle, not a kill switch) and (b) the harm-perception readout is unchanged. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, refusal-direction steering (should flip refuse/comply, not smoothly modulate detail), and confirm specificity steering does not change harm perception. Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (actionability-judge score, uplift score, refuse/comply outcome, harm-probe output). Establish the throttle causally sets granularity.
4) THROTTLE-vs-UPLIFT DECOUPLING (H3): For each complied dual-use answer, measure the per-prompt specificity throttle readout and the answer's true UPLIFT (verifiable label). Test whether the throttle is DECOUPLED from true uplift: high-throttle (dangerously specific) answers occur on high-uplift prompts (leakage) and low-throttle (vague) answers on low-uplift prompts (needless over-vagueness), i.e., the throttle does not track uplift (report mutual information / regression of throttle on uplift, predicting weak coupling). Contrast with the ideal (throttle should fall as uplift rises).
5) UPLIFT-COUPLED THROTTLING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads a harm-uplift readout (from a probe / the harm-perception readout calibrated against verifiable uplift labels on a held-out split) and sets the specificity-throttle injection strength as a monotone decreasing function of uplift: throttle DOWN operational detail when uplift is high (safe completion) while allowing full detail when uplift is low. Gate off clearly-benign prompts (full helpfulness) and route clearly-harmful prompts to refusal. Calibrate the mapping, layer, and gates on a held-out split.
6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, binary refusal-direction addition (refuse-or-comply), a prompt-based safe-completion instruction, HiddenGuard-style post-hoc redaction, and Uplift-Coupled Throttling on: REAL-UPLIFT LEAKAGE (fraction of complied answers that cross into operationally-actionable, uplift-conferring detail on high-uplift prompts — primary), SAFE-COMPLETION HELPFULNESS (high-level usefulness on dual-use prompts, per Health-ORSC-Bench/safe-completion rubrics), OVER-VAGUENESS (uselessly vague answers on low-uplift prompts), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and latency. Central test: Uplift-Coupled Throttling reduces real-uplift leakage AND over-vagueness simultaneously while preserving safe-completion helpfulness — a graded Pareto improvement the binary refuse/comply knob and post-hoc redaction cannot achieve, because it modulates the model's own detail-generation rather than blocking or scrubbing output.
7) ABLATIONS: which layer hosts the specificity throttle vs harm/refusal; single-direction vs low-rank throttle subspace; whether the throttle generalizes across domains (fit on biology dual-use, test on cyber/medicine); whether teacher-forced vs prompt-derived specificity directions agree; uplift-coupled throttling vs constant throttling at matched average detail (isolating the value of uplift-conditioning); transfer of the throttle and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models throttle detail across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive prompt that elicits maximal detail while suppressing the throttle readout (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) DUAL-USE CARE: measuring uplift leakage and steering answer specificity up is sensitive; we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content, cap the detailed-reference (G3) answers at documented, non-uplift levels, release probes/metrics rather than elicitation recipes, and frame the deliverable as a defense (Uplift-Coupled Throttling that throttles DOWN on high-uplift prompts) plus a diagnostic — the applied controller only reduces detail, never adds operational capability. Upward steering is used solely for the diagnostic dose-response, reported at aggregate/non-operational granularity. (2) The central risk is separating a genuine RESPONSE-SPECIFICITY throttle from generic verbosity/length or from the refuse-vs-comply direction; matched-content high-vs-low-detail pairs, a verbosity/length control direction, separability tests, and the specificity-vs-refusal steering contrast (smooth granularity modulation vs binary flip) are designed to isolate it, and if the throttle collapses into verbosity or refusal that is itself an informative refinement of the safe-completion picture. (3) If no graded throttle exists (specificity is not internally controllable independent of refusal, H1/H2 false), the hypothesis is refuted — but adjudicating whether safe-completion granularity has a dedicated internal lever is a valuable, publishable finding that directly informs the safe-completion training agenda. (4) Scoring 'operational uplift / actionability' is delicate and rubric-dependent; we use verifiable dual-use items, expert-informed rubrics, multiple judges, and human spot-checks, and report labeling reliability; residual judge noise is a caveat. (5) Uplift-Coupled Throttling could over-throttle legitimate benign detail (harming helpfulness) or under-throttle if the uplift readout mis-estimates; the benign-detail utility, safe-completion helpfulness, and over-vagueness benchmarks bound this genuine trade-off, and the controller is paired with (not replacing) refusal for clearly-harmful prompts. (6) The specificity direction may be incomplete/nonlinear; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The throttle/uplift-readout may transfer poorly across domains or models; we test cross-domain and cross-model transfer. (8) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: harm_belief_frequency_competence_law
Title: You Only Truly Know the Harms You Saw Often: A Data-Frequency Law Governing the Robustness of an LLM's Internal Harm Belief
Short Hypothesis: The ROBUSTNESS of an LLM's internal harm belief (its harm-perception readout) on a given harm category is governed by a data-frequency law: categories that appeared densely in safety-relevant training data yield a harm belief that persists under jailbreaks and paraphrase, while low-frequency categories yield a belief that is present but FRAGILE (easily suppressed, surface-cue-dependent). Prior work found that jailbreaks 'leave the harm belief intact' — we hypothesize this is true only for high-frequency categories, and that per-category harm-belief robustness is predictable from a training-frequency proxy and repairable by frequency-aware calibration. This reframes belief-intact-vs-belief-erased (the crux of whether jailbreaks suppress refusal vs perception) as a graded, data-driven property rather than a universal fact.
Related Work: 'LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately' (2025) shows harm and refusal are distinct directions and that jailbreaks/adversarial finetuning 'leave the harm belief largely intact' — but treats belief-persistence as a UNIFORM property and never asks whether it varies by category or tracks training frequency. 'Understanding Refusal with SAEs' (2025) shows jailbreaks suppress refusal features while harm features remain, again uniformly. 'False Sense of Security' (2025) shows safety probes rely on surface trigger-words and fail OOD — a surface-reliance finding, not a frequency-graded belief-robustness law. Harm-category geometry work (Geometry of Harmfulness 2025) and taxonomies (SORRY-Bench 2024; Cannot-or-Should-Not 2024) characterize categories but not the frequency-dependence of belief robustness. My own prior proposals cover harm-CATEGORY ACQUISITION ORDER (a training-time developmental claim about WHEN categories consolidate) and a REFUSAL GENERALIZATION GRADIENT (semantic distance from harmful exemplars driving over/under-refusal); NEITHER makes the distinct claim here: that the INFERENCE-TIME robustness of the harm BELIEF (not refusal execution, not acquisition timing) obeys a per-category data-FREQUENCY law, that this frequency-dependence explains WHEN the 'belief-intact' finding holds vs fails, and that frequency-aware calibration repairs fragile-category belief. This is a Location+Causal-Intervention+Formation-Tracing claim (belief robustness ↔ training frequency) absent from the literature and my priors.
Abstract: A pivotal recent finding is that when jailbreaks defeat an aligned LLM, they suppress its refusal while leaving its internal 'this is harmful' belief intact — implying the model still knows, it just fails to act. This has been treated as a universal fact and motivates belief-based defenses (Latent Guard). We challenge its universality with a data-frequency law: the harm belief is robust only for harm categories that appeared densely in safety-relevant training, and is present-but-FRAGILE (readily suppressed under jailbreaks and unstable across paraphrases) for low-frequency categories. Consequently, the 'belief-intact' phenomenon holds for common harms and breaks for rare ones — exactly where belief-based safeguards are then unreliable. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B (plus small models with dense checkpoints for a formation check) across a broad harm taxonomy. We extract a per-category harm-perception readout, define belief ROBUSTNESS (how much of the belief survives jailbreaks/paraphrase, and its OOD probe transfer), and estimate a training-frequency proxy per category (public safety-corpus counts + the model's own next-token 'familiarity'/perplexity on category-canonical harmful phrasings). We test three claims: (H1) per-category belief robustness correlates with the frequency proxy, so the belief-intact-under-jailbreak result is strong for high-frequency and weak for low-frequency categories; (H2) causally, low-frequency-category belief is disproportionately suppressible (steering/jailbreak flips it more) while high-frequency belief resists; (H3) a frequency-aware belief-calibration that reinforces the harm signal for low-frequency categories restores robust belief-based detection where Latent-Guard-style safeguards currently fail. We evaluate belief-robustness-vs-frequency correlation, belief-based detection AUROC by category, jailbreak belief-suppression rates, and over-refusal.
Experiments: 1) TAXONOMY & FREQUENCY PROXY: Assemble a broad harm-category taxonomy (~40-60 categories from SORRY-Bench + HarmBench, non-uplift public content). Estimate a per-category training-FREQUENCY proxy two ways: (a) counts of category-canonical harmful phrasings/concepts in a large public corpus (e.g. an open pretraining/safety-SFT corpus subset), and (b) the model's own FAMILIARITY — next-token perplexity / a 'do I know this concept' readout on category-canonical harmful phrasings (a model-internal frequency proxy validated to correlate with (a) on categories where corpus counts are reliable). Report proxy reliability. 2) PER-CATEGORY HARM-BELIEF & ROBUSTNESS (Location): Extract a per-category harm-perception readout via difference-in-means at the last instruction token (per LLMs-Encode-Harmfulness-Separately), validated by held-out probes (per-category AUROC). Define belief ROBUSTNESS per category as: (i) fraction of the harm-belief readout that SURVIVES under jailbreaks (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona) — belief-suppression rate; (ii) belief STABILITY across meaning-preserving paraphrases (ParaGuard-style); (iii) OOD probe TRANSFER (train probe on other categories, test on this one). 3) FREQUENCY LAW TEST (H1, core): Test whether per-category belief robustness correlates with the frequency proxy (Spearman; held-out predictive R^2), and specifically that the 'belief-intact-under-jailbreak' effect (belief survives jailbreak) is STRONG for high-frequency categories and WEAK (belief actually suppressed, contra the universal claim) for low-frequency ones. Report the belief-suppression-rate-vs-frequency curve across the four models; this directly qualifies the prior 'belief intact' finding as frequency-conditional. Baselines: category semantic-typicality and probe in-distribution AUROC as alternative predictors (test frequency adds unique variance). 4) CAUSAL SUPPRESSIBILITY TEST (H2): For high- vs low-frequency categories, measure how easily the harm belief is flipped by (a) steering the harm-perception direction down at fixed magnitude and (b) a fixed jailbreak dose. Test that low-frequency-category belief is disproportionately suppressible while high-frequency belief resists, with random-direction/corruption controls and multiple metrics (harm-probe output, P(refusal token), realized refusal). 5) FORMATION CHECK (Formation Tracing, optional-small): On small models safety-SFT'd with a KNOWN, controllable category-frequency mix and dense checkpointing, test whether up-weighting a low-frequency category's data specifically increases its end-state belief robustness at matched total compute — establishing frequency as a CAUSAL origin of belief robustness, not just a correlate. 6) FREQUENCY-AWARE CALIBRATION DEFENSE (H3): Training-free controller that reinforces the harm-perception readout for prompts detected as low-frequency-category (scaled by the frequency deficit) before belief-based detection/refusal; gate off high-frequency/benign prompts. Compare a Latent-Guard-style belief-based safeguard with vs without frequency-aware calibration on: belief-based detection AUROC by category (especially low-frequency), jailbreak belief-suppression, ASR (JailbreakBench, HarmBench), over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), latency. Central test: frequency-aware calibration restores robust belief-based detection on the low-frequency categories where Latent-Guard-style defenses currently fail, without hurting high-frequency/benign performance. 7) ABLATIONS: corpus-count vs model-familiarity proxy (which better predicts robustness); which layer hosts the belief; single-direction vs low-rank; transfer of the frequency law across the four model families; whether reasoning models show flatter frequency-dependence (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The training-frequency proxy is the crux and is imperfect — closed training sets are unobservable and public-corpus counts may not match a given model's safety data; we mitigate by using TWO proxies (corpus counts + model-internal familiarity/perplexity), validating their agreement where possible, and — decisively — the small-model formation check (Exp 5) manipulates frequency directly to establish causality independent of proxy quality; if the proxies disagree or fail to predict, that is itself an informative negative bounding the law's testability. (2) The central claim contradicts a published 'belief-intact is universal' finding, which is the point — but if belief turns out uniformly robust across categories (H1 null), the frequency-law hypothesis is refuted and we instead confirm and sharpen the universality claim (still a valuable, publishable qualification). (3) Belief robustness may be confounded with category semantic-typicality or probe in-distribution accuracy rather than genuine frequency; we control by including these as competing predictors and reporting frequency's unique variance. (4) Per-category harm-belief directions are noisy for data-scarce categories (a confound with the very quantity we study — low frequency may just mean a noisy probe); we report per-category probe reliability, exclude unreliable categories from quantitative claims, and use the causal suppressibility test (which does not depend on absolute probe quality) as corroboration. (5) Frequency-aware calibration could raise over-refusal by over-reinforcing low-frequency benign-adjacent prompts; the over-refusal benchmarks and gating bound this and may reveal a trade-off. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally. (7) The small-model formation check may not transfer to frontier RLHF pipelines; stated as scope. (8) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark-derived, non-operational content and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (frequency-aware belief calibration) plus a diagnostic, strengthening safeguards on exactly the under-covered categories, with bounded over-refusal as the only failure mode. (9) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: refusal_evidence_accumulation_boundary
Title: Refusal as Bounded Evidence Accumulation: An Adjustable Decision Boundary That Jailbreaks Lower and Defenses Can Raise
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the drift-diffusion / bounded-evidence-accumulation account of decision-making (a choice is committed when accumulated evidence crosses an adjustable BOUNDARY, and the boundary collapses under conflict/uncertainty and can be set separately from the evidence), we hypothesize that LLM refusal is not a fixed threshold on a harm signal but an evidence-accumulation process: harm evidence accumulates across layers/tokens toward a refusal DECISION BOUNDARY, and this boundary is encoded separately from the harm-evidence signal and is causally adjustable. Jailbreaks succeed disproportionately by RAISING the boundary (demanding more evidence to refuse) while leaving harm evidence intact, rather than by lowering the harm signal; reading the per-prompt boundary predicts jailbreak success, and re-lowering the boundary at inference restores refusal without hurting benign helpfulness.
Related Work: A large decision-neuroscience literature (drift-diffusion / bounded-accumulation models; Evidence Bounds on Decision-Making 2012; basal-ganglia collapsing decision boundary under conflict/uncertainty 2025; Confidence Is the Bridge 2016; distinct encoding of confidence vs boundary-distance in medial PFC 2018) robustly establishes that (a) decisions are made by accumulating evidence to an adjustable boundary, (b) the boundary collapses under conflict/uncertainty and can be raised/lowered as a control setting, and (c) the boundary distance is encoded SEPARATELY from the evidence/confidence signal. In LLM safety, refusal is treated as a fixed one-dimensional direction/threshold (Refusal Is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024; Geometry of Refusal concept cones 2025), the safety entropy gap is used as a static self-reward (SIRL 2025), overrefusal is framed as boundary MISALIGNMENT at inference (RASS 2025; MOSR 2025), harm and refusal are separable directions (harm evidence vs refusal execution), and entropy/confidence-regulation neurons exist (2024). CRITICALLY, no safety work models refusal as a bounded-EVIDENCE-ACCUMULATION process with an adjustable DECISION BOUNDARY that is (i) encoded separately from the harm-evidence signal, (ii) causally raisable/lowerable, and (iii) the primary lever jailbreaks exploit (boundary-raising, not evidence-erasure). This reframes 'safety boundary' from a static geometric hyperplane (RASS/BOOST) into a dynamic, controllable evidence-threshold, and unifies jailbreaks (boundary raised), over-refusal (boundary too low), and instability under conflict (boundary collapse) under one accumulation account. It is distinct from my prior gating-direction proposals: the object here is the boundary/threshold quantity itself, not a content-framing signal that shifts harm perception.
Abstract: One of the most robust findings in the neuroscience of decision-making is that choices are made by accumulating evidence to an adjustable decision BOUNDARY, that this boundary collapses under conflict and uncertainty, and that it is encoded separately from the evidence itself. We port this account to LLM safety. We hypothesize that refusal is not a fixed threshold on a harm signal but a bounded-evidence-accumulation process: harm evidence accumulates across the forward pass toward a refusal decision boundary, the boundary is represented separately from the harm-evidence signal, and it is a causally adjustable control setting. On this view, many jailbreaks succeed by RAISING the boundary (requiring more evidence before the model commits to refusing) while the harm evidence remains intact, over-refusal reflects a boundary set too low, and instability under adversarial conflict reflects boundary collapse. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B. We extract a harm-evidence signal and, separately, a decision-boundary readout (the accumulated-evidence deficit-to-commit), verify they are separable, and fit whether refusal follows an accumulation-to-boundary law across layers/tokens. We test three claims: (H1) the boundary is a decodable quantity distinct from the harm-evidence signal and jointly they predict refusal better than harm evidence alone; (H2) jailbreaks disproportionately RAISE the per-prompt boundary while leaving harm evidence intact, and the boundary readout predicts jailbreak success better than the harm signal; (H3) causally lowering the decision boundary at inference restores refusal on jailbroken prompts, whereas raising it induces compliance, with harm evidence unchanged, and a boundary-lowering defense beats blanket refusal-direction addition on the safety-vs-over-refusal frontier. We evaluate attack success, boundary predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval), and the boundary's causal effect and specificity.
Experiments: 1) SIGNAL EXTRACTION & SEPARABILITY (H1): For each model extract (a) a HARM-EVIDENCE signal via difference-in-means over matched harmful/benign prompts (per Refusal-Is-Mediated / harm-perception direction), validated by a held-out probe (AUROC); and (b) a DECISION-BOUNDARY readout operationalized as the accumulated-evidence-deficit-to-commit: for each prompt, measure how much additional harm-evidence (in the harm-direction) must be injected before the model flips to refusal (a per-prompt titration giving the boundary distance), and train a linear probe to predict this boundary distance from a single forward pass. Test separability: the boundary probe must be distinct from the harm-evidence magnitude (cross-probe transfer, low cosine) and add predictive value — refusal predicted by (harm-evidence, boundary) jointly should beat harm-evidence alone (report AUROC gain), mirroring the neuroscience dissociation of evidence vs boundary. 2) ACCUMULATION-TO-BOUNDARY LAW (H1b): Test whether refusal follows an accumulation-to-boundary form: measure the harm-evidence signal's trajectory across layers (and across generated tokens for prefill settings) and test whether the model commits to refusal when the accumulated evidence crosses the boundary readout (fit an accumulation-to-threshold model vs a static-threshold null; report fit and whether commitment timing tracks evidence-vs-boundary crossing). Test the conflict/uncertainty prediction: under adversarial-conflict prompts the boundary COLLAPSES (drops), mirroring collapsing-boundary findings. 3) JAILBREAK-RAISES-BOUNDARY TEST (H2, core): For harmful prompts and jailbroken variants (GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, template), measure per-prompt harm-evidence and boundary readouts before/after attack. Test H2: successful jailbreaks disproportionately RAISE the boundary (larger evidence-deficit-to-commit) while harm-evidence stays roughly intact (belief-preserved boundary-raising), as opposed to lowering harm evidence; classify each attack as boundary-raising vs evidence-lowering and report the fraction. Test whether the pre-attack/under-attack boundary readout predicts per-prompt jailbreak success (AUROC), beating harm-evidence magnitude, refusal-direction projection, and perplexity; report cross-attack and cross-model transfer. 4) CAUSAL TEST (H3): Steer the decision-boundary readout down (fixed-norm dose-response) on jailbroken prompts and measure restored refusal; steer it up on clean-harmful prompts and measure induced compliance. Specificity controls: random-direction steering, harm-evidence-direction steering (should change the evidence readout, not act as a pure threshold), and a check that boundary steering does NOT change the harm-evidence readout (it moves the threshold, not the evidence). Corruption baselines and multiple metrics (refusal-direction projection at output onset, P(refusal token), realized refusal by a harm judge). Establish the boundary as a separately-controllable threshold. 5) BOUNDARY-LOWERING DEFENSE: Training-free controller that reads the boundary readout and lowers it (toward its clean-harmful value) when harm evidence is present, gated on a harm-likeness readout so benign/low-evidence prompts are untouched (avoiding blanket over-refusal). Contrast with blanket refusal-direction addition, which adds a constant to the evidence/output rather than lowering the threshold. Calibrate on a held-out split. 6) EVALUATION: Compare base model, uniform refusal-direction addition, an SIRL-style entropy-reward baseline (where reproducible), a RASS/MOSR boundary-alignment baseline, and Boundary-Lowering on: attack success (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, GCG, AutoDAN, prefill, persona, and BOOST/eos-token boundary attacks), boundary predictive AUROC, over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), utility (MMLU, GSM8K, AlpacaEval win-rate), and latency. Central test: Boundary-Lowering reduces jailbreak success AND lowers over-refusal on benign prompts (by right-sizing the threshold in both directions) — a Pareto move on the safety-vs-over-refusal frontier that a constant refusal-direction addition (which raises over-refusal) cannot achieve. 7) ABLATIONS: which layer/position hosts the boundary vs harm-evidence; single-direction vs low-rank boundary readout; titration-based vs probe-based boundary estimation; whether the eos/BOOST attack works specifically by raising the boundary (mechanistic account of context-segmentation); whether over-refusal cases have anomalously low boundaries; transfer of the boundary predictor and defense across the four model families; whether reasoning models show boundary collapse across CoT (optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill); adaptive attacker that jailbreaks while keeping the measured boundary unchanged (arms-race stress test).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The central risk is that the 'decision boundary' is not separable from the harm-evidence signal — refusal may be a simple monotone threshold on one quantity, in which case a distinct, independently-adjustable boundary does not exist (H1 false); the separability and beyond-harm-evidence predictive tests, plus the causal check that boundary steering leaves harm evidence unchanged, adjudicate this cleanly, and either outcome (a genuine evidence-vs-boundary dissociation vs a single-quantity threshold) is an informative, publishable characterization of the safety decision. (2) Operationalizing the boundary via evidence-injection titration is a construct choice; if refusal does not follow an accumulation-to-threshold law (H1b null), the drift-diffusion framing is refuted — but adjudicating whether LLM refusal is bounded-accumulation vs static-threshold is itself a valuable finding grounded in a heavily-cited human account, and reframes the 'safety boundary' notion in RASS/BOOST from geometric to dynamic. (3) The titration is compute-heavy; we bound cost by sampling prompts and rely on the cheap boundary probe at inference. (4) If jailbreaks turn out to lower harm evidence rather than raise the boundary for most attacks (H2 partial), the boundary-raising account holds only for a subset — the boundary-raising-vs-evidence-lowering census is a primary contribution regardless, and cleanly complements belief-intact findings by locating WHERE the belief-intact jailbreaks act (the threshold). (5) Boundary-Lowering could raise over-refusal if the boundary is over-lowered, or degrade utility; the harm-gated design and over-refusal/utility benchmarks bound this and the two-directional right-sizing is the intended advantage over constant addition. (6) Difference-in-means/single-direction may be incomplete given concept-cone/nonlinear refusal geometry; we use low-rank subspaces and corroborate causally with multiple metrics and corruption baselines. (7) The boundary predictor may transfer poorly to unseen attacks; we test cross-attack and cross-model transfer. (8) Adaptive attackers could jailbreak while keeping the measured boundary unchanged; we test this as an arms-race limitation. (9) DUAL-USE CARE: we use only public benchmark harmful prompts and standard published attacks for measurement; the deliverable is a defense (Boundary-Lowering) plus a diagnostic, and its net effect is right-sizing refusal (bounded over-refusal on the safety-raising side), not new attack capability. (10) Findings may be model/scale-specific and may not transfer to closed models; stated as out of scope.

Name: merge_safety_collision_predictor
Title: Predicting Which Merge Will Break Safety: A Pre-Merge Adapter-Safety Collision Geometry That Forecasts Post-Merge Alignment Loss
Short Hypothesis: How much safety a model-merge or adapter-composition will lose is largely predictable BEFORE merging from a per-adapter, per-layer 'safety-collision' geometry: how much each task vector/LoRA update projects onto (and rotates) the aligned model's safety-critical weight subspace.
